News.title: Woman, 26, arrested for ‘murder’ after another woman’s body found in house
News.content:
MURDER PROBE Woman, 26, arrested for ‘murder’ after another woman’s body found in house







Next

A 26-YEAR-OLD woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after another woman’s body was found.

Emergency services scrambled to a property in Moss Side, Manchester, at around 1.30pm yesterday after reports of a disturbance.



The woman was tragically pronounced dead at the scene.

Crime scene investigators remain at the address as they probe how the tragedy unfolded.



Detective Chief Inspector Louise Edwards said: “We understand an incident of this nature will cause concern however we would like to reassure the public that we believe this is an isolated incident and there is no wider threat to the community.

“We would ask that people stay away from the scene and we’d like to thank the local community for their patience whilst officers undertake their work.



“If you have any information in relation to this incident, please get in touch via the reporting function on our website, Live Chat or by calling 101 quoting log 1631 of 19.10.26. Alternatively you can speak to Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

A spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police said: “We were called to a disturbance at an address on Crondall Street, Manchester shortly before 1.30pm on Monday 19 October 2026.

“Emergency services attended and sadly found the body of a woman.

“A 26-year-old woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder and currently remains in custody for questioning.



“A scene is in place as officers conduct their enquiries as part of this investigation.”

News.title: Shocking moment shark circles surfers in ankle-deep water at LA beach as fin spotted slicing through shallows
News.content:
Next

THIS is the terrifying moment a shark slices through ankle-deep water just feet away from unsuspecting surfers off a popular California beach.

Shocking video shows the predator lurking in the surf as oblivious beachgoers wade nearby.



In one clip, a paddleboarder can be seen smiling and pointing with his paddle after spotting the beast’s sharp dorsal fin gliding through the shallows.

The unnerving footage was captured by social media influencer Josh Hubilitz off El Porto beach in Los Angeles on October 16.



“Surfing with sharks in Los Angeles…I’ve actually never seen a shark in El Porto before,” he said on Instagram.

He added: “This is the first. Ankle deep water – that is super sketch.”

Several viewers commented that the creature appeared to be a “baby thresher” shark – a species typically measuring between three to five feet in length at birth.

The species of the shark spotted in the incident is yet to be confirmed.



The hair-raising scare is the latest in a worrying surge of shark sightings along the Californian coast.

Back in July, a massive 10ft great white shark was spotted lurking just feet from kids splashing in the sea off Southern California.

Chilling footage showed the predator stalking the youngsters, who appear oblivious to the danger as the shark draws closer.



Carlos Gauna, who filmed the encounter, said: “I don’t often get nervous but this was one of those instances where I did.

“When it involves kids I do get nervous and that shark was a lot bigger than those kids. The young swimmers had no idea.”

That sighting came after a great white hunted down two paddleboarders in California.

Terrifying footage captured the monster preparing to strike Robert Kagan and Kayla Ross as they paddled furiously to escape.

In April, an “aggressive” 10ft great white was seen feeding on a sea lion just feet away from swimmers near Los Angeles.



Experts say sharks are fleeing warmer waters in Mexico and heading north due to a Super El Niño pushing ocean temperatures to record highs.

That has triggered a spike in close encounters – though experts insist humans are not on the menu.

Dr Chris Lowe, director of the Shark Lab at California State University Long Beach, said: “Humans don’t look like prey, they don’t sound like prey.

“If it doesn’t feel like prey, they ignore it. It’s not a threat, it’s not food.”

California typically averages just 2.5 fatal shark attacks per decade, with only 17 deaths recorded since 1950.

News.title: Aldi urgently recalls £12 Dyson dupe over risk of electric shock as shoppers warned ‘stop using it immediately’
News.content:
Next

ALDI has urgently recalled a £12 Dyson dupe over fears it presents a risk of electric shock and fire.

Customers who have bought the popular Specialbuy have been urged to stop using the product immediately and to return to stores.

A batch of the Ambiano Ionic Hairdryer, sold between August and September 2025, has been pulled by the discount supermarket “as a precautionary measure”.



According to the retailer, the power cord on the hairdryer may become damaged, allowing access to live parts or causing overheating.



If users were to touch live parts of the hairdryer, they could receive an electric shock.

Ultimately, this means the product does not meet UK electrical appliance standards, therefore prompting the recall.



The Ionic Hairdryers in colours Black (4061462195075) , White (4061462195211), Yellow (4061462195310) and Orange (4061462195372) have all been pulled.

The hairdryer is set to hit middle aisles this Sunday for just £11.99 each, coming in Black, Berry and Cream designs, but only hairdryers sold last year are impacted.

The Ionic Hairdryer is widely known as a budget-friendly alternative to the bestselling Dyson Supersonic hairdryer, which is priced at £250.



Customers who think they have bought the recalled product should check the underside of the hairdryer, where the middle code will correspond with its specific colour code below.

Full list of product codes for recalled Ambiano Ionic Hairdryer If the middle code on the underside of the hairdryer is the one below, you are entitled to a full refund 4061462195075 – Black

4061462195211 – White

4061462195310 – Yellow

4061462195372 – Orange

If this is the case, customers should not use the product and return to the nearest Aldi store where a full refund will be given.

Aldi has said on its website: “We apologise for any inconvenience caused.”

News.title: Criminals locked up in secure hospital including Nottingham triple killer to be banned from receiving benefits
News.content:
LOOPHOLE CLOSED Criminals locked up in secure hospital including Nottingham triple killer to be banned from receiving benefits







Next

CRAZED criminals who have been locked up in hospital will finally be banned from receiving benefits to stop them double-dipping on the taxpayer.

More than 2,500 serious offenders with mental health issues are currently claiming up to £800 in welfare payments every month despite getting full-time NHS care.



It includes Nottingham killer Valdo Calocane who was detained indefinitely in a high security ward after his stabbing spree.

Welfare Secretary Pat McFadden will today lay the new regulations in Parliament following a campaign by victims’ families.



He said: “We said we’d act to tackle this gross unfairness and we’re delivering on that promise.

“For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

“That ends today because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it.”

The ban will cover the most serious crimes including manslaughter, attempted murder and rape.

Murder itself is not included because a Hospital Order is not available for the offence of murder.

The criminals will not be entitled to Universal Credit, Pension Credit, the State Pension and Employment and Support Allowance.



The families of victims killed by unhinged criminals last night welcomed the changes.

Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber who was killed by Calcocane, said: “This is long overdue, and simply the right thing to do.

“It was a disgrace that Calocane and offenders like him have ever received taxpayers’ money.”

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, father of fellow Calocane victim Grace O’Malley Kumar said: “Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness.

“Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount.



“On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits.

“On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated.”

The mum of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche who was killed by partner Gogoa Lois Tape added that “it is a matter of moral responsibility”.

Tape pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility and was handed a hospital order.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Linda Westcarr said: “For many victims’ families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society.”

News.title: Billionaire blow-in is turning our cute countryside idyll into a snooty celeb haven…even the station has been taken over
News.content:
Next

AS passengers pull into this quaint Somerset town, they might notice something unusual about its signage.

The words ‘Castle Cary: For The Newt’ tell weary travellers they’ve arrived on the doorstep of £900-a-night upmarket country hotel owned by billionaire South African businessman Koos Bekker.





And Bekker’s ventures don’t end with his celeb-loved hotel. The mogul has been described as a “feudal lord” after taking over thousands of acres of Somerset countryside to create an empire for posh people.

He’s bought up land, pubs and shops where he sells chocolate buttons for £12.

One local man in his 70s said: “It’s hard to argue with someone with that much money.”

His £900-a-night upmarket country hotel The Newt has bought him an army of celebrity fans and guests including Kate Moss and Charlie XCX.

Indeed, some locals gush about the property mogul; his generosity towards community events, the way everything he does, “he does so well” and how many jobs he’s created.

But while he continues to build a realm of boutique hotels and shops in the posh town of Castle Cary there is an undercurrent of anger over his growing Estate.

Locals have signed a petition against his use of pesticides.

While others fume about an “egocentric” sign at the town train’s station – used by thousands of Glastonbury festival-goers.





“Castle Cary – For The Newt” reads the sign to anyone embarking onto the platform, and visitors can walk straight into the first of several businesses Bekker has launched.

His farm shop and café, The Creamery, sells Buffalo mozzarella from his own 500-strong herd, which you can watch them make, and salted caramel chocolate buttons in a Reindeer pouch at £11.95.

He serves afternoon teas at £45-a-pop from a vintage Pullman carriage out the back.

One local woman told us: “I find the new signage diabolical and frankly egocentric.

“It’s not like there aren’t many other fantastic businesses in the town and if they had the money, they’d probably all like their own signs at the train station too. It’s a bit much.

“The amount of businesses and land he’s got – it’s a monopoly, which is never good.

“It’s like having a feudal lord.”

As well as the swanky Newt, nestled on 900 acres with its own orchard mazes, and spa hotel, Bekker has bought The George pub on the High Street of Castle Cary, as well as The Angel.



He now also owns a beauty parlour behind the George.

In total, his company which runs the Newt and his other businesses in the area – Emily Estate Ltd – turned over a staggering £23.5milllion last year.

One business owner who did not want to be identified, said they had spoken out about the “monopoly” in the past, but did not want to do so again.

They said: “I do have problems with all of it.

“But I won’t put my neck on the line again.

“I have a business to run and a family to feed, and my shop has another few years on the lease.

“What I will say is that none of it is ok.

“Many of the other residents are unhappy, but it’s hard to argue with someone who has that much money.”



The George is a former Greene King pub which was popular with pensioners as it served meals for as little as £12 before its recent closure.

On the sunny day The Sun visited, staff were selling off the fixtures and fittings to make way for the developers, with one commenting, “anyone with deep pockets” would fit the future clientele.

Bekker has also launched boutique hotels similar to The Newt.

Yarlington Lodge and Cattle Hill Gate are nestled between Castle Cary and nearby celeb-heavy town Bruton.

Bruton has been dubbed the “new Notting Hill” and is the home of a litany of celebs.

Caroline Sharley, 59, is the owner of the Giggling Grape, based in the rear of husband Jan Schimmel’s shop, Schimmel’s Hardware.

She is also the chair of the Castle Cary Commerce Association.

Caroline said: “My view is that the whole development of The George is more nuanced, it’s not black or white.



“Some parts of The George building were falling down, and Greene King weren’t going to invest in that.

“If someone can afford to invest that kind of money in a lovely, small, town, then it’s great for the economy and for the community.

“It will bring a different kind of tourist, it will bring people with money into the town.

“He arranged a public consultation for people to meet with the architects and project manager even before planning, so he’s been very good.

“Because our businesses are so close, the only concern is the noise and dust the development will cause.”

Bekker is believed to be investing £40 million into the pub, converting rear buildings into apartments in a five-year project.

Meanwhile, up the road is another of his investments, The Angel pub, which is also being redeveloped.

One local resident of almost 50 years said: “I think it’s brilliant, it’s a positive for the town and will revitalise it, so it’s wonderful.



“It will create lots of jobs and everything he does, he does it well. We’re lucky he’s so invested in improving the town.”

Meanwhile the owner of coffee shop Burnt Honey Jesse Gilchrist, 41, said: “Anything that brings more people into the town is good for all businesses.

“If it wasn’t him, it would be someone else.

“There is always competition in business, and if they come to the new pubs, maybe they’ll discover our shop too.”

Businessman Bekker is believed to have a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms.

He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to The Guardian – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited.

One business owner cryptically said: “It’s difficult to speak about, isn’t it?

“On the one hand he sponsors the carnival and the flower show and takes part in all the community events, which helps business, so no business owners are going to speak against him.

“On the other hand, residents are not happy with everything he’s doing.”

People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built.



The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.

Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about Bekker’s business practices.

Writer Emma Craigie, who is not part of the group, but also lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on.

“In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”

She claimed the worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”.

The Sun contacted Bekker’s representatives for comment.

News.title: Tributes to ‘kind’ man, 23, killed in horror crash after his motorcycle collided with lorry
News.content:
SMASH TRAGEDY Tributes to ‘kind’ man, 23, killed in horror crash after his motorcycle collided with lorry







Next

A MOTORCYCLIST who was killed in a horror crash with a lorry has been described as a “kind, loving and likeable young man”.

Tyler Ellis was riding a black Kawasaki motorcycle when it collided with a red Volvo HGV on the Old North Road in Cambridge at around 12.50pm on October 5.

Tyler was raced to Addenbrooke’s Hospital in Cambridge but despite best efforts he died the next day.

The lorry driver, 76, was arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by careless driving and has been bailed until January.





Tyler’s family said in a heartbreaking tribute: “Today, we pay tribute to our beautiful, loving son, whose life was tragically taken following a road traffic collision.

“Tyler was loved beyond words by his family and friends. He was such a kind, loving and likeable young man, with a smile that could light up any room and a laugh that was truly infectious. He had a special way of bringing happiness to those around him, and his presence made life brighter for everyone who knew him.

“There are simply no words to describe the heartbreak and devastation we feel at losing our precious boy.

“Our world has been shattered in a way that words can never explain, and there will forever be an emptiness in our hearts that can never be filled.



“Tyler, you were taken from us far too soon, and we will carry you in our hearts every single day.

“The love we have for you will never fade, and although we cannot hold you in our arms, you will forever be a part of us. Your memories, your smile and your laughter will live on in everyone who was lucky enough to know you.

“Fly high, our beautiful boy. Until we meet again, may you rest peacefully, knowing just how deeply you are loved and how terribly you will be missed.

“Forever our son, forever in our hearts, forever 23.



“Rest in peace, Tyler. We love you always.”

News.title: Australian MP Helen Haines loses leg after left-wing climate activist ‘reversed to hit her 2nd time in car ram attack’
News.content:
Next

AUSTRALIAN MP Helen Haines has lost a leg and is fighting for her life after a left-wing climate activist allegedly reversed to hit her a second time in a “deliberate” car ram attack.

Doctors are fighting to save the Independent politician’s other leg after she was struck in a horror ramming.



Haines, 65, was repeatedly struck by the Toyota Land Cruiser and pinned underneath on Monday outside her regional Victoria office.

The man allegedly behind the wheel was anti-Israel environmentalist activist Brendan Nugent, 43, according to The Age.



Nugent’s dad revealed the independent MP has been a family friend for decades, calling the attack “devastating and unfathomable”.

The suspected attacker is said to have made a U-turn before ramming the 65-year-old as she was taking items out of her car boot.

Witnesses saw the alleged attacker reverse his car and strike Haines a second time, according to home affairs minister Tony Burke.

Footage appears to show the car reversing from the MP’s car as bystanders run to get help.



Witnesses said she was hit “at least three times”.

Nugent’s social media included a slew of anti-Israel and anti-logging posts, where he described himself as a “plant person”.

On a handful of occasions, Nugent replied to Haines’ X posts, but was not aggressive.

In October 2019, he wrote: “Would’ve been nice to include a politician who takes climate change seriously, such as yourself.”

His posts, which became increasingly toxic over three years, are the focus of a terror probe, the Australian reported.



Nugent complained of being “broke” and living in “chronic pain” online and railed against Israeli military contracts, accusing Australian PM Anthony Albanese in 2023 of “starting WWIII” for working with Joe Biden.

He is from Tarrawingee – a short 15-minute drive from Wangaratta where the attack unfolded – and has a history of activism in the area.

Cops have not established that his political or environmental views were behind the alleged attack and the motive remains unclear.

One source told the Age he strayed into “darker” things after once protesting logging in the local forest.

The alleged attacker’s dad Rod said: “Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community.



“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable.



“All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends.”

Hero barber Ricky Jefferies has revealed how he ran out of his shop to take down the alleged attacker, pulling him from his car and disarming him.

The dad-of-three told 7News he had heard a “loud bang” and rushed out of his shop to help.

He said: “I was just trying to not get injured and trying to not let anyone else be injured after the initial incident.

Ricky said he had “no choice” but to pull the alleged attacker out of his car because “it was the right and safest thing to do”.



The barber said he grabbed a knife from the rammer’s pocket and threw it away, and pinned him down until the cops came.

Ricky said he didn’t think he was a “hero”, just “a person who had the opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way”.

Cody Lepoidevin was working across the road from Haines’ Wangaratta office at the time of the attack when he heard screams.



Lepoidevin said he saw the Land Cruiser drive into her at least three times before the attacker tried to flee.

He told The Age: “I was there to restrain him against the wall, but yeah, more or less they got him out of the car.

“He was quite delirious, I suspect pretty riddled with drugs, but yeah, from there on it was pretty much just blur. We did what we could.”

PM Albanese described the incident as an “attack” and said counter-terrorism units were investigating the ordeal.

He said: “This wasn’t an accident. There was a deliberate act it would appear.”



Witnesses said the driver passed her in a car park before doing a U-turn and ramming the mum-of-three politician.

The MP was airlifted to a Melbourne hospital with “severe” lower body injuries and underwent surgery on Monday night.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Albanese said the hero barber serves as “a reminder that at the worst of times we see the best of the Australian character”.

He said: “All of our thoughts are with Helen Haines today, with her family, her team, her many many friends and indeed her community as well.”

News.title: Aldi customers urged 'stop using immediately' as 'high risk' item recalled
News.content:
Aldi customers urged 'stop using immediately' as 'high risk' item recalled

The supermarket is providing refunds to affected customers

View 3 Images Aldi has issued a recall notice (Image: Getty)

Aldi has issued an urgent product recall notice for one of its Specialbuy items. The budget supermarket sells much more than just food and drink thanks to its special offers.

‌



‌



Its middle aisles are often filled with products ranging from toys to camping equipment, home décor and appliances. However, a "high risk" alert has been issued for a hairdryer sold in stores.

‌



Aldi is recalling its Ambiano Ionic Hairdryers due to a high risk of electric shock. The Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) has published a recall alert to warn customers.

‌



It said: "The product presents a risk of electric shock or fire as, over time, the power cord may become damaged, allowing access to live parts or causing overheating. If the user were to touch an accessible live part, they could receive an electric shock.

View 3 Images A range of hairdryers have been recalled (Image: Aldi)

"The product does not meet the requirements of the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016."

‌



The OPSS added: "The product has been recalled from end users by Aldi. Consumers who have purchased the product should stop using it immediately and return it to their nearest Aldi store for a full refund."

News.content:
Revolut users are experiencing problems with the app this morning, with reports of issues with the UK-based bank surging on outage-tracking website Downdetector

Revolut is experiencing an outage, with users reporting problems making payments through the banking app.

More than 1,500 Revolut users had reported issues with the UK-based bank by 8.09am, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.

Almost 65 per cent of reports related to problems with the app, while around 20 per cent related to problems accessing funds and eight per cent involved login issues.

News.title: PIP payments update for claimants with anxiety, depression, ADHD or autism
News.content:
PIP payments update for claimants with anxiety, depression, ADHD or autism

A major review of the PIP benefit system is underway

View 2 Images A major review of the PIP system is underway (Image: Getty)

A benefits support charity has spoken out to clarify some misunderstandings about the reality facing PIP claimants (Personal Independence Payment). Financial help group Money Wellness spoke about some of the extra costs that people can face living with mental health conditions such as anxiety or depression, or with neurodivergent conditions such as autism or ADHD.

‌



‌



The update comes after a report came out with a series of findings about people with these conditions who claim the DWP benefit. Depression and anxiety are the top two health conditions that people with PIP report having, while autism and ADHD are also in the top 10 most commonly reported conditions. There have been concerns raised in the media about the rapid rise in recent years in the diagnosis of mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.

‌



Some argue that people are to an extent incentivised to get such a diagnosis so they can claim certain benefits or a higher award. A recent Government-commission report also raised concerns that ADHD and autism are being overdiagnosed.

‌



View 2 Images A major review of the PIP system is underway (Image: Getty)

PIP is intended to help with the extra costs associated with living with a long-term health condition or disability. There are varying levels of payment depending on to what extent your health condition(s) impact your in your daily life or mobility. The Money Wellness team explained why people with conditions such as anxiety or ADHD may well need this support.

Not always visible

Rebecca Lamb, external relations manager at Money Wellness, said: "Living with anxiety, depression, ADHD or autism can cost more in ways that aren't always visible from the outside. That might mean taking a taxi because a crowded bus feels impossible, paying more for ready meals or delivery on days when cooking is out of reach, or running the heating more because you spend more time at home."

‌



She explained how people with these conditions can face higher bills as a result of their condition: "For people with ADHD, missed bills and forgotten renewals can mean late payment fees and rolling on to more expensive tariffs. And people with autism may need things such as noise-cancelling headphones or specific foods because of sensory needs.

Ensure our latest DWP headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

"Long NHS waiting lists mean some people end up paying for therapy or assessments privately too." The Resolution Foundation recently published a report having spoken to PIP claimants to hear their real-life experiences being on the benefit.

‌



The study found that 89 per cent of PIP claimants with ADHD have extra costs as a result of their disability, similar to the proportions for those with back pain (87 per cent) and arthritis (94 per cent). Less than one per cent of PIP recipients report only having anxiety, ADHD or autism, meaning the vast majority of people with these conditions have other health conditions or disabilities that they live with.

Makes dealing with money harder

Looking at these findings, Ms Lamb said: "The picture of someone claiming for a single mild condition doesn't match the reality for most people. Many of these conditions also make dealing with money harder in the first place, because opening post, making phone calls or keeping track of bills can feel overwhelming, so debts can build up quietly.

"If that sounds familiar, organisations like us can help you check you’re getting everything you're entitled to and work through any bills that have mounted up." One curious finding in the report is that 16 per cent of those spoken to said they don't currently have extra costs as a result of their health condition.

‌



Expert tips to save money on energy bills

Ms Lamb spelled out the reality here. She said: "The 16 per cent figure needs to be read alongside what PIP tests. The assessment looks at what you can and can't do day to day, not at what you spend, so it was never set up to measure extra costs directly.

"People's health also changes. Someone who had high costs when they were first assessed may be in a better place now, which is what everyone would hope for. The report found nearly nine in 10 people have conditions that go up and down, so some may have simply answered on a good day."

‌



In contrast, the report found that in some cases, people are struggling to cover their extra costs even with their PIP payments. The benefits expert said: "What concerns us more is the other side of the picture. Among people who pay more for heating because of their condition, more than a third say they can never or rarely afford it.

"So for many people, PIP isn't stretching far enough to cover the costs it's meant for. There's clearly room for the test to match support to need more closely, and asking about costs at the assessment would help with that."

PIP review

Major changes to the PIP system could be on the way soon. The Government is carrying out a review of the benefit, co-chaired by DWP minister Sir Stephen Timms.

Article continues below

An interim report said the review team had heard from many people that the benefit was "not fit for purpose". Some disabled people described the process of applying for the benefit as "dehumanising" and "soul destroying". The final report for the review with its recommendations to the Government is expected to come out in November 2026.

News.title: Midwife says pregnant women must 'never ignore' worrying sign on hands and feet
News.content:
Midwife says pregnant women must 'never ignore' worrying sign on hands and feet

A midwife with is urging pregnant women not to ignore symptoms they get on their hands and feet, as it could be much more sinister than they initially think

View 2 Images A midwife is urging pregnant women not to ignore a worrying sign on their feet and hands (stock image) (Image: Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images)

A midwife has urged pregnant women not to ignore a worrying sign on their feet and hands as it could be more sinister than they initially think. There are a number of weird symptoms and effects of pregnancy, including a sudden intense sensitivity to smells, increased gum sensitivity and even unexplained cravings for non-food items.

‌



‌



Although health professionals may tell pregnant women not to worry about many weird and wonderful symptoms that come with growing an entire human being, there are some things mums-to-be must take more seriously.

‌



Lara Basini-Millar, a former senior NHS midwife who appeared on One Born Every Minute, has urged pregnant women not to hesitate in getting in touch with a midwife if they suffer with itching on the palms of their hands or feet.

‌



Lara said: "I've been a midwife for 23 years, and here are things that I would never ignore if I was pregnant again. Some of these might surprise you. Itching, particularly on the palms of your hands or the soles of your feet, and if it's worse at night.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

"Because, although itching can be completely harmless, it can also be a sign of a liver condition called intrahepatic cholestasis. And that needs investigating."

‌



What is Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP) and how does it impact pregnant women?

Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP) is a condition that affects how a pregnant woman's liver works. In the UK, ICP affects about 7 in 1000 women (less than 1%), but the condition is much more common among women of Indian-Asian or Pakistani-Asian origin, with up to 15 in 1000 women (1.5%).

It usually happens towards the end of a pregnancy and will get better after a woman has given birth. ICP can cause a number of risks in pregnancy including anxiety or low mood, jaundice, pre-eclampsia and an small, but increased risk of a baby being born early.

View 2 Images Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy is a condition that affects how a pregnant woman's liver works (stock image) (Image: Antonio_Diaz via Getty Images)

‌



There are no long-term health risks for babies of women with ICP, but it could increase the risks of a child opening their bowels before they are born, which could cause them to get unwell if it enters their lungs during labour.

There is a small increased chance that a baby will need to go to the neonatal unit when they are born, especially if they have been born early.

One a woman has suffered from ICP, there is also an increased chance they will get the condition again in future pregnancies.

Article continues below

Women who are pregnant and have itchy skin should get in touch with a GP if the itchy skin is affecting their daily life, it does not get better after treatment from a pharmacist, or it keeps coming back, they have eczema, or have a new rash, lump or swelling.

However, woman should call 111 or their dedicated maternity unit to get urgent medical help if they're pregnant and have very itchy skin that keeps them awake at night, have itchy palms or soles of your feet or the itching is worse at night.

News.title: Angela Rayner warns of 'silent majority' being radicalised online after Australian MP attack

Angela Rayner warns of 'silent majority' being radicalised online after Australian MP attack

View 2 Images Angela Rayner warned people are being radicalised online (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

Angela Rayner has warned a "silent majority" are being radicalised online after the horrific attack on an Australian MP.

‌



‌



The Communities Secretary was asked about Dr Helen Haines, who lost a leg after being allegedly rammed twice by a vehicle outside her office in rural Victoria.

‌



Ms Rayner told Sky News intimidation was driving people out of politics, and that the algorithms were fuelling hate online.

‌



She said: “Many Prime Ministers and international people have spoken about this, in this context of violence, which I think undermines our democracy.

Barber refuses to be called hero after rushing to help Australia MP Helen Haines who was mowed down by car READ MORE :

‌



“I've mentioned in many interviews that I might disagree with what the leader of the opposition in the Conservatives says, or the leader of Reform, or the leader of the Greens. It is completely unacceptable to intimidate people and to threaten them. These are democratically elected individuals, whether we like it or not.

“I've been in parliament since 2015 — I saw Mhairi Black, I saw Anna Soubry, these were strong women that have said, ‘You know what? It was too much. The threats were too much,’ and they pulled back from public life.

“Therefore, we're all losing out when that happens. Even one of my colleagues, luckily enough the police were informed about a plot to murder her, and thankfully that didn't happen, Rosie Cooper, there is a documentary made about it. This is just in my time in parliament, in the decade that I've been, two of my colleagues have been murdered.”

‌



Ms Rayner said she had panic buttons at her house, had suffered threats against her children, but that 99.9% of the public were “good and decent”.

Warning the “online space is radicalising a lot of this”, she said: “A lot of it what is said to me is in communications electronically or online, they wouldn't say it to my face, and I don't feel that they come at me in person. But I really feel there's an issue around the radicalisation, and the violence, and the imagery that is projected on a lot of online platforms.

“The government is taking action on that, but I really feel that we have to push back, because that is not the experience or what the British people are about.

Article continues below

“It's this silent majority that are radicalised, that are angry, that are driven to the algorithms to see more of the hate that is, I think, fuelling a lot of this.

It's not just against politicians, but actually you can see people who go online, if they put something in a forum, then there's this like pile-on. People are starting to withdraw because they don't want to express their views because they get attacked for it.”

News.title: Doctor explains '4-7-8 method' to get to sleep faster
News.content:
Doctor explains '4-7-8 method' to get to sleep faster

Dr Deborah Lee has also outlined four other tips to help people fall asleep

View 3 Images A sleep doctor has some advice (Image: Curly_photo via Getty Images)

A doctor has outlined five ways to get to sleep at night if you're struggling.

‌



‌



Dr Deborah Lee, a GP and sleep expert from Doctor Fox working with Comfybedss, has discussed five weird ways that might send you off to sleep faster. They include a counting method and a bit of reverse psychology.

‌



Doctor's five ways to get to sleep faster

Breathe only through one nostril

Dr Lee said: “If you lie on your side and breathe only through your left nostril, it may help you drift off a little bit faster. By covering your right nostril with your finger, this could help you lower your blood pressure and calm the body ready for bed time. It should start making you feel a bit dozier.”

‌



Welsh might have cured dementia by mistake, new dads dying at alarming rate, giant tortoise's secrets for a long life, and what are the side-effects of weight-loss drugs? All this and more in our weird science newsletter

View 3 Images Struggling to sleep? Give these a try (Image: Tero Vesalainen via Getty Images)

Tell yourself to stay awake

“Reverse psychology at its finest. By telling yourself to sleep constantly, it’ll drive stress and anger around the fact that you’re not falling asleep. However, by doing the complete opposite, and telling yourself to stay awake, it’ll help you drift off a bit quicker.

‌



"Just keep repeating the phrase, in your head, “do not fall asleep”. Eventually, your eye muscles will tire out and you’ll be asleep before you know it!”

The 4-7-8 breathing method

“Put your tongue to the roof of your mouth and exhale through your mouth. You might find that a weird noise comes out of your mouth, but this is part of the process.

"Once you’ve done this, close your mouth and inhale through your nose for four seconds. Then, hold your breath for seven seconds. Once you’ve gotten the four and seven out of the way, we’re onto the eight. Exhale through your mouth for eight seconds. Keep repeating this until you’re fast asleep.”

‌



View 3 Images There are a few ways to try (Image: nong2 via Getty Images)

Take yourself through your day

“Take yourself through the day, but not just in any order, in reverse. Keep it detailed, remind yourself what you had for breakfast, lunch and dinner, what you did at work and what music you listened to in the car on your commute.

"Start from what you watched on TV before bed and go back through the day taking you right back to when you first woke up. This will keep your mind occupied, not letting you think of something that might be the reason that you’re keeping up.”

Article continues below

Tense your toes

“Another weird one, but something I’ve recommended to clients is tensing their toes for 10 seconds. Tense your toes for 10 seconds, and then relax your toes for 10 seconds. Keep doing this until you start to feel tired. This will help you draw tension away from the rest of the body.”

News.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
News.content:
Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT).

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times, external, Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.

The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.

If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

Last year, HMRC estimated that lifting the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by Â£3.6bn in 2028-9.

The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits.

"I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said.

Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".

But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.

Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work".

Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to the Financial Times, external.

Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget.

Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living.

It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices.

The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year.

The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers.

The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt.

In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to urge the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing.

She will tell the prime minister and the chancellor to "live within our means" and signpost her party's plan to save Â£70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid.

The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise Â£14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks.

The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses.

News.title: We asked teens what schools should teach them about work. This is what they said
News.content:
More than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests.

The online survey, by Survation,, external asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education.

Some called for more support with their communications skills and raised concerns about stress management and personal finances.

Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was the government's "mission" to ensure teenagers leave school "confident about their next step and equipped with the skills and experience they need to succeed".

In England, the government wants to guarantee two weeks' of work experience for every young person, external during secondary school.

It's an opportunity not all teenagers are currently given, the survey for the BBC suggests, with more than half of respondents saying they had not done any.

When teenagers were asked in the survey what skills or guidance they would like more of at school, the most common responses were more work experience opportunities (44%) and help managing finances (43%).

Respondents said they also wanted guidance on how to apply for jobs (42%) as well as how to manage stress and mental health (39%) and develop their communication skills (38%).

As part of the Teen Summit project by Radio 5 Live and Bitesize, the BBC followed four students from Newcastle - Param, McKenzie, Jasmine and Javaris - as they tried out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements.

"I'm terrified about the future. I feel very uncertain about it," 15-year-old Jasmine said.

News.title: Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
News.content:
Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.

Regulations due to be laid out in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to Â£800 a month in universal credit over several years.

Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, who was stabbed to death by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham, before the killer was sentenced to a hospital order, said she would now "demand" ministers reallocate the funds, which she said was a "no-brainer".

The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds a year.

The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to parliamentary approval.

Currently, serious criminals on hospital orders - where their bed and board is funded by the NHS - continue to receive any benefits they were paid on the outside.

Students Barnaby and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital.

The parents of Barnaby and Grace met Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden to discuss the change on Monday.

Emma Webber said the move was "long overdue".

News.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
News.content:
Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.

The prime minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished.

In one case, a woman was taken to court in a Â£1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped.

Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".

Burnham said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."

The new rules will give drivers:

A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to park

A 10-minute window to leave without facing a penalty

Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parks

Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines

Maximum charges of Â£20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking

A freeze on the maximum parking charge at Â£100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice

Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.

News.title: US church on front line of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
News.content:
America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities.

President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction".

But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq".

While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction.

BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more.

Read more on this story: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis.

News.title: Job vacancies fall as small firms cut back on recruitment
News.content:
Job vacancies in the UK have seen their largest fall since the start of the year as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate.

Vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), which said small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring.

Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff.

The ONS figures also showed the unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the lowest for more than a year.

The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before Chancellor John Healey presents his first Budget next week.

ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment".

"The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said.

"The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor."

The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs.

Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms.

News.title: Can a simple photo of your face reveal how ill you are?
News.content:
Mak and colleagues are also evaluating an AI tool for predicting biological age, or how old someone looks, as opposed to their birthday age.

The 'FaceAge' tool suggests the skin below the nose and near the mouth - the so-called nasolabial folds and marionette lines - plus the forehead (frown lines), temples (crows' feet) and cheeks are a good indicator of how fast we age.

Some lifestyle habits can speed that process up, like heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking.

Mak says the tool was "surprisingly consistent" across common real-world photos despite variations in pose, lighting, facial expression and make-up.

"It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty [a nose job]," he says.

But the researchers stress they need much more data and photos of faces, particularly from lots of different ethnic groups, to determine how well the tools work. They are still very much under development.

The research team is inviting the public to take part, external and receive a personalised biological age estimate by uploading their own facial photo the research team.

Prof Miroslaw Bober, an expert in video processing and machine learning at the University of Surrey in the UK, says any claims that the tool could track ageing or lifestyle changes over time would be "premature".

"This is a promising proof of concept, but it is not ready for clinical use," he said.

"The tool still needs testing against doctors' own judgement and across different hospitals and patient groups."

And he warned: "Predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it."

News.title: Watch: Ukraine says it carried out first drone airlift of wounded soldier from front line
News.content:
The Ukrainian military has released footage of what it says is the world's first drone airlift of a wounded soldier from the front line.

The 92nd Assault Brigade said a ground rescue mission was not possible as the wounded serviceman was surrounded by landmines and there was high Russian drone activity in the area.

It says a "heavy" hexacopter, piloted by a remote operator, was able to maintain stability during the "very difficult" operation.

BBC Verify has confirmed the identity of the army personnel involved in the video, and found no signs of AI generation or manipulation.

News.title: Troubles legacy bill is not an amnesty for soldiers - NI secretary
News.content:
The secretary of state for Northern Ireland has rejected claims that planned changes to the government's Troubles legacy bill amount to an "amnesty" for former soldiers.

Sir Chris Bryant said it was "completely wrong" to suggest a requirement for the attorney general to consent to serious Troubles-related prosecutions was designed to pardon veterans.

The proposal is among a series of government amendments being debated by MPs on Monday after the long-awaited legislation returned to the House of Commons.

Speaking to BBC News NI, Bryant said it was a "sensible measure" to ensure there was "more consistency" in how decisions are made.

The legislation seeks to deal with the unresolved legacy of the decades-long violent conflict in Northern Ireland, which cost the lives of more than 3,500 people.

It was first introduced to Parliament last year following agreement on a joint framework with the Irish government.

News.title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.

In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.

The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.

She has accused Brand of grabbing her breasts at the bar in Soho in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet and allegedly raping her.

The pair had been attending a birthday party when the alleged incidents happened.

She said she waited two decades to come forward to the police because the thought of doing so "terrified" her.

She said his celebrity status meant "it would be his word against mine".

"I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends."

The complainant worked for MTV at the time and said she was often surrounded by famous people.

From behind a blue screen in the witness box she said times had changed.

In those days - she said - "you weren't believed as a woman and it was a lad culture of 'you wearing this, so you were asking for it' and all that rubbish you were told back then".

The complainant recalled Brand's "big weird grin" which she compared to the face of a clown as he allegedly launched forward and grabbed hold of her.

Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested during cross examination that Brand and the woman went to the toilet consensually for a "kiss and a cuddle", but they abandoned the attempt to have a sexual encounter because of the filthy state of the flooded toilet.

The woman, who became tearful while giving evidence, has rejected this version of events.

She said she felt "dazed" after the alleged attack.

Pressed on her claim of being dragged into the toilets against her will, the defendant's barrister suggested it would have been "perfectly easy" for her to have struggled or asked for help.

She said she did not agree because he had been holding her quite strongly, saying "part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

She described feeling numb and ashamed afterwards.

She told the jury she had later confided in a friend, telling them Brand had "tried to do it" - but held back from saying he had "succeeded" in raping her.

The woman told the prosecution barrister that she didn't even know at the time that the alleged oral attack would be legally considered as rape.

Earlier on Monday, the jury was shown a 2023 video interview with an officer in which the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs".

A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.

She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock".

"The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said.

"Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".

"I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.

After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."

Brand denies all the charges he faces.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

News.title: Man accused of mass train stabbing admits wounding
News.content:
A man accused of a mass stabbing on a train in Cambridgeshire last year has pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent.

Passengers and staff were injured on the 18:25 Doncaster-London service on Saturday, 1 November after it left Peterborough, causing it to make an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon railway station.

Anthony Williams, 33, has denied 14 counts of attempted murder, relating to the train and to incidents in London and Peterborough, and is due to stand trial next week.

Appearing at a pre-trial review at Cambridge Crown Court, Williams, of Langford Road in Peterborough, pleaded guilty to the lesser wounding charges and several other offences.

He appeared via video link from Rampton Hospital in Nottinghamshire.

At an earlier hearing, Williams pleaded not guilty to attempting to murder Jonathan Gjoshe, Sachin Balakrishnan, David Presland, Scott Bletcher, Scott Green, Kevin Deely, Stephen Crean, Raza Aslam, Michael Paffett, and Samir Zitouni on the train near Huntingdon on 1 November.

In front of Mr Justice Calver this Monday, Williams pleaded guilty to 12 counts of wounding with intent and two of attempting to wound with intent in relation to incidents on the train, and earlier in Peterborough and London.

News.title: Rantzen felt 'deprived of choice' over her own death
News.content:
A posthumous note written by Dame Esther Rantzen said she was "deprived of any choice over my own death".

The farewell message was released as the 86-year-old broadcaster and campaigner's family confirmed she had been laid to rest in an "incredibly beautiful" private funeral last week.

The Childline founder, who was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in 2023, died at her Bramshaw home in the New Forest, Hampshire, on 30 September.

A larger memorial service is expected to take place at a later date.

Rantzen's daughter Rebecca Wilcox said the family had been inundated with messages since her death.

"It's been hugely comforting to know that people around the world felt the same way about her as we did," she said.

Dame Esther became a prominent campaigner for assisted dying in her later years, something MPs voted against legalising in September.

In her note, she wrote: "It would have transformed the way I died if the law had allowed me to ask for assistance to die when my life had become unbearable.

"I was extremely lucky because I had the talent, skill and support of my local Oakhaven Hospice.

"But I was still deprived of any choice over my own death by the current messy criminal law."

She said she had become "too physically frail to take the flight" to an assisted dying clinic in Switzerland.

News.title: NHS trust prosecuted over children's sepsis deaths
News.content:
An NHS trust is being prosecuted over the deaths of two children who had sepsis, the BBC has learned.

Two charges relate to Zadie Ajetunmobi, three, who died within hours of being taken to Broomfield Hospital, Essex, with a temperature of 40C (104F) in November 2022.

A third regards two-year-old Selina Samarina, who was sent home by a doctor at Broomfield in April 2024, only to die two days later.

Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust (MSE), which runs the hospital, said it was "working closely" with investigators. It is due before Chelmsford Magistrates' Court in December.

Care and treatment was allegedly "not provided in a safe way" to the girls, court documents revealed.

The prosecution is being brought by the Care Quality Commission under the Health and Social Care Act.

Zadie died within 10 hours of being taken to Broomfield on 10 November 2022, having suffered a cardiac arrest.

A post-mortem examination showed her death arose from complications associated with sepsis, external.

She was not given a potentially life-saving dose of intravenous antibiotics for more than seven hours.

News.title: Four arrested after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Four people have been arrested - including a woman on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm and possessing a firearm - after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects at a bus stop in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The male officer remains in hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.

Two women, 27 and 25, and a 24-year-old man were arrested after police stopped a vehicle in the Radford area of Nottingham on Sunday evening, while a 30-year-old man was arrested in Bedfordshire in the early hours of Monday.

The 27-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm with intent, and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

The 24-year-old man and 25-year-old woman were also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

Separately, after stopping a vehicle in Bedfordshire, the 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: Man held after three Jewish women report assaults
News.content:
A man has been arrested after three Jewish women, one of whom was pushing a baby in a pram, reported being assaulted in north-east London.

Police were called to the Clapton Common area of Hackney at about 13:40 BST on Monday after a man had been detained by members of Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group.

Officers arrested a 33-year-old man on suspicion of racially aggravated common assault. The women are believed to have suffered minor injuries.

The Metropolitan Police said it was treating the incident as a suspected antisemitic hate crime and had increased patrols in the area.

The man has since been further arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in connection with a separate incident in Islington on Friday, the force said. He remains in custody.

Ch Insp Erica Crawshaw said it had been "an alarming and distressing incident" and thanked Shomrim volunteers for detaining a suspect before officers arrived.

"We recognise the concern that this incident will have caused the Jewish community here in Hackney," she said.

"We have increased patrols in the area and we are speaking to community leaders to provide further reassurance."

The Met has appealed for anyone with information, or anyone else who believes they may have been assaulted, to come forward.

News.title: Trial hears Robinson 'intimidated' Daily Mail reporters
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson used "bully-boy, intimidatory tactics" to frighten two Daily Mail journalists, forcing them to employ security or leave home, a court has heard.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence towards reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber.

Opening the trial, prosecutor Ben Holt said the case was about Yaxley-Lennon's reaction to what he perceived to be "an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday" in the aftermath of the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson, who founded the English Defence League, entered not guilty pleas to the charges in July last year.

Holt said Dirnhuber had to move house because of the alleged harassment, while Young was given a close protection officer by the Daily Mail after photographs of his wife and children were posted on Robinson's X account.

The judge at Southwark Crown Court, Mr Justice Cavanagh, told the jury: "This is not a trial about or an assessment of the defendant's political views."

Ben Holt, for the prosecution, described Yaxley-Lennon as a "well-known public figure" with a "large, vocal online following" that now included more than two million followers on social media website X.

Robinson posted on X before the trial began to thank the social media platform's owner Elon Musk for funding his case â and said his court fees to date had cost him Â£400,000.

News.title: Who is Brendan Nugent? Suspect in attack on Australian MP Helen Haines as parents say they are ‘family friends’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The man arrested on suspicion of ramming Australian MP Helen Haines has been identified as an environmental campaigner whose family have been friends with the politician for years.

Dr Haines, 65, was hospitalised in a serious condition and reportedly had a leg amputated after a man struck her with his car and then reversed to hit her a second time in Wangaratta on Monday.

Anti-terrorism police are investigating but yet to establish a motive, as local media identified the 43-year-old man arrested at the scene as Brendan Nugent.

The suspect's father, Rod Nugent, and his partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement that the attack was “devastating and unfathomable”.

“Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” they said on Tuesday.

open image in gallery Independent member for Indi Helen Haines in February last year ( Reuters )

“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable. All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends.

“We would like to sincerely thank members of the local community and police who came to Helen's aid yesterday after the shocking and horrific crime.

“We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.”

Who is Brendan Nugent?

Brendan Nugent, 43, was arrested at the scene on Monday after being detained by a witness to the incident, according to Australia’s ABC.

The campaigner, from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared to be a “longtime local” to the Indi electorate that Dr Haines had served since 2019, the broadcaster reported.

Mr Nugent had posted on his social media channels about the environment and politics for some years, and was an active member of the Save Our Strathbogie Forest group.

Online records show he played football for the Wangaratta High School in his youth.

He has claimed since at least 2022 to be living with a disability and in “chronic pain”, and said that despite receiving benefits for his condition, he was “constantly broke” from the associated costs.

He had posted about medicinal cannabis use but it was unclear whether he had used the drug.

An account linked to Mr Nugent posted on domestic and foreign policy issues, and followed a large number of climate-related groups.

The account in 2019 responded to one of Ms Haines’ posts about the future of Australian farming in the face of climate change, saying: “Would’ve been nice to include a politician who takes climate change seriously, such as yourself.”

What happened to Dr Helen Haines?

Dr Haines, the Independent MP for Indi, a rural electorate north of Melbourne, was airlifted to hospital after being struck outside her office by a 4x4 vehicle in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon.

Early investigations suggested the car hit Haines as she was loading or unloading things from the trunk of her car, prime minister Anthony Albanese said.

A knife was found inside the Toyota Landcruiser, police said, adding that there was no further threat to the public.

Witness Ricky Jefferies ran from his barber shop, restraining the attacker and removing a knife from him after initially believing the incident was a car accident, Australian media reported.

open image in gallery Barber Ricky Jefferies speaks to the media a day after tackling a man accused of attacking Australian politician Helen Haines ( AFP/Getty )

“I heard a loud bang with no brakes. It was crazy, I just ran out to the front to see what's happening,” Jefferies told reporters outside his shop.

“I didn't realise the seriousness of the situation initially, and once it became relevant I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do.”

Dr Haines underwent surgery overnight and remained in critical condition on Tuesday. Australian media, citing unidentified sources, reported she had lost one leg as a result of her injuries and that doctors were working to save the other leg.

Mr Albanese told a news conference on Monday that it was too early to determine the motive for the attack, but later pointed to how social media had raised the temperature of politics in a country where such violence is extremely rare.

Dr Haines' family posted on her Facebook page, saying: “We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.”

open image in gallery Helen Haines, the Independent member for Indi ( Reuters )

Who is Helen Haines?

The former nurse and midwife has served as an MP since 2019, when she became the first independent to succeed another independent in the same seat in Australia’s parliament. She was re-elected in 2022 and again in 2025.

Dr Haines worked in nursing and midwifery and as an academic before being elected to parliament as an independent in 2019 in the seat of Indi.

Her website says she has opposed proposals including making political donations to the major parties more secretive, banning mobile phones in immigration detention and spending billions on fossil fuel subsidies.

She grew up with four brothers on a dairy farm near Colac in Victoria's South-West, according to a biography on her website, and now lives with her husband on a small working farm.

Dr Haines spent three decades working in rural healthcare, completing a doctoral thesis at Sweden's Uppsala University on childbirth.

In her first speech to parliament, she spoke of the “privilege” to have been able to care for people “as they take their first breath of life and as they take their last”.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and MP Helen Haines ( Reuters )

“Midwives are the hand that guides the hand that rocks the cradle that rules the world,” she said, laying out the challenges in access to healthcare for many Australians, and the constraints especially squeezing those in rural areas.

She turned to politics in 2019 as part of a community movement in Indi, traditionally a conservative stronghold, called "Voices for Indi". Three years later, she held her seat with a significantly larger margin of 8.9 per cent.

In parliament, she has championed causes including climate change, regional housing and worked with the ruling Labor government to establish a National Anti-Corruption Commission.

“As an Independent I work in partnership with the community, councils, small business and local industry – to figure out what we need and how to make it happen,” she wrote on her website.

“Together, we’ve achieved a lot; a record number of mobile phone towers, funding for major projects, recovery from natural disasters, and more housing infrastructure.

open image in gallery Helen Haines (2nd-L) speaks to the media in November last year ( Getty )

“We’ve pushed to improve integrity, for better support for regional Australia and against funding cuts to essential services.”

"She's someone who is very passionate about her community,” Albanese told public broadcaster ABC. “She's someone who's not shy about coming forward about what she thinks that community needs, but she's also someone who plays a role in the parliament.”

"She's just a thoroughly decent, respectful human being who is a delight to work with, and her presence in the Parliament adds to it."
