Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni reflected on Hurts' season-ending injury and their relationship, saying: "I always talk to our guys, and I never put our conversations out there. I think you guys can understand that. Like that's private conversations with myself and him.

"I can just say to you I haven't been without Jalen for an extended period of time. I have the utmost confidence in Tanner (McKee).

"But you know, I miss him, right? I miss him, and I know that will be the case. I mean, because Jalen and I have been together, head coach and quarterback, for six years. So that's natural.

"But I don't want to speak for him in any sense of the matter. I just deeply care about him and hope that he continues to improve with what he's going through."

Sports.title: Bills safety Gardner-Johnson suspended for spitting
Sports.content:
Buffalo Bills safety CJ Gardner-Johnson has been suspended for one game without pay for spitting in the direction of Las Vegas Raiders players on Sunday.

Gardner-Johnson was ejected late in the second quarter for unsportsmanlike conduct following an exchange with a group of Raiders players, including tight end Brock Bowers.

In issuing the suspension, the NFL cited its rule applying to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Buffalo Bills against the Los Angeles Rams from Week 5 of the NFL season

With Buffalo (5-1) entering their bye week, Gardiner-Johnson's suspension will begin on October 26 and run through November 2, a day after the Bills host the Baltimore Ravens.

The player has the right to appeal the suspension.

Gardner-Johnson apologised to his team-mates immediately following Buffalo's 33-30 win and posted a note on social media apologising to fans.

"I owe my team-mates an apology and to be a man about it," Gardner-Johnson said following the game.

"You got to understand that as a grown man you can't be doing [stuff] like that in a game," he added. "As a vet, I'll be better. I'll take my consequences as it is, handle it like a man and move on."

The 28-year-old won a Super Bowl with the 2024 Philadelphia Eagles and is on his sixth team in eight seasons, and signed a one-year contract with Buffalo in March.

Coach Joe Brady referred to Gardner-Johnson's spitting act as being "inexcusable" and said he discussed the matter privately with the player.

"It can't happen. That's not what we're about. That's not what the game of football is about, and he knows that," Brady said.

Gardner-Johnson arrived in Buffalo with an established reputation of being a noted trash-talker and as someone who has on occasion crossed the line with illegal hits.

"I don't need a roster of everybody being the same person," Brady said.

"Obviously, he crossed the line yesterday and that can't happen. It won't happen again. Personality-wise, I'm not afraid to have people who are going to try to toe the line in everything they do."

Sports.title: Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’
Sports.content:
Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.”

The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media.

He is tired of the shorthand way he is described during these high‑profile job hunts. People focus on his playing accolades, including calling him the treble winner, a label he says belongs to one season in a run of three Premier League titles at Manchester United from 1999-2001. “I’m a manager,” he says.

Over the past four years, Yorke has quietly built a coaching résumé far removed from Old Trafford. His first taste of management came in May 2022, taking charge of Australia’s A-League All Stars against Barcelona in front of more than 70,000 people in Sydney. They lost 3-2. “I realised then that I enjoyed it,” he says.

Macarthur, based in Sydney, followed that July. “We went to a relatively unknown team in the A‑League and managed to win the cup.” The Australia Cup success, three months into his spell, was the club’s first trophy.

It did not last. Macarthur sacked him in January 2023, with the club sixth, after a post-match address when he reportedly called the club a “pub team” run by “muppets”.

A Fifa chamber found Macarthur had dismissed him without just cause. The court of arbitration for sport upheld that in 2024 and ordered the club to pay AU$212,500 (£111,300 at current exchange rates).

“I wish I’d had the opportunity to finish what I started,” Yorke says. The job taught him communication and the importance of being transparent. “There was a disagreement. It was resolved amicably and I’ve moved on.”

Between Macarthur and his next role, he kept his hand in. He worked as a pundit for beIN Sports and on the Saudi Pro League and travelled the world watching coaches at work.

In November 2024, Trinidad and Tobago came calling. The Soca Warriors finished third in their World Cup qualifying group behind Curaçao and Jamaica, missing out on the finals tournament, and Yorke’s tenure ended soon after. The Trinidad and Tobago Football Association said talks over revised terms had not produced an agreement and the contract was ended by mutual consent, announced in March. “The decision to end things was out of my control,” Yorke says.

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke smiles on the sidelines as he leads the A-League All Stars to a narrow friendly defeat by Barcelona in May 2022, his first taste of management. Photograph: Rick Rycroft/AP

He does not accept that missing the World Cup defines his time in charge. “People can be blind to success because they focus on whether you qualified.”

He lost once in six qualifiers, 2-0 in Jamaica in September 2025. He had been handed a brief: make people care about Trinidad and Tobago again, boost recruitment and qualify. “I was given three tasks and completed two,” he says.

With Yorke as the head coach, crowds came back and a number of US-born players with Trinidadian and Tobagonian heritage, such as the CF Montréal winger Dante Sealy and Real Salt Lake’s Kobi Henry, opted in and made their debuts. Yorke gave a new generation a fighting chance to emulate the team he captained to the finals in 2006. “I left Trinidadian football in a far better place than I found it,” he says.

The TTFA president at the time described Yorke’s mandate as qualification alone. The team were ranked 102nd by Fifa when Yorke was hired, behind Curaçao (91st) and Jamaica (62nd). “I miss management,” Yorke says. “I miss what we were creating.”

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke says he tends to fast for nearly 20 hours a day and eats one meal: ‘I’m a fitness fanatic who trains every day.’ Photograph: Christopher Pike/The Guardian

The players are understood to want him back because his successor, Derek King, is struggling with two draws and eight defeats from his 10 games. Ghana, though, is the live opportunity. “It’s a job I’d be interested in, given Ghana’s history and the players available.”

The Ghanaian FA has not confirmed any approach. The team are bottom of their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying group with no points, after a 2-0 defeat in Côte d’Ivoire and a 4-2 home loss against the Gambia in which they led by two goals. It is a sharp decline for a side that reached the last 32 of the World Cup this summer, losing 1-0 against Colombia.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“You look at the squad and your eyes open even wider,” Yorke says. He says an agent called to tell him Ghana were interested. “The conversation started there and then reached the media before I really knew it.”

From the outside, he says, Ghana “sometimes looks disjointed”. The GFA has said its women’s head coach, Kim Björkegren, will take temporary charge of the men’s qualifying double-header against Somalia next month. In Yorke’s view, outside noise unbalances things, from the administration to the players. So how would he fix it? Organisation, transparency and everyone speaking the same language. “The talent is there. Build the culture and get the players to buy in and the football will follow.”

double quotation mark Pep said that I can’t be him or any other manager – I have to be myself Dwight Yorke

He has considered the effect that diaspora players could have in the role, pointing to Ghana’s Antoine Semenyo and Brandon Thomas-Asante as proof that countries can benefit immensely from UK-born talent. It reflects a broader trend: at the World Cup, 23.6% of the 1,248 squad players represented countries outside their place of birth. For Yorke, the approach is simple: identify the players, establish their heritage and quality and sell them a vision. “I’d make sure that what I say is what I do.”

Older managers might have screamed and shouted to get messages across, but he says: “I’m not sure that approach can last in the current environment.” He would not berate a player in public. “That can be done behind closed doors, while still being assertive.” Respect and punctuality are non‑negotiable. He has sat in dressing rooms with big egos and says nobody gets special treatment. “Everyone starts equally.”

He borrows, but he does not copy. Sir Alex Ferguson, who managed him at United, is the shadow over any such comparison. Among contemporary managers, Pep Guardiola offered him the best advice. “He said, in effect, that I can’t be him or any other manager. I have to be myself.”

View image in fullscreen Dwight Yorke fends off Dominic Matteo in Manchester United’s FA Cup fourth-round win against Liverpool in January 1999. Photograph: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto Ltd

Other labels have stuck anyway. “People still call me a ‘party boy’. That stigma has been overused and has followed me since I retired from football. I’m not saying I didn’t enjoy myself as a player.” But he says: “You never hear that I didn’t turn up for training or wasn’t fit.”

In Dubai, he tends to fast for nearly 20 hours a day and eats one meal. “I’m a fitness fanatic who trains every day.”

Ask Yorke how he wants to be remembered as a coach and he sits up and answers with a list. Committed. Transparent with players. Decisions made for the team, never for an individual. “I’m straightforward. I don’t mess around, take shortcuts or do the job halfway.”

Yorke has the interest and, by his own account, the answers. “If anyone doubts me, I can prove them wrong.”

Sports.title: Villarreal’s Iñigo Pérez ready to meet Iraola again in test of old bond
Sports.content:
On Iñigo Pérez’s first day as a head coach he took a call from Andoni Iraola, just as he had every day for months. They had known each other for 22 years, lived in the same residency, come through the same academy and played in the same team; they had worked side by side, manager and assistant, and embarked on an adventure together. Now, though, Pérez was having to go it alone. At 36, he had become what his friend thought he would be from the moment they met, just not so soon. “He wished me luck and said he was there for me,” Pérez said, “said that if I ever needed anything …”

Well, maybe not anything.

“Sometimes life brings what you never imagined,” Pérez said after his coaching debut. Now he is off to Anfield. It’s funny the way it goes. Had he not been denied a work permit by the Home Office, had a Football Association panel not declared him incapable of contributing to English football, a partnership broken and a family turned back, a career seemingly derailed from the start, Villarreal’s manager wouldn’t be sitting on the bench to the left of the halfway line at Anfield tonight. He would be sitting on the bench to the right.

This time, the man who should have been Iraola’s assistant is instead his opponent, nothing given for 90 minutes. “I’m looking forward to seeing him; we speak continuously, always there,” Pérez says. “To encounter each other pitchside is emotional. When the referee blows, it all ends, but it’s a very nice story.”

The story starts in 2002, when Pérez arrived at Athletic Club Bilbao’s academy, aged 14. Iraola was 19, six months from his first‑team debut. They first played together in the first team in October 2009 but, teenagers and tenants, something had already drawn them together and would do again. If Pérez was more open, Iraola more private, timid even, there was much they shared: an inquisitive mind, an ability to observe and listen, a humility befitting a club where presumptuousness is prohibited.

“Intellectually they’re brilliant,” says a teammate from that time, Carlos Gurpegui, intelligent a word that keeps coming back and with warmth too. “Andoni had a privileged mind and Iñigo was so intuitive. We played [Fantasy Football] and Andoni always won,” the goalkeeper Raúl Fernández recalls.

View image in fullscreen Iñigo Pérez celebrates a goal with Athletic Bilbao teammates, including Andoni Iraola (far left) in the Europa League in March 2012. Photograph: Dennis Grombkowski/Bongarts/Getty Images

If that gave them natural leadership, it was worn lightly, not imposed. As one coach notes: “If everyone was going left and Andoni said: ‘Go right,’ they’d all be like: ‘Yeah, yeah, go right!’ They are two unusually intelligent guys, always rationalising, able to reach others.”

Iraola saw it in the kid coming through, ideas explored together. “Iñigo was always aware of tactical [shifts],” he said later. “At 14 or 15, the way he thought about the game was mature. Ever since I knew Iñigo, I thought he had the personality to be a coach. In fact, he had a clearer idea about being a coach than I did.”

David López, who played alongside them, says: “It’s no surprise they became coaches.” Eneko Bóveda, who came through the academy with Pérez, says: “They might have become coaches individually; together, they were bound to. Iñigo was extremely impressive in personal relationships, inside every dressing‑room circle: emotionally intelligent, empathetic.”

The age difference was no barrier, a product of their place, the communal culture that made them. “When we reached the first team, that generation [above] was established, but it was very easy to talk to them, even take life advice,” recalls Fernández, born in 1988, like Pérez. “I remember asking Andoni what to do about my contract. Under Marcelo Bielsa, the players would come together before games with a hot chocolate, a croissant and talk. Bielsa was super‑demanding, always at your throat; we took refuge in each other.”

Pérez might not have been there at all, unwanted by Bielsa until the training session when he crashed into the goalkeeper Gorka Iraizoz. “There was blood everywhere, his lip split open, but Iñigo carries on and Marcelo thinks: ‘I can follow this guy to the end of the world,’” Gurpegui recalls. Picturing the scene, Fernández starts laughing: “Iñigo didn’t know what would happen to him. I seem to remember him even sleeping at Lezama [the training ground] on a mattress, which showed how committed he was. And that day Bielsa was shouting at the physios: ‘Leave him! Leave him! He wants to carry on!’ He’s going to Iñigo: ‘Bravo! Bravo! That’s it, lad!’”

An opportunity opened at full‑back and Pérez did what he always did: adapted. Above all, they observed, took it all in. “Iñigo and I would speak a lot about the way Bielsa coached,” Iraola recalled. They would ask endless questions of assistants Claudio Vivas, Pablo Quiroga and Diego Reyes, always wanting to know why. “But then they’re football nutcases who learned from everything,” Boveda says.

View image in fullscreen Andoni Iraola, then at Bournemouth, invited Iñigo Pérez and his Rayo Vallecano side to England for a pre-season friendly in August 2024. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

Their last game together was in October 2013. Iraola retired in 2016 and started coaching two years later. Unseen, Pérez was drifting in the same direction. Common friends and a shared agent meant they were never far away and in February 2022 they crossed paths again. Pérez didn’t play when Osasuna won 3-0 at Rayo but their conversation that night stuck in Iraola’s mind, a mental note made.

Aged 34, Pérez had told Iraola his role now was really about helping the coaches. Indeed, Osasuna’s manager Jagoba Arrasate was already referring to him as a “player-assistant coach” and soon invited him to join the staff. Bielsa approached him too, furious when Pérez turned down Uruguay. When Iraola heard Pérez was retiring, he called immediately, convincing him to come to Rayo. The assistant coach Unai Mendia was leaving and his old teammate was perfect. The impression made was immediate: “Iñigo’s top,” a member of Rayo’s coaching staff says. “He was special, a phenomenon. Super‑elite, like Andoni.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Together with the fitness coach Pablo de la Torre, who constructed a physical model around which the whole, wild ride was built, they were a revelation, practitioners of organised chaos. Nowhere was football more fun, a shared vision soon enticed to the Premier League.

“When we found out that Andoni was leaving for Bournemouth, I told Iñigo he should be our head coach,” the Rayo striker Sergio Camello recalls, and the club hierarchy agreed. Pérez, though, thought it would be morally wrong: this was Iraola’s construction, not his to take. Besides, he wanted to continue with his friend. Iraola wanted that as well, taking only two staff to England: Pérez and De la Torre. It was a new start, a new life, and he needed his partners there.

But then Pérez was denied a work permit. Bournemouth took it to an FA exceptions panel. Supporting letters were sent, a case made. Iraola wrote, too, explaining their history and describing Pérez as “fundamental”. The panel, though, remained unsatisfied that he was “of the highest calibre and able to contribute significantly to the development of the game at the top level in England”.

“We did everything we could,” Pérez said, which was true: they even requested a permit as youth‑team coach, earning a telling off for trying it on. As he awaited a final resolution, Pérez kept working: he couldn’t wear a club tracksuit, appear publicly or sit on the bench, but he was at the training ground daily. Until, in the late autumn, they had to admit defeat. That hurt, personally as much as professionally. “It was very difficult, an uncomfortable situation for all of us,” Iraola says. “You can’t [work], you can’t put your kids in school.”

Between them, Shaun Cooper, Tommy Elphick and De la Torre had to assimilate Pérez’s duties, Iraola impressed and grateful at the staff he inherited. His tourist visa expiring, Pérez returned to Spain. Calls from Bournemouth continued, some consultation and a lot of conversation, not always about football. Then when Rayo sacked Francisco Rodríguez in early 2024, the club offered him the manager’s job again. Iraola encouraged Pérez to go for it. “In the summer, I didn’t feel ethically comfortable and I wanted to continue with Andoni,” Pérez said. “The circumstances changed.”

View image in fullscreen Iñigo Pérez shows the way during Villarreal’s Champions League 3-2 defeat against Borussia Dortmund in September 2026. Photograph: Jürgen Fromme/firo sportphoto/Getty Images

Camello admits: “I think the transition from assistant to head coach here was hard. He had been so close to us. Iñigo loved us too much: he felt so responsible for us that the inevitable frictions as No 1 were taken to heart. But he opened up to us, reached us. The relationship is still so good: he messaged me yesterday with some bands to listen to. And I doubt I’ll ever come across someone so capable in football terms. It’s amazing how many solutions he gives you on the pitch. Seeing him and Andoni in the Champions League doesn’t surprise. They have no limits; we’re just grateful that two monsters coached us.”

Their paths had separated, but the courses set were similar, the styles too. “My football belongs to Andoni,” Pérez said. Chaos still reigned many miles away and only a phone call apart. Iraola took Bournemouth to Europe for the first time; Pérez achieved Rayo’s first European qualification, and led them to the only final in their history. This summer greater challenges awaited, so here they are at Anfield, where there is relief that a friend’s career was not ruined but rather launched. “I am so, so happy for Iñigo,” one staffer says, “because you want good things to happen to good people and he’s very, very good people.”

They will watch in Bilbao, where it all began. “It’s special: I’m so proud of them,” says López. Gurpegui says: “Iñigo suffered in England but that situation opened another opportunity and now look: Andoni at Anfield. Bloody hell, I’m so pleased, because they’re two incredible people: humble, always there when you need them. Football needs more people like that.” Fernández adds: “And knowing them, it will be fun too: bold, brave football, a great game.”

Iraola says: “These games aren’t good for your relationship. We usually talk a lot but when you’re facing each other you talk less. It’s a special game because he’s my friend. He knows me very well. We’ve been through a lot together.”

Sports.title: ‘Like a family’: De Zerbi credits players’ talk and bonding trip for improving Tottenham
Sports.content:
Roberto De Zerbi said that Tottenham are playing with more togetherness after holding a clear-the-air meeting before their recent game with Manchester United.

Spurs went on to draw 1-1 with 10 men against United and are out of the bottom three after beating Coventry 3-1 at home on Monday night. De Zerbi felt the performance against Coventry could have been better but was happy with his side’s attitude as they claimed their first Premier League win of the season.

“It’s important,” the Spurs manager said. “The result is important but most important, two things. First one, we are able to realise we can win a game like other teams in the Premier League. The second thing, if we put [in] something from ourselves like we have done in the last two weeks. The day before Old Trafford we had a big meeting and spoke about the situation. We can’t accept and can’t move on if we don’t accept responsibility.”

De Zerbi took his squad to Marbella for a bonding trip and warm weather training last week. “This week has been important because we spend time together and want to be like a family,” he said. “During the game if you have a problem and there is a tough situation you have to play for your friend and your brother, not like 11 robot players on the pitch.”

Spurs took the lead when James Maddison marked his first start in 536 days with a brilliant goal. Coventry equalised through Jack Rudoni but Omar Marmoush responded with his first goal since leaving Manchester City and Ben Davies sealed the result.

Spurs are up to 16th and De Zerbi was happy that Maddison’s first goal since May 2025 was joined by Dejan Kulusevski coming off the bench to make his first appearance since suffering a serious knee injury in the same month.

“They are different players,” De Zerbi said. “Different talent, different experience, different personality. With them in the dressing room there is another atmosphere.”

Frank Lampard was happy with Coventry’s fight but was surprised that Marmoush’s goal was not ruled out after the Egyptian elbowed Milan van Ewijk. “I did think that,” Coventry’s manager said. “If you roll and your elbow is that high and it connects with Milan, I thought VAR would cancel it.”

Sports.title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes.

This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League?

Brentford began the weekend in third and with, perhaps, a slight sense of frustration that they had drawn four games. Again, they will feel they might have done rather better on Saturday; they were leading Liverpool 1-0 when Yehor Yarmolyuk foolishly flicked his head towards Jérémy Jacquet and was sent off just before half-time. The result was a 2-1 defeat and a sense of an opportunity missed. Bournemouth have not had the easiest start under Marco Rose, but Sunday’s 2-0 win over Sunderland perhaps hints at a brighter future.

Which left Brighton to carry the charge of the B clubs, which they did in emphatic style, ending a run of four derbies without success with a crushing 5-0 win. Crystal Palace had been extremely fortunate to survive a first-half battering from Nottingham Forest last week. They were thoroughly outplayed in the early stages again, and this time found themselves 3-0 down inside 10 minutes. Perhaps the opening goal, a cross headed into his own net by Jaydee Canvot, was fortunate, but it was an error induced by the intensity of Brighton’s start. The second goal, a perfectly weighted drive from just inside the Palace half from Diego Gómez, spoke of a side playing with immense confidence. Already this season, 11 different players have scored for Brighton in the league. They have become the image of a side without stars, the whole far greater than the individuals who comprise it.

The difference from February, when Brighton last played Palace, is stark. They lost that game 1-0, meaning they had won just one of their previous 12 Premier League games. Generalised grumbling had begun to curdle into calls for Fabian Hürzeler to be sacked. When they lost Carlos Baleba, Jan Paul van Hecke, Danny Welbeck and James Milner over the summer, there were reasons to wonder whether they could keep going with the process of continuous renewal.

There were the usual assorted signings, the usual mix of Premier League experience and exotic unknowns. The 19-year-old centre-back Luka Vušković, who spent last season on loan at Hamburg from Tottenham, already looks at home (and who really thought, when Spurs and Brighton effectively swapped centre-backs, with Van Hecke moving to London, that Brighton would not end up with the better of the deal?). The 21-year-old Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés, who arrived from Stuttgart, sparkled from the bench against Arsenal and has excelled in the two games since.

But the stand-out performer this season has been a far more familiar name: Pascal Gross, who returned in January after a season and a half at Borussia Dortmund. No player in the Premier League has registered more than his four assists this season. Nobody has run further. He has three goals. He averages a league-high 3.0 key passes a game. To bring back a player who is now 35 has been a masterstroke.

The victory over Arsenal before the international break suggested a team capable not merely of accumulating points against the league’s lesser lights, or even of challenging the elite, but of overwhelming them. Arsenal were suffocated by the Brighton press and, while a couple of low-xG long-range finishes in the first half helped, the fact is that Brighton dominated the match to a remarkable extent.

The question is whether they can keep it going. Just as their transfer policy is now an accepted feature of the Premier League, so too is Brighton’s mid-season slump. They haven’t won a game in December since 2023. Is this squad strong enough to sustain the challenge? Europe seems not to be unsettling Brighton as it did on their first foray, or as it appears to be draining Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Sunderland – which may be a reflection on the relative quality of the Conference League.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They are doing this without Kaoru Mitoma, Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer, all of whom should be back at some point over the next month. That suggests the depth of this Brighton squad. It’s always a major step for a club unfamiliar with the Champions League to haul themselves into the top five. At times it often feels a mental barrier as much as anything.

But if any of those B clubs are ever going to break into the Champions League, they may never have a better opportunity than Brighton do this season.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace to give Sage more time but manager under serious scrutiny
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage has been granted more time to fix Crystal Palace’s defensive issues but he has been warned that things must improve quickly after the 5-0 defeat at Brighton on Sunday.

The Frenchman’s future was in serious doubt after his side conceded three times inside the opening 10 minutes before equalling the 70‑year record for the club’s heaviest defeat against their arch-rivals. The thrashing means Palace have conceded the most goals in the Premier League: 17 from seven games.

The club chair, Steve Parish, is understood not to have been fully convinced by Sage since the 47‑year‑old was appointed to replace Oliver Glasner in the summer. Parish is believed to have considered parting company with Sage on Sunday after 10 matches but decided against a change given that Palace are 14th and not in immediate danger.

Sage is expected to remain in charge not only for the Europa League game at Besiktas on Thursday but also the Premier League match against Newcastle on Sunday. But it has been made clear to the former Lens manager that his position is under heavy scrutiny. Kieran McKenna, who Parish approached while the Northern Irishman was at Ipswich, and Thomas Frank will be among the contenders if Sage is sacked.

Tensions between Sage and Parish date to the summer transfer window when Palace failed to secure the manager’s main targets to replace Maxence Lacroix in central defence. Two loanees, Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor –, were signed instead from Chelsea and Atalanta respectively. Palace also missed out on Malick Fofana to Sunderland on deadline day despite Sage making the Belgium forward, whom he coached in Lyon’s youth teams, a priority. Palace instead signed Darío Osorio on an initial loan and the Chile forward has played only a handful of minutes.

Parish was unhappy with Sage’s treatment of Jaydee Canvot after the France Under-21 international was dropped from the squad for the home defeat by Ipswich last month. He is also understood to have been angered by Adam Wharton being substituted in that match after Disasi was shown a red card in the first half.

Some behind the scenes at Palace have been pushing for Sage to be sacked, but Parish is thought to recognise the headache caused by Disasi’s three-match suspension and injuries to Chadi Riad and Takehiro Tomiyasu and would prefer to give him an opportunity to turn things around.

Chris Richards has apologised to Palace supporters after failing to acknowledge them after the Brighton game. “I want to apologise for walking off after the game,” the USA defender wrote on Instagram.

“I was emotional and embarrassed with the result – I know how much this club means to all of you. We have to take responsibility, do better and show that on the pitch.”

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo receives 30-day suspension and £215 fine over Portugal walkout
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been suspended for 30 days by the Portuguese ⁠FA after leaving the national team camp following a rift with the coach, ⁠Jorge Jesus, over ⁠his role in the side. The federation’s disciplinary council said it had upheld the charge against ⁠the 41-year-old forward in full and imposed a fine of €255 (£215).

Ronaldo left Portugal’s base in ⁠Copenhagen before their Nations League match against Denmark this month, having accused ‌Jesus of twice ‌breaking his word about his role after he was an ‌unused substitute against Norway. Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return after Portugal’s 2-1 win.

The disciplinary council’s non-professional section found Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) ‌of the federation’s disciplinary regulations. Proceedings were opened on 9 October over facts reported two days earlier.

The statement did not specify which matches or activities the suspension would cover, or whether time already served under a provisional suspension would count towards the 30-day sanction.

Ronaldo later ⁠apologised for failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates, saying he remained available for selection after serving any ‌punishment arising from the incident.

The Portuguese FA president, Pedro Proença, has said everyone within the federation wanted Ronaldo to return to the national team once the matter was resolved.

Meanwhile, Fifa has suspended the Egypt coach, Hossam Hassan, and the forward Mostafa Ziko for ⁠three and five matches respectively, the Egyptian Football Association said on Monday, after they ⁠criticised the referee ⁠following their ​3-2 defeat by Argentina in the World Cup.

The 60-year-old Hassan was sanctioned after blaming ⁠refereeing errors for his country’s elimination from the tournament in the last 16, while Ziko insulted the ⁠referee in a post-match interview.

Ibrahim Hassan, Hossam’s twin and ​Egypt’s national team director, ‌has also been suspended ‌for three matches.

“The decisions include the suspension of Hossam Hassan ‌and Ibrahim Hassan for three matches each, while Ziko has been suspended for five matches,” the EFA said in a statement.

Sports.title: Football Australia chair Anter Isaac dismisses recent Fifa ructions as ‘growing pains’
Sports.content:
Football Australia chair Anter Isaac has played down concerns around the controversial World Cup privatisation push engineered by Gianni Infantino ahead of a meeting of Asian confederation officials in Tokyo this week.

Isaac’s sentiments come amid a global rebound in support for the embattled Fifa president, who at one stage appeared unlikely to be able to continue in his role following criticism led by officials in Europe and North America.

The Swiss lawyer now enjoys backing from South America, Africa and growing chunks of Asia, which would represent a bloc large enough for him to win March’s Fifa presidential election.

Continental powerbrokers are converging on Tokyo this week for the Asian Football Confederation congress. Fifa’s leadership and governance do not form part of the formal meeting agenda, but will be discussed by those present alongside the likelihood of January’s Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia going ahead.

Isaac, the most senior football official in Australia, was asked about the situation at Fifa in an episode of a little-known sports business You Tube channel earlier this month that has been viewed fewer than 200 times.

“We can look at it and be unsophisticated and say, what a mess,” he told Beyond the Game with Dillon and Rafael. “Or we can take a more responsible, mature view and say, you know what, these are growing pains.”

Isaac pointed out that Fifa’s revenues have exploded in recent World Cup cycles, and “systems and processes” at the organisation may not have kept pace. He was adamant that the intentions and motivations of people in football are “always in the best interests” of the sport.

“Maybe it’s not always aligned, but everyone involved in football really does want that, right? Everyone, at least in my experience and my interactions with them, that’s not even a question. So where has it become misaligned? Maybe it is in approach, maybe in communications and so forth.”

View image in fullscreen FA chair Anter Isaac spoke to a little-known podcast about the situation at Fifa. Photograph: Mark Metcalfe/Getty Images for Football Australia

FA’s previous statement on the controversial proposal dubbed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), issued in August, called for “clear and credible action” but stopped short of calling for Infantino’s resignation.

It was broadly in line with a letter co-signed by Asian Football Confederation president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa which demanded from Fifa “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.

Since then Salman appears to have softened his stance against Infantino, instead calling for strengthened Fifa governance, as a growing bloc of Asian nations including Qatar and the UAE indicate support for the Fifa president.

Isaac said people will criticise bodies like Fifa, AFC and Uefa but will not have the same knowledge of those within the system.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Football Desk Australia 

“If I had the same information that most critics or the general public have, I would probably draw the same conclusions as them. But I don’t. I have a lot more information. I see a lot more that happens,” he said.

“So when I reflect on Fifa and major institutions in football, I see a lot of the incredible work that they do, that confederations do, even our association [does], that goes unnoticed in supporting and serving and servicing different stakeholders, especially the ones that need the greatest help.”

Uefa sent a letter to Fifa this week asking it to explain the proposed sale of 20% of its commercial rights under the now-abandoned FFE, the Folarin Balogun affair and relations with Donald Trump.

The missive follows last week’s meeting of the Fifa council in Zurich, the first since FFE came to light. Infantino listened to questions there, but declined to provide comprehensive answers, and called for questions in writing to be submitted before the next meeting in Doha on 16 December.

Isaac said it was “premature” to talk about whether he would support Infantino at next year’s election. While he noted he has his “own views” – and he wanted to avoid being openly critical himself – he sees criticism of Fifa’s president as largely about “process”.

“I’ve been encouraged that, right across the board, everyone is now focusing on that [process] with a view to, OK, let’s try and diagnose, what maybe could have been done differently or better, so that in future – and we codify it – so that in future we avoid it and what’s happened in this particular situation.”

Sports.title: Semenyo’s eight-week injury absence leaves Manchester City short on cover for Haaland
Sports.content:
Antoine Semenyo has been ruled out for eight weeks with a knee injury, leaving Enzo Maresca short of alternatives to Erling Haaland, who is a doubt for Manchester City’s Champions League game at home against AEK Athens on Tuesday.

Semenyo limped off against Ipswich on Saturday and Haaland hobbled off at full time with a foot injury. City are eager to get their European campaign back on track after losing against Paris Saint-Germain last Wednesday. Maresca has said he will make changes and has admitted previously that Haaland will require resting at some point. Semenyo would have been the most obvious replacement but Phil Foden and Iliman Ndiaye could be utilised.

“To replace Erling it’s always difficult but we have some different options; we’ll see tomorrow,” Maresca said. “To lose Antoine or any player for us is not good. Then in terms of Erling, we said that we can use Antoine as a 9 but also we have different players that we are going to try and to find new solutions.”

Maresca witnessed a number of his players limp away from the win against Ipswich: Haaland, Semenyo, Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O’Reilly, who all featured at the World Cup. Maresca had made six changes, showing the need to rotate amid a hectic schedule of seven games in 21 days in October for City, many of whose players also had international commitments at the start of the month.

“We try to manage all the players in the best way, try to keep them fit,” Maresca said. “Even sometimes things happen that you cannot control, like Antoine’s injury. We try to save him, we try to keep him fresh.”

The fixtures mean it is difficult for Maresca to get training time as he tries to instil his style. “We try and do what we can on the pitch to go through a few things and tactics before the games,” the defender Marc Guéhi said. “It’s just a lot of recovery, sleep, to make sure the body is right for the next game,. It’s been enjoyable, to be honest; not to train, just playing games, which is fun.”

Guéhi was among the players who opted not to take a knee at the weekend as part of the Premier League’s “No Room For Racism” campaign. “I haven’t been taking the knee for a while now,” he said. “I’d always clap just because of what that actually signifies.” He wants greater action to combat racism in sport. “I hope we can do a bit more but we will just see. Hopefully the message is still getting out there, which is important.”

Sports.title: The top five goalkeepers in the world right now according to Premier League winner
Sports.content:
The top five goalkeepers in the world right now according to Premier League winner

Ex-Premier League goalkeeper Asmir Begovic has revealed his top five shot-stoppers in world football.

The former Stoke and Bournemouth star was wading into the debate over Jordan Pickford's status as England No.1.



7 Pickford and Begovic were teammates at Everton between 2021 and 2023 Credit: Getty

Pickford's place in Thomas Tuchel's team was called into question during the most recent international break as Leeds goalkeeper James Trafford nabbed his place for two of the four games.

Nevertheless, Premier League winner Begovic believes Everton's Pickford is still one of the best around.

"He is definitely in the top ten in the world without a doubt," Begovic said.



"I think maybe he is just a little bit outside that top five. There isn't a huge difference between all these goalkeepers.

"I've seen it first hand working with him every single day at Everton. How he performed in the most pressurised situations... which is when you need your goalkeeper and your key players and he's done some amazing things.



"What he's done for England for so many years... how consistent he's been and some of the big games that he's had there.

"So he's right up there with the best of them."

But if Pickford does not quite make the top five, who does? These are Begovic's selections...



7 Begovic earned a Premier League winner's medal during his career at Chelsea - and he scored a top-flight goal during his time at Stoke! Credit: Getty

5. Mike Maignan (AC Milan)

Age: 31

Major Trophies: 1x Serie A, 1x Ligue 1, 1x Nations League.

Clean Sheets: Over 180 total career clean sheets across Lille, AC Milan, and the French national team.

AC Milan star Maignan became the new France No.1 after Hugo Lloris retired in 2023.

Known as 'Magic Mike', Maignan boasts one of the highest career penalty save rates in elite European football, having stopped over 30 per cent of the penalties he has faced.



In his debut season in Italy, Maignan kept 17 clean sheets in 32 matches, winning the Best Goalkeeper award and inspiring AC Milan to their first Serie A Scudetto in 11 years.

He is forever linked with a move to the Premier League - most notably Chelsea - although the Blues opted for a bargain deal to sign Argentina's Emiliano Martinez earlier this year instead.

7 Maignan is AC Milan's talisman and wears the captain's armband for the iconic Italian club Credit: Getty

4. Jan Oblak (Atletico Madrid)

Age: 33

Major Trophies: 1x La Liga, 1x Europa League, 1x UEFA Super Cup, 1x Supercopa de Espana, 1x Primeira Liga, 1x Taca de Portugal, 1x Taca da Liga.



Clean Sheets: Around 295 career clean sheets, holding one of the highest clean-sheet percentages in European football history (nearly 45 per cent of his total appearances).

Oblak has won La Liga's prestigious Ricardo Zamora Trophy five times, tying the all-time historic record shared with legendary Barcelona goalkeepers Antoni Ramallets and Victor Valdes.

He also broke the all-time La Liga record by reaching 100 clean sheets in just 182 appearances, shattering the previous mark held by Miguel Reina (222 matches).

During Atletico Madrid's 2015/16 season, Oblak conceded just 18 goals in 38 La Liga games, equaling the lowest goals-conceded record for a 38-game European top-flight season.



7 Oblak has written his name in Spanish football history on numerous occasions - he is a brick wall Credit: Getty

3. Gianluigi Donnarumma (Man City)

Age: 27

Major Trophies: 1x Champions League, 4x Ligue 1, 2x Coupe de France, 1x FA Cup, 1x EFL Cup, 1x European Championship

Clean Sheets: Approaching 200 total career clean sheets across AC Milan, PSG, Manchester City, and Italy.

Donnarumma has been around for so long, it is easy to forget he is still relatively youthful for a goalkeeper.



The Italy star made his professional Serie A debut for AC Milan at just 16 years and 242 days old, making him the second-youngest goalkeeper to start a match in Italian top-flight history.

He later became the youngest goalkeeper ever to play for Italy at 17 years and 189 days.

Donnarumma has never lost a competitive penalty shootout - as England fans will know all too well - as he became the first ever goalkeeper to win UEFA's Player of the Tournament for his performance at Euro 2020.

7 Donnarumma completed a surprise move to Man City in 2025 and picked up two trophies in his first season Credit: Getty



2. David Raya (Arsenal)

Age: 31

Major Trophies: 1x Premier League, 1x European Championship, 1x World Cup, 1x Nations League.

Clean Sheets: Over 130 professional clean sheets recorded across Southport, Blackburn Rovers, Brentford, Arsenal, and Spain.

Incredibly, the second-best goalkeeper in the world does not even start for his country.

Raya played just one match across Spain's three recent international triumphs - with Unai Simon preferred between the sticks - but he is nevertheless invaluable to Arsenal.



The 31-year-old began his English football journey on loan at non-league side Southport before climbing through League One and the Championship to win back-to-back Premier League Golden Glove awards.

Besides his extraordinary shot-stopping ability, Raya is renowned for his long-range passing ability, changing the game when it comes to goalkeeper distribution.

7 Raya [left] is widely considered the best goalkeeper in the Premier League and gets the nod here over Donnarumma Credit: Getty

1. Thibaut Courtois (Real Madrid)

Age: 34

Major Trophies: 2x Champions League, 4x La Liga, 2x Premier League, 2x Club World Cup, 1x Europa League, 1x FA Cup, 2x Copa del Rey.



Clean Sheets: Over 335 clean sheets across KRC Genk, Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Real Madrid, and the Belgian national team.

Despite his exceptional career, it only took one game to cement Courtois' position as the greatest goalkeeper in world football.

The Belgium star holds the record for the most saves ever in a single Champions League final, making nine incredible stops against Liverpool in the 2022 final to secure a 1–0 victory for Real Madrid.

He also delivered an outstanding performance at the 2018 World Cup to win the Golden Glove award.

Sports.title: Football news LIVE: Ten Hag says Ronaldo ‘let the team down’ in bombshell revelation, Spurs claim first win, Champions League action
Sports.content:
Ronaldo 'let the team down'

Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has slammed Cristiano Ronaldo for his conduct at the club.

Ten Hag and Ronaldo had a fallout during the icon's second stint at the club between 2021 and 2022.

The Portuguese legend was dropped by the ex-United boss amid tensions between the pair - and now Ten Hag has revealed details of their feud when speaking to The Athletic.

“He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag admitted.

"I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United. Obviously, he’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."

Ten Hag then revealed that Ronaldo pulled out of training sessions at the time and didn't train to the right level when taking part, with the Dutchman also unhappy with his overall work ethic.

“I confronted him with this,” he added. “Many times I say, ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score’.

"He was not capable to do this. It’s the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he’s exhausted. But he couldn’t. He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn’t prepare himself.

“Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team.

“He was telling the players, ‘Save your legs at the training’. I understand it when you are top fit; you have sessions, you can save the legs. But first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels.”

Sports.title: Arsenal and Liverpool backed to take advantage of Barcelona’s mad decision to sell best defender
Sports.content:
Arsenal and Liverpool backed to take advantage of Barcelona’s mad decision to sell best defender

France defender Jules Kounde has been tipped to move to the Premier League if Barcelona choose to cash in on him.

The LaLiga giants have been warned it would be a 'mad' decision to offload Kounde anytime soon, though.

5 Kounde has been with Barcelona since 2022 Credit: Getty

That is according to European football journalist Andy Brassell, who has named the two Premier League clubs the right-back could join.

Kounde has made 196 appearances for Barca since signing from Sevilla in 2022.

He has also won three LaLiga titles in four years, with another potentially on the cards this term.

Hansi Flick's side are already five points clear at the top of the table having won each of their opening nine matches.

Kounde has helped contribute with a goal and an assist in their last two victories.

However, Brassell believes Barca may chose to sell the 27-year-old sooner rather than later despite handing him a new five-year deal as recently as August last year.

Could Kounde leave Barcelona?

Speaking exclusively to talkSPORT.com, he explained: "I do get the feeling that Barcelona are going to sell Jules Kounde at some point in the near future, which I think is a bit mad.

"Obviously they're going to have to sell someone of value at some point in the medium term. It looks like they're limbering up for it to be him.

"He's an underrated right-back and a really underrated centre-back because he doesn't get to play there that often anymore."

Kounde has shown his versatility for club and country at both right-back and in central defence.

5 Barca have been warned selling Kounde would be a 'mad' decision Credit: Getty

As well as his title triumphs with Barcelona, the former Sevilla and Bordeaux man has won 58 caps for France.

He was part of the side which reached the 2022 World Cup final having won the Nations League the previous year.

Kounde made five starts during the tournament in Qatar, including the final defeat to Argentina.

Didier Deschamps later included him in his squad for both Euro 2024 and last summer's World Cup in North America.

Arsenal and Liverpool told to sign Kounde

As for which clubs Brassell believes Kounde could join, he continued: "I think he'd be brilliant for Arsenal, for example. I think he'd be really good there.

"You could argue that maybe that's the place that Arsenal don't need to spend £50-60million on a player because they've got so many accomplished defenders.

5 Kounde was handed a new five-year deal by Barca last summer Credit: AFP

"I think he'd be good for Liverpool as well because he can be an attacking full-back but he's an authentic defender as well."

Arsenal currently have just two senior right-backs in their squad in the form of Jurrien Timber and Ben White.

However, the latter is currently out of contract at the end of next season.

As for Liverpool, the Reds' centre-back options could see them move for Kounde next summer.

Both Virgil van Dijk and Joe Gomez's deal will expire at the end of the current campaign.

Their exits would leave Andoni Iraola with only three recognised centre-backs, provided Ronald Araujo's loan from Barca is made permanent.

5 Arsenal have an embarrassment of riches in defence but Arteta surely wouldn't say no to Kounde Credit: Getty

5 Van Dijk's potential departure from Liverpool in the summer leaves a hole in their defence Credit: Getty

Kounde's ability to play both centrally and at right-back would also provide a boost, with Araujo deputising in the role in recent weeks.

It comes amid Conor Bradley's injury lay-off, with a return not expected before December for the long-term absentee.

Sports.title: Furious Jamie O’Hara demands Tottenham sell £52m summer signing in expletive-laden rant
Sports.content:
Tottenham finally got their first Premier League win of the season against Coventry, but it wasn't a stress-free watch for Jamie O'Hara.

At the seventh time of asking, Spurs got themselves up and running with a 3-1 home victory against Frank Lampard's newly-promoted side.

5 Ben Davies was the unlikely man that sealed the points for Tottenham Credit: AFP

5 Omar Marmoush had set Spurs on their way as he restored their lead in the second half Credit: Getty

Roberto De Zerbi's side headed into Monday night's clash as the only team in England's top five divisions yet to win a league fixture this season.

But Spurs finally shed their unwanted tag on home turf with a first three points that moved them out of the Premier League's bottom three.

Coventry youth product James Maddison opened the scoring with a stunning curled effort after just 14 minutes - marking his first Tottenham start in 18 months with a goal.

Despite a dominant first-half, Spurs' lead was then wiped away on 49 minutes when Jack Rudoni's initial shot rebounded into his path and he found the net at the second attempt to equalise.

But De Zerbi's men restored their lead ten minutes later, as Omar Marmoush curled home to ease their nerves, before Ben Davies sealed the points with a stoppage-time effort.

Van Hecke leaves O'Hara fuming

While Tottenham megafan and former player O'Hara was delighted to see his club finally deliver the goods, he was left raging at Jan Paul van Hecke when his mistake helped Coventry find their equaliser.

The £52million defender gave the ball away further up the pitch in the build-up, before failing to recover to stop Rudoni from scoring.

With O'Hara taking part in a special live watchalong of the game alongside Jason Cundy on 'Sports Bar: The Lock In', he did not hold back in his assessment of Van Hecke's role in the goal.

In an X-rated outburst, he ex-Spurs midfielder exclaimed: "What the f*** is Van Hecke doing? He is s***. He is absolute toilet.

"It is toilet, it is so Spurs. What is [Antonin] Kinsky doing? Van Hecke, I'm sick of it, get him out of here. We sold (Luka) Vuskovic for that pile of c***."

5 Van Hecke endured a hairy moment as Spurs were briefly pegged back by Coventry Credit: AFP

5 Rudoni equalised for Coventry minutes into the second half Credit: Getty

With Chelsea man Cundy earning a reputation for winding up O'Hara over Spurs' struggles, he made sure to deliver while his co-host raged.

Repeating his favourite catch phrase in recent months, Cundy gleefully taunted him: "You're going down!"

"F*** off," came the response from a furious O'Hara.

Despite a much-needed three points for Spurs, the talkSPORT host wasn't done with slating Van Hecke after the match either.

O'Hara continued to question why promising young defender Luka Vuskovic was allowed to be sold to Brighton, while Van Hecke moved in the opposite direction.

He said on the Sports Bar: "He's running through treacle, people say he's good on the ball but he is a problem for us.

5 Jan Paul van Hecke was one the first of Spurs' big-money arrivals this summer when he joined in a £52m deal Credit: Getty

"Brighton got Vuskovic out of the deal, they've got a better player."

Thankfully for O'Hara, Van Hecke's moment to forget was unable to prevent Spurs from getting their all-important win.

This isn't the first time the Dutcham has come in for criticism since reuniting with former Brighton boss De Zerbi in north London this summer.

In Spurs' 3-2 defeat to Aston Villa in September, Stuart Pearce questioned his £52m price tag after he struggled against Nicolas Jackson.

The England great said of Van Hecke on air: "Was that £52million worth of central defending?"

While Van Hecke's struggles came under scrutiny again against Coventry, O'Hara and Spurs fans up and down the country will simply be relieved to see their team get their first three points.

The victory lifts them out of the Premier League relegation zone and into 16th place, with six points from their first seven games.

Sports.title: UEFA piles pressure on FIFA demanding more from Gianni Infantino in damning letter
Sports.content:
UEFA piles pressure on FIFA demanding more from Gianni Infantino in damning letter

UEFA has sent FIFA a letter demanding answers to 42 questions surrounding Gianni Infantino's presidency, including his relationship with Donald Trump.

The letter, seen by talkSPORT, is addressed to General Secretary Mattias Grafstrom, and seeks answers by November 2.



3 Gianni Infantino has faced mounting scrutiny over his presidency in recent months Credit: Getty

It follows FIFA President Infantino telling FIFA Council members in a meeting in Zurich last Thursday to put their questions in writing.

UEFA is seeking further clarity on a number of concerns raised in the meeting, including Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

The letter also questions how Folarin Balogun’s red card came to be suspended at the World Cup, which allowed him to play against Belgium despite being sent off in the round before against Bosnia-Herzegovina.



UEFA want details as to how the FIFA Peace Prize was founded, and given to Trump at the 2026 World Cup draw in Washington DC.

Among their other grievances, European football's governing body ask for more transparency FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), the failed plan to part-privatise FIFA.



UEFA's letter to FIFA

“We formally request a substantive written response to each question, together with all supporting documentation by Monday, November 2,” the UEFA letter reads.

“Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon.



“These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the FIFA Council — nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.”

Senior UEFA executives are still spearheading a move to find a candidate to run against Infantino at the next election.

The deadline to put forward a name is November 18.

3 Aleksander Ceferin heads up UEFA, who have long questioned Infantino's suitability for his role as FIFA president Credit: Getty

Infantino has vowed to fight on, but there remain several unanswered questions despite the FIFA President apologising for FFE in Zurich last week.



UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin and his CONCACAF counterpart Victor Montagliani have both called for Infantino to resign, as has UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister and English FA chair Debbie Hewitt.

Among the major issues over which UEFA are seeking answers are the origins of FFE, where Infantino planned to sell off stakes in the world football governing body's competitions to private investors

FIFA are asked by UEFA, "When was the idea of FFE first explored, by whom and with what objective?"

FIFA are also tasked with explaining why Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital were granted exclusivity as an investor without consultation. Kusher is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. president Donald Trump.



UEFA also ask whether Infantino had a financial interest in FFE.

3 infantino's decisions throughout the summer have put him under serious pressure to keep his job Credit: AFP

The letter goes on to demand further information on "a series of decisions, transactions and interventions involving the FIFA President, the President of the United States [Trump] and individuals associated with him".

These are outlined in detail as follows:

UEFA's question on Infantino-Trump dealings " • The FIFA Peace Prize, which was not submitted to the FIFA Council for approval; - The reported seven-year, approximately USD 4 million lease of office premises in Trump Tower, New York, involving Eric Trump, for premises reportedly unused for much of the year; - The proposed agreement with Thrive Capital, led by Mr Joshua Kushner, a member of the US President’s family; - The US President’s telephone call to the FIFA President requesting intervention in the Balogun disciplinary case; - Reported advanced discussions involving the US President and individuals associated with him concerning a FIFA cryptocurrency; - The World Cup sponsorship arrangement with Kalshi, a company reportedly advised and partly owned by Donald Trump Jr., including reports that Kalshi received extensive advertising exposure without providing financial consideration to FIFA; - The last-minute relocation of the World Cup draw, reportedly at significant additional cost to FIFA, to the JFK/Donald Trump Center in Washington, D.C., instead of Las Vegas; - The involvement of the US President’s daughter and grandson in the Club World Cup draw; - The announcement of a USD 75 million investment in Palestine during the US President’s Board of Peace meeting, apparently without prior information being provided to, or approval sought from, the FIFA Finance Committee or Council; - Public statements by White House representatives, including Andrew Giuliani and the US President himself, defending the FIFA President, supporting his continued presidency and criticising those questioning his leadership."

UEFA want all documents relating to Balogun's red card against Bosnia in the World Cup round of 32 to be shared.

The US striker saw his automatic one-game ban suspended following a call from President Trump to Infantino to review the matter, as talkSPORT exclusively revealed.



Infantino has always claimed he had no involvement in the decision to suspend Balogun’s red stressing FIFA's disciplinary committee, which is independent, took the call.

The lack of clarity as to why the decision was made has led Infantino’s critics to question whether Infantino directly influenced the decision despite his denial.

And there are questions about Infantino's use of a private jet, and the hosting of celebrities at World Cup final, and whether any FIFA costs were incurred in doing so.

Sports.title: Ex-Premier League star opens up on unemployment struggle as he targets manager role
Sports.content:
Ex-Premier League star opens up on unemployment struggle as he targets manager role

Steven Caulker has provided an update on his search for coaching opportunities following a viral social media post.

The former defender took to LinkedIn on Sunday to share details of a 'stressful' spell away from football.

3 Caulker's phone has 'not stopped ringing' since his viral LinkedIn post Credit: Getty

Caulker has been without a job since leaving his role as assistant manager at Turkish side Konyaspor last month.

The 34-year-old spent eight months with the club, joining their coaching staff in February.

It followed his decision to retire from football in November 2025 after a spell in Iceland with Stjarnan.

Caulker had juggled playing with a role as assistant manager during his time at the Scandinavian club.

Meanwhile, he was previously a player-coach for Spanish outfit Malaga Juniors back in 2024.

Since leaving Turkey, though, Caulker has been unable to secure a role in England despite his experience and coaching badges.

The former Sierra Leone international joined Hawksbee and Jacobs on Monday to provide an update on his employment search.

Asked about the response to his LinkedIn post, he revealed: "Do you know what? I wrote that post yesterday morning and I think my phone has not stopped ringing."

Caulker continued: "It’s a good thing. I’m just in a situation where I wanted to leave Turkey.

"I wanted to come back and look to develop my coaching in the UK or maybe Europe, but I felt that it was time to come back closer to home.

3 Caulker made 123 Premier League appearances as a player Credit: Getty

"I spent a long time on the road and I’ve come back and I’ve been applying for jobs, I’m doing all the networking. It’s just a case of waiting for the right opportunity to appear.

"The difficult thing when you’re in a situation like this, or what I’m finding difficult, is to then say no to jobs that don’t align with my vision.

"Ultimately, I want to be a Premier League manager and I know that I’ve got a lot of work to get there, but I want to make sure that I’m on the right path, learning from the right people and making the right decisions along the way."

Caulker made 123 Premier League appearances as a player for Cardiff City, QPR, Swansea City, Tottenham Hotspur, Liverpool and Southampton.

He also represented Wigan Athletic in the EFL and had a brief spell in Scotland with Dundee.

As well as winning 18 caps for Sierra Leone, the centre-back was capped once by England in 2012.

3 Caulker has coached in Spain, Iceland and Turkey already in his career Credit: Getty

It followed his inclusion in the Team GB squad at the London Olympics earlier that year.

Alongside his coaching career, Caulker founded his own wellbeing consultancy firm last November following his retirement.

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford’s lack of form has created dressing room headache for Michael Carrick
Sports.content:
Marcus Rashford doesn't seem to have the trust of Michael Carrick and his current form is causing an issue for the under-pressure Manchester United boss.

That's the view of talkSPORT's chief football correspondent Alex Crook, who has shared his thoughts on the forward after he was an unused substitute in United's 1-1 draw with Leeds.

4 Rashford's goalless start to the season saw him left on the bench against Leeds Credit: Getty

The Red Devils' worst ever start to a Premier League season continued on Sunday, as their winless run extended to six games.

It piles the pressure on boss Carrick, whose side have won just once in the league - a 5-2 victory against Ipswich in their second game - and sit just two points above the bottom three in 13th.

As for Rashford, he has struggled to have a positive impact since returning to Old Trafford following his loan spell at Barcelona.

Rashford has been struggling with a hip injury suffered during the World Cup, meaning he needs regular treatment to ensure he is available for selection.

Despite the England forward being yet to register a goal contribution this term, having started six of his eight games this season, United sources insist Carrick is still backing his player.

The manager was heavily consulted before the club decided to bring him back from Barcelona and reintegrate him into the first team.

Rashford return questioned

With Rashford having little influence as United continue to struggle, United fan Crook has claimed his return is only proving a hindrance.

An academy graduate, Rashford quickly established himself as one of England's brightest young talents after bursting onto the scene as an 18-year-old.

He remained a key player for United in the years that followed, and signed a five-year deal worth in excess of £325,000-per-week in 2023 after a 30-goal season, which he remains under contract now.

However, after two loan spells away at Aston Villa and Barcelona, Crook told talkSPORT Breakfast: "I think he's probably peaked.

4 Rashford has scored 138 goals for United, but wasn't called upon against Leeds Credit: AFP

4 The 28-year-old has failed to pick up where he left off last season at Barcelona Credit: Getty

"That season, when he scored so many goals under Erik ten Hag [30 in 2022/23 term], that convinced them to give him this huge, big-money contract, which has been a real problem, I think, for the football club.

"And since he came back in, I was hoping that maybe his spell away at Barcelona would have sparked a new lease of life out of Marcus Rashford, but we haven't seen it, in all honesty.

"And I think Michael Carrick was absolutely right to put him on the bench yesterday, and the fact he didn't bring him on at the end of the game when United are short of goals and chasing a winner probably tells you he doesn't trust him at this moment in time."

United finished an impressive third in the Premier League last season, with Bryan Mbeumo, Benjamin Sesko and Matheus Cunha all hitting double figures in league goals.

Rashford's return was expected to boost their attacking threat having registered 14 goals and 15 assists on loan at Barcelona in 2025/26.

However, with United's forward line struggling to deliver the goods this term, Crook believes Rashford's return has upset the squad -particularly Cunha, who has scored just once so far.

4 Matheus Cunha hit 10 Premier League goals in his debut season for United last term Credit: Getty

He continued: "I think his return has been a problem, I think there's probably some unhappy players in that dressing room that he's earning so much money.

"I think it's been an issue for Matheus Cunha, because it's his place that he took and you can see that Cunha is sulking a little bit.

"And there was such a good balance at the top end of the pitch last season with Cunha and Mbeumo and Bruno Fernandes, Amad Diallo, Sesko when he was fit.

"But Marcus Rashford, I think, not on a personal level, but just because those players feel aggrieved, I think he's upset the balance of the attack and isn't putting the numbers on the board at the moment to justify that huge salary."

Sports.title: Husband of tennis's divorcing power couple loses his wife AND career all at once: Gael Monfils 'hit like a ton of bricks' by split from Elina Svitolina - as she cites war in Ukraine as the reason
Sports.content:
Husband of tennis's divorcing power couple loses his wife AND career all at once: Gael Monfils 'hit like a ton of bricks' by split from Elina Svitolina - as she cites war in Ukraine as the reason

Gael Monfils abruptly confirmed his retirement from tennis with the sport having 'lost all meaning' after Elina Svitolina's decision to end their marriage.

Svitolina, 32, had confirmed her separation from her fellow tennis star on Monday, where she cited the devastating toll Russia's war in Ukraine has taken on her mental health.

Monfils, 40, and Svitolina had been a couple since 2018 and married three years later. They shared a four-year-old daughter, who Svitolina stressed that their child will remain their top priority as they navigate their separation.

According to L'Equipe, the divorce led to Monfils bringing forward his retirement from the sport.

The French newspaper stated that the news had 'hit him like a ton of bricks' and that tennis 'lost all meaning as a result', with Monfils deciding he was 'no longer able to play'.

Tennis fans had been surprised last week when Monfils was listed as being inactive on a retired players list overseen by the International Tennis Integrity Agency.

Gael Monfils abruptly retired following his split from fellow tennis star Elina Svitolina

Svitolina announced the end of the couple's marriage in a social media post on Monday

His place on the list meant that Monfils is no longer able to play in professional events.

Monfils announced in October last year that he planned to retire at the end of the 2026 season, with the Paris Masters event at the start of November expected to be his swansong in front of a home crowd.

He had also been granted a wildcard entry to appear at the Grand Prix Auvergne-Rhone-Alpes, an ATP 250 event in Lyon, this week.

Monfils was due to take part in an exhibition at the event with retired French tennis stars Jo-Wilfried Tsonga, Gilles Simon and Richard Gasquet. The quartet had been dubbed as the 'New Musketeers' by French media during their careers.

Organisers had confirmed earlier this month that Monfils had withdrawn for 'personal reasons', with Lucas Pouille stepping in as his replacement.

Monfils' career officially ended at the US Open in September, when he was beaten in the second round by Learner Tien.

'I'm just me, Gael Monfils,' he said following the match. 'I think I have been the same since I came on tour, with a lot of joy.

'The most important for me is how my family lived all these years and how they will remember this ride was unbelievable.'

In an emotional post, Svitolina revealed devastating toll Russia's war in Ukraine has taken on her mental health and urged she needs to rediscover herself separately from Monfils

Monfils and Svitolina had played together in the US Open mixed doubles back in August

Monfils, who is viewed as one of the best players never to win a major, had competed in the mixed doubles competition at the US Open with Svitolina.

The star was previously treated to a lengthy send-off at his home major Roland-Garros in May.

Monfils, who was ranked as high as world No6 at his very peak and reached two Grand Slam semi-finals in 2008 and 2016, confirmed at the US Open that he will embark on a career in finance after joining a Swiss management firm.

Svitolina had confirmed their separation in a social media post, which featured a black and white picture of her and Monfils embracing.

The Ukrainian opened up about sleepless nights and self-doubt amid the ongoing conflict in her homeland, admitting on Instagram that she needs to rediscover her identity after 'slowly losing myself'.

'This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share. Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside,' she wrote.

'Gael saw all of it. He never let go of my hand. We fought through this together for a long time, with everything we had. But some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you.

'Please know that there is no one to blame here. There are only two people who loved each other deeply and a story that is changing shape.'

Svitolina, the world number six, this week was confirmed to have qualified for the season-ending Women's Tennis Association Finals.

Sports.title: Untidy Tottenham settled by James Maddison ending 610-day drought on a night of hope that things can only get better against Coventry - but it won't cause Chelsea sleepless nights
Sports.content:
Untidy Tottenham settled by James Maddison ending 610-day drought on a night of hope that things can only get better against Coventry - but it won't cause Chelsea sleepless nights

They came to salute the return of Dejan Kulusevski, and they rose to applaud James Maddison as he fired in the goal to finally give Tottenham lift off in this Premier League season.

Two creative forces back in Spurs colours offering hope that things can only get better.

Kulusevski came off the bench in the 87th minute to make his first appearance for close to 18 months after a serious knee injury which for a time threatened to end his career.

Maddison had not started a game for even longer, with his own recovery from cruciate knee damage complicated by a setback, a hip niggle in the summer and then a shoulder injury after coming on as a sub in the first game of the season at Brentford.

Roberto De Zerbi threw Maddison back into the team against Coventry, a club where his career began before leaving for Norwich more than a decade ago, and whose fans made the mistake of jeering his early touches.

Maddison repaid the Spurs boss and silenced the those in the away end with a wonderful goal to give his team the lead in the 14th minute and settle a few of the jitters.

James Maddison scored his first Premier League goal in 610 days to give Tottenham lift-off

Dejan Kulusevski made his first outing since May 2025 and received a rapturous reception

Roberto De Zerbi's side finally have a win - and the rocking Tottenham faithful loved it

It swerved from his right boot just outside the penalty box and traced through an elegant arc into the top corner of the net, his first Premier League goal for 610 days.

By the time he left the pitch exhausted to a standing ovation in the 69th minute, his team were 2-1 up.

Jack Rudoni had equalised for Coventry before Omar Marmoush scored his first since arriving from Manchester City to restore the lead and Ben Davies added a third in the sixth minute of stoppage time.

Coventry goalkeeper Carl Rushworth should have saved the effort from Davies but the home fans did not care, Finally, they could celebrate their first victory of the Premier League win of the season and with it climb off the foot of the table.

It was a positive return from a training break last week on the Costa del Sol even if Spurs were far from emphatic.

They were untidy at times in possession and vulnerable at the back. There are injury problems piling up. Tosin Adarabioyo, Andy Robertson and Marmoush all limped off in a nervous closing spell.

On top of injuries to Pedro Porro, Savio, Lucas Bergvall, Mykhailo Mudryk and Destiny Udogie, the casualty list is lengthening once again.

Nor will this performance cause sleepless nights across London at Chelsea, the opponents for Spurs on Saturday and yet this was a night De Zerbi desperately needed.

First for the win to release the pressure and instil belief that they can win at home, and then to have Maddison making them tick, always looking to move the ball at a slick tempo and Kulusevski back in the picture.

Ben Davies netted late on to make it a comfortable finish for Spurs, who climb to 16th

De Zerbi deployed a lopsided tactical shape with three centre halves, and Jan Paul van Hecke on the right of the trio sliding across to play at times as a right back.
