MATCH FACTS AND PLAYER RATINGS TOTTENHAM (3-1-4-2): Kinsky 6; Adarabioyo 7 (Fernandes 71min, 6), Van Hecke 6, Van de Ven 6; Tonali 6; Kudus 7 (Tel 87), Gray 6, MADDISON 8 (Gallagher 69, 6), Robertson 6 (Davies 69, 6); Solanke 6, Marmoush 7 (Kulusevski 87) Scorers: Maddison 14, Marmoush 58, Davies 90+6. Booked: Solanke. Manager: Roberto De Zerbi 7 COVENTRY CITY (4-2-3-1): Rushworth 5; Van Ewijk 6, Thomas 6, Pinnock 6, Dasilva 6; Yirenkyi 7 (Onyeka 60, 6), Grimes 6; Sakamoto 6 (Hamer 78), Rudoni 7 (Kesler-Hayden 87), Thomas-Asante 6 (Mason-Clark 78); Cherif 6 (Awoniyi 60, 5) Scorer: Rudoni 49. Booked: Dasilva, Yirenkyi, Rudoni Manager: Frank Lampard 6 Referee: Andy Madley 6 Attendance: 60,913

Toni Kinsky saved at the feet of Rudoni inside 15 seconds. Van Hecke deflected a shot from Tatsuhiro Sakamoto and Bobby Thomas went close with a header from the corner. All of this within the first 15 minutes.

Mohamed Kudus proved difficult to pick up in the first half in his role as a wing back seemingly devoid of defensive duties and was involved in Maddison's opener, carrying the ball forward after Tosin won it in the air and Archie Gray moved it wide.

The goal though was all about Maddison's exquisite finish, swept first time beyond the dive of Rushworth who is struggling with quality of long-range shooting in the Premier League.

Brighton's Lewis Dunk and Newcastle's Sven Botman have both crashed screamers past him and there was more pain from distance for him in the second half.

Spurs dominated possession, although Maddison's goal was their only shot on target in the first half and they wobbled against a Coventry team quick on the turnover and threatening from set pieces. Tosin's presence helped Spurs to cope with their aerial strength.

The Van de Ven afterburners were required towards the end of the first half when Brandon Thomas-Asante darted clear of Van Hecke. Van de Ven was alert to the danger and quick on the cover with a sliding tackle.

Frank Lampard's Coventry have lost their two-match winning streak but remain above the relegation zone

DE ZERBI HAILS SPAIN TRAINING BREAK AND SUMMIT FOR CHANGING THE MOOD AT SPURS Roberto De Zerbi hailed the impact of a training break in Spain and a summit meeting with his players for transforming the mood inside the Tottenham dressing room. Spurs claimed their first win of the Premier League season at the seventh attempt, beating Coventry 3-1 after returning from a trip to Marbella. But De Zerbi detected a change of attitude among his players before the previous game, the fight back to draw with 10 men at Manchester United. The Spurs boss said: 'The day before Old Trafford, we had a big meeting, and we spoke about the situation and said we can't move on if we don't accept responsibility. 'Then we spent time together and want to be not a family but like a family, because during the game if you have a problem and there is a tough situation you have to play for your friend and your brother, not like robots on the pitch. 'Life is like this. If we don't react together in tough moments we have to change and play golf or another sport.' James Maddison scored the opener on his first start for almost 18 months and Dejan Kulusevski came on as a late substitute for his first appearance in just as long. 'With them in the dressing room there is another atmosphere,' said De Zerbi, who eased fears about Tosin Adarabioyo, Andy Robertson and Omar Marmoush, who all limped off before the end. 'Not injuries, nothing important.' Coventry boss Frank Lampard disputed the second Spurs goal because goalscorer Marmoush caught Milan van Ewijk in the face with an arm as he rolled clear but chose his words carefully. 'I did think that,' said Lampard. 'If you roll and elbows are that high and he connects with Milan I thought VAR would cancel it, I did. 'Have to be careful, there's no point after the event to get too deep into it.' By Matt Barlow

Coventry started the season with four defeats but kicked into life with a win at Nottingham Forest before thumping four past Newcastle on their previous outing.

They travelled to London with the look of a team who knew the plan and were level early in the second half.

Van Hecke lost the ball dribbling out into midfield and was punished by Rudoni who linked up well with Caleb Yirenkyi and then forced a shot past Kinsky when his initial cross rebounded his way.

Spurs have seldom responded well to setbacks in recent months, especially not at home in the Premier League and the fact they did will encourage De Zerbi. They went forward with purpose after the equaliser.

Sandro Tonali fizzed shots over and wide before Marmoush struck. Coventry disputed the goal. They thought there was a foul by the Spurs goalscorer as he rolled out of a challenge and threw out an elbow and catching Milan van Ewijk flush in the face, but the goal would stand.

Then on came Kulusevski to a rapturous ovation. And in went the third. Spurs have lift off.

Sports.title: 'Reckless on a catastrophic level': Medical expert's damning verdict on the Eagles' decision to play Jalen Hurts with a blood clot that could have killed him… now their NFL reputation and his career lie in tatters as 'fall guy' hunt begins
Sports.content:
'Reckless on a catastrophic level': Medical expert's damning verdict on the Eagles' decision to play Jalen Hurts with a blood clot that could have killed him… now their NFL reputation and his career lie in tatters as 'fall guy' hunt begins

Jalen Hurts was at risk of dying in the days before multiple blood clots were found in his lungs, an expert claims, as the Philadelphia Eagles face growing questions over their handling of the star quarterback's health.

Hurts is set to miss the rest of the NFL season after doctors made the terrifying discovery on Wednesday - three days after he played against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London before flying home to Philadelphia and 10 days after a cleat to the calf against the Los Angeles Rams that sparked the problem.

An ultrasound initially found a blood clot after the team arrived in London to face the Jaguars, with Hurts placed on the injury report with a calf injury on Friday. According to reports, Hurts barely slept the night before the game after being evaluated in a London hospital. But the quarterback was nevertheless allowed to take the field.

Now, sports medicine specialist Dr. Jesse Morse - who has not personally treated Hurts - has told the Daily Mail that the 'fact they let him play in the game is the craziest decision that I can fathom,' as he outlined the terrifying risks he faced then and in the days that followed.

The Daily Mail has contacted Hurts' representatives and the Philadelphia Eagles for comment.

Morse claimed that even Hurts' tiredness put him in danger, noting that lack of sleep 'significantly reduces reaction time', and in an NFL game 'you're at very high risk for suffering concussion or possible injury if your reaction times are slow.'

Jalen Hurts is set to miss the rest of the NFL season due to multiple blood clots in his lungs

The Eagles have faced questions over the handling of Hurts' situation after his diagnosis

ESPN initially reported that Hurts was up all night before the Jaguars game, due to the risk that the clot could move. But the quarterback's agent, Nicole Lynn, has since claimed that he was able to sleep after rejoining the team. Lynn said the Eagles set aside a room for him at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

After returning to the United States following Philadelphia's loss to the Jaguars, Hurts said he had faced a 'very unique' situation when he practiced. It was not until Wednesday, October 14 that the Eagles said a follow-up ultrasound revealed the clot had moved. The Eagles have not responded to comment to confirm whether or not he had any more ultrasounds between the Jaguars game and that finding.

The fact he played the game in London indicates he had not started taking blood thinning medication before the game, as that would have prevented him from being able to take to the field due to extremely high risks from being hit.

Morse said: 'Rather than being smart and putting him on the blood thinner to prevent that blood clot from moving, they decided to say, you know what, we're just going to let him play.

'The crazy part, after that, is them saying, you know what? He just played a stressful game, which is very stressful in the body and increases the risk for further clotting, but not only that, could have caused it to move. Then they decided to send him back internationally from London to Philly.

'So he was at risk of having a blood clot, going through his lungs, his brain or his heart and potentially killing him, from the date of that diagnosis. So probably from last Friday, through the game, through the international flight, and then each of the days afterwards until he was put on a blood thinner.'

Morse believes allowing Hurts to play in the game and subsequent details of his treatment could amount to a 'fireable offense' and told the Daily Mail: 'There has to be a fall guy, probably, multiple fall guys. But this is reckless on a catastrophic level.

'Whether this is the coach, the GM, the doctor, the medical team... somebody, several people have to be the fall guy, because this isn't just a random, one off, small player, that like, "we could just sit him, it's not a big deal."

'This is the quarterback of the team. This is the leader. So everybody is in the know about what's going on with this situation. This is not, you know, we're going to keep this hush hush.

'Everyone was in on this decision, but this is on the medical staff to say, "hey, I am not medically clearing you to play in that game. I don't care if you want to play in that game. I know you're going to want to play."

'Players want to play. But it is my medical judgment that is not worth the risk. For you to play in that game and potentially this blood clot from the blood vessel, go into your lungs, cause a saddle embolus and die.'

Hurts threw for over 200 yards against the Jaguars in London in a narrow 19-17 loss

Hurts later told reporters he had faced a 'very unique' situation before the Jaguars game

Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni insisted Monday he has 'full trust and full faith' in the team's medical staff and added: 'We always put our players health first and foremost in every situation.'

Attention is now turning to whether Hurts will be able to return at all, with concerns the situation could end his career. He will need to be cleared after months on blood thinners, which Morse says is far from guaranteed now he faces increased risk of blood clots after a 'unique' sequence of events.

'It could be (career-ending),' Morse said. 'At the minimum, this is three months. And we've had several players suffer blood costs and come back. But to my knowledge, and I studied this stuff really well, I don't think we've ever had an NFL player get confirmed multiple blood clots in his lungs. Which means this is not the first time, and this was not only one.

'The only way you could potentially prevent a new blood clot from forming is to be on a blood thinner. You cannot be on a blood thinner and a play contact sport. You will bleed out and you can't stop the hose when the faucet is turned on, which is what a blood thinner does. You can't turn it off until like 34 days later. So it's not worth the risk.

'Unless they decide to make this a unique exception to the rule, this could be career ending. At the minimum it is season ending, but this is a very unique situation.

'Just the fact that this was a trauma-induced clot. That was probably worsened by the international flight each way. Diagnosed, acknowledged that it existed, recommended not to sleep, because if he slept, the immobility could potentially cause the blood clot to move into his lungs, yet you allowed him to play in an NFL game? And then flew him back on a flight for 6 to 7 hours? I don't know how they could medically clear him, safely.'

Morse also points to increased risk, albeit a rare one, of suffering blood clots after getting a COVID-19 vaccine. In 2021, it was found that around 4 in one million people who got the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine later got a blood clot syndrome. The vaccine is no longer available in the United States and medical experts say the benefits of getting a COVID-19 vaccine generally outweigh the risks.

Hurts is set to remain with the team while he is ruled out of football due to his health condition

Hurts initially suffered the injury when he took a cleat to the calf against the Los Angeles Rams

'They're calling this provoked versus unprovoked, is usually the term we use. So this would be a provoked blood clot, meaning it was a trauma which led to it.

'The trauma that caused it could potentially cause a new one. So if this was an unprovoked blood clot, meaning he just developed blood cloth out of the blue, he wasn't doing anything, he didn't get hit, then that is permanent career-ending. No questions.

'That's what happened to Chris Bosh for the for the Miami Heat. But at the same time, knowing the sport that he plays, how can you justify the risk?'

Sports.title: Crystal Palace's nightmare start to the season unpacked: The blunders that could cost Pierre Sage his job, how Steve Parish and Matt Hobbs sold him short in the transfer market - and why players feel worried and confused
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage is understandably under intense scrutiny after Crystal Palace's shambolic 5-0 thrashing by rivals Brighton.

But that must not distract from the inexcusable failures of Sage's bosses, chairman Steve Parish and sporting director Matt Hobbs, who have failed to create the conditions for him to succeed over multiple transfer windows.

It does not absolve the Frenchman of blame. He is not helping himself with how he is setting his side up defensively. But it does provide important context to the conditions he is working under.

Palace have conceded the most goals in the Premier League, 17 in seven matches. And it is not as though they have been unlucky: they have faced the most shots and shots on target of any team, conceded a league-high 252 touches in their penalty area and have the highest expected goals (xG) against. They have been inviting teams to score – and repeatedly failing to do things as basic as winning headers and clearing their lines at corners.

Ultimately, that comes down to the manager and his tactics. Sage's emphasis on an intense press is leaving an already vulnerable Palace defence exposed. In his 3-4-3 formation, both wing-backs push into extraordinarily advanced positions and desert the back three. Under Oliver Glasner last season, one wing-back would hold a deeper position when Palace attacked, ensuring four defenders were in place to cover and react to transitions.

But now, the set-up is unbalanced – allowing teams to pick Palace apart quickly and attack their fragile backline. The midfield is not helping either, with Adam Wharton increasingly isolated as Quinten Timber marauds forward. There is too much focus on being front-footed and not enough caution with the personnel Sage has to choose from.

Pierre Sage is under serious pressure at Crystal Palace after a disappointing start to the Frenchman's tenure

Palace have looked shambolic at the back, especially in their 5-0 thrashing by Brighton (pictured)

Palace have frequently tried to play out in tight areas with the back three and Wharton while the rest of the team push forward, leaving them just one sloppy pass – of which there have been plenty – away from disaster.

Palace have taken seven points from seven games this season, matching Manchester United, and have won twice. In that respect, they are not yet in crisis. But both of their victories were fortuitous. Against Nottingham Forest, they should have been 5-0 down inside the first 40 minutes and rode their luck before punishing the visitors' profligacy.

Similar could be said about their victory at Fulham, where the hosts scored twice despite having 3.14 xG and Palace overperformed theirs with freakish goals. Their defensive performances have been consistently unconvincing, to say the least.

Sources at the club have echoed that view, too. Some in the dressing room are concerned about the lack of control in games and have been left confused by Sage’s ideas. Questions have also been raised about whether Palace have done enough defensive work on the training pitch and been given enough instructions. Sage remains well-liked on a personal level, however.

Again, there is mitigation: Sage, who impressed in taking Lens to a historic second-place finish in Ligue 1 with a similar system last season, has been unable to field a consistent back three due to injuries and Axel Disasi’s suspension.

Perhaps he does not have the personnel to play how he wants at Palace, especially with a back three that lacks recovery pace to deal with counter attacks. But even if that is true, the onus is on the manager to be pragmatic and adapt. Aside from an anomaly at Leeds, where Palace kept a clean sheet and were solid defensively, there has been no sign of that.

Sage was fighting to save his job against Leeds, with Parish considering sacking him over Palace’s defensive vulnerability. Daily Mail Sport understands Parish and Sage met on the week of the game, and the Palace chairman urged his manager to concentrate on defending.

Sage's job is once again at risk and if Palace fail to improve against Besiktas on Thursday night, Parish may be forced to act. However, Sage’s saving grace could be the quick succession of fixtures, which would leave limited time to find a replacement.

Palace chairman Steve Parish (centre) must take some of the blame after appearing complacent about the club leaving their business late in the transfer window

Sporting director Matt Hobbs has also failed to give Sage the conditions to succeed

HOW SAGE WAS SET UP TO FAIL

Sage has created plenty of problems for himself and his relative inexperience has done little to help him navigate adversity.

However, the root of the problem lies with errors made by the club’s hierarchy. Sage’s predecessor, Glasner, was brave enough to call out their deficencies in several scathing press conferences. His public criticism raised eyebrows but it was never misplaced.

Glasner grew tired of inadequate transfer business and repeatedly scolded Parish for it. Sage does not seem the type to air his dirty laundry in public, although he surely holds a similar opinion behind closed doors.

Palace are paying the price for a lack of urgency in the summer window. Glasner criticised the club for two things: late transfer business and a failure to build a deep enough squad. In fairness, they addressed the latter ahead of their second European campaign, with options in each position. But the late panic buys continued, most damningly at centre back – the position where Palace most urgently needed to strengthen.

Two centre backs arrived after the season started, despite Palace selling England international Marc Guehi in January without a replacement and losing France international Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea during the World Cup.

Not only did those signings arrive too late, leaving Sage limited time to implement his ideas amid a hectic schedule, but both represented a significant downgrade. Palace received £72million for Guehi and Lacroix but replaced them with an 18-year-old loanee in Honest Ahanor and Chelsea cast-off Axel Disasi.

Disasi, to his credit, significantly improved West Ham’s defence in the second half of last season, albeit as a wide centre back. At Palace, he has been forced into the middle simply because they lack a natural option for the role. It is, quite frankly, poor squad planning.

Ahanor is an exciting prospect but remains a work in progress. With Palace also developing their own young centre back, Jaydee Canvot, their back three lacks the experience and proven quality required at this level, as the thumping at Brighton demonstrated.

Lacroix and Guehi lifted those around them, whether Canvot, Chris Richards or both. Palace no longer have that commanding, standards-raising figure and look feeble as a result. In fact, Takehiro Tomiyasu, signed as an understudy on a comparable wage to Nathaniel Clyne, who left the club in the summer, has been Palace’s best performer in the back three when available this season. He is now sidelined with injury.

Palace have lost two high-quality international centre backs this year, and replaced them with an 18-year-old loanee in Honest Ahanor (pictured) and a Chelsea cast-off in Axel Disasi

Youngster Jaydee Canvot (left) is among the defenders suffering from a lack of experience around him and Sage's bold set-up

Parish was naive when reviewing the club’s transfer business in an interview with The Athletic last month. Five of Palace’s summer signings arrived after the season began, four of them on deadline day, denying Sage vital time on the training ground in an already curtailed pre-season because of the World Cup.

Parish claimed the fact business was done late becomes irrelevant as the season progresses, but that disregards the difficult position it places the manager in to begin with. Particularly heading into a campaign in which Palace will be playing every three days for much of the season.

Parish said: ‘The important thing is that you get to the end of the transfer window and you say: “Have we done good business for the club?” We needed to make a bit of money on transfers, we needed to strengthen the squad in a different way with loans so that we had the squad depth but we weren’t necessarily carrying that cost going forward. In three months’ time, nobody cares if you did it early.’

The reality is Palace were hamstrung this summer because they overspent in January, splashing £83m on Brennan Johnson – a Glasner request – and Jorgen Strand Larsen. And those January signings were only necessary because Palace had failed to build a deep enough squad in the previous summer window. Consistently poor planning – it has consequences.

Hobbs and Parish took the importance of recruiting genuine quality at centre back far too lightly and are now paying the price. At some point, Sage will likely be the fall guy. But at least one of the Palace chiefs should take responsibility for their errors.

Sports.title: Graeme Souness labels Bukayo Saka a CHEAT: Liverpool legend claims Arsenal star 'dives all over the place' - leaving Piers Morgan in shock
Sports.content:
Graeme Souness labels Bukayo Saka a CHEAT: Liverpool legend claims Arsenal star 'dives all over the place' - leaving Piers Morgan in shock

Graeme Souness has accused Bukayo Saka of being a 'cheat' who 'dives all over the place'.

And the Liverpool legend believes Arsenal have a strategy of ganging up on referees to convince them that a 'screaming' Saka has been fouled.

It is an accusation commonly levelled at the England man, 25, who is often among the most-fouled players in a given Premier League season.

Fans may remember the controversy that erupted in the Champions League quarter-finals in 2024 when he tried to buy a last-minute penalty against Manuel Neuer in a tie which Arsenal eventually lost.

And Souness dug into the winger on Piers Morgan's Football Uncensored show, leaving his host outraged.

'Your man Saka dives all over the place. I don't want to hear about him. The minute he looks like losing possession, he's down,' he said.

Graeme Souness has accused Bukayo Saka of being a 'cheat' who 'dives all over the place'

Fans may remember his 'dive' against Bayern Munich in the Champions League in 2024

Souness says that Saka 'screams' when he goes down and that Arsenal's players work to convince the referee

'He simulates a foul. Anyone who simulates a foul in my book would be a cheat.

'He dives when he should be staying on his feet. He's not alone. So Saka gets tackled, he screams as he's going down.

'The referee thinks there's nothing in that but wait a minute, he's stayed down. And then worse than that, everyone in the immediate area - all Arsenal players - put their hands up and scream foul.

'The referee at that point panics and blows his whistle when it wasn't a foul - his first instinct was the right one.

'But he blows a foul because he's thinking, wait a minute, something I'm not understanding here.

'Simulation is a form of cheating, yes. But it's all over football today.

'If you asked 100 people what is it you dislike about the modern game, 50 per cent would say simulation, another 50 per cent would say VAR.'

With the game moving at such speed, it is difficult to always know exactly how hard a player has felt contact, or how a tiny amount of contact may genuinely throw them off.

Piers Morgan was unhappy with Souness' suggestion, saying: 'I wouldn't call him a cheat

Saka's notoriety for diving has lasted for years, but he is far from the only player to have that criticism levelled at him.

The incident with Bayern in 2024 attracted a lot of attention and debate. It initially looked as if the goalkeeper had brought him down, and the winger had got to the ball first.

However, replays showed Saka moving his leg in Neuer's direction to collide with him to try and buy a penalty - a move which backfired.

Some pundits came down on him with disapproval, with Paola Di Canio telling Sky Sports Italia: 'He moves blatantly the leg towards Neuer, it’s never a penalty.

'He didn’t behave as an experienced player. He behaved like a baby with no experience.'

But Rio Ferdinand took Saka's side, saying: 'I can’t believe that’s not been given! That is a penalty, I’m in disbelief.'

Sports.title: Zlatan Ibrahimovic's acrobatic brilliance against England, Jamie Vardy's volley and a belter at Blackpool... after Diego Gomez's halfway-line stunner for Brighton, our experts pick their favourite goal
Sports.content:
Zlatan Ibrahimovic's acrobatic brilliance against England, Jamie Vardy's volley and a belter at Blackpool... after Diego Gomez's halfway-line stunner for Brighton, our experts pick their favourite goal

Diego Gomez's incredible strike from the halfway line was the highlight of Brighton's 5-0 demolition of Crystal Palace on Sunday - and a contender for goal of the season.

On the back of that, we asked our experts for their favourite goal they have ever witnessed live...

MATT BARLOW: Zlatan Ibrahimovic (Sweden 4-2 England, 2012)

Zlatan's overhead kick from about 35 yards for Sweden against England. Simply the most Zlatan moment you could imagine. The opening of a new stadium in Stockholm came with a general feeling of underappreciation in the media for Zlatan's enduring qualities. Me included to be honest.

He had rarely turned it on against English opposition in the Champions League, but this was the night he scored four in a 4-2 win as the England choir serenaded him with a song comparing him unfavourably to Andy Carroll.

His fourth was an outrageous acrobatic finish not only from distance but also off centre, wide on the right with Joe Hart marooned out of his goal. Off came the shirt.

Asked by a gaggle of English reporters to rate his own career out of 10 after the game, Zlatan thought carefully for a moment or two and said, "10". Nobody argued. Still makes me smile.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic's amazing strike towards the end of the match sealed Sweden's 4-2 win

JACK GAUGHAN: Phil Clarkson (Blackpool 2-1 Northampton, 1998)

A header has popped up in the direction of Clarkson. Six yards out, back to goal and with a defender touch tight. A goal down, Blackpool’s No 8 takes the knock down with the instep of his right foot, passing over to his left and then uses his left to impishly volley a backheel with proper force into the corner.

Remarkably he watches the ball all the way and follows it into the net, pirouetting and almost breaking into an Eric Cantona celebration.

It’s Division Two (League One these days) - a moment of genius so far removed from its surroundings that it sticks in your mind for decades to come. Sat on a wall level with that penalty area, there was a seven-year-old going crazy who’d had a perfect view of the magic unfolding.

Hopefully in his second career, Clarkson delivers the post to the people of the Fylde Coast with the same panache.

JAMES SHARPE: Jamie Vardy (West Brom 1-4 Leicester, 2018)

As someone who has watched - and cheered - many a Jamie Vardy goal for Leicester over the years, you might think my pick of the bunch would be his glorious 30-yard volley against Liverpool in the title-winning season. Or the one to break Ruud van Nistelrooy’s record by scoring in 11 consecutive games. Or…never mind.

Belters, of course, but not the best nor my favourite. That one is saved for his ridiculous over-the-shoulder volley against West Brom in 2018, a strike that would be crowned Carling goal of the month and Leicester’s goal of the season.

Riyad Mahrez’s floating ball over the top, dropping over Vardy’s shoulder as he runs in behind and never breaks stride as he hooks it first-time - with his weaker left foot - straight into the bottom corner. I make a noise every time I watch it back. He makes it look ridiculously easy.

All from a man who Michael Owen once described as ‘not a natural finisher’.

Jamie Vardy's volley levelled the game against West Brom and Leicester went on to win 4-1

IAN HERBERT: Paul Mullin (Wrexham 2-0 Stockport, 2022)

A 90th-minute goal which sent Paul Mullin running onto a ball sent from his own half into the left channel. He’d taken nine strides and was just outside the area when, with a defender approaching, he looked up, saw the goalkeeper moving out and dug out looping a left foot shot over him, into the net.

It was the goal which co-owner Ryan Reynolds always said had switched him on to the beauty of football and, for what it’s worth, the film star’s tweet of it generated 2.1 million views.

For we Wrexham fans, though, it was the most graphic evidence we’d seen that we really did have the talent to end our non-League exile. The club had gambled on paying Mullin big wages. This proved his value.

And another vote from NATHAN SALT...

A goal that I felt I was watching in slow motion when witnessing it in real time. The game had ticked over into stoppage time, Stockport were breaking and an inch-perfect Liam McAlinden tackle stopped them in their tracks.

From there it was poetry in motion as Jordan Davies, a local lad who grew up a stone’s throw from the ground, sent Mullin clear and he chipped the goalkeeper from best part of 30 yards to send us to Wembley.

I lost my voice, picked up a few bruises in the celebrations, and can still picture it as vividly now as I did at the time. Technique, context, euphoria, the goal had it all.

Paul Mullin scored 110 goals for Wrexham in a stellar spell at the club

LEWIS STEELE: Nick Powell (Cheltenham 0-2 Crewe, 2012)

Nick Powell for Crewe Alexandra against Cheltenham in the League Two play-off final, 2012. What do you mean, dear reader, when you say you've never seen it?

The technique is outstanding and, to this day, I think he would have made it at Manchester United had Sir Alex Ferguson not left - the subsequent managers were under pressure so could not give youth players a chance.

Honourable mentions for Alejandro Garnacho for United at Everton and several Rodri goals for Manchester City. I also once saw someone back-heel a ball into their own goal from near the halfway line in Sunday League but I suppose that doesn’t count.

Nick Powell earned a move from Crewe to Manchester United in the summer of 2012 at the age of 18, just a month after his play-off final strike

WILL PICKWORTH: Dean Campbell (Aston Villa 1-2 Stevenage, 2023)

I can still vividly picture every part; David Amoo winning the corner, Jake Reeves taking it quickly, Ollie Watkins' half-hearted attempt to close Dean Campbell down, the ball squirming under Robin Olsen's arms, and the incredible away-end scenes.

As a Stevenage fan, I have never felt emotions quite like those provided by the 90th-minute winner to knock out Unai Emery's Aston Villa in the FA Cup in January 2023.

The fact it was scored by Campbell, an OK but unspectacular loanee with just seven career goals in 247 games only adds to its allure, and ensures that Boro fans will never, ever, forget the Scottish midfielder.

Sports.title: Why HAS football gone soft on diving? It appears that 'simulation' is a plague we have chosen to live with
Sports.content:
Why HAS football gone soft on diving? It appears that 'simulation' is a plague we have chosen to live with

‘It just wasn’t a penalty for me.’ Football fans have become accustomed to hearing managers say this in post-match interviews. They’re just not particularly used to hearing it from the man whose side profited from the decision.

Fair play, then, to Mark Wilson. Partick Thistle’s head coach was charitable enough to concede that the spot kick awarded to his side in Friday’s Scottish Championship match at Ayr United – a decision that ultimately decided the match – should not have been given.

‘I need to be honest because everybody’s bored of managers coming out and going, “Oh well, I didn’t see it”,’ he added. ‘I did see it. I said to the fourth official at the time, “I don’t think that’s a penalty.” And he says, “Well, we’re kind of blocked [in our view] here”.

‘We are, but I think you can kind of tell, can’t you? When you’ve been in the game a long time, you can tell what’s a foul and what’s not a foul.’

The incident in question occurred on the stroke of half-time, Thistle’s Seb Drozd tumbling inside the box – in instalments, it must be noted – under pressure from Ayr’s Liam Dick.

Standing just yards away and with a perfect view of it all, referee Matthew MacDermid had no hesitation in pointing to the spot, much to the incredulity of, well, just about everybody who saw it.

Partick Thistle front man Seb Drozd was captured smirking on the turf after his tumble

Commentating on the match for the BBC, James McFadden said: ‘I’m still struggling to see anything wrong there.’ Former Celtic striker Chris Sutton described it as ‘a contender for BBC 606’s Simulation Game’. The Ref’s View podcast, hosted by former officials, called it a ‘horrific decision’, adding: ‘Matthew MacDermid has been conned there.’

Ayr boss Gary Naysmith was understandably seething, not least because his side had been on the receiving end of a similar injustice against Dunfermline Athletic a week earlier.

‘I’ve now seen it back more than once and I think it’s another really poor decision that has gone against us,’ said the former Scotland international. ‘I think it’s a dive and I think the one last week was a dive.’

In a league where fine margins are routinely the difference between challenging for promotion and avoiding relegation, these two decisions – and the subsequent goals scored – could yet prove to be season-defining for Ayr, and potentially even affect the future of Naysmith, his staff and some of their players.

Referee Matthew MacDermid didn't cover himself in glory with the preposterous penalty call

And whilst referee MacDermid has rightly fielded considerable criticism for his part in it all – this is far from the whistler’s first controversy – the incident raises a further, more important question.

When did football get so soft on diving?

Where, for example, is the contempt for Drozd, who lay smirking on the Somerset Park turf after the penalty was awarded? His reckoning may – and should – yet come in the form of retrospective sanctions. If Thistle boss Wilson wanted to polish his own halo, he could even punish Drozd himself. A week’s wages would surely remind his squad of the standards required.

But Drozd’s tumble is merely a symptom of a bigger, enduring problem.

Once upon a time, to dive was to imperil your reputation. Fans, players, pundits – they didn’t so much take a dim view of the behaviour as regard it with unambiguous disgust. Those caught in the act were forever tainted; not quite pariahs but besmirched, for sure.

Thistle boss Mark Wilson was honest in the aftermath but should look to fine his errant player

Sometime between then and now, however, diving has become a plague that we have apparently chosen to live with, to tolerate instead of eradicate, and nobody knows exactly when or why.

Maybe it was around the time Jurgen Klinsmann laundered his reputation for such antics with a supposedly self-deprecating celebratory dive after scoring his first goal for Tottenham Hotspur in 1994, a stunt that immediately endeared the German striker to fickle fans. ‘He might be prone to cheating but at least he’s got a sense of humour,’ they cooed.

Maybe it was when the first referee dispensed with IFAB protocol and elected not to book a player for trying to con them. Maybe it was when ‘simulation’ – the acceptable face of diving, its sanitised, much cuddlier identity – transcended the rulebook and became part of the sport’s uber-trendy modern lexicon, gleefully tossed around by podcasters and pontificators galore.

Regardless, diving is cheating. It’s deliberate, disrespectful and dishonest. Unlike other forms of sporting chicanery, it should also be relatively straightforward to police.

Intent, for example, is often easier to discern. For what reason, other than an attempt to deceive, would players throw themselves to the ground, arms flailing and faces contorting as though they’d stared directly into the Ark of the Covenant? By dint of their inherently laughable theatricality, the most blatant dives are easy to distinguish from a stumble or a trip, particularly for properly trained officials.

Jurgen Klinsmann made diving fashionable by making it his signature celebration in his heyday

And yet it feels like it’s not regarded as the offence it once was. Where referees once flashed yellow cards, they now mostly motion to the players responsible to ‘get up’; a tsk-tsk in lieu of a caution.

By the midway point of last season, and despite a ‘crackdown’ by PGMOL, the body responsible for professional match officials that now goes by Pro Ref, there had been only 16 bookings for simulation in the English Premier League.

Call me cynical, but the implication that just 16 dives warranted punishment across 190 matches – 285 whole hours of football – feels far-fetched. Still, at least it was an improvement on the equivalent period the previous season, by which point only seven dives had been punished with a caution.

At a time when football appears hell-bent on tackling other forms of cheating – hello, Manchester City – it would do well to tackle all forms of it. They don’t all require litigation and thousand-dollar-an-hour lawyers. A consistent application of the game’s very own rules will suffice.

Sports.title: Brentford report fan to police after rugby ball is kicked onto the pitch from high-rise flat during Liverpool defeat
Sports.content:
Brentford report fan to police after rugby ball is kicked onto the pitch from high-rise flat during Liverpool defeat

Brentford have reported a fan to the police after he kicked a rugby ball from a rooftop into their stadium during their 2-1 defeat by Liverpool on Saturday.

The club highlighted the 'dangerous and potentially harmful' behaviour after footage of the misdemeanour went viral on social media.

Brentford's Gtech Community Stadium is bordered by a jungle of high-rise apartment blocks and while nobody appeared to get injured, the ball did land near the field of play and had to be confiscated by a member of staff.

The ball is believed to have been kicked from the luxury Memento Kew Bridge apartment complex, where flats can cost as much as £37,860 per year to rent.

Each of the 487 apartments has its own private balcony and many offer VIP views of the state-of-the-art stadium.

A club statement read: 'Brentford are aware of an incident involving an item being kicked from a height towards the field of play during Saturday’s match against Liverpool.

Police are investigating after a male booted a rugby ball into Brentford's stadium during their match with Liverpool

The falling ball was 'dangerous and potentially harmful' according to a club statement

View this post on Instagram

'Such behaviour is dangerous and potentially very harmful.

'The matter has been referred to the police and the club are supporting the relevant authorities in their investigation to help identify those responsible and take appropriate action, which may result in criminal prosecution.

'The matchday safety of fans, staff, players and officials is of utmost importance, and the club will support all efforts to ensure action is taken.'

Rugby union club London Irish did play at the stadium between 2020 and 2023 before their suspension from the Premiership due to financial trouble, but this latest intervention at the weekend was rather unexpected.

Brentford were leapfrogged by Liverpool on Saturday as the visitors completed a comeback victory.

The hosts were 1-0 up against Liverpool after Keane Lewis-Potter's header but Yehor Yarmolyuk's red card for a headbutt on Jeremy Jacquet on the stroke of half-time changed the game.

Liverpool got level thanks to in-form winger Victor Munoz before Alexander Isak scored his fifth goal of the season on his return from injury.

Brentford sit sixth in the Premier League and are pushing for Europe after a strong first season under manager Keith Andrews which saw them finish ninth.

Noemi Oberhauser lives in a flat overlooking Brentford's Gtech Community Stadium - and claims men have tried to date her to get a view of the game!

The lucky tenant - who is a singer from London - often shares TikTok videos showing off her view of the games

It is an ambitious era for them under owner Matthew Benham and they have a tidy £71million, 17,250-capacity stadium in west London which opened in 2020.

The flats around them have been in the news before - in 2024, singer Noemi Oberhauser revealed how men were asking her on dates simply so they could visit her address and watch the football from the window.

'I have quite a few people messaging me on Instagram about the apartment,' Oberhauser told What's The Jam.

'Mostly offering to come to watch the match with me and turning it into a little date.

'A lot also comment saying things like "Marry me". So, it is quite funny.'

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
