Some Moroccans are already asking what was the point of holding elections if the same people are brought back to govern.

Challenges ahead

The new government has an ambitious programme to respond to growing domestic pressure as the cost-of-living crisis deepens. At the first Council of Ministers meeting chaired by the king on October 17 , a 2027 Finance Bill was put forward that featured greater emphasis on addressing social issues, citizens’ purchasing power and youth inclusion.

However, this agenda is facing an unfavourable international economic and financial environment, marked by rising energy prices and increasing costs of inputs for some of Morocco’s leading sectors, including phosphate production.

The state-owned OCP Group, which is in charge of phosphate extraction and the industrial processing of phosphate derivatives and is one of Morocco’s principal sources of wealth, is now experiencing difficult times.

There are also concerns about the potential effects of El Nino, which could bring more dry weather and threaten food security in a country that just endured seven consecutive years of drought.



Tourism, another major source of revenue, could also suffer from the global slowdown in travel, rising transport costs and the uncertainties arising from tensions in the Gulf and Europe.

The circumstances are therefore far from favourable for the new government, and public opinion appears broadly sceptical.

Last but not least, this government will face an experienced and outspoken opposition, represented by both the Islamist PJD and the radical left.

Even the ministers holding the so-called sovereign portfolios face serious challenges. The foreign minister must contend with public opposition to the normalisation of relations with Israel. The interior minister has to tackle allegations of electoral manipulation.

The minister of religious affairs is facing the fallout of controversial statements concerning Morocco as a secular country and remarks about Ceuta, known in Morocco as Sebta, made during a religious ceremony. These comments were poorly received by the Spanish authorities.

The new government has an ambitious agenda, indeed, but its tenure will be shaped by difficult circumstances – both at home and abroad – that are largely out of its control.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Alberta voters reject separation from Canada, early results show
World.content:
With more than one million votes counted, about 76 percent supported remaining in Canada.

Alberta residents have voted to remain ⁠part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he ‌attempts to unify the country amid an ongoing trade war with the United States.

With more than one million votes counted, about 77 percent supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23 percent who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation, early results showed on Tuesday.

The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path towards a future vote on separation from Canada.

Carney welcomed the result and said Albertans had made a “clear choice” in favor of unity.

“They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,” he said in a statement on X.

Jeffrey Rath, a top leader of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters his push for an independent Alberta will “absolutely” continue, despite the result from Monday’s vote.

“We’ve learned a lot of lessons from this fight,” he said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative, said she voted against independence but called the referendum to settle an issue that has divided the province.

She has said a win for the federalists would close the secession question.

Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the separatist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management.

Smith has blamed Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the separatist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.



Alberta’s independence push has also drawn sustained interest from Trump allies, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who called Alberta a “natural partner” for the US. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and key Trump supporter, also posted on X that Alberta “should separate.”

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office last year. He has partnered with Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a nonstarter during Trudeau’s tenure.

World.title: US-Ukraine relations sour as Trump, Zelenskyy clash over talks, arms
World.content:
Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as negotiator, while Ukraine’s president says arms shipments delayed.

United States President Donald Trump says someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf in talks to end Russia’s war.

“Zelenskyy is a man that should have had settled this war a long time ago. If he would’ve listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Monday. “Maybe it’s time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate.”

The US president has been verbally swiping at his Ukrainian counterpart for several days as a rift between the leaders deepens.

On Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that Zelenskyy does not want to end the war. Earlier this month, he called for him to be replaced as president, and labelled him a “warmonger” over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Trump has also defended sanctions waivers for Russia, saying in the same Truth Social post that he wants to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

Zelenskyy said the decision “will hurt Ukraine” and strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

Trump also announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.

The decision has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and US officials, who say it rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told US senators at a meeting on Monday that decisions taken by the Trump administration “are hard to explain between friends”.



He said arms shipments had been delayed and intelligence sharing restricted.

“We also know that … the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) programme,” he said.

To his knowledge, he added, one missile package was waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US approval.

In remarks posted in a video on Telegram, Zelenskyy said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of Russian attacks generally provided by its partners.

Last week, Zelenskyy suggested a disruption of Starlink services in Ukraine was “deliberate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected the claim.

The sparring comes as Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is ⁠set to travel to Norway this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, the Reuters news agency reported, citing three people familiar with the matter.

Two of the sources said they expected Zelenskyy to attend the meetings.

The Oslo discussions are expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland – the European Union, and NATO.

World.title: Palestine weekly: Israeli settlers attack journalist and diplomats
World.content:
With more than a month left of the olive harvest season to go, United Nations deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq said on Friday that the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) had recorded more than 200 Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers since September 1, eclipsing the 185 that OCHA documented across the entire 2025 harvest season.

The attacks have already killed one Palestinian, injured more than 120 and damaged more than 2,500 trees. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 34 Israeli attacks on Friday that injured at least 19 people, with another 40 on Saturday.

Israeli settlers are carrying out such widescale attacks and thefts with backing from some religious figures. On Friday, Rabbi Dov Lior, spiritual guide of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, ruled that settlers may take olives from Palestinian orchards, proclaiming “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land and thereby fulfill the commandment of conquering the land”.

“An olive tree today is more significant in the campaign for Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank] than an M16 rifle,” said one post in a settler chat group this week.

“Settlers are stealing the Palestinian olive crop on a vast scale, never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue,” said Sarit Michaeli, formerly the international advocacy director of the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem.



Under this ideological push, dozens of attacks on olive harvesters have been reported each day. On October 16, in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, about 80 masked settlers armed with clubs charged at Palestinians picking olives. During the attack, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, fell and was beaten for more than 10 minutes by settlers, videos and her own account attest. She suffered broken ribs and needed hand surgery, while her camera, phone and passport were stolen. Israeli activist Jonathan Pollak reported that soldiers later shot a village council member, Abdel Jaber Obeid, in the thigh.

Then, on Saturday, masked settlers with clubs attacked a delegation visiting Taybeh, east of Ramallah, that included Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats, and church representatives. A window of a Belgian consulate vehicle was smashed. French mayor Bernard Baudoux, 78, was kicked and beaten during the attack.

In response to these incidents, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was “very disturbed”, while US Ambassador Mike Huckabee called Levine’s attack “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”. France demanded arrests and the European Union said it expected “full accountability”.

In response, Israel’s military called the Taybeh attack “severe”, and leader of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, described settler violence as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the government of Israel”, according to The Times of Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, however, offered a conditional condemnation of Levine’s attack, saying questions remained about “who initiated the violence”. After the attack in Taybeh, his office equivocated on the matter, too, remarking that “the more serious the accusation, the stronger the evidence required”.

On Monday, police and the domestic intelligence agency Shin Bet launched “Operation Olive Leaf”, arresting 10 Israelis in raids near Ofra and Shiloh in connection to these attacks on foreign journalists and diplomats.

Attacks across the West Bank

However, no other arrests or investigations have been announced for the dozens of other settler attacks against Palestinians reported this weekend alone. Beyond the headline incidents, masked settlers – often alongside soldiers – targeted farmers, flocks, homes and land.

Attacks included:

Settlers beat two women in Beit Lid on Tuesday and injured an American citizen, Haytham Tayseer, in Burqa on Thursday, leaving him with deep head wounds.

Six people, including four women and a child, were injured in Ma’in, in Masafer Yatta, on Saturday, the Red Crescent said.

Settlers burned four vehicles in Turmus Aya, including a civil defence vehicle, and set fire to a mosque in Mikhmas, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Settlers stabbed to death about 20 sheep in Kafr Malek, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.

Bulldozers uprooted hundreds of olive trees in Kafr Malek, and settlers cut down 120 olive trees in Kisan, near Bethlehem, Wafa reported.



Gaza: Halted trade deepens hunger fears

In Gaza, the ever-worsening humanitarian situation is now deteriorating even more rapidly. Israel declared on October 14 that no commercial goods would be allowed to enter Gaza, blaming a dispute between merchants and Hamas over a 10,000-shekel ($3,220) per-truck fee. Gaza’s Government Media Office called that a “blatant disinformation campaign”, saying the sum was a voluntary contribution to a fund for widows and orphans. By Sunday, prices had jumped significantly: a carton of eggs rose in price from 35 shekels ($11.30) to 60-70 shekels ($18-$21), and a sack of flour from 25-35 shekels ($7.50-$10.50) to about 80 shekels ($24), residents said.

Such price increases are taking place just as the World Food Programme announced this week it would cut the number of people it feeds monthly in Gaza from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. Gaza’s Health Ministry said 466 people have died of malnutrition since 2024 and 67 percent of the population faces crisis-level food insecurity or worse through year-end.

Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in Gaza each day. As of October 19, Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since last year’s “ceasefire” at 1,522 killed and 5,421 wounded – 27 killed in the past week, against 33 the previous week and 38 the week before. The cumulative death toll has reached 74,480 since October 7, 2023.

Among the Palestinians killed:

Three children, including Muhammad Riyad Abu Hammad, 14, in Deir el-Balah – the Education Ministry said shrapnel pierced his school bag on his way home from school on Saturday – and Misk Hazem al-Dalu and Tamer Shadi Subh, who were killed in the Maghazi camp and Beit Lahiya, respectively, on Sunday. UNICEF said more than 340 children have been killed since the ceasefire.

Drone strikes in the past week killed Ahmad Raja al-Shaer and Basel Nabil Qeshta in al-Qarara; Reem Awad in a strike on a Gaza City apartment; Mahmoud al-Madhoun and Ubaida Murtaja in Gaza City; Abdullah and Imad Jaber and Sheikh Majid al-Sabbagh, a Quran school director in Tuffah, on October 17; Amer al-Horani near a Jabalia clinic the same day; and police officer Abd al-Jawad Joudeh in Rafah.

Shootings killed Saddam al-Za’anin in Jabalia, Hatem Abu Hasanein by quadcopter fire, Huda Abu Adwan, 49, in al-Mawasi and Wijdan Shurrab, 28, in eastern Khan Younis, according to Wafa and local activists.

Israel’s military said several of those killed this week were Hamas members. None of its claims has been independently verified.

Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued advancing the “Yellow Line” deeper into Shujayea on Saturday, placing concrete blocks on al-Qa’qa Street. The line demarcates areas under Israeli control, which now extend across about 65 percent of Gaza, far beyond what was envisaged under last year’s “ceasefire” agreement.

World.title: Egypt’s Hassan and Zico suspended over FIFA World Cup refereeing criticism
World.content:
FIFA punishes Egypt’s head coach, forward and team manager for their comments after their World Cup loss to Argentina.

Egypt’s head coach Hossam Hassan and forward Mostafa Zico have paid the price for criticising the referee after their World Cup knockout loss to Argentina, with FIFA suspending the duo for three and five matches, respectively.

FIFA’s Disciplinary Committee handed down the sanctions, the Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said in a statement on Monday.

Hossam’s twin brother, Ibrahim, who is the national team’s manager, was also given a three-match suspension.

The EFA said it had submitted a request to the committee, seeking “the detailed reasons and justifications for the decisions”. The national football body is planning to appeal after assessing the legal aspects of the punishment.

The suspensions could rule Hossam and Ibrahim Hassan out of Egypt’s upcoming matches against Malawi in the next rounds of Africa Cup of Nations qualifying in November, as well as the first match of the March international window.

Zico will be unavailable until June.

Egypt were knocked out in the round of 16 by Argentina, who came from 2-0 down to win the tense encounter in Atlanta, United States, on July 6.

The Pharaohs were left furious after a number of controversial calls went against them, including a disallowed goal early in the second half, and a member of their coaching staff was red-carded in the aftermath of the winning goal.

Hassan claimed his side was “cheated” out of a place in the quarterfinals after Argentina’s stunning late comeback.

“I do not want to put it nicely and talk about hard luck. We have been cheated unfairly today; we have suffered injustice,” Hassan said in an explosive post-match news conference.



Egypt had a Zico goal ruled out when they were leading 1-0 as the video assistant referee (VAR) intervened to spot a foul on Lisandro Martinez much earlier in the move.

Zico then put Egypt on the brink of a place in the last eight for the first time by doubling their lead.

However, the defending champions hit back as Cristian Romero reduced the arrears before Lionel Messi, who had a first-half penalty saved, smashed in the equaliser with his eighth goal of the tournament.

The controversy did not end there, though, as in the build-up to Argentina’s winner scored by Enzo Fernandez, Egypt believe they should have instead been awarded a penalty for a pull by Alexis Mac Allister on Hamdy Fathy.

“We haven’t seen respect or fair play. There has not been respect or fair play,” Hassan said.

“A penalty was ruled out; it was not even checked by VAR. A second goal was remarkably disallowed. There has not even been a VAR check when we have all seen the image of the [shirt] being pulled back.”

Zico had a goal ruled out for a foul in the build-up, before Egypt’s players appealed for a penalty near the end when the score was 2-2.

However, FIFA refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina defended the officiating in the match, saying such allegations could provoke threats against referees and their families.

World.title: Southeast Asia’s haze crisis will persist until polluters pay
World.content:
Across Southeast Asia, the haze has returned with a familiar cruelty. Malaysia has closed schools as air quality deteriorated, Singapore has experienced dangerous levels of air pollution, and even parts of the Philippines have been affected, underscoring how far the smoke has travelled. In Indonesia, meanwhile, forest and peatland fires, a major source of the region’s haze, have threatened communities and livelihoods, particularly in parts of Kalimantan. What begins as land burning in one country can become a public health emergency across an entire region.

The immediate response is predictable: extinguish fires, distribute masks and seek regional cooperation. All are necessary, but none explains why the emergency keeps returning. Malaysian children missing school, Singaporean residents breathing polluted air, Filipino communities exposed to drifting smoke and Indonesian families living near burning land all bear different costs from the same regional failure.

Dry weather and El Nino can intensify fires, but many are deliberately started to clear land for agriculture. The deeper question is why practices that create enormous public losses can remain attractive to those who benefit from them. When the gains from cheap land preparation are concentrated while the costs of smoke are dispersed across communities and national borders, the market signal is distorted and political responsibility becomes easier to evade.

The haze is therefore not merely an environmental emergency or a test of diplomatic goodwill. It disrupts ordinary life, strains public services and exposes how easily environmental costs can be shifted away from those who create them. It is a failure of economic accountability. Unless Southeast Asia changes who pays for the damage, how land-clearing decisions are monitored and what consequences follow proven violations, each dry season will bring another round of emergency measures followed by familiar arguments over blame.



The economics of cheap land clearing

Fire can be an inexpensive way to clear vegetation, especially where land governance is weak, alternative methods are costly and enforcement is uncertain. The private calculation is straightforward: spend less on land preparation and capture the returns. The fires cause respiratory illness, lost working days, school closures and transport disruption, while also damaging ecosystems and releasing greenhouse gases. Those costs are rarely borne in full by those responsible for the burning.

The World Bank’s assessment of Indonesia’s 2015 fire crisis estimated losses of at least $16.1bn, equivalent to 1.9 percent of that year’s gross domestic product (GDP). Government figures put the area burned between June and October at 2.6 million hectares. The bank linked the fires to cheap land preparation, drought and weak enforcement. Its estimate covered agriculture, trade, tourism, transport, healthcare and emergency response, but excluded some long-term health damage and lost ecosystem services.

That figure is not a price tag for the 2026 fires. It shows the scale of losses a recurrent crisis can impose. More recent estimates put the area burned in Indonesia this year at between 637,000 and 900,000 hectares, while Ministry of Health data recorded 283,270 cases of respiratory illness linked to the fires in seven provinces as of October 13. In West Kalimantan province, fires have also threatened communities and livelihoods, underscoring that Indonesians living beside the flames bear costs long before smoke reaches neighbouring countries.

This is the central economic distortion: the cost of burning is not fully reflected in the decision to burn. When benefits accrue privately, but health costs, lost income and ecological damage are borne by society, fire can remain economically attractive even when its total cost is enormous. Small farmers need affordable, practical alternatives to burning; companies must face credible liability when evidence links them to fires; and peatlands need sustained restoration and water management, not emergency attention only when smoke becomes politically embarrassing.

ASEAN’s accountability gap

Smoke travels across borders, but responsibility and enforcement remain largely national. Tracing pollution to a particular fire, identifying those responsible and proving cross-border harm can be difficult. A satellite hotspot is a warning signal, but not by itself proof of who started a fire or whether a company is liable.



The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is not without rules. Its Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution was signed in 2002 and entered into force in 2003; Indonesia ratified it in 2014. The region also has a Haze-Free Roadmap and a strategy for sustainable peatland management for 2023-30. But agreements cannot substitute consistent implementation, transparent enforcement or incentives that make prevention economically rational.

The challenge is translating these commitments into effective action. Cooperation can improve monitoring and preparedness, but ASEAN’s consensus-based diplomacy has limited leverage when national enforcement is inconsistent or commercial interests resist scrutiny. Its investment framework for haze-free land management aims to mobilise $1.5bn by 2030. Yet money alone will not suffice without transparent spending, measurable outcomes and accountability for repeated fires.

This does not mean every fire is caused by a large corporation or that all pollution in Kuala Lumpur or Singapore originates in Indonesia. Local emissions and weather conditions matter, and fires may involve companies, smallholders or other actors. Accountability requires investigations that identify those responsible and distinguish proven violations from suspicion. Blanket blame lets offenders disappear into arguments about sovereignty, while a lack of transparent evidence erodes trust between neighbours.

Making polluters bear the cost

ASEAN foreign ministers are due to discuss the haze crisis at preparatory meetings before the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Their discussions should be judged by whether they shift the region from managing haze to preventing it.

First, member states should publish comparable data on burned areas, fire recurrence, concessions and enforcement outcomes. Satellite detections should be cross-checked with field investigations, and concession maps should be made available for scrutiny by communities and independent researchers. Greater transparency would make it harder to obscure responsibility through competing claims.

Second, governments should put the polluter-pays principle into practice. Where investigations establish responsibility, penalties and restoration orders should reflect the damage caused, while repeat violations should trigger stronger consequences. Environmental liability must be evidence-based and applied consistently, not used as a political weapon. Penalties must also be substantial enough to deter violations rather than simply become a cost of doing business.

Third, prevention must be economically viable. Smallholders need machinery, technical assistance, credit and access to markets to make alternatives to burning affordable. Peatland rewetting, firebreaks and community-based monitoring require predictable funding before the dry season, rather than ad hoc budgets after fires spread. ASEAN’s investment framework can help mobilise resources, but governments should disclose where funds go and assess their impact on reductions in fires and smoke exposure.



Finally, ASEAN should publish a regional scorecard tied to its 2030 haze-free goal. It should track not only hotspots and hectares burned, but also repeat fires, response times, enforcement, peatland restoration, school closures and population exposure to dangerous air. No regional mechanism can replace Indonesia’s responsibility to prevent fires on its territory. But sovereignty cannot mean that the costs of domestic land-use decisions are ignored once smoke crosses a border. The principle should be simple: those who profit from risky practices must not be allowed to transfer the bill to children missing school, workers losing wages, sick families or neighbouring states.

For more than two decades, ASEAN has had agreements, strategies and roadmaps. The haze’s return does not make these efforts worthless; it shows prevention remains inadequate. If leaders leave November’s meetings with another declaration but no transparent metrics, credible enforcement and funding for alternatives, the region will once again treat the symptoms while preserving the incentives that produce them. Economic accountability is not an add-on to haze policy. It is the condition for making that policy work.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Israel’s elections 2026 explained in maps and charts
World.content:
Israelis vote on October 27 in the sixth election since 2019. Here’s how the system works and who gets left out.

Israelis go to the polls on October 27 to elect the 26th Knesset, in the first general vote since the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza and the wars on Lebanon and Iran.

Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history, with 19 years in office, is seeking another term while standing trial on corruption charges. His Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads are locked in a close race with a Jewish-led opposition bloc, with neither side appearing on track to win an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament.

About 7.3 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. Most polling stations open from 7am to 10pm, and anyone still queuing when they close is entitled to vote. Election day is a national holiday.

Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, which sits for a four-year term. There are no term limits for a prime minister.

How voting works

Israelis vote for a party, not a candidate.

A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats and no party has ever won that outright. Finishing first does not guarantee power. Parties then have 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days, to assemble a coalition reaching 61. If nobody manages it, the country votes again.

Seats are shared out in proportion to each party’s share of the national vote, so a party winning 30 percent of votes takes roughly 30 percent of seats. The votes for parties failing to secure 3.25 percent are discarded, which explains why small parties routinely merge before every election.

Who can and cannot vote?

About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in this election, but they are not the only adults living under the government they choose.



Roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no vote in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status.

Jewish Israelis and Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million, can vote. So can adult settlers among the more than 750,000 Israelis living in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, who help elect the parliament that legislates over the land they live on.

Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem hold Israeli residency, not citizenship. They can vote for Jerusalem’s city council but not for the Knesset.

The result is a sharp anomaly in the occupied West Bank, where a settler votes and a Palestinian family living nearby, under the same military authority, does not.

Most Israeli citizens living abroad also cannot vote, because Israel has no general absentee ballot and requires voters to be physically in the country on election day. Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception, casting their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.

What are the main issues?

Israelis are dealing with a series of domestic and international issues this election cycle, including:

October 7 security failures – Three years on, the government is yet to form a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-headed attack led to the killing of some 1,200 people, with about 250 taken captive. Israel launched the genocidal war against Palestinians in the wake of the attack, killing at least 74,000 people and leaving most of the besieged territory in ruins.

– Three years on, the government is yet to form a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-headed attack led to the killing of some 1,200 people, with about 250 taken captive. Israel launched the genocidal war against Palestinians in the wake of the attack, killing at least 74,000 people and leaving most of the besieged territory in ruins. Ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions – Supporters of the exemptions say they protect full-time Torah study, but critics argue they place an unfair military burden on everyone else.

– Supporters of the exemptions say they protect full-time Torah study, but critics argue they place an unfair military burden on everyone else. Judicial reform – Netanyahu’s push to curb the Supreme Court’s powers, which sparked mass protests before the war on Gaza, remains a deep fault line. Critics see it as a threat to democracy, while supporters argue that the court has overstepped its authority.

– Netanyahu’s push to curb the Supreme Court’s powers, which sparked mass protests before the war on Gaza, remains a deep fault line. Critics see it as a threat to democracy, while supporters argue that the court has overstepped its authority. War and security – The public wants stability but remains wary of concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. Netanyahu promised “total victory”, but Hamas and Hezbollah remain operational.

– The public wants stability but remains wary of concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. Netanyahu promised “total victory”, but Hamas and Hezbollah remain operational. Cost of living – High prices and modest wages are being further squeezed by soaring defence spending. Since 2023, Israel’s defence budget has doubled, increasing pressure on public finances.

Israel’s outgoing government

Netanyahu’s coalition held 60 of the Knesset’s 120 seats when parliament dissolved in July. It comprised Likud with 32 seats, Shas with 11, Religious Zionism with seven, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit with six, and New Hope with four. Shas left the government in July 2025 but remained in the coalition and New Hope will merge into Likud for this election.



The opposition held 59 seats: Yesh Atid with 24, Blue and White with eight, United Torah Judaism with seven, Yisrael Beiteinu with six, Hadash-Taal and Raam with five each and Labor with four. Noam’s single seat was unaffiliated.

Who are the main contenders?

Netanyahu is seeking re-election while facing a trial on corruption charges, which he denies.

His far-right coalition is up against a bloc comprising of four major Jewish-led opposition parties, whose leaders have signed a declaration promising not to attack each other ahead of the vote and to join forces in forming a government after the polls.

Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister, with his new Yashar party evenly matched with Likud in the opinion polls.

The opposition alliance includes the Together list, led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.

Other key players include far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, the ultra-Orthodox parties, and the Arab-majority lists Ra’am and the Joint List.

Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List from the election, but the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bans on October 2, ruling that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold for exclusion.

Sami Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel who leads Balad, one of the parties in the Joint List, withdrew from the race after the court signalled that a majority of its judges would uphold his disqualification.

The Arab-led parties could hold the balance of power after the vote, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them.

Sixth election in seven years

October 27 will be Israel’s sixth national vote since 2019, but the first in 38 years to arrive at the natural end of a full Knesset term.

The instability began in April 2019, when Netanyahu’s Likud party and Benny Gantz’s Blue and White party tied on 35 seats each. A second vote that September produced another deadlock, with Blue and White on 33 and Likud on 32, and neither round yielded a coalition able to reach a majority.

A third election in March 2020 gave Likud 36 seats to Blue and White’s 33, and produced a Netanyahu-Gantz unity government that collapsed within a year. In March 2021, Likud won 30 seats to Yesh Atid’s 17, but an eight-party coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that also included Ra’am, an Arab party, ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run. It lasted a year.

Netanyahu returned in November 2022, with Likud on 32 and Yesh Atid on 24, at the head of what has been described as Israel’s most right-wing government. Polls now show neither bloc clearly reaching 61.

Israel’s prime ministers

The state of Israel has had 14 prime ministers since its foundation in 1948. Netanyahu is by far the longest-serving, with 19 years in three separate stints: 1996 to 1999, 2009 to 2021 and from 2022 to now



Only David Ben-Gurion, who led the country from 1948 to 1954 and again from 1955 to 1963, comes close.

Whatever happens on October 27, Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in.

World.title: US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
World.content:
Share US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions on social media

The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students.

The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland.

The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.

Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied.

If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.

The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June.

‘The Pandemic Plan’

The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic.

It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.

The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool.



Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.

“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.

Previously thrown out

The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools.

Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.

The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.

“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”

Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.

World.title: French cities calm overnight after curfews imposed to quell violence, PM says
World.content:
Targeted curfews across France contributed to a quiet night following a weekend of riots and looting across the country, the Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has said.

Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.

Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they are necessary.

Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.

World.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
World.content:
Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."

The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.

The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.

Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.

On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."

Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.

"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."

But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.

"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."

He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."

However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."

Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.

Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).

This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.

Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.

Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.

He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."

Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.

He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.

"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."

On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."

World.title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
World.content:
Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.

"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."

The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.

She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.

"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.

"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."

At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.

"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.

Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.

"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.

Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

World.title: Canadian tourist found guilty of animal cruelty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
World.content:
A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.

Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.

Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.

Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.

A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".

"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.

"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.

Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.

He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.

The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.

During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.

It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.

Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.

A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

World.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
World.content:
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.

If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.

The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.

"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.

World.title: Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
World.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".

Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".

One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".

Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.

One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.

Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.

Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.

But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.

He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

World.title: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
World.content:
Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player GaÃ«l Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.

The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".

"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.

She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".

"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.

It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.

"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.

Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."

The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.

Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".

Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.

However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.

Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.

Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

World.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support, says court filing
World.content:
A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.

The 35-year-old engineer was on Monday deemed a flight risk and denied bail, pending trial.

The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.

The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.

A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.

He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.

It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.

"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.

US district judge Alex Tse on Monday denied Alfozan's attorneys request for his release on bail, saying "there is a risk of non-appearance that is significant".

The FBI investigation is ongoing.

Alfozan was scheduled to âappear â in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (Â£188,000) fine.

World.title: FRSC orders probe into Otedola bridge tanker inferno
World.content:
The ​‌‌‍​‌‍⁠⁠‍​⁠⁠‍​⁠⁠‍‌​Corps Marshal, Shehu Mohammed, gave the directive following the incident, which occurred at about 4:10 p.m. on Monday.

The incident involved a diesel-laden tanker that plunged into the underpass beneath the bridge on the outward section of the expressway.

This is contained in a statement issued by the Corps Public Education Officer (CPEO), Osondu Ohaeri, on Monday in Abuja.

Mr Mohammed said the crash triggered a raging inferno, raising concerns over the dangers associated with reckless driving, particularly by operators of heavy-duty vehicles transporting petroleum products.

He, however, said no fatalities were recorded in the initial report, while two adult male occupants of the tanker sustained injuries and were taken to the Lagos State Accident and Emergency Centre for medical attention.

According to him, preliminary findings forwarded by the Lagos Sector Command identified excessive speed as the cause of the crash.

“The FRSC rescue team arrived at the scene at about 4:20 p.m., following a report received at 4:15 p.m., and joined other emergency responders in efforts to contain the fire, manage traffic and prevent further casualties.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The agencies involved in the response included the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, Lagos State Traffic Management Authority (LASTMA), the Police and other emergency responders.”

The corps marshal described the crash as a grave reminder that irresponsible driving could have consequences extending far beyond the driver and the vehicle, especially when hazardous cargo and heavily trafficked public infrastructure were involved.

He stressed the need for a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash, adding that appropriate action would be taken in accordance with the findings.

He also emphasised that transporting petroleum products required exceptional discipline, professional competence and strict adherence to safety standards.

He noted that tanker drivers must understand that the size of their vehicles, the weight of their cargo and the potential consequences of losing control left little room for error.

“Speeding, dangerous manoeuvres, poor vehicle maintenance and failure to comply with prescribed safety requirements can turn an ordinary journey into a disaster with devastating consequences,” Mr Mohammed said.

Mr Mohammed also warned fleet operators and tanker owners against placing commercial considerations above human safety.

He said unrealistic delivery schedules, inadequate driver supervision and poor maintenance practices must not be used as excuses for exposing Nigerians to preventable danger.

He called for stronger driver training, effective monitoring of driving behaviour, regular vehicle inspections and strict compliance with applicable speed limits and other road safety regulations.

He commended the emergency responders for their coordinated intervention, noting the importance of prompt and collaborative action in containing emergencies and preventing additional casualties.

The corps marshal urged motorists to exercise extreme caution around emergency scenes and obey traffic control instructions to allow emergency personnel to carry out their duties effectively.

He particularly cautioned members of the public against approaching burning tankers to collect spilled petroleum products or take photographs and videos of such incidents.

He warned that such actions could expose members of the public to potentially fatal consequences, urging motorists and other road users to avoid obstructing emergency responders.

The FRSC boss said the corps would continue to intensify public education, operational surveillance and enforcement to promote responsible driving and protect all road users.

He added that the corps remained committed to preventing avoidable crashes, investigating incidents and ensuring that negligence was held accountable wherever established.

Mr Mohammed reiterated that road safety was not merely a regulatory obligation but a collective national responsibility, stressing that every driver, fleet operator and road user had a duty to ensure that individual decisions do not become a source of tragedy for innocent Nigerians.

He urged tanker operators and other motorists to prioritise safety, exercise caution and comply with traffic regulations to prevent similar incidents.

(NAN)

World.title: Nigerian troops kill 103 suspected terrorists, destroy logistics hubs – Official
World.content:
The military has sustained precision air strikes against Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) terrorists in the North-east, killing 103 fighters and destroying several logistics hubs and storage facilities between 10 and 18 October.

The Acting Military Information Officer, Headquarters Joint Task Force (North-East), Operation Hadin Kai (OPHK), Mohammed Goni, disclosed this in a statement on Monday in Maiduguri.

Mr Goni said the operations involved coordinated air assets from Nigerian Army Aviation, the Nigerian Army Remotely Piloted Aircraft Regiment (NARPARS) and the Air Component.

He said the campaign comprised seven strikes targeting terrorist locations around Gudumbali in Guzamala Local Government Area (LGA), Badu and Mairari in Monguno LGA, Duste Uku in Gombi LGA of Adamawa, and the Arina Woje area of Monguno LGA, Borno.

According to him, a major success was recorded on Sunday when the air component conducted a precision strike against the alternate residence of Abu Saleem, the ISWAP Wali of South Lake Chad, following intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance activities.

He said subsequent human intelligence confirmed the killing of Jindullah, a prominent ISWAP fighter reportedly serving as Abu Saleem’s chief security guard, and Abul Kissa, a member of the group’s Shura Council.

Mr Goni added that other prominent fighters were also killed during the strike.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the targeted structure was completely destroyed alongside key logistics assets, including nine boat engines and several motorcycles stored within the premises.

He also said that the destruction of the facility had further undermined the group’s ability to use the location as a safe haven and logistics base within the forested area.

Mr Goni added that an earlier operation on 13 October involved a Guardian air asset tracking a group of 16 terrorists from the Mairari axis to a gathering of more than 100 fighters accompanied by several motorcycles.

He said the gathering was located approximately 23 kilometres east of Badu and 19 kilometres west of Monguno.

According to him, a subsequent precision strike on the gathering resulted in the assessed killing of about 30 terrorists, although the extent of damage to the motorcycles remained unconfirmed.

He said other strikes during the period targeted terrorist elements and facilities around Gudumbali, Badu, Mairari and Duste Uku.

MrGoni said the operations reflected sustained military pressure on terrorist concentrations, leadership structures and logistics networks across the theatre.

He added that the coordinated use of air assets and ground forces remained central to efforts to degrade terrorist capabilities, disrupt command structures and deny insurgents freedom of action.

The military, he said, remained committed to sustaining operational momentum and advancing efforts to restore lasting peace and security across the North-East.

(NAN)

World.title: Nigeria vs Puerto Rico Preview: Flamingos target first win at 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos will be desperate to get their 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup campaign back on track when they take on Puerto Rico in their second Group B fixture in Morocco on Tuesday, 20 October.

Head coach Akeem Busari’s side have little room for another slip-up after opening their campaign with a 2-1 defeat to Poland, while Puerto Rico also enter the encounter under pressure following a heavy 6-0 loss to Korea DPR.

With both teams seeking their first points of the tournament, Tuesday’s clash gives Nigeria a chance to respond to their opening setback and strengthen their chances of reaching the Round of 16.

For the Flamingos, the challenge is clear: turn their attacking promise into goals, eliminate costly mistakes and deliver a performance that reflects their ambition on the world stage.

Flamingos seek redemption after Poland defeat

Nigeria will enter the encounter knowing their opening defeat to Poland exposed areas that must improve if they want to make a deep run in Morocco.

Despite creating chances to trouble the European side, the Flamingos struggled to make their attacking efforts count, allowing Poland to build a two-goal lead before mounting a late response.

Wiktoria Skrzypczak broke the deadlock from the penalty spot in the 33rd minute before Natalia Skrok doubled Poland’s lead in the 65th minute.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria eventually found a breakthrough in the 79th minute through Oluebube Umejiaku, who finished off a promising attacking move initiated by substitute Kanyinsola Yusuf.

However, the late goal proved insufficient to rescue a point, leaving Busari’s team with the task of recovering quickly ahead of their second group outing.

Against Puerto Rico, the Flamingos must show greater composure in the final third and more urgency when opportunities arise. Their ability to convert chances could prove decisive against an opponent equally determined to recover from an opening-day defeat.

Defensively, Nigeria will also need to stay disciplined and avoid giving Puerto Rico chances to build momentum.

Puerto Rico seek response after historic World Cup debut

While Nigeria look to recover from disappointment, Puerto Rico will aim to put their difficult opening performance behind them and make history with their first-ever FIFA World Cup victory.

The tournament in Morocco represents Puerto Rico’s maiden appearance at a FIFA World Cup at any level, marking a significant milestone for the island nation’s women’s football programme.

Puerto Rico booked their place at the tournament after finishing as the best-ranked runner-up in the final round of the 2026 Concacaf Women’s U-17 Qualifiers.

Their qualification campaign featured two wins and one loss, with impressive victories over Haiti and Bermuda that secured their historic ticket to Morocco.

They defeated Haiti 3-1 before recording a commanding 9-0 victory over Bermuda. Giselle Falcón played an important role in those results, scoring a penalty against Haiti and finding the net twice against Bermuda.

However, the step up to the global stage proved challenging in their opening fixture against Korea DPR, who won convincingly 6-0.

Yu Jong Hyang and Kim Won Sim both scored twice as the Asian side underlined their attacking quality, leaving Puerto Rico with plenty to consider ahead of Tuesday’s encounter.

Puerto Rico will need a significant improvement in defensive organisation to contain Nigeria’s attacking players. At the same time, they must find a way to threaten the Flamingos rather than spend long periods absorbing pressure.

Despite their opening defeat, the tournament debutants will be motivated by the prospect of securing their first points at a FIFA World Cup.

What Nigeria must get right against Puerto Rico

For the Flamingos, Tuesday’s encounter is about more than simply recovering from their defeat to Poland. It is an opportunity to demonstrate resilience, improve their execution and keep their knockout-stage ambitions firmly on course.

Nigeria showed against Poland that they could create chances, but their inability to convert them ultimately contributed to their defeat. Against Puerto Rico, they must be more clinical in front of goal and avoid allowing frustration to creep into their performance if an early breakthrough proves difficult.

Busari’s players will also need to strike the right balance between attacking intent and defensive discipline. Puerto Rico’s 6-0 defeat to Korea DPR may suggest vulnerability, but Nigeria cannot afford to approach the contest with complacency.

With both sides seeking a response, the team that settles in quicker and makes better use of its opportunities could gain the decisive edge.

Korea DPR’s emphatic opening victory has already given them an early advantage in Group B, increasing the importance of the remaining fixtures for the other teams.

Under the tournament format, the top two teams in each group qualify automatically for the Round of 16, while the four best third-placed teams across the six groups also advance to the knockout stage.

That means Nigeria must begin collecting points if they are to avoid leaving their qualification hopes to the uncertainty of the third-placed rankings.

Flamingos face crucial test of character

The meeting with Puerto Rico offers Nigeria an immediate chance to respond to their opening disappointment, but the Flamingos must back their ambition with a more convincing display.

A win would provide a timely confidence boost and put them in a stronger position ahead of their remaining Group B fixture. Another disappointing result, however, would leave them facing a much more difficult route to the Round of 16.

Puerto Rico are equally motivated to secure their first points after a bruising introduction to the tournament, setting up a contest between two teams with something to prove.

For Busari and his players, the priority will be to show that the defeat to Poland was a setback rather than a sign of what is to come.

The Flamingos now have a chance to deliver the response their campaign demands, with their finishing, discipline, and mentality likely to determine whether they can secure their first victory at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

World.title: Uba Sani breaks ground for NASENI Skill Development Centre in Kaduna
World.content:
Governor Uba Sani has maintained that skills development is central to economic renewal and social inclusion in Nigeria and that government should create the enabling platforms.

The governor who said this during the ground breaking of NASENI Skill Development Centre at Rigachukun on Monday, noted that young persons in Nigeria posses the energy, ambition and ingenuity to tap from.

‘’Government has a responsibility to create conditions in which these qualities can flourish through relevant training, recognised qualifications and fair access to productive opportunities.This conviction informs our investment in the Kaduna State Institute of Vocational Training and Skills Development.

‘’In August, we celebrated 4,050 graduates from its campuses in Rigachikun, Soba and Samaru Kataf. Their training covered 14 trades, including Electrical Installation, Aluminium Fabrication, Solar Installation, Mechatronics, Computer Hardware Repairs and Maintenance, Catering and Hospitality, and Fashion Design,’’ he recalled.

Uba Sani disclosed that ‘’the Institute secured accreditation from the National Board for Technical Education, while instructors received training as Quality Assurance Assessors and Internal Quality Assurance Managers.’’

According to him, ‘’these measures strengthen the credibility of assessment and certification, giving employers greater confidence in the competence of our graduates.’’

‘’Today, we lay the foundation for an institution that will expand opportunity, strengthen productive capacity and prepare our people for the demands of a changing economy.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

‘’The NASENI Skill Development Centre represents an investment in the knowledge, competence and enterprise through which individuals build secure livelihoods and societies achieve lasting prosperity,’’ he added.

He expressed optimism that the NASENI Skill Development Centre will deepen the efforts of Kaduna State Government towards Human Capital Development.

He pointed out that the NASENI Skill Development Centre’s value will depend on how effectively it complements existing institutions, responds to industry and equips trainees with capabilities that employers need.

Uba Sani further said that Kaduna State Government looks forward to programmes grounded in practical competence, credible certification and clear pathways into employment and enterprise.

‘’Access must be integral to that ambition. Women, persons with disabilities and young people in underserved communities must have meaningful opportunities to participate. Their inclusion will broaden our pool of talent and ensure that the benefits of development reach households too often excluded from opportunity,’’ he added.

‘’Kaduna State has provided the required site and remains fully committed to facilitating this project. I commend the contractors for mobilising equipment and demonstrating readiness to commence work.

‘’I urge NASENI, the project team and contractors to uphold agreed standards and timelines. Timely delivery and sound construction must be matched by careful preparation for effective operation,’’ he added.

According to him, ‘’our shared responsibility is to build an institution that earns public confidence through the quality of its training and the achievements of its graduates.

‘’Working together, we can make this Centre a dependable bridge between the aspirations of our people and the opportunities of a productive economy. It should become a place where discipline meets ingenuity, and where useful knowledge translates into greater dignity for families,’’ he added.

World.title: Iheanacho extends record-breaking scoring run to 11 league matches in Turkey
World.content:
Super Eagles forward Kelechi Iheanacho continued his extraordinary goalscoring form in Turkey after finding the net for the 11th consecutive league match in Bursaspor’s 2-0 victory over Pendikspor on Monday.

The Nigerian striker scored Bursaspor’s second goal in the 62nd minute, putting the game beyond Pendikspor’s reach after Halil Akbunar had given the hosts an early lead with the opening goal in the 10th minute.

Iheanacho’s latest effort further underlined his growing influence at Bursaspor, where he has emerged as one of the division’s most dangerous attacking players since the start of the campaign.

The former Manchester City and Leicester City forward had registered 14 goals and three assists in 10 league appearances before Monday’s encounter. His strike against Pendikspor took his league tally to 15 goals, strengthening his position among the competition’s leading scorers.

Beyond his impressive numbers, the 30-year-old has continued to rewrite the record books with a remarkable run of consistency in front of goal.

Iheanacho had previously established a new Bursaspor record by scoring in nine consecutive league matches, surpassing Brazilian forward Fernandao’s previous club record of eight successive games during the 2014-15 season.

He then moved beyond club history to set a new benchmark in Turkish football, surpassing the nine-match scoring streaks of Galatasaray legend Metin Oktay in the 1962-63 campaign and former Turkey international Saffet Sancaklı in the 1995-96 season.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Nigerian international reached that milestone with a brace in Bursaspor’s 3-0 victory over Muğlaspor on 15 October, extending his remarkable run to 10 consecutive league matches.

Monday’s encounter against Pendikspor provided another opportunity to extend that record, and Iheanacho duly delivered with his 62nd-minute finish to make it 11 successive league games with a goal.

His continued scoring exploits represent an impressive return for the former Premier League forward, whose clinical finishing and consistency have made him a key figure in Bursaspor’s attacking setup.

With 15 league goals already to his name, Iheanacho will now look to maintain his remarkable momentum as the season progresses, with his latest achievement further enhancing his reputation in Turkish football.

World.title: Northern Nigeria’s tech turn: Solar, biotech and digital innovation can drive the change, By Mukhtar Yau Madobi
World.content:
Northern Nigeria’s opportunity lies in combining its agricultural strength, scientific capabilities, solar potential and youthful population into productive enterprises. With sustained investment and practical collaboration, the region can build a more resilient, prosperous future… The real test is simple: Do these innovations improve people’s lives?

Northern Nigeria is a region of contrasts — rich in sunlight, land and youthful energy, yet constrained by insecurity, unreliable electricity, unemployment, climate pressures and limited industrial capacity. States such as Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Jigawa, Zamfara and Borno possess the raw materials for a productive, technology‑driven economy. What they need now is a coordinated push to convert potential into prosperity.

That conversation resurfaced recently at an executive training organised by the Bureau for Public Service Reforms (BPSR) in partnership with Image Merchants Promotion Limited (IMPR). At the sidelines of the event, the Director‑General of the National Biotechnology Research and Development Agency (NBRDA), Professor Abdullahi Mustapha, argued that the future of Northern Nigeria lies at the intersection of biotechnology, information technology, and solar energy.

His message was simple: these three sectors, working together, can boost agricultural productivity, expand renewable energy, support local manufacturing and create jobs for millions of young people.

But another voice is equally central to this transformation — Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, director‑general of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA). Under his leadership, NITDA has championed digital literacy, innovation hubs, tech skills development, startup incubation, data governance and smart agriculture solutions. These digital foundations are essential for supporting biotechnology research, renewable energy expansion and the broader technology ecosystem emerging across the North.

Together, NBRDA and NITDA represent two pillars of a new Northern economy: scientific innovation and digital capability.

Solar Energy: The North’s Most Abundant Resource

Northern Nigeria receives some of the highest solar irradiation in the world. The Global Solar Atlas confirms that states like Kano, Jigawa, Katsina, Zamfara and Borno enjoy year‑round sunshine — a natural advantage waiting to be harnessed.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Reliable solar power can support irrigation systems, cold storage, food processing, biotechnology laboratories and digital innovation hubs.
