The impact is already visible. According to the World Bank’s March 2025 mini‑grid report, the Nigeria Electrification Project supported 125 mini‑grids and one million solar home systems, giving 5.5 million Nigerians access to electricity and creating over 5,000 green jobs.

For Northern Nigeria, this is a blueprint. Kano and Jigawa can scale solar‑powered irrigation; Katsina and Zamfara can energise rural enterprises; Kaduna can link solar power to manufacturing; Borno can use renewable energy to rebuild livelihoods in conflict‑affected communities.

Biotechnology: Strengthening Food Security

Agriculture remains the backbone of Northern Nigeria, yet farmers face drought, heat stress, pests, declining soil quality and insecurity. Biotechnology offers practical solutions.

The IITA Cowpea Breeding Programme shows how improved crop varieties can be tailored to local conditions. NBRDA’s Agricultural Biotechnology Department is working on tissue culture, improved soybean varieties, ginger blight research, biofertilisers, biopesticides and waste‑to‑biogas technology.

These innovations can reduce dependence on imported inputs and create new agro‑businesses. But research alone is not enough. The real challenge is commercialisation — moving discoveries from laboratories to farms.

This requires partnerships among NBRDA, universities, farmers, cooperatives and private investors. Affordable seeds, accessible biological inputs and strong extension services will determine whether biotechnology becomes a real driver of food security.

Digital Innovation: The Backbone of Modern Agriculture

This is where NITDA, under Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, becomes indispensable.

NITDA’s digital transformation agenda — innovation hubs, tech‑skills development, data governance, digital agriculture and startup incubation — provides the infrastructure needed to support biotechnology and renewable energy expansion.

In May 2026, NBRDA launched the National Genomics and Bioinformatics Infrastructure, a platform for managing genomic data on plants, animals, humans and microorganisms. Such systems rely heavily on digital tools, cloud infrastructure and data‑management standards — areas where NITDA’s expertise is crucial.

Digital tools are also reaching farmers directly. Nigeria’s Digital Precision Agricultural Extension platform sends automated Hausa language voice messages on weather, pests and crop management. Its pilot covered eight northern locations, including Kano and Kaduna.

Expanding such services can help farmers make informed decisions, especially where traditional extension services are limited.

Building a Northern Technology Economy

Northern Nigeria’s technology ambitions should extend beyond agriculture. Electronics repair, component assembly and accessory production can create jobs for young people with technical skills.

Potential innovation clusters include Kano’s industrial corridor and Kaduna’s research and manufacturing ecosystem.

Early activities could include mobile phone repairs, charger and accessory production, the assembly of imported components and quality control services. Advanced manufacturing (e.g. smartphone screens) will require heavy investment and specialised expertise. A gradual approach — starting with repair and assembly — is more realistic.

Solar‑powered workshops, technical training centres and digital hubs can support this emerging ecosystem. NITDA’s innovation cluster model and startup‑support programmes can accelerate this growth, while NBRDA strengthens the scientific backbone through biotechnology and bio‑enterprise development.

Technology and Security: A Delicate Balance

Insecurity has disrupted farming, displaced households and discouraged investment across the North. Technology cannot replace security operations, but it can strengthen resilience.

A World Bank analysis (July 2026) found that partial crop losses in Nigeria rose from 6 per cent in 2018/19 to over 20 per cent in 2023/24, driven by environmental shocks and insecurity.

Investments in agricultural processing, improved seeds, renewable energy, vocational training and small‑scale manufacturing can diversify incomes and support displaced families. NBRDA and NITDA can contribute through research, training, digital tools and bio‑enterprise support — but such interventions must be evaluated alongside governance and conflict‑resolution efforts.

Climate Resilience: Protecting the North’s Future

Biotechnology, digital monitoring and renewable energy can strengthen environmental management. Climate‑resilient crops, biofertilisers and biopesticides can reduce chemical dependence. Waste‑to‑biogas technology can support cleaner production.

Satellite imagery, weather forecasts and early‑warning systems can help communities prepare for floods and droughts. The Agro‑Climatic Resilience in Semi‑Arid Landscapes (ACReSAL) initiative provides a framework for climate‑smart agriculture and landscape restoration.

But technology must be paired with effective environmental regulation, sound water management, proper drainage infrastructure and community preparedness.

Turning Research into Economic Value

Northern Nigeria’s transformation will require coordinated investment by federal and state governments, NBRDA, NITDA, universities, manufacturers and local communities.

Progress should be measured through jobs created, higher crop yields, improved farmer incomes, reduced post‑harvest losses, reliable electricity access, responsible water use and commercialised research innovations.

Under Professor Abdullahi Mustapha, NBRDA can help bridge the gap between scientific research and commercial application. Under Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, NITDA can ensure that digital infrastructure, innovation ecosystems and tech‑skills development support this transformation.

Northern Nigeria’s opportunity lies in combining its agricultural strength, scientific capabilities, solar potential and youthful population into productive enterprises. With sustained investment and practical collaboration, the region can build a more resilient, prosperous future.

The real test is simple: Do these innovations improve people’s lives?

If they do, Northern Nigeria’s quiet tech awakening has already begun.

Mukhtar Yau Madobi is a Research Fellow, Centre for Crisis Communication (CCC), Abuja.

World.title: Journalists, media leaders honour Dele Giwa at book unveiling
World.content:
Journalists and prominent figures from Nigeria’s media industry on Monday gathered in Lagos to honour Dele Giwa, the late founding editor-in-chief of Newswatch magazine, 40 years after his assassination.

The gathering, held at the Sir Kessington Adebutu Auditorium of the Nigerian Institute of Journalism (NIJ), Ogba, Lagos, featured the unveiling of Dele Giwa’s Granite Journalism, edited by veteran journalist Ray Ekpu, with a foreword by Yemi Ogunbiyi.

Among those in attendance were Sam Amuka, publisher of Vanguard Newspapers, who chaired the occasion; former Ogun State Governor Segun Osoba, Mr Ogunbiyi, a former managing director of Daily Times, Nduka Obaigbena, chairman and editor-in-chief of THISDAY, and Biodun Shobanjo, founder of Insight Communications.

Mr Ekpu, a former colleague of Mr Giwa, said the book was intended to preserve his legacy and draw attention to the enduring importance of journalism, truth and accountability.

“We are not here to mourn the death of Dele, even though his death comes as a predictable mystery. We have done a lot of that, publicly and privately, in the last 40 years.

“We are here to give presence to his absence by presenting to the public a book that will immortalise him,” he said.

Mr Ekpu said the publication brings together selected articles written by Mr Giwa for Daily Times, The Sunday Concord and Newswatch, as well as interviews and contributions examining his journalism and influence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He recalled his close relationship with Mr Giwa, including the period when they lived in a duplex in Ikeja, Lagos, with their families.

Mr Ekpu also recounted how his young son abandoned his ambition to become a journalist after Mr Giwa was killed, saying the incident reflected the risks journalists face while covering protests, riots, elections and wars.

Citing figures from the International Federation of Journalists, Mr Ekpu said 128 journalists and media workers were killed worldwide in 2025. He lamented the inadequate protection of journalists and the failure to ensure accountability for attacks against them.

“Whoever said that the pen is mightier than the sword did not have Nigeria in mind,” he said.

He urged journalists to continue holding those in power accountable, saying much remained to be done to build a better Nigeria.

Kolawole reflects on Giwa’s legacy

Reviewing the book, founder of The Cable, an online newspaper, Simon Kolawole, described Mr Giwa as a writer whose work was driven by intellectual curiosity, a commitment to truth and a sense of public responsibility.

Mr Kolawole said Mr Giwa’s journalism extended beyond reporting on Nigeria to international politics, race relations, the Western media, capital and questions about human existence.

Mr Kolawole said the book did not present Mr Giwa as a saint, acknowledging that he could be combative and critical. Rather, he said, Mr Giwa was a journalist deeply engaged with society and unwilling to remain indifferent to its problems.

He said the collection offered lessons in curiosity, courage, clarity, storytelling, discipline and originality.

Mr Kolawole also described journalism as a public responsibility rather than merely a profession.

“Forty years after his assassination, the remarkable thing is not simply that Nigerians still remember his book. It is that his writing can still command our attention, challenge our assumptions, and give us considerable reading pleasure,” he said.

He urged journalists, students of journalism and history, writers and other readers to engage with the collection.

Family, colleagues celebrate Giwa

Mr Giwa’s widow, Funmi, and daughter, Aisha, attended the event alongside journalists from different generations and media organisations who gathered to celebrate his contribution to Nigerian journalism.

Aisha said she remained proud of her father and the legacy he left behind.

READ ALSO: Newswatch to unveil book honouring Dele Giwa 40 years after assassination

The gathering also featured reflections on press freedom, professional courage and the responsibility of journalists to hold public officials accountable.

The late Dele Giwa

Mr Giwa was killed by a parcel bomb delivered to his Lagos residence on 19 October 1986. His assassination remains one of the most prominent unsolved killings of a journalist in Nigeria.

His killing, widely blamed on the then-regime of military president Ibrahim Babangida, remains unresolved. Mr Babangida, 85, has consistently denied complicity in the murder. The late legal icon, Gani Fawehinmi, championed the cause of justice for Mr Giwa until he himself passed away in September 2009.

Mr Giwa, who was 39 at the time of his death in 1986, co-founded Newswatch magazine in 1985 with Mr Ekpu, Yakubu Mohammed and Dan Agbese. Mr Giwa served as the magazine’s editor-in-chief, with Mr Ekpu as his deputy.

The magazine, under Mr Giwa’s editorship, helped advance investigative journalism in Nigeria.

World.title: Nigeria is not doomed: Countering the forces of polarisation, By Chris Ngwodo
World.content:
Ultimately, national cohesion cannot be sustained by exhortation alone. It must be cultivated through equitable institutions, shared prosperity and empathetic leadership at all levels. Nigeria’s diversity is not a death sentence. Our differences need not become divisions, nor must competition degenerate into conflict. The Republic’s future remains ours to shape. Nigeria is not doomed to destruction. With intelligent policymaking, inclusive citizenship and leadership sufficiently empathetic to recognise our common humanity, polarisation can be defeated.

Since the inception of the modern Nigerian state, observers have repeatedly contemplated its bewildering diversity and issued earnest forecasts of its impending disintegration. Across successive decades, scholars, intelligence services, think tanks and assorted professional obituarists have confidently predicted the Republic’s demise. Yet Nigeria endures, in stubborn defiance of its prophets of doom. As one born after the Civil War, I have witnessed repeated invocations of imminent national calamity. With another electoral season approaching, polarisation has again assumed topical significance. Some commentators contend that Nigeria’s ethnic and religious heterogeneity makes it fundamentally unworkable. I disagree.

Nigeria is neither uniquely divided nor exceptionally afflicted by communal prejudice. Every diverse society contends with varying degrees of mutual suspicion, chauvinism and bigotry. If Nigerians were constitutionally incapable of coexistence, the federation would have collapsed long ago. Its survival through civil war, economic upheavals, authoritarian rule and recurrent political crises suggests something more complicated than the familiar narrative of irreconcilable antagonisms.

The fundamental problem is not that Nigerians viscerally hate one another. It is that our political economy has made identity a principal currency of access to opportunity. In a society where public employment, political appointments, economic patronage and access to state resources are frequently mediated through communal affiliations, citizenship becomes less a shared entitlement than a contest for preferential access to the proverbial national cake.

This competition often manifests through the pernicious distinction between indigenes and settlers, an exclusionary framework that elevates ancestral provenance above constitutional citizenship. Elsewhere, socioeconomic grievances are conveniently repackaged as ethnic or religious hostilities. Complex struggles over land, livelihoods, political representation and public resources are reduced to supposedly primordial hatreds. The resulting polarisation is neither inevitable nor immutable. It is substantially manufactured by institutions, incentives and political choices.

…combatting polarisation requires more than ceremonial appeals to national unity. It demands an economic transformation capable of generating opportunities at a scale commensurate with Nigeria’s demographic pressures. Sustained, inclusive, ideally double-digit economic growth should be a national ambition, accompanied by investments in education, employment and social protection.

Economic adversity compounds the problem. Where legitimate opportunities are scarce, the impulse to retreat into narrower circles of communal solidarity becomes especially powerful. Political entrepreneurs exploit this insecurity, offering ethnic and religious protection as substitutes to effective governance. This is hardly an exclusively Nigerian pathology. Economic dislocation has energised nativist movements across Western democracies, while xenophobic violence in South Africa illustrates how socioeconomic frustrations can be redirected against perceived outsiders.

Consequently, combatting polarisation requires more than ceremonial appeals to national unity. It demands an economic transformation capable of generating opportunities at a scale commensurate with Nigeria’s demographic pressures. Sustained, inclusive, ideally double-digit economic growth should be a national ambition, accompanied by investments in education, employment and social protection.

There are, however, encouraging signs that the integrative forces within Nigerian society remain formidable. The Africa Polling Institute’s 2026 Nigeria Social Cohesion Survey recorded a Social Cohesion Index of 48.8 per cent, up from 46.8 per cent in 2025, and the highest since its surveys began in 2019. Remarkably, for the first time, a majority of respondents identified primarily as Nigerians, rather than through ethnic, religious or regional affiliations. Furthermore, 77 per cent expressed willingness to cooperate with citizens of other ethnic groups to strengthen national unity. These findings do not suggest that our divisions have disappeared. Indeed, perceptions of polarisation remain troubling. They do, however, challenge the fashionable assumption that Nigeria is irredeemably fractured.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We need enforceable guarantees of equal citizenship, civic education that interrogates inherited prejudices, and a more historically literate understanding of the longstanding interactions among Nigeria’s peoples. Government must confront discriminatory practices, while ensuring that public institutions reward merit, fairness and inclusion.

Meanwhile, rapid urbanisation is producing increasingly cosmopolitan, culturally hybrid Nigerians whose identities transcend inherited communal boundaries. Across our cities, interethnic commerce, professional relationships, friendships and marriages continually renegotiate the meaning of belonging. Even social media, frequently condemned as an amplifier of prejudice, enables new solidarities across traditional fault lines. Intelligent public policy must accelerate these tendencies.

We need enforceable guarantees of equal citizenship, civic education that interrogates inherited prejudices, and a more historically literate understanding of the longstanding interactions among Nigeria’s peoples. Government must confront discriminatory practices, while ensuring that public institutions reward merit, fairness and inclusion. Equally important is restoring security to highways and commercial corridors. Insecurity discourages travel, interrupts trade and enlarges the psychological distances between communities. Roads, railways and safe transportation networks are therefore not merely economic infrastructure; they are instruments of nation-building.

Ultimately, national cohesion cannot be sustained by exhortation alone. It must be cultivated through equitable institutions, shared prosperity and empathetic leadership at all levels. Nigeria’s diversity is not a death sentence. Our differences need not become divisions, nor must competition degenerate into conflict. The Republic’s future remains ours to shape. Nigeria is not doomed to destruction. With intelligent policymaking, inclusive citizenship and leadership sufficiently empathetic to recognise our common humanity, polarisation can be defeated. Our history demonstrates our capacity to endure. Our task now is to learn how to flourish together.

Chris Ngwodo is the director general of the Office for Strategic Preparedness and Resilience (OSPRE).

World.title: Anambra confirms Lassa fever case, activates emergency response
World.content:
The Anambra Government has confirmed a Lassa fever case involving a patient linked to Omasi in Ayamelum Local Government Area (LGA), who is currently receiving treatment at the Federal Teaching Hospital, Abakaliki (FETHA), Ebonyi.

The State Commissioner for Health, Dr Afam Obidike, disclosed this on Monday at an emergency stakeholders’ meeting in Awka.

Obidike said the state had activated an emergency response to prevent further transmission.

“The state has intensified disease surveillance and public awareness.

“The meeting, attended by health partners, including the World Health Organisation and Médecins Sans Frontières, led to the activation of the Incident Management System.

“Health officials will follow up on the affected household in Omasi, identify people who had contact with the patient and classify them according to their level of exposure for appropriate monitoring,” he said.

The commissioner urged residents experiencing persistent fever or malaria-like symptoms that do not improve with appropriate treatment to seek medical attention promptly.

He warned against relying solely on self-medication, stressing that early diagnosis and proper medical care were essential to managing the disease.

Also speaking, the State Epidemiologist, Dr Chuma Emembolu, advised residents to keep food covered and store it in rodent-proof containers to prevent contamination by rats.

Emembolu also urged residents to maintain clean surroundings and prevent rodents from contaminating food and household items with their urine and droppings.

He further warned against direct contact with the blood and other body fluids of suspected or confirmed Lassa fever patients.

The epidemiologist called for strict compliance with infection prevention measures and the guidance of health professionals.

“We urge residents of Omasi and other communities in Ayamelum and the state at large to remain vigilant, cooperate with public health officials and avoid spreading unverified information.

“These measures are aimed at strengthening preparedness, monitoring potential contacts and reducing the risk of further transmission,” he said. (NAN)

World.title: Champions League: Bayern set for Arsenal test without red-hot Olise
World.content:
Champions League hopefuls Bayern Munich are set for an early test of their title credentials when they host English champions Arsenal on Wednesday without in-form winger Michael Olise.

The London-born Olise, who started in Arsenal’s junior system, is suspended after picking up two yellow cards inside a minute in Bayern’s 3-3 draw with Viking last week.

After seeing a first yellow for a foul, a clearly frustrated Olise responded to some verbal provocation from Viking captain Zlatko Tripic by throwing the ball at his head to be sent off for the first time in his career.

After being thrust into Ballon d’Or contention due to last season’s stellar showing, the former Crystal Palace winger has continued his excellent form this campaign.

Olise has nine goals and five assists from 10 games in all competitions for Bayern.

With Jamal Musiala struggling with injury and illness and both Serge Gnabry and Lennart Karl well off their best form, Olise and the ever-reliable Harry Kane have shouldered Bayern’s attacking burden so far this season.

The England captain has nine goals and six assists in 10 games. With Bayern 2-0 down away at Viking last week, Kane almost single-handedly engineered a comeback, scoring twice and setting up another.

Speaking after Bayern’s ruthless 6-1 victory over RB Leipzig in the Bundesliga on Saturday, Kane said Bayern would miss Olise but called on the rest of their star-studded squad to step up.

“Missing one of your biggest players, you’re going to feel it for sure, but that’s where other people have to step up and show they can take their opportunity,” Kane said.

“We talk about the squad a lot, we talk about being ready for your moment and whoever plays will have to be ready.”

One of the many positives to come out of Saturday’s thumping win over Leipzig was the performance of Luis Diaz.

The 29-year-old had cut a frustrated figure after a poor start to the season but scored three goals and set up another in one of his best performances since moving from Liverpool in 2025.

– ‘One of the best’ –

Despite swapping north London for the Bavarian capital back in 2023, former Tottenham captain Kane has seen plenty of Arsenal since joining Bayern.

Bayern faced the Gunners in two quarter-final legs in 2023-24, progressing by just a goal, but were outclassed in a 3-1 defeat in the league phase of last year’s competition.

With domestic and international matches coming thick and fast, Kane has not had time to exchange pleasantries with any of his Gunners rivals.

“I spoke to them a bit in the international break previously and we knew the game was coming up, but I think we’re all too busy right now to text each other, with a game every three days,” he explained.

Saturday’s thrashing of Leipzig once again showed the perennial German champions are a cut above their domestic rivals and Kane said Bayern were relishing a chance to take on Mikel Arteta’s side.

Still smarting from last year’s painful loss on penalties to Paris Saint-Germain, Arsenal have started strongly, winning 10 of 11 games in all competitions.

“It’s a big game and we’re playing against one of the best teams in Europe, you have to always enjoy these occasions,” Kane said.

“We’re testing ourselves against one of the best, we’re here at home, the energy, the fans, it’s going to be a special night.”

World.title: Tinubu’s reforms spare Nigeria deeper economic crisis – Shettima
World.content:
FILE PHOTO: Vice President Shettima met with President Tinubu at the Presidential Villa in Abuja on Friday, July 10, 2026.

Vice President Kashim Shettima says President Bola Tinubu’s economic decisions have spared Nigeria a deeper crisis that further delays in implementing critical reforms would have caused.

Shettima said this on Monday while addressing leaders and members of the City Boy Movement at the State House Conference Hall in Abuja.

He acknowledged the economic pressures Nigerians have endured, stressing that their sacrifices must translate into better livelihoods, more opportunities and improved living conditions.

The vice president said the administration had demonstrated the courage to address structural weaknesses rather than postpone difficult decisions.

“What distinguishes this administration from its predecessors is our refusal to pay lip service to the structural reforms Nigeria needs.

“We owe that resolve to the visionary, audacious, tenacious, sagacious architect of our renewal, His Excellency, President Bola Tinubu.

“His courage has drawn Nigeria back from the edge of an economic calamity that continued delay would have made inevitable,” he said.

Shettima maintained that Tinubu understood the consequences of postponing necessary reforms.

The vice president, however, acknowledged the hardship associated with the implementation of those reforms.

“We recognise the pressures Nigerians have endured, and our obligation is to ensure that their sacrifices yield better livelihoods.

“We must earn that patience by listening attentively, correcting what fails and measuring progress against the daily experience of households,” he added.

The vice president also credited Tinubu’s inclusive leadership with strengthening political cooperation and accommodating diverse interests.

“Beyond the science of developing solutions, governance is also the art of managing people.

“The All Progressives Congress (APC) has become a template for unifying diverse groups, because Mr President understands the calculus of inclusion.

“He listens to those who disagree with him, recognises talent beyond familiar circles, and gives competing interests a stake in shared success,” he also said.

On the City Boy Movement, Shettima said its members had helped explain government policies, counter misinformation and encourage issue-based political engagement.

“Thanks to you, we lead in issue-based politics; policies find interpreters in communities far beyond the reach of official statements; falsehood encounters resistance; difficult decisions receive a patient hearing, and the distance between government and the governed continues to narrow,” he said.

He further described Tinubu as a leader whose development vision extended beyond electoral cycles.

Shettima cited his support for the development of reclaimed land along the Atlantic coastline as an example of long-term planning.

“He thinks beyond the calendar of an administration. He treats the future as a responsibility owed to those who cannot yet vote, plans for citizens yet unborn, industries yet to be established, and possibilities that timid minds dismiss before examining them,” he added.

Shettima described the involvement of young Nigerians in governance and political advocacy as vital to the country’s democratic future.

“Your participation in politics and governance gives us confidence that the next generation will inherit the responsibilities of citizenship with conviction.

“We owe your faith an honest account of our stewardship and a country in which your talents can flourish,” he said.

He urged members of the movement to sustain their commitment to national unity and responsible political engagement, while appreciating them for their continued support. (NAN)

World.title: Chemical Engineers seek private control of moribund refineries
World.content:
By Providence Ayanfeoluwa

The Nigerian Society of Chemical Engineers (NSChE) has called on the Federal Government to adopt a transparent, competitive and time-bound privatisation process for Nigeria’s moribund state-owned refineries, with majority private ownership and professional management.

The society’s National President, Engr. Bayo Olarewaju-Alo, made the call at a press conference titled, “Nigeria’s Moribund Refineries Need New Governance.”

He said further public spending on rehabilitation should give way to a new ownership structure that transfers operational control, investment responsibility and execution risks to technically and financially credible private investors.

According to him, repeated attempts to rehabilitate the Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna refineries over more than two decades had failed to deliver reliable and commercially competitive production.

He proposed a 22-month timeline for completing the privatisation process, including asset assessment, investor prequalification, due diligence, competitive bidding, regulatory approvals and transfer of ownership and operational control.

His words: “Further public rehabilitation expenditure should give way to a transparent divestment of majority equity holding to credible private investors, with enforceable obligations and professional operational control.

“Government may retain a minority, non-controlling interest to protect strategic public interests, while avoiding responsibility for financing shortfalls or day-to-day operations.

“The purpose is not simply to sell assets, but to create a governance and investment model that can deliver reliable production, commercial discipline, national value and public accountability.

“Nigeria has spent substantial public resources over more than two decades trying to restore the Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna refineries. Despite repeated rehabilitation efforts, the refineries have not achieved reliable, sustained or competitive production.”

He also called for binding investment and production milestones, environmental safeguards, workforce protection, transparent allocation of legacy liabilities and penalties for non-performance

World.title: Dele Cole’s death leaves vacuum in family, friends’ circle – Agbahor
World.content:
Dr Dele-Cole

By Jeremiah Urowayino

Dr Aghogho Agbahor has expressed sadness over the death of diplomat Dele Cole, saying in a world where true friendship is scarce, Cole showed what loyalty, respect and genuine friendship should look like.

Cole died in London on Saturday, October 17.

Agbahor said he knew the late diplomat as his father’s friend, who never let a day pass without asking about his welfare, studies and life. He described Cole as a rare man who carried integrity like a garment.

His words: “You were humble despite all you had achieved. You were wise, calm, full of stories, and always ready with a smile and good advice whenever I met you. You never passed without asking about my welfare, my PhD studies, and life, and you left without celebrating the final award.

“What I will miss most is the brotherhood you shared with my Dad (Engr Eddy Agbahor) and Uncle Tom Fabyan. In a world where true friendship is scarce, the three of you showed us what loyalty, respect and true friendship look like over decades. You stood by each other through good times and hard times. That bond alone is a legacy for us, your children, to learn from.

“You came, you saw, and you conquered. You lived a life of impact. You raised wonderful children, you built a good name, and you served humanity with kindness.

“Your death has left a big vacuum, not just in your family but in the circle of all who knew and loved you. On behalf of my Dad and our entire family, I say thank you. Thank you for being a true friend to my father. Thank you for being a father figure to us.

“We take solace in knowing you lived well, loved well, and left this world with a good name, which is better than gold. May the Almighty God forgive your shortcomings and grant you eternal rest. May He give your children the strength and fortitude to bear this painful loss.”

World.title: Sanwo-Olu appoints Sanuth as new LAWMA MD
World.content:
Hassan Sanuth, new LAWMA MD

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, has appointed Dr. Hassan Sanuth as the new Managing Director of the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), following reports that the incumbent, Dr. Muyiwa Gbadegesin, had been asked to resign over persistent waste management challenges across the state.

However, relevant state authorities had yet to officially confirm the development as of press time.

Sources familiar with the matter said the governor had become dissatisfied with the continued accumulation of refuse on major roads, residential streets and drainage channels despite directives to improve waste collection.

One of the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Sanwo-Olu had asked Gbadegesin to resign over the weekend, although the outgoing managing director was reportedly seeking more time to address the situation.

“The directives aim at addressing the waste challenges in the state,” the source told Vanguard.

Sanuth, before his reported appointment, was the Director of Sanitation Services in the Office of Environmental Services, Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources.

The reported development comes amid renewed concerns over waste collection and disposal across Lagos, despite the state government’s recent interventions to address the problem.

Sanwo-Olu Declares Emergency on Waste Management

Recall that Sanwo-Olu, during a visit to the Olusosun Dumpsite in Ojota about a month ago, expressed dissatisfaction with the heaps of refuse across the state, describing the situation as “embarrassing”.

The governor ordered immediate action, directed a comprehensive overhaul of LAWMA’s operational structures and management, and declared a state of emergency on waste management.

Accompanied by his deputy, Dr. Obafemi Hamzat, Sanwo-Olu met with stakeholders in the waste management sector at the dumpsite to assess the challenges affecting municipal waste collection and outline immediate, medium- and long-term solutions.

He acknowledged the slow pace of waste collection, attributing the situation partly to the failure of Private Sector Participation (PSP) operators to meet their obligations in the preceding weeks.

The governor also said waste compaction activities were ongoing at the Olusosun and Solous 3 dumpsites, adding that completing the exercise would facilitate faster evacuation.

He explained that recent fire incidents at the dumpsites had slowed operations but said work had resumed, with contractors working to clear the sites for daily waste disposal.

According to him, completing the projects would enable each dumpsite to receive about 450 trucks of municipal waste daily, effectively doubling the capacity of PSP operators.

Refuse Accumulation Persists Across Communities

Despite the interventions, residents have continued to report refuse accumulation in several parts of Lagos, including Mushin, Egbeda, Surulere, Ajegunle, Ikorodu, Ojo, Obalende, Apapa and Mile 2.

The situation has prompted repeated complaints about decomposing waste along streets, road medians, major highways and drainage channels.

A source familiar with the matter said the governor was dissatisfied that the situation had not improved despite his earlier directives.

“The governor was upset when he observed that the situation had not improved despite his clear directive,” the source said.

The source added that Gbadegesin was reportedly appealing for more time and seeking the intervention of prominent individuals.

In a weekly update on waste management posted on his X handle on Saturday, however, Gbadegesin reported progress in clearing some affected areas and sustaining collection services on selected routes.

He said Mile 2 had been cleared, with routine collection sustained, while three additional trucks had been deployed to Doyin-Orile and its environs.

READ ALSO: Lagos evacuates Ago Palace Way refuse bins after Vanguard report

“11 of the 15 routes in this week’s programme now have field updates,” he wrote.

According to the update, daily waste collection had been maintained on Ijesha Road and Itire-Ikate, while Bucknor-Ijegun had been cleared and placed on a three-times-weekly collection schedule.

He also said Okeira and Oluodo had been placed under LAWMA’s interim service following the termination of their PSP arrangements, while collection continued at Ogolonto and Igbokusu.

Obalende, he added, had been cleared, provided with a waste bin and placed under surveillance, while clearance operations continued at Iraye.

Gbadegesin identified Apapa, Abesan Estate, Idimu-Ejigbo Road and the Isheri-Igando corridor as the four routes awaiting field updates.

“The objective is to progress from clearance to sustained collection and prevention of recurrence, not simply remove visible waste,” he said.

Gbadegesin was reappointed to head LAWMA by Sanwo-Olu following the governor’s re-election.

Meet the Reported Successor

Dr. Hassan A. Sanuth holds a PhD in Environmental Microbiology and a master’s degree in Microbiology from the University of Ibadan.

His research interests include epidemiology, biodegradation and bioremediation, and environmental monitoring.

He also holds certificates in Environmental Monitoring and Modelling from the Institute for Water Education in Delft, the Netherlands, and Multilevel Water Governance from The Hague Academy for Local Governance.

Sanuth has more than 23 years of public service experience and has worked in various environmental management and protection departments, including pollution control, billing and monitoring, conservation, and ecology.

He also served as Nigeria’s focal point for environment under the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation-sponsored Collaborative Action for Sustainable Tourism programme in sub-Saharan Africa.

Sanuth is a member of the Science Association of Nigeria, Nigeria Environmental Society and American Society for Microbiology, as well as an associate of the Nigerian Institute of Management.

Vanguard Newspaper

World.title: ‘My message twisted’  -  Obi denies telling UK-based Nigerians to abandon loved ones
World.content:
Peter Obi

The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has denied asking Nigerians living in the United Kingdom to abandon relatives who depend on them for financial support, saying his message about hardship in Nigeria was distorted by political opponents.

Obi said he appreciated Nigerians in the diaspora who made sacrifices to support their families at home, stressing that his concern was the country’s dependence on remittances to meet basic needs.

In a statement titled “My Message Has Been Twisted”, posted on X on Tuesday, the former Anambra State governor said he never asked Nigerians abroad to stop supporting their loved ones.

“I deeply appreciate Nigerians in the diaspora who work tirelessly and make enormous sacrifices to support their families back home,” he said.

“Their remittances pay for school fees, hospital bills, rent, and feeding expenses. Their patriotism and sacrifices deserve our profound respect. I never asked them to abandon their loved ones.”

Obi said his message was aimed at drawing attention to the economic conditions forcing millions of Nigerians to rely on relatives abroad for their survival.

“My concern is that Nigeria should not remain a country where millions depend on relatives abroad for basic survival,” he said.

“Our goal must be to build a nation that provides jobs, affordable healthcare, quality education, and economic opportunities for its citizens.”

He accused political opponents of misrepresenting his comments, insisting that his position was about addressing the causes of hardship rather than discouraging financial assistance to families.

“Political opponents may twist my message, but the truth remains clear: I am not asking Nigerians abroad to abandon their families. I am advocating for a Nigeria that will no longer abandon its own people,” he said.

The clarification followed backlash over comments Obi made during a town hall meeting with diaspora supporters in Manchester on Sunday.

In a video that went viral, Obi urged Nigerians in the UK to stop giving money to relatives and others at home who asked them for financial assistance, arguing that such support could ease hardship without addressing its underlying causes.

“You have people at home in Nigeria today who are begging you for money. Tell them no!” he said.

Obi attributed the country’s economic difficulties to poor leadership and urged Nigerians abroad to encourage their relatives and friends at home to vote for leaders who would prioritise productivity and economic opportunities.

World.title: Fuel subsidy return could push Naira to N4,000/$ — Oyedele
World.content:
Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele

Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has warned that a return to petrol subsidy could trigger capital flight, weaken investor confidence and push the naira to between N3,000 and N4,000 to the dollar.

Oyedele gave the warning on Monday during a press briefing at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

He said investors had repeatedly questioned whether the Federal Government would abandon its economic reforms ahead of the next election cycle.

The minister ruled out reversing the reforms, warning that even a signal that President Bola Tinubu’s administration was considering reinstating petrol subsidy could unsettle financial markets, increase borrowing costs and worsen economic pressures on households.

“In all the meetings I have had, I came to a conclusion that the markets, including the domestic market, which you can read from the capital market, and the international market, have largely written off the opposition in Nigeria as being unserious,” he said.

Oyedele warned that any indication of a possible return to subsidy would trigger an immediate market reaction.

“If, for any reason, the President were to say we are merely considering the return of fuel subsidy, capital would react immediately.

“Airfares would struggle, the naira would come under severe pressure, potentially moving towards 3,000, 3,500 or even 4,000. The very fuel people want subsidised would become far more expensive in naira terms,” he stated.

The minister added that capital flight could extend beyond foreign investors, as wealthy Nigerians, business owners and middle-class investors might also turn to the dollar as a hedge against uncertainty, further increasing demand for foreign exchange.

Oyedele also rejected suggestions that the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited’s temporary reduction in petrol retail margins amounted to a return to subsidy.

He explained that the reduction was a commercial decision rather than a payment funded by public resources, arguing that a company’s decision to lower its profit margin to make a product more affordable should not automatically be classified as a subsidy.

World.title: High Expectations as Oyebanji Begins Second Term in Ekiti
World.content:
Biodun Oyebanji became the first governor in the history of Ekiti State to secure a consecutive second term, and was sworn in Friday before a gathering of political heavyweights from the Fountain of Knowledge, Abuja and across the country. The question begging for answer is: will he be able to meet up with the high expectations of Ekiti people in the next four years? Raheem Akingbolu writes.

Biodun Oyebanji was sworn in on Friday in Ado-Ekiti for a second term as Governor of Ekiti State, becoming the first holder of the office in the state’s history to win a consecutive second term.

The ceremony drew political leaders from Ekiti, Abuja and across the country, underscoring the weight of Oyebanji’s renewed mandate and his growing political profile. Those present included Vice President Kashim Shettima, who represented President Bola Tinubu; Senate President, Godswill Akpabio; Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele; Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu; Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma; All Progressives Congress National Chairman Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda; Ooni of Ife, Oba Adeyeye Ogunwusi; former Ekiti Governor Dr Kayode Fayemi; and other traditional rulers, federal lawmakers and political leaders.

Beyond the colour and political weight of the occasion, the inauguration opens a more demanding phase for the governor. With a fresh four-year mandate, Oyebanji must now turn the confidence placed in him into economic opportunity, better livelihoods and more visible development across the state.

The second term also comes with the benefit of experience. Oyebanji returns with a clearer understanding of Ekiti’s challenges, stronger relationships at the federal level and an agenda built around electricity, agriculture, education, skills development, job creation and infrastructure.

But that agenda must be pursued against real economic hardship, which the governor acknowledged in his inauguration remarks. Rising costs of food, transport, education and other essentials have changed what citizens expect from government. The effect of public spending on household incomes, businesses, farms and public services will therefore be an important measure of his second term.

This explains the emphasis Oyebanji placed on livelihoods. At this stage, the question is no longer simply whether projects are being conceived or executed. It is whether they improve the economic circumstances of the people. A road must help farmers move produce and reach markets. Electricity must help businesses operate. Schools must prepare young people for productive lives.

Electricity deserves particular attention because it affects almost every part of the economic agenda. Reliable power can lower operating costs for small businesses, support artisans and manufacturers, improve agricultural processing and make Ekiti more attractive to investors. For households already under pressure, a more dependable supply can also reduce the cost of relying on alternative sources of power.

Infrastructure must be judged in equally practical terms. Ekiti cannot realise the full value of its agricultural and commercial potential if farmers struggle to move produce, businesses face poor transport links and communities remain disconnected from economic centres. Roads and other infrastructure are important not simply because they are projects, but because they can reduce the cost of doing business and open up markets.

Education carries an even deeper significance in Ekiti because it is part of the state’s identity. Generations of parents have invested heavily in their children’s education, building a culture in which learning is regarded as one of the surest routes to advancement. The challenge now is to ensure that this strength remains relevant to an economy that is changing rapidly.

This is why Oyebanji’s pledge to link education more closely with enterprise and practical skills matters. Educational progress cannot be measured only by enrolment figures or certificates. Young people also need the ability to start businesses, enter the modern workplace, use technology and adapt to changing forms of employment. The link between education and opportunity must become stronger.

Agriculture offers another important opportunity. The task is not simply to increase production, but to ensure that more of the value created remains within Ekiti. Processing, storage, packaging, transportation and marketing are all part of the agricultural economy. Investment in these areas can create jobs and businesses far beyond the farm.

That wider value chain could also change the way younger people see agriculture. With technology, capital, processing facilities, reliable electricity, good transport and access to markets, farming can become a serious business rather than an occupation associated mainly with subsistence. It can attract young people with ideas, skills and entrepreneurial ambition.

The real strength of the second-term agenda will depend on how these priorities work together. Education can produce skilled young people, but those skills need an economy capable of creating opportunities. Farmers can increase production, but they need roads, electricity, storage and markets. Businesses can expand, but they need infrastructure and an environment in which the cost of operation is manageable.

This is where Ekiti’s political advantage at the centre becomes important. Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, who is Senate Leader, occupies one of the most influential positions in the National Assembly. For Oyebanji, that provides an important political link to Abuja at a time when the state will need federal support for projects, partnerships, funding and other interventions.

Bamidele’s role did not begin with this inauguration. He has been part of efforts to advance Ekiti’s interests at the federal level, working within the national political structure and using his influence to strengthen the state’s engagement with the centre. His continued position gives Oyebanji a valuable partner as the governor begins a second term with bigger ambitions and higher expectations.

The combination is significant. Oyebanji has the executive authority to drive Ekiti’s development agenda, while Bamidele has considerable influence within the National Assembly. If properly aligned, that relationship could help the state attract federal projects, strengthen infrastructure, support electricity and industrial development, expand educational and healthcare opportunities and deepen investment in agriculture.

But political access, by itself, is not an achievement. Its value will ultimately depend on what it produces. The people of Ekiti will be more interested in completed roads, functioning infrastructure, stronger businesses, productive farms, better schools and new opportunities for young people than in the political strength of the relationships that made those things possible.

There is also a wider historical dimension to the moment. As Bamidele has noted, Ekiti’s development has been shaped by successive leaders and by a political class that has contributed to the state’s progress since its creation. Oyebanji’s own journey now forms part of that history, from his emergence as governor to his return for a second consecutive term.

His place in that history will be determined by what he does with the mandate he now holds. His first term established his administration and gave him the political capital to win re-election. The second gives him four more years to deepen the work, address weaknesses, pursue bigger opportunities and show how much of the confidence placed in him can become lasting value for the state.

Friday’s ceremony was therefore both an achievement and a beginning. The historic nature of the second term is settled, and the goodwill around the governor is clear. His relationships in Abuja are stronger, his understanding of the state is deeper and his priorities are clearer. What remains is the harder work of turning those advantages into results.

For the people of Ekiti, the final test will be simpler than the political calculations around the inauguration. They will look for businesses that survive and grow, farms that generate better incomes, young people who find meaningful opportunities, schools that prepare students for life beyond the classroom, infrastructure that works and public services that ease the pressures of everyday life.

The crowd in Ado-Ekiti on Friday showed the political importance of Oyebanji’s second term. The next four years will show its practical importance. History may record that he became the first governor of Ekiti to win a consecutive second term.

The more consequential question is whether that mandate becomes a period in which political goodwill, federal influence and public investment produce a better economic and social reality for the people of Ekiti.

World.title: Putting Nigeria First in 2027 Presidential Poll
World.content:
Olusoji Onobun in this piece lauds Governor Ademola Adeleke of Osun State for setting aside party politics for national interest and continuity to support President Bola Tinubu ahead of the January, 2027 poll.

Some people have expressed disappointment in Governor Ademola Adeleke for openly endorsing President Bola Tinubu (PBAT) for re-election in 2027. But we must ask ourselves a fundamental question: Should partisan loyalty and political sentiments matter more than Nigeria’s national interest?

I remember a story about two farmers whose fields were separated by a narrow stream. They belonged to different communities and often disagreed about politics. One year, heavy rains destroyed the small bridge they both used to reach the market. Instead of arguing over which community should take responsibility, they worked together, rebuilt the bridge, and restored access for everyone. The anecdote here is that their differences did not disappear, but they understood that a shared need required a shared solution.

Nigeria is much like that bridge. Our political differences may be real, but our future is shared. When national interest is at stake, cooperation and wise judgment should come before party loyalty.

Politics is about more than party affiliations; it requires strategic thinking, political maturity, and the ability to recognise leadership that can move a nation forward. President Tinubu has taken bold steps to reform the economy and address longstanding structural challenges. While there is still work to be done, we must assess his administration objectively, considering both the challenges and the progress made.

The support PBAT is receiving across party lines deserves serious consideration. When governors from opposition parties are willing to endorse his re-election, it is worth asking what informs their decisions. These are political leaders who understand the complexities of governance and the realities of national development. Their decisions should encourage us to look beyond partisan sentiments and examine the bigger picture.

The international community is also closely watching Nigeria’s economic reforms. Rather than dismissing every positive assessment or political endorsement, we should engage with the available evidence and judge the administration on its policies, results, and long-term impact.

Governor Adeleke’s endorsement demonstrates that political differences do not have to stand in the way of supporting a candidate. It reinforces the principle that national interest should be greater than party loyalty. Those who disagree with his decision are entitled to their opinions, but disagreement should not prevent us from considering the reasons behind it.

As we approach the 2027 presidential election, the real question is whether Nigeria should continue with the current reform agenda or change direction. My position is clear: I support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election because I believe continuity, sustained reforms, and experienced leadership offer Nigeria a strong path towards economic stability and long term prosperity.

Ultimately, our loyalty should be to Nigeria and its future. Let us rise above political sentiments, evaluate the issues objectively, and make decisions that serve the greater good of our nation.

-Onobun writes from Lagos.

World.title: Again, Tinubu Forecloses Fuel Subsidy Return, Says Nigeria Won’t Go Back
World.content:
• Oyedele: Petrol subsidy restoration ’ll devastate economy, hurt Nigerians

•Argues capital flight may push dollar to N3,000, petrol to N5,000 per litre

•Minister predicts Nigeria ’ll outperform IMF’s 4.1% growth forecast for 2026

Deji Elumoye and Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





President Bola Ahmed Tinubu last night revisited the issue of fuel subsidy removal and once again foreclosed its return, saying the nation won’t go ‘back to Egypt’ on the matter.

Also, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, has warned that restoring fuel subsidy would devastate Nigeria’s economy, trigger capital flight, weaken the naira and ultimately impose a heavier burden on Nigerians through higher petrol prices.

But speaking at a special engagement tagged: “An Evening with the Original City Boy,” at the Conference hall of the State House, Abuja, the president likened the fuel subsidy removal to passages in both the Bible and the Quran.

“I remember my scripture studies, both in the Bible and in the Holy Quran. When Moses and Musa left Egypt, they faced a challenge, and the Red Sea parted and gave way. You cannot ask Moses to go back to Egypt,” he maintained.

He stressed that the decision to remove petrol subsidy on his first day in office was necessary to confront longstanding economic challenges, insisting that the country could not afford to reverse the reforms despite renewed promises by some political opponents to restore the subsidy regime.

“I removed the fuel subsidy on my first day in office. Nigeria will not go back to that era. I hear my political opponents promising a return to the subsidy regime, but Nigeria must win this election before any candidate does,” he said.

Tinubu declared that Nigeria would not reverse the economic reforms introduced since he assumed office in May 2023, despite the challenges associated with their implementation.

He defended his administration’s economic policies and reaffirmed his determination to build a more prosperous Nigeria.

The president recalled the economic difficulties inherited by his government, including what he described as excessive currency printing, fiscal pressures and structural weaknesses, explaining that his government had since embarked on reforms in taxation, monetary management and other critical sectors to reposition the economy.

He added: “Currency was being printed as if there was no tomorrow. That was a challenge, but rather than looking back, we took steps to address it and rebuild our tax system.”

Tinubu expressed satisfaction with the support of young Nigerians for his reform agenda, noting that despite predictions that the younger generation would reject the difficult policies, their continued engagement demonstrated confidence in the country’s future.

The president said the enthusiasm and commitment of members of the City Boy Movement reinforced his conviction that the sacrifices associated with the ongoing reforms would contribute to building a stronger nation.

“I did not see a crowd. I saw Nigeria,” Tinubu declared, explaining that the gathering reminded him of the reasons he sought the presidency and his daily commitment to national development.

He commended the movement for establishing extensive grassroots structures across states, local government areas and wards, describing its organisational approach, verifiable membership database, communication platforms and community engagement initiatives as an example of purposeful youth participation in national affairs.

Highlighting his administration’s youth-focused interventions, the president identified the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), which had supported more than one million students, as a significant initiative designed to ensure that financial limitations did not prevent young Nigerians from accessing higher education.

He also referenced the Nigerian Consumer Credit Corporation (CREDICORP), established to expand access to credit for workers seeking to acquire essential assets, including laptops, vehicles, motorcycles and solar energy systems.

Similarly, he highlighted the Three Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme as part of the administration’s efforts to equip young Nigerians with globally competitive digital skills and opportunities to participate in the international technology economy.

Tinubu reaffirmed his commitment to appointing more qualified young Nigerians into positions of responsibility, maintaining that those who would inherit the consequences of today’s policy decisions deserved opportunities to participate in shaping them.

In a direct speech to his son and Patron of the City Boy Movement, Seyi Tinubu, the president urged him to deepen his commitment to public service, youth engagement and responsible leadership.

“My son, Seyi, you have only started. Do more. Go further. Serve harder. Set an example that your own children, my grandchildren, will be proud to follow. Nigerians are watching, and they should know that serving your country is the highest honour,” he said.

Shettima Attacks Atiku, Defends Tinubu

Earlier, Vice President Kashim Shettima picked on former Vice President Atiku Abubakar over his criticism of the Tinubu government, recalling how the president provided a political platform for Atiku during his disagreement with the then ruling Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) ahead of the 2007 presidential election.

He recalled that Atiku found political accommodation in the defunct Action Congress (AC), a party associated with Tinubu, when he sought to contest the presidency after falling out with the PDP leadership.

According to Shettima, Atiku “found refuge in the land of the Jagaban”, referencing Tinubu’s political support during that period.

He queried the consistency of some of Atiku’s present political positions, maintaining that political disagreements should not obscure important events in the country’s democratic history.

The vice president also warned opposition politicians against insulting or disrespecting Tinubu, declaring that the ruling APC would not condone malicious attacks, deliberate falsehoods or personal vilification of the President in the name of political opposition.

He noted that political competition must be conducted within acceptable standards of decency and mutual respect.

Shettima maintained that while the APC welcomed robust political engagement and constructive criticism of government policies, it would not allow opposition figures to hide behind democratic freedoms to engage in what he described as malicious fabrications against the president.

“Desperation is not insanity,” the vice president declared, warning that the pursuit of political power should not become an excuse for abandoning basic standards of responsible public conduct.

He stressed that political actors, irrespective of their affiliations or ambitions, must maintain a minimal threshold of decency in their public statements and engagements.

The APC, he said, would continue to engage opposition parties on substantive issues of governance, economic policy and national development, but would firmly challenge attempts to misrepresent the president’s record or undermine his person through what he considered unfounded attacks.

He, however, maintained that political opponents were not enemies, describing them as fellow Nigerians with competing visions for the country’s future and stressing that disagreements should not erode mutual respect or the shared responsibility of building a stronger nation.

While defending the government’s economic policies, Shettima said the administration inherited enormous financial challenges, including approximately N27 trillion in ‘Ways and Means’ obligations, weak public finances and considerable pressure on the foreign exchange market.

On his part, Deputy Senate President, Senator Barau Jibrin, urged the City Boy Movement to deploy artificial intelligence and other digital technologies to educate Nigerians about the administration’s programmes, the records of opposition politicians and the factors responsible for the country’s cost-of-living challenges.

Barau commended the movement for its technological presentation, saying its approach to communicating government policies and achievements represented a significant departure from conventional political mobilisation.

Also, Speaker of the House of Representatives, Hon Tajudeen Abbas, announced plans to launch a comprehensive public accountability initiative tagged: “The PBAT Stewardship Account,” aimed at providing Nigerians with verifiable information on projects, interventions and legislative achievements under the Tinubu administration.

Abbas disclosed that within 14 days, he would hold a media briefing to present a detailed account of interventions associated with the president, including their locations, financial values and implementation status, alongside a scorecard of the legislative achievements of the 10th House of Representatives.

Oyedele: Petrol Subsidy Restoration ’ll Devastate Economy

Meanwhile, the debate over whether to return Nigeria’s petrol subsidy has continued, with the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Oyedele, warning that restoring it would devastate Nigeria’s economy, trigger capital flight, weaken the naira and ultimately impose a heavier burden on Nigerians through higher petrol prices.

Oyedele, who spoke in an interview with Arise News Business Correspondent, Rotus Odiri, in Bangkok, Thailand, at the just-concluded International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings, said Nigeria could not afford to reverse the removal of the subsidy, insisting that the country lacked the crude oil required to sustain such a policy.

He argued that renewed subsidy commitments would undermine investor confidence, trigger a fresh depreciation of the naira and potentially push the exchange rate to between N3,000 and N4,000 to the dollar, with petrol prices rising to as much as N5,000 per litre. The interview was aired yesterday.

The minister’s comments came amid renewed political discussions around fuel prices and calls for government intervention to ease the burden of rising living costs. The call has been largely spearheaded by the candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku.

But Oyedele said the economic consequences of a return to subsidies would outweigh any immediate relief consumers might enjoy, warning politicians against presenting the policy as a viable solution to the country’s economic challenges.

“We’re at the tail end of it, which is why I keep saying if it’s a joke, anybody that is talking about reversing the subsidy should please stop it. Stop that joke. They should just stop the joke,” he said.

Explaining the rationale behind the federal government’s recent clarification on fuel prices and a 30-day discount arrangement, Oyedele said the Ministry of Finance had a responsibility to provide Nigerians with accurate economic information, particularly when political promises threatened to create unrealistic expectations.

He disclosed that the government had initially been reluctant to engage in the political debate surrounding fuel prices but eventually decided that it could not remain silent while politicians made competing promises about how cheaply petrol could be sold.

“I don’t qualify to be a politician. So I know politicians have a way of trying to hold on to something. So when this whole thing about subsidy started, I honestly thought it was a joke. It was repeated many times. Some people started believing it. Other politicians jumped on the bandwagon.

“They were giving numbers, N700, me I can even do N500, somebody said I can do N300, I said very soon it will be, I can give out for free,” he said, mocking the proponents of fuel subsidy removal.

The minister said the government’s intervention was intended to explain the economic realities behind petrol pricing and demonstrate why promises to restore subsidies could not be implemented without serious consequences.

He added that Nigeria did not have sufficient crude oil available to support such an arrangement, noting that expanding production could not be achieved within a few months.

“We have to clarify. Number two, we actually do not have the crude to give. You can’t give what you don’t have. You can blame whatever past administration for why you don’t have the crude, but it doesn’t change the fact that today, you do not have crude. And to produce crude oil is not a matter of months. It takes years,” he said.

Oyedele explained that the exchange rate remained the biggest determinant of petrol prices, warning that any policy that undermined investor confidence could worsen the very problem it was designed to solve.

He cited Indonesia as an example of the risks associated with subsidy discussions, arguing that even the announcement of a return to subsidies could influence investment decisions and capital flows.

Minister Says Capital Flight May Push Dollar to N3,000

Oyedele maintained that the government’s body language merely favouring the restoration of subsidy will not only lead to capital flight, but will generally worsen the economic state of Nigerians, saying that it was a no go area.

“When you do any subsidy, like is happening to Indonesia, just say you want to do it, not that you have even started. The capital will leave. Investment will go. And when that happens, the Naira will crash, and then the same subsidy that you are hoping will bring down the cost of fuel will now be the reason why it will go up, because the Naira exchange rate will be like N3,000, N4,000,” he maintained.

The minister also rejected the characterisation of the recent fuel discount arrangement as a subsidy, arguing that a genuine subsidy would require the government to pay from the treasury while selling petrol below its market price.

He said the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) remained wholly owned by the government, through the Ministry of Finance Incorporated and the Ministry of Petroleum Incorporated, but that government ownership alone did not make a commercial price adjustment a subsidy.

“ It’s one of the reasons why some people say it’s still a subsidy, but it’s not a subsidy unless you’re paying from the treasury and you’re selling below market price,” he said.

On the wider implications of the government’s economic reforms, Oyedele said the priority was to complete the adjustment process, stabilise the economy and ensure that income growth eventually outpaced increases in the cost of living.

He acknowledged the hardship associated with the reforms but maintained that suppressing prices artificially was not a sustainable route to prosperity.

“The objective should be that instead of trying to suppress prices, which hasn’t worked for us, it hasn’t worked for any country in the world, not one, instead of trying to suppress prices, think about how to grow income faster than prices rise. That’s how you bring prosperity and grow the middle class. And that’s exactly what we are doing as led by Mr. President himself,” he said.

On the possibility of introducing fuel taxes in the future, the minister said the government was not ruling out the policy but would only consider it when economic conditions and household incomes could accommodate the additional burden.

He explained that fuel taxes could provide dedicated funding for road infrastructure and strategic fuel reserves, allowing the government to cushion the impact of future international oil price shocks.

Oyedele admitted that several countries had reduced fuel taxes to cushion consumers during periods of elevated energy prices, but Nigeria lacked such a mechanism because it did not have a comparable fuel tax regime.

He stressed, however, that any decision to introduce the taxes would be transparent and would follow the legal process, including publication of the required order in the official gazette.

On mounting concerns about government revenues, debt servicing and conflicting fiscal statistics, the minister admitted that Nigeria had significant weaknesses in the way public financial data were reported and reconciled.

He said the Ministry of Finance had begun work to improve the quality, consistency and accessibility of fiscal information, with the aim of giving investors, development partners and Nigerians a clearer understanding of the country’s revenue position and debt obligations.

“One of our top priorities over the next few months before the end of the year is fiscal data. I’ll be honest with you, we’re not doing well in terms of reporting government data. And so different stakeholders, depending on where they get the information from, are confused. And so they report different numbers,” he said.

The minister was responding to questions about discrepancies between figures reported by the World Bank and those published by the Debt Management Office (DMO) on interest payments, as well as differing assessments of Nigeria’s tax-to-gross domestic product ratio.

He said some of the discrepancies arose because the federal government makes certain external debt payments on behalf of state governments and other subnational entities before recovering the amounts from them, sometimes after delays.

According to him, comparing federation-wide interest payments with only federal government revenue could produce misleading conclusions about the government’s capacity to service its debt.

He added that revenue figures were often drawn from different sources and presented without adequate explanations of how federal, state and federation revenues related to one another.

Oyedele said the government intended to publish clearer fiscal indicators, accompanied by explanations and detailed breakdowns, on the Ministry of Finance’s website to improve transparency and ensure that international assessments were based on properly reconciled figures.

On the growing revenue allocations to state governments, the minister said the federal government was seeking greater cooperation among the three tiers of government to translate increased public revenue into better living conditions.

He said the federal government’s primary responsibility was to maintain macroeconomic stability, while state and local governments had a central role in delivering basic education, primary healthcare, sanitation and access roads connecting farms to markets.

Although he acknowledged that some states needed to improve their spending priorities and the quality of their expenditure, he said the federal government lacked the statutory authority to compel subnational governments to act in particular ways.

“The thinking behind it is that if you look closely at the primary responsibilities of different levels of government, you’re likely to conclude that the primary responsibility of the federal government is economic, macroeconomic stability. So when inflation is moving in the wrong direction, you can’t blame the states. Maybe you can blame some of them, but just blame the federal government.

“But once those ones have been stabilised, how you deliver shared prosperity is with sub-national. So whether there’s primary school for basic education, whether there’s a clinic, whether there’s sanitation, whether the access road from farm to the market is working. It’s not the federal government,” he pointed out.

Oyedele argued that the distribution of federation revenue was more complicated than the commonly cited allocation formula suggested, pointing to derivation payments, value-added tax, stamp duties and personal income tax as revenue sources that significantly benefit states.

He said strengthening the federal government’s revenue base would enable it to support state governments with funding tied to agreed national development priorities.

On the economic outlook, the minister expressed confidence that Nigeria would outperform the IMF’s growth projections of 4.1 per cent for 2026 and 4.3 per cent for 2027.

“We will exceed the forecast that the IMF has for us for 2026. We would exceed the one for 2027. We will exceed it for 2028. We’ll exceed all of it because they’re conservative. And you know they have the opportunity to always revise it. We expect they will revise it again very soon, upwards,” he assured.

World.title: Tinubu, Oborevwori, Others Mourn as Ex-Delta Gov, Emmanuel Uduaghan, Dies at 71
World.content:
• State govt declares three days of mourning

•I love you yesterday, today and forever,’ daughter, Orode, grieves

Deji Elumoye, Chuks Okocha, Sunday Aborisade, Kuni Tyessi in Abuja, Sunday Ehigiator in Lagos and Sylvester Idowu in Warri





President Bola Tinubu has mourned former Governor of Delta State, Dr Emmanuel Uduaghan, who died yesterday aged 71.

The Uduaghan family announced his death in a statement by a family member, Toju Anire Uduaghan, describing his passing as a profound loss to the family, the people of Delta State, and Nigeria.

“It is with hearts weighed down by immeasurable grief and profound sorrow that we announce the passing to glory of our beloved Father, Brother, Uncle, and Patriarch, His Excellency, Dr. Chief Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, former Governor of Delta State, who departed this world on the morning of 19th October 2026,” the statement read.

The family said Uduaghan’s death had left a deep void, describing him as a beloved family patriarch, respected elder, and a figure whose life and public service touched many people across Delta State and the country.

“His passing is an immeasurable loss to our family, the people of Delta State, and Nigeria at large,” the statement added.

The family also expressed gratitude for his life and service, praying for the repose of his soul and for comfort for relatives, friends, associates, and others mourning his death.

In a condolence message, Tinubu extended his commiserations to the Uduaghan family, the government, and the people of Delta State.

The president stated, “Dr Uduaghan was a public servant whose leadership was devoted to Delta State’s development and service to our nation.

“He served as Commissioner for Health, Secretary to the State Government and was elected Governor of Delta State in 2007. His two-term tenure, which ended in 2015, placed him at the centre of the state’s political and developmental journey.

“During this period, he pursued developmental strides to improve infrastructure, healthcare delivery, and the overall welfare of Deltans.

“After his tenure as governor, Dr Uduaghan continued to feature prominently in Delta State’s political and socio-economic landscape, contributing to the sustenance of democratic governance and the advancement of public service in Nigeria. His passing is a great loss to his family, his community, Delta State, and the nation at large.

“At this difficult time, I urge the people of Delta State to draw strength from the late governor’s years of service and the enduring relationships he built across the political and social terrain of our country.

“On behalf of my family, the government, and the people of Nigeria, I extend my deepest sympathies to his wife, Roli; his children; his cousin, former Governor James Ibori; and friends and political associates whose lives he impacted.

“May Almighty God grant his soul eternal rest and comfort all who mourn him.”

Delta State Government

Delta State Government declared three days of mourning in honour of Uduaghan.

The mourning period took effect from Monday, October 19.

In honour of the late former governor, the incumbent governor, Hon. Sheriff Oborevwori, directed that all flags on public buildings across the state should be flown at half-mast throughout the three-day mourning period.
