World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: The rioting across France is a symptom of a much larger public and political crisis
World.content:
“We have a mess on our hands, to put it bluntly,” French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said Monday.

If anything, he might be guilty of understatement. After widespread rioting at the weekend – estimated to have cost several hundred million dollars in property damage and theft – France faces a toxic mix of urban rebellion, political drift and economic crisis.

The disorder at the weekend occurred in major cities across the country, leading Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to offer his resignation because of the police’s failure to contain the rioting.

There was rampant looting in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities, while the city hall in Limoges, which survived two world wars, was badly damaged by fire and its clock spire collapsed.

The violence at the weekend, which led to some 2,400 arrests, followed weeks of protests by French students angry about crumbling schools, a lack of teachers and dismal job prospects. More than 6,000 arrests were made during the school protests that began at the start of the fall term and more than 100 schools were damaged.

More demonstrations are scheduled for next weekend. In November, labor unions plan to strike.

France faces a winter of discontent in the run-up to a presidential election next spring. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls.

Political drift

French President Emmanuel Macron meets with the Emir of Kuwait (unseen) at Bayan Palace in Kuwait City on October 19, 2026. The French president arrived in Kuwait on October 19, beginning a tour of four Gulf countries, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain and Qatar. (Photo by Benoit Tessier / POOL / AFP via Getty Images) Benoit Tessier/Pool/AFP/Getty Images

In a national televised address Sunday, President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence but did not set out ideas to deal with it or seize the initiative. Instead, he warned of politicians seizing on the chaos for political gain – before leaving France for a three-day visit to the Gulf states.

Lecornu similarly deployed the blame game. After far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the government of “opening the door to chaos” with its policing tactics, Lecornu shot back: “You cannot call for an end to the violence while providing excuses to those who commit it. This is YOUR political responsibility.”

Le Pen, who is standing in the presidential election for the far-right National Rally party, has sought to inject the issue of migration into the debate, blaming the violence on delinquents from France’s banlieues, poor urban areas where much of the country’s migrant population lives.

“Our country is caught in a vice…between violence and powerlessness,” she said, suggesting only her firm hand could restore order amid Macron’s “chaos.”

The president of her National Rally party, Jordan Bardella, poured fuel on the fire, demanding that “Antifa militias, far-left extremist groups and Black Bloc groups” be designated as terrorist organisations.”

Black Bloc groups wear matching or similar black clothing along with face masks during protests to hide their identity.

Analysts say this political fragmentation, which led to the paralysis of parliament after snap elections called by Macron in 2024 backfired, is likely to persist – and is at the core of France’s deepening crisis.

The political center in France has evaporated, allowing the National Rally and Mélenchon’s far-left France Unbowed party to harvest growing public exasperation, while Macron’s successive prime ministers have been unable to pass a budget through Parliament.

The multitude of candidates in the center, “most with relatively few supporters, will ultimately help secure the second-round election for one of the two contenders who represent the greatest danger to democracy in France,” wrote Robert Zaretsky, a professor of modern French history at the University of Houston, in an essay for the Atlantic.

Debt and déclinisme

Protesters hold signs during a demonstration as part of nationwide protests called by the “Yellow Vests” movement against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, joined by French high school and university students, teachers and parents demanding better school conditions and government action, as well as labour unions, workers, farmers and retirees, in Nantes, France, October 17, 2026. Stephane Mahe/Reuters

The current crisis has polarized an already deeply divided society. Besides the shock and anger at the weekend’s mayhem, there is an air of defeatism. In a recent Ipsos-BVA poll, 85% of respondents said that France was in decline, and 98% were dissatisfied with the present state of the country.

Whoever governs France next will have shrinking room for maneuver, even if they can stitch together a stable coalition.

The French economy is stagnating. Farmers were hit by an extremely hot and dry summer, while global energy prices stoked inflation.

Tourism remains a strong earner for France, but the videos of violence on the streets circling the globe in the past two days may deter some travelers.

French businesses are wary of the drift and indecision. Investment has fallen about 1% in the first half of this year amid climbing interest rates.

Above all, there is the debt.

“France carries one of the highest government debt burdens in Europe, and political deadlock means we expect its debt level to continue rising,” researchers at Oxford Economics said in July.

France will have to issue a record high of €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds next year, according to analysts. Its debt as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP) rose to 119% in the second quarter of this year, double the European Union’s target.

Jittery investors sent the country’s 10-year government bond yield up to 4.9% on Monday.

Its reputation in bond markets is not helped by Mélenchon’s plan to freeze or wipe away the French sovereign bonds held by the Bank of France.

A vandalized Serge Lutens storefront a day after clashes during a national day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris, France, October 18, 2026. REUTERS/Benoit Tessier TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY Benoit Tessier/Reuters

“Political fragmentation may persist well after the 2027 elections, meaning that France’s next government will continue to kick the public-finance can down the road,” said Oxford Economics. This would “prolong the existing climate of high uncertainty, weighing on confidence and domestic demand.”

The man most revered by the French, General Charles de Gaulle, once declared that “France cannot be France without grandeur.” De Gaulle had soaring ambitions for the country’s global role and independence.

But during his long presidency he also told an aide: “I keep the theater going as long as I can and then, after me, have no illusion, things will go back to where they were.”

De Gaulle stepped down a year after the 1968 riots that shook France – events that some commentators are likening to today’s shock.

When he became president, Macron was seen as the antidote to what the French call déclinisme (a word that first appeared in the French Larousse dictionary in 2016.)

“He delivers an extremely positive, constructive message, full of hope for the future. He shows that there is also another France,” wrote one commentator.

A decade later, Macron’s approval rating is hovering at about 15 to 17%, according to multiple polls Déclinisme is still very much on the lips of a citizenry that is demanding more from a beleaguered state that has less.

World.title: She made an anti-war drawing as a child in Russia. Four years on, she’s still living with the fallout
World.content:
Masha Moskalyova has spent a quarter of her life in jeopardy or on the run because of a picture she drew when she was just 12 years old.

Four years on, she and her father are living in hiding in a small village in eastern France and still worry about their safety. One of the few things they still have of their former lives in Russia is the drawing itself.

“Even though it’s a child’s drawing and seems so simple, who could have expected it to have such consequences?” Masha says, as we consider the drawing together. Drawn in colored pencil, it shows a mother protecting her child from the bombs being launched from Russia. A Ukrainian flag reads “Glory to Ukraine,” while a Russian flag beside says, “No Putin, no war.”

She drew it just a few weeks after Russia had invaded Ukraine in 2022. In her hometown of Yefremov, about 300 kilometers (185 miles) south of Moscow and about halfway to the border with Ukraine, Masha’s teacher had asked the class to draw pictures supporting Russian troops. Most of the children drew tanks, or the letter Z, used by Russia as a pro-war symbol. Masha, who is now 16, decided to do something else.

“I drew the situation as I actually saw it, what I believed to be the truth,” she says. “After the lesson, one of my classmates, who had seen the drawing, came up to me. Perhaps she was the one who reported it, leading to everything that followed. In any case, the drawing ended up in the hands of the police. And that was when all our problems began.”

Shortly after that her father, Alexey Moskalyov, was charged with “discrediting the Russian military” and sentenced to two years in a penal colony. Masha, whom he’d been raising alone, was sent to an orphanage.

After his release, the pair fled, traveling through Armenia and onto France, where they arrived earlier this year and where they have been given a temporary visa.

A dog that Masha had been given in the orphanage has now arrived from Armenia, which she is pleased about. Still, what’s striking is how alone they seem, with nothing of their former lives and only each other for company.

Alexey’s health is fragile because of his time in jail and Masha is now schooled in a language she doesn’t speak. Both fear for their safety. But Alexey says he is just proud of his daughter.

“Everything I’ve lost, everything I had in Russia, is compensated for by the fact that we can now speak freely and tell the truth,” he says. “By the fact that we are now in a country where people are not persecuted for their words or their opinions.”

Masha meets her father at the prison gates after his release on October 15, 2024. OVD-Info

And words are exactly what Masha intends to keep using. Outside of school, Masha spends her time trying to reach audiences inside Russia and beyond, through YouTube and social media. And her criticism now extends to US President Donald Trump’s handshake with his Russian counterpart.

“I want to say that what Trump is doing is terrible,” she tells CNN. “The fact that the president of a free country shakes hands with a murderer,” she says, holding Russian President Vladimir Putin responsible for the deaths caused by the war in Ukraine. “The fact that you could say he is being controlled by him is another matter altogether.”

Going home remains a distant prospect. “I would return to Russia with enormous joy,” Masha says. “But when will this regime change? I don’t know. How many decades will it take? How many decades before Russia becomes a democratic and free country?”

It is hard to fathom that a single child’s drawing could have angered the Russian authorities as much as this one did, but Masha seems to get it. After all, the point of authoritarianism is that it cannot allow any dissent, however childish.

“I would return to Russia with enormous joy,” Masha told CNN. Courtesy of Alexey Moskalyov

“Here was a child who spoke the truth, who wasn’t afraid,” she says. “And if that child isn’t alone, if there are many children like her, if it’s not just one teenager but a thousand teenagers, not just one adult but a million, then that is what will change Russia for the better.”

The last four years have clearly taken their toll on Masha, who seems mature beyond her years and graver than any 16-year-old should be.

Perhaps the most surprising thing is that after everything she has endured – being sent to the orphanage, her father’s incarceration and their time on the road – she still has the drawing in her possession.

It was as they were preparing to flee their home that she found it on a shelf by chance, among her childhood notebooks.

“It hadn’t been confiscated,” she says. “They hadn’t found it or paid any attention to it. Perhaps because the police hadn’t thought to search through a child’s belongings.”

So, today, one of Masha’s only belongings from her former life is the very drawing that ended it.

World.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery
World.content:
Rome —

Pope Leo XIV left hospital Saturday, four days after undergoing lung cancer surgery in a swift return to his duties following the first health scare of his papacy.

Leo walked out of hospital unaided, greeting well-wishers, including a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl who gave him a stuffed toy as a gift.

The 71-year-old first American pope was admitted to the Gemelli hospital on Tuesday with doctors removing a nodule that was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

Leo was deemed ready to leave hospital after blood tests and an X-ray, his doctors said ahead of his release.

He is due to offer the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St. Peter’s Square on Sunday, a week after he announced he would need surgery.

News of the pope’s illness has been met with shock and concern inside the Vatican, while raising questions about what this means for his papacy.

Pope Leo was elected last May at the relatively young age of 69 and is in good physical shape. As a cardinal living in Rome, he had a personal trainer and is known to enjoy sports such as tennis and swimming.

The pope is scheduled to make a packed trip to Latin America from 6-17 November, including Uruguay, Argentina, and a “homecoming” to Peru where he served as a missionary and bishop for years. The Vatican is remaining cautious about those travel plans.

“We need to see how the Pope feels once he is discharged—what his state of health is—and based on that, he will decide whether to keep or cancel his trips,” Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Holy See Secretary of State, told reporters Friday.

Since his surgery, however, the pope has worked from the hospital, receiving cardinals and having a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, where he raised the plight of civilians in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

The pontiff’s doctors told reporters on Saturday there were “no clinical reasons” why his visit to Latin America next month should not take place. They said they expected it would take a couple weeks for Leo to make a “truly complete physical recovery.”

Past popes have written letters of resignation in case of a severe illness or medical emergency that impedes them from carrying out their duties.

Parolin, however, told reporters that he didn’t think Leo had made such a provision. “I don’t think he left anything. It didn’t even seem to me that there was any need and that the matter was so serious to be able to foresee an absence of government.”

Just days before his surgery, however, the pope had confirmed Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle as the Dean of the College of Cardinals.

The dean, who is the “first among equals” leader of the college, plays a crucial role in presiding over a conclave (providing he’s under 80) and the pre-conclave meetings. Any future papal election is considered far into the future. But the appointment of the 69-year-old Tagle, a charismatic figure previously tipped as a possible pope, was an important piece of housekeeping.

This story has been updated. Sharon Braithwaite, Barbie Latza Nadeau and Stefano Pozzebon contributed reporting.

World.title: Elon Musk says he will give a SpaceX share to ‘every kid in America’
World.content:
London —

Elon Musk has said he will give every child in America a stake in SpaceX, his $2 trillion aerospace and artificial intelligence company, as tech firms face intensifying scrutiny over their impact on society.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” he wrote on X on Monday. “This will be the first of many.”

SpaceX only began trading publicly in June (and had the biggest initial public offering in history). The company’s shares were trading for about $146 when the market closed on Friday.

Musk’s proposal was thin on detail. It is not clear how those shares would be distributed to the tens of millions of American children or whether all of them would even be eligible.

According to the United States Census Bureau, there are roughly 73 million people under the age of 18, making Musk’s potential giveaway worth about $10.7 billion at SpaceX’s current share price.

Offering young people a stake in the US stock market isn’t a new idea. This month, the Treasury Department automatically signed up millions of under-18s to Trump Accounts, a new federal savings and investment vehicle, with children born between the start of 2025 and the end of 2028 eligible for a one-off $1,000 government contribution.

Damage control?

Musk’s offer came in response to Anthropic’s announcement on Sunday that it will commit at least 5% of its shares — worth $48 billion at the private company’s latest valuation — to a “Public Benefit Fund” that will donate money to social causes.

The fund could make “large donations” to non-profit organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations,” the company wrote on its website, adding that the money could help mitigate the impact of artificial intelligence on people’s jobs.

Musk retorted on X: “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public… This is what I will be doing.”

Both offers come as AI companies face intense backlash over the safety of their products (Anthropic itself recently warned of the “existential risk to humanity” posed by the technology), the potential for AI to push humans out of their jobs en masse, as well as the social and environmental impact of the industry’s gargantuan data center build-out.

Tech titans more broadly are catching heat.

New movies like “The Social Reckoning” — about a Facebook employee blowing the whistle on unsafe company practices — and documentary “You Can See Everything” — following blood testing start-up founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes — are helping to remind audiences of the long-running recklessness of some in Big Tech.

Musk himself is the subject of the new documentary “Musk,” charting his life and career. It is unsparing in its criticism of some of his business practices and controversial foray into politics.

World.title: France’s Macron vows to hold accountable those who ‘sought to bring down the Republic’ during major protests
World.content:
France’s President Emmanuel Macron addressed the nation on Sunday evening as communities reeled from one of the most violent nights of unrest in recent years after largely peaceful anti-government protests descended into rioting, leaving government buildings torched, one police officer and one protester dead.

Macron said that the full force of the law would be brought to bear on those who had damaged property or participated in rioting.

“Those who destroyed must pay,” Macron said. “Those who looted must pay back. Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.”

Macron described the violence as the work of “seditious elements from far-left factions, joined by numerous delinquents.”

“Watching these images, we were all wondering: what had got into them? How can French people do that to France?”

“Nothing can justify it, explain it or excuse it,” Macron said. “Tonight we all feel both anger and shame.”

The president added that the government should listen to public grievances, and that many protesters did not participate in violence.

“Yesterday, hundreds of thousands of our compatriots demonstrated to state legitimate claims,” Macron said. “Never must we confuse the latter with those who destroyed and vandalized.”

Macron said that he had asked the government to convene stakeholders – including students, teachers, trade unionists and others – this week to discuss “concrete proposals.”

There were at least two deaths connected to rioting and protests over the weekend. A 22-year-old police officer died after being “struck by a third-party vehicle” in the city of Nantes, about 250 miles southwest of Paris, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.

One protester died just north of Paris following a “cardiorespiratory arrest,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported on Sunday, citing the Paris Police headquarters.

Police have detained more than 2,000 people, Nunez said,adding that more than 600 police officers were injured.

Scenes unfolded again on Sunday of police officers launching tear gas into the hallowed Place de la République, where dozens of people gathered in response to messages on social media to “continue the movement,” BFMTV reported. In the central city of Limoges, the 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze on Saturday, with video showing its spire collapsing. In Marseille, masked protesters dressed all in black broke into city hall and defaced the building, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.

Lawmakers and regional officials launched mounting criticism over the government’s law enforcement plan, BFMTV said, with French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu set to meet the mayors of Paris, Lyon and Marseille, who called for greater reinforcement to repair the damage.

As night fell in Paris on Saturday, groups of young people looted shops and started fires as protests wound down, prompting police to respond with tear gas and baton charges in the narrow streets. Alexandre Bompard, CEO of retail giant Carrefour, said in a social media post Sunday that around 1,500 stores across the country were affected by violence.

More than 600 police officers have been injured, France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nunez posted on X on Sunday, warning that “nothing can justify” the unrest. Earlier this weekend, Lecornu also condemned “unacceptable levels of violence.”

The destruction followed what had been largely peaceful protests, which have grown out of sweeping student-led rallies that gripped parts of France last month, sparking a broader movement against crumbling schools, the spiking cost of living, and perceived government inaction. The rallies have become emblematic of long-simmering, intergenerational anger among people who say their calls for social and political change are going unmet by negligent governments.

Some 550,000 protesters hit the streets across France, including 110,000 in Paris, Nunez said on Saturday. Organizers said far more people turned out.

“There’s an accumulation of wealth and power that’s completely out of control,” one protester, who gave her name as Pauline, told CNN in Paris on Saturday.

“We’re also here to support the youth. There are victories, but if we look at the bigger picture, it’s not going in the right direction,” the 36-year-old added.

Another demonstrator complained of “less democracy” and a “concentration of power” under Macron’s leadership. “There are billionaires who control the media,” Louise, 38, told CNN. “We are fighting to change things.”

Macron slammed “sowers of chaos” for interfering with peaceful protests, and warned late on Saturday that “those who have broken, attacked (police) prefectures, as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.”

French police detain a protester during clashes prior to the start of a demonstration in Marseille, southern France, on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty Images

“We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who’ve come to attack law enforcement,” said the Paris Police Prefecture – the body that oversees the Paris Police Force, emergency services and various other administrative departments – adding that its staffers stood “their ground with courage and professionalism.”

‘Two worlds, two realities’

The police response to the weeks of protest has come under scrutiny. Earlier in the week, that response had left a 14-year-old boy with a fractured jaw. Another police officer was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in the northwestern area of Alençon, an action now prohibited by law.

This is the second reported instance of a demonstrator losing their hand in the current wave of student protests.

A student in the northeastern city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade earlier this month, prompting the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police. That ban, which still allowed police to use several different grenades, has now been rescinded.

Overall, authorities said that the “vast majority of individuals” had demonstrated peacefully on Saturday, according to BFMTV.

Police officers charge at demonstrators at Place de la Republique in Paris on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Geoffroy Van Der Hasselt/AFP/Getty Images General view of the Place de la Republique as protesters walk through tear gas during a demonstration at the Place de la Republique in Paris on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Jack Taylor/Reuters

Posting on X, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left La France Insoumise Party, emphasized that the majority of demonstrators on Sunday had made their point peacefully. “While news channels are flooded with images of violence in dozens of cities, everything is unfolding peacefully with tens of thousands of people calmly mobilized. Two worlds, two realities.”

Masked protesters raise their arms as they face off with French riot police during a demonstration in a street near the Gare du Nord train station in Paris on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Abdul Saboor/Reuters

Youth activists also led solidarity protests in Belgium, Albania and Italy, where police arrested more than 70 people for identification in the city of Milan on Sunday, according to CNN affiliate SkyTG24.

Reuters reported Sunday that police in Milan clashed with stone-throwing demonstrators for a second day, with law enforcement firing tear gas and water cannons in response. SkyTG24 shared video from a supermarket in Milan, showing the windows smashed out and merchandise scattered over the floor after looting.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the looting in a statement posted on social media, and said that she will convene a meeting in Rome on Monday to “evaluate further measures against those who exploit legitimate demonstrations to sow violence and chaos.”

The wave of protests in France has its roots in the country’s public school system. Earlier this fall, French high school students organized scattered protests demanding reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investments in infrastructure designed to withstand the climate crisis and an end to police violence against young people.

In the past decade and a half, a rise in fertility coupled with funding cuts has led to more students, but fewer teachers in classrooms. The French Education Minister Edouard Geffray has met with student protesters multiple times in recent weeks, although an agreement is yet to be made.

This story has been updated with additional information.

World.title: Amid US pressure on settler violence, Israel arrests at least 10 suspected of West Bank attacks on journalist, diplomats
World.content:
Jerusalem — Amid US pressure on a surge of settler violence in the occupied West Bank, Israeli police arrested at least 10 suspects in the weekend attacks on a Washington Post journalist and an entourage of European diplomats.

Police said the operation to locate and arrest the suspects was called “Olive Leaf,” an apparent reference to the recent start of the olive harvest in the West Bank, which has seen a dramatic rise in settler attacks.

On Friday, settlers attacked and hospitalized veteran Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine as she traveled with a group of Palestinians at the start of the olive harvest. One day later, settlers attacked a group of European diplomats visiting the Palestinian Christian town of Taybeh.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee welcomed the arrests as a “very positive development in finding & punishing those who severely attacked and beat Heidi Levine.”

American freelance photojournalist Heidi Levine leaves the emergency room of the government hospital in the Israeli-occupied city of Ramallah, after being treated following an attack by Israeli settlers as she photographed Palestinian farmers harvesting their olives, in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah on October 16, 2026. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

According to police, security forces worked with the Israeli military to locate and arrest the suspects across the area with the attacks took place. “During this activity, 10 suspects were arrested, findings linking them to the incidents were sized and several vehicles were confiscated,” police said.

“We are working to collect evidence, findings and testimonies and to consolidate an evidentiary infrastructure that will enable bringing those involved to justice,” said Israel Police Superintendent Moshe Pinchi in a statement.

Israeli human rights group Yesh Din documented more than 530 incidents of settler violence since the beginning of the olive harvest in late-September, averaging 27 violent incidents each day. According to Yesh Din, Israeli soldiers were present at roughly one quarter of the attacks over this period.

Palestinians harvest their olive trees in the Israeli-occupied West Bank village of Deir Abu Mashal on October 19, 2026. Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images Palestinian Amal Abu Awad, 62, collects olives during the harvest in the West Bank town of Turmus Ayya, Sunday, October 18, 2026. Leo Correa/AP

On Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Trump administration has told Israel that the US “doesn’t want to see a new spark” in the West Bank and called on Israel to take action against settler violence.

“We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff,” said Rubio before his flight to India and Uzbekistan. “The President has been very clear. He’s said this repeatedly. He does not want to see friction or anything – a crisis – going on in the West Bank.”

Despite video of the attacks on both Levine, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has tried to cast doubt on the violence, saying afterwards that “serious questions remain.” In an apparent attempt to avoid upsetting his right-wing voter base so close to Israel’s elections, Netanyahu has repeatedly downplayed the severity and scale of settler violence, claiming it’s carried out by a rogue group.

Palestinian farmers, accompanied by Israeli and international activists, return to the land where an attack took place the previous day to harvest olives during olive harvest but are prevented from proceeding by Israeli forces on October 17, 2026 in Abu Falah, West Bank. Faiz Abu Rmeleh/Getty Images

Meanwhile, Israel’s defense minister said on Monday he would not reinstate administrative detention against Jewish Israelis, which allows authorities to hold suspects without charge or trial. The draconian measure was one of Israel’s most effective tools against settler extremism, but the defense minister cancelled its use against Jewish Israelis as one of his first decisions nearly two years ago.

On Sunday, President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election, which will take place on October 27, calling him “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant.” For weeks, Trump had sidestepped questions on whether Netanyahu should be re-elected, including just days earlier when he said, “I don’t trust anyone in the world of politics.”

World.title: Egypt highlights private sector role in healthcare development, pharmaceutical localization
World.content:
Minister of Health and Population Khaled Abdel Ghaffar stressed the private sector’s central role in Egypt’s healthcare development, particularly in localizing pharmaceutical and vaccine production, which currently meets more than 91 percent of domestic market needs, as well as managing healthcare facilities and delivering high-quality services.

He made the remarks during a high-level roundtable organized by the American Chamber of Commerce in Egypt, attended by healthcare and pharmaceutical industry leaders and representatives of major international and local companies operating in the medical and pharmaceutical sectors.

Abdel Ghaffar outlined the main pillars of Egypt’s national healthcare strategy and the government’s efforts to ensure equitable access to high-quality medical services for citizens across all governorates.

He highlighted the gradual shift from reactive curative care to proactive preventive healthcare through expanded screening and early-detection programs. He also cited President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s support for efforts to reduce hepatitis C infection rates, culminating in Egypt’s receipt of international Gold Tier recognition on the path to eliminating the disease.

The minister also highlighted the Universal Health Insurance System and legislation regulating private-sector investment in healthcare infrastructure, saying these measures provide investors with a secure and stable legislative framework.

The ministry is accelerating digital transformation and automating administrative procedures for licensing medical facilities and registering pharmaceutical products, in full coordination with the Egyptian Drug Authority, he said.

Abdel Ghaffar underscored the government’s efforts to establish a transparent investment climate underpinned by predictability and regulatory stability, reducing paperwork and facilitating the introduction of advanced technologies and modern treatment solutions to the Egyptian market, thereby encouraging innovation and investment.

He also said Egypt’s healthcare system had demonstrated its capacity to withstand ongoing regional challenges and crises, reaffirming the government’s commitment to removing obstacles facing domestic and foreign investors and strengthening Egypt’s position as a leading regional hub for healthcare and medical tourism.

World.title: Madbouly stresses commitment to developing social protection system
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly affirmed the government’s commitment to continuing to develop the social protection system and enhance integration among government policies and programs in a manner that helps meet citizens’ basic needs, ensures the efficient allocation of resources, and reaches the most vulnerable groups.This came during a meeting held by the prime minister on Sunday, October 18, 2026 to follow up on the latest developments regarding the session entitled “Market Regulation and a More Effective Social Protection System,” as part of ongoing preparations for the “Egypt Forum 2026,” which is scheduled to begin tomorrow and run through October 24 in the New Administrative Capital.

The meeting was attended by Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy, Supply and Internal Trade Minister Sherif Farouk, Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom, and Head of the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS) Akram al-Gohary.

At the beginning of the meeting, Madbouly stressed that it was being held as part of the follow-up to preparations for the “Market Regulation and a More Effective Social Protection System” session at Egypt Forum 2026, given the importance of this issue and its direct connection to the state’s efforts to improve citizens’ quality of life and strengthen social stability.

During the meeting, the main themes of the session were reviewed to ensure that it addresses the various dimensions of social protection and security, highlights the state’s efforts to strengthen the social protection system and support food security, and promotes integration among government policies and programs. These efforts aim to ensure the efficient allocation of available resources and improve citizens’ living standards.

The meeting also reviewed the government’s efforts to ensure that essential commodities are available in adequate quantities and that supplies remain regular. Discussions covered measures to enhance market stability through continuous monitoring of stock levels, intensified inspections of markets and retail outlets, and action against monopolistic practices and attempts to manipulate prices, thereby protecting consumer rights and helping ease the cost-of-living burden on citizens.

The meeting further addressed the objectives for the coming phase and mechanisms for developing relevant programs and initiatives. It emphasized the importance of highlighting achievements and existing challenges in order to improve government performance, enhance responsiveness to the needs of target groups, and support the state’s efforts to consolidate social protection and security.

World.title: Liberia Bets Its Future on Iron, Gold and Power
World.content:
MONROVIA — For most of the past half-century, Liberia’s mineral wealth has been a story told in the past tense. In the 1960s and 1970s, iron ore from the Nimba and Bong ranges made this small West African nation one of the world’s leading exporters of the steelmaking ingredient. Then came 14 years of civil war, and the mines, railways and ports fell silent.

By Rodney D. Sieh

This month, the government is staking its economic future on rewriting that story in the present tense.



On October 28 and 29, Liberia will host the first Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference & Expo, known as LIMEC 2026, a gathering of ministers, mining executives, energy developers, financiers and development partners. Organized jointly by the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the Liberia Chamber of Mines and the London-based events firm AME Trade Ltd, the conference will be held at the Farmington Hotel under the theme “Powering Prosperity: Sustainable Mining and Energy as Catalysts for Liberia’s Economic Transformation.” Organizers say ongoing and planned projects could draw more than $3 billion in new investment.

Launching the event at a news conference over the weekend, Mines and Energy Minister R. Matenokay Tingban framed it as a turning point.

“Our message to the international investment community is clear: Liberia is open for responsible business, committed to reform, and ready to build mutually beneficial partnerships,” he said.

But he attached a condition that will be closely watched by the companies already operating here. “Our natural resources must serve not only the interests of investors but also the broader aspirations of the Liberian people,” he said.

That tension — between courting capital and capturing a fairer share of its rewards — runs through every part of Liberia’s resource economy today.

From boom to ruin, and back

Liberia, founded in 1847 and Africa’s oldest republic, built much of its post-war-era economy on concessions: rubber, timber and, above all, iron ore. The Liberian American-Swedish Minerals Company (LAMCO) in Nimba County and the German-backed Bong Mines were among the largest mining operations in Africa, linked by dedicated railways to the ports of Buchanan and Monrovia.

The civil wars of 1989 to 2003 destroyed that system. Rail lines were stripped for scrap, ports decayed, and an industry that once underpinned the national budget vanished.

The revival began in 2005, when Mittal Steel — now ArcelorMittal, the world’s second-largest steelmaker — signed a Mineral Development Agreement to restart mining in Nimba and rebuild the 250-kilometer (155-mile) railway to Buchanan. First exports followed in 2011. But the Ebola epidemic of 2014-15 and a collapse in iron ore prices slowed ambitions, and for more than a decade the company shipped around 5 million metric tons a year.

Liberia also opened its first commercial gold mine, New Liberty in Grand Cape Mount County, which began production in 2016 after Turkey’s MNG Gold rescued the Ebola-stricken project.

What has changed in the past 18 months is scale.

The ArcelorMittal factor

ArcelorMittal Liberia remains the anchor of the sector, accounting for roughly 90 percent of the country’s iron ore exports. Its $1.8 billion expansion, built around a new concentrator at Tokadeh in Nimba County, lifts the company’s total investment in Liberia to about $3.5 billion — the largest foreign direct investment since the war.

In January, lawmakers ratified a third amendment to the company’s agreement, extending it to 2050 with an option to renew for a further 25 years. In return, ArcelorMittal agreed to pay $200 million upfront for the extended mining rights and reserved rail capacity, and annual license fees rose tenfold, from $50,000 to $500,000. The payment alone represented roughly 16 percent of the national budget, according to the credit insurer Coface.

The results are already visible. ArcelorMittal Liberia set production and shipment records in 2025, shipping about 10 million tons. The company initially targeted 20 million tons for 2026 but now guides to 18 million, citing heavy rains that slowed mining and port operations in the second quarter. It is also upgrading the railway to carry up to 30 million tons a year should it decide to expand further.

For the government, the deal secured long-term certainty from its largest investor. For ArcelorMittal, LIMEC is likely to be a stage on which it can present itself as a partner in Liberia’s ambitions — while watching carefully how far the reform agenda reaches into existing contracts.

Breaking the rail monopoly

The most consequential structural change in Liberia’s mining economy may not be a mine at all, but a railway.

For two decades, ArcelorMittal held exclusive use of the Yekepa-to-Buchanan line. Under President Joseph Boakai’s multi-user rail policy, that is ending. In December 2025, the Legislature ratified a 25-year Concession and Access Agreement with Ivanhoe Atlantic, a U.S. company founded by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, valued at $1.8 billion.

The deal allows Ivanhoe to haul ultra-high-grade iron ore from its Kon Kweni project in neighboring Guinea — which holds about 752 million tons of direct-shipping ore, including 209 million tons grading 67.8 percent iron — across Liberia to Buchanan. The company plans initial output of 2 million to 5 million tons a year, with exports through Liberia expected from 2027, and an eventual second phase of up to 30 million tons.

The amended ArcelorMittal agreement now requires new rail users to invest in expanding capacity to meet their own needs, an arrangement designed to turn the corridor into shared national infrastructure rather than a private asset.

The stakes are geopolitical as well as commercial. Ivanhoe markets Kon Kweni as a source of high-grade ore for Western supply chains, an alternative to the China-led Simandou mega-project elsewhere in Guinea, and the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia has publicly endorsed the deal. The corridor sits atop an estimated 12 billion tons of iron ore reserves straddling the border, much of it still under exploration licenses.

If the model works, Liberia could become a transit hub for Guinea’s landlocked southeastern deposits — earning fees, jobs and port traffic from minerals it does not even own.

Gold, grievances and the 3 percent question

If iron ore is Liberia’s success story, gold is its flashpoint.

Bea Mountain Mining Corporation, controlled by Turkish businessman Murathan Günal through Avesoro Resources, is the country’s largest industrial gold producer. It plans to double plant capacity and says the expansion will create more than 2,000 jobs. But the company has faced mounting scrutiny. A joint investigation by The Associated Press and The Gecko Project published in January documented cyanide spills into waterways, 2,200 hectares (5,436 acres) of cleared rainforest and community anger that turned deadly during 2024 protests. The company says it has reinforced its tailings dam and points to its record of rescuing the mine and safeguarding more than 1,200 Liberian jobs.

Politically, the sharpest issue is money. With gold prices near record highs — approaching $4,200 an ounce earlier this year — both senators from Grand Cape Mount County have called for the company’s agreement to be renegotiated, arguing that its flat 3 percent royalty no longer reflects the value leaving the country. The government holds a 5 percent stake in the operation. A visit by Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung, at which figures of about $1.6 billion in company revenue were discussed, stirred public outrage over the gap between that wealth and conditions in host communities.

Liberia remains a modest gold producer, at roughly 10 tons a year, and an estimated 70 percent of gold activity is informal, according to Senator Francis Dopoh, who has co-sponsored a bill to create a state-owned National Gold Company and a domestic refinery.

Rewriting the rules

These pressures have converged on a single question: Liberia’s mining law, written in 2000, is widely seen as out of date.

In February, Minister Tingban told Reuters at the Mining Indaba conference in Cape Town that a new mining code would be ready within three months. It would create a national mining company entitled to a free-carried equity stake of 10 to 15 percent in new projects, rising over time to 25 percent. Royalties would remain at 4.5 percent for iron ore and 3 percent for gold, with a new 8 percent rate for heavy mineral sands.

“We are moving from a royalty-only approach to equity participation to maximise returns,” Tingban said at the time. Whether the new equity terms would apply to existing projects, he added, would be determined by the Ministry of Justice.

Eight months on, the overhaul is still working its way through the Legislature. The House of Representatives opened public hearings in July, where the minister pressed for tougher penalties against illegal mining and mineral smuggling. The Senate has advanced an amendment reserving small-scale Class B licenses for Liberians. The Liberia Chamber of Mines, which represents the industry, has urged lawmakers to pursue a comprehensive rewrite rather than piecemeal fixes, saying investors expect fairness, consistency and transparency.

For existing operators, LIMEC arrives at a moment of regulatory uncertainty. The government’s message — welcome, but on better terms — will be tested by how it treats contracts already signed.

Power: the missing ingredient

The “energy” half of LIMEC’s title addresses what may be Liberia’s biggest structural handicap. Only about a third of Liberians — 32.7 percent — have access to electricity.

The government aims to raise that to 75 percent by 2030 under a national energy compact backed by the World Bank, while lifting renewables to 75 percent of the power mix.

There has been progress. The 88-megawatt Mount Coffee hydropower plant, rebuilt after the war, supplies nearly 70 percent of the country’s electricity. In June, President Boakai inaugurated the country’s first utility-scale solar plant, a 20-megawatt park at the Mount Coffee site, and signed a $57 million World Bank financing agreement to expand it and add battery storage. With Mount Coffee’s full capacity restored, the state utility has begun cutting costly imports from Côte d’Ivoire and Guinea through the regional CLSG power line.

For miners, reliable grid power would lower costs and make processing — and the value addition Tingban champions — more viable.

Without it, ambitions to refine gold or process ore at home will remain largely aspirational.

What it means for the economy

The macroeconomic picture is encouraging. The International Monetary Fund estimates Liberia’s economy grew 5.1 percent in 2025, up from 4 percent in 2024, and projects 5.5 percent growth this year, driven chiefly by iron ore, with support from manufacturing and construction. Inflation stood at 5.3 percent in May, and the country remains on a $210 million IMF Extended Credit Facility running through 2027.

Mining’s weight is growing fast. Extractives already accounted for more than 21 percent of domestic revenue in 2023, according to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, and mining drove roughly two-thirds of economic growth in the first three quarters of 2025, Coface estimates.

Tingban has projected that mining’s share of national output could climb from 15 percent in 2024 to as much as 50 percent as new producers — including Cavalla Resources, Westcrest, Zodiac and a revived Bao Chico — come online, with national iron ore output potentially reaching 25 million to 30 million tons.

That concentration is also the risk. The IMF projects Liberia’s current account deficit will widen sharply this year, to 18 percent of GDP from 7 percent, as fuel and mining equipment imports surge. A single company still dominates exports, and the country’s fortunes are tightly bound to iron ore prices — and therefore to Chinese steel demand — at a time when vast new supply from Guinea’s Simandou is coming to market.

And Liberia’s history offers a sobering lesson: in the decades of the LAMCO era, iron ore generated enormous export earnings while much of the population remained poor, a disparity that fed the grievances behind the country’s collapse.

The real test

Tingban himself has set the bar. “LIMEC 2026 must be measured not only by the quality of its discussions,” he said, “but also by the investments it attracts, the partnerships it builds, the jobs it helps create, and the lasting benefits it delivers to the Liberian people.”

For international investors, Liberia offers rare advantages: a rebuilt rail corridor, deep-water access, a stable currency, an IMF-backed reform program and a government openly courting capital. For Liberians, the questions are older and harder — whether this boom will build schools and power lines in Nimba and Grand Cape Mount, whether communities will be heard, and whether the country can finally turn the wealth beneath its soil into prosperity above it.

Next week’s conference will not answer those questions. But it will show whether Liberia, a generation after the guns fell silent, is ready to be judged by them.

World.title: Liberia: Rising Poverty, Economic Constraints and Drug Addiction Push Young Liberian Women Into Transactional Sex; Plea For Help, Empowerment
World.content:
MONROVIA – By eight o’clock on most evenings, the young women have already taken their places. Near an unfinished building in the VOA community of Brewerville City, outside Monrovia, they stand in the spots they know are best for catching the attention of passing men. They have a name for those men: “customers.” They have a name, too, for what they do. They call it “hustling.”

By Obediah Johnson

The word sounds like ambition. In this place it means survival. The young women are mostly between 18 and 24 years old, although teenagers are among them. They sell sex for sums so small that they would barely cover a snack in some parts of the world, and they do it night after night, driven by poverty, grief and, for some, the pull of drug addiction.



Their faces, observers say, show frustration, anger and despair. Behind those expressions lie stories of lost parents, interrupted schooling and a country where economic hardship continues to squeeze families who had little to begin with.

A Night That Begins at Eight

Rita, who asked that her real name not be used, is one of the regulars. She is 18 years old. She usually arrives at the site by 8 p.m. and does not leave until between 3 and 4 a.m. the next morning. Hers is a night shift in the most literal sense, and it is one she has worked for two years. She began selling sex at 16. Before then, she earned a living selling auction goods, the second-hand items traded in markets across Liberia. Then her mother died. With her mother gone, Rita says, nobody was left to take care of her.

“I am here to hustle because I was living with my mother, but she passed away. I don’t have anyone to take care of me, so I came on the road to hustle with my friends on the street. I used to sell auction goods before. I am doing this to support myself,” she said in an interview with FrontPage Africa in Brewerville City on Sunday, October 19.

Her explanation is plain, almost matter-of-fact. There is no suggestion that she chose this life over a better one. In her telling, the road simply replaced the family that had been taken from her, and her friends on the street showed her how to survive on it.

The Arithmetic of Survival

The money is meagre. Rita charges between L$200, which is about US$1, and L$300 for one round of sex. On a typical night, she sleeps with between three and five men. “Sometimes I make L$2,000 (US$11.7) or L$3,000 (US$17.6). I sleep with between three to five men at night. Some men who have feelings for us can give us L$400 (US$2) or L$600 (US$3),” she said.

Consider what these figures mean. A night of work that stretches for seven or eight hours, in the open air and among strangers, produces an income of roughly twelve to eighteen United States dollars at best. Some of the men pay a little more because, in her words, they “have feelings” for the girls. Most do not.

For Rita, that money must stretch across food, shelter, and every other need that comes with living alone. There is nothing in these numbers that suggests savings, and nothing that suggests a way out. Each night’s earnings are spent on the next day’s survival, and the cycle begins again at dusk.

When Drugs Set the Price

For others at the site, poverty is only half of the story. The other half is addiction. Miatta, also not her real name, is 22 years old and a junior high school dropout. She has spent nearly four years on the street, selling sex to feed a drug habit. According to her account, it was her sexual partner who introduced her to drugs several years ago. Today she sells sex to pay for the drugs and to cover a few basic needs.

“I am hustling here in the night. Sometimes when business is on our side, I make L$2,500 (US$14.7) or L$2,000 (US$11.7); sometimes when the business is rough, I make L$1,000 (US$5.8). Sometimes I sleep with about eight to 10 men. I use the money I make to smoke drugs,” she said.

The contrast with Rita’s account is striking. Where Rita speaks of three to five men a night, Miatta speaks of as many as eight to ten. Her earnings on a rough night are less than six United States dollars. The need to find enough money to satisfy her habit pushes her toward more encounters, and more encounters mean more exposure to danger and disease.

Her story shows why the crisis cannot be explained by poverty alone. Hardship pushes young women onto the street, and drugs keep them there. Each problem feeds the other, and breaking the cycle will require more than any single intervention can offer.

Pain Behind the Hustle

The dangers do not end with poverty and addiction. Many of those engaged in commercial sex in Liberia have suffered severe assaults and attacks, including from first-time customers and from disadvantaged youths who see them as easy targets.

The injuries that can be seen are only part of the harm. The scars carried in the heart, according to the account, are heavier than the ones on the body. The young women are sexually abused and assaulted, and the money they have earned is taken away from them by their attackers.

Miatta described how it can happen. “Some of them can even beat us; they can carry us behind here (pointing at the back of the unfinished building), have sex with us, take advantage of us (because of our look and habit) and take the money from us,” she said.

Her words capture a double injury. The attackers take the bodies of these young women and then take their pay as well. Those who work at night and use drugs are especially exposed, because the very qualities that mark them out also make it easy for others to dismiss them. They carry out their work in the shadows, and the shadows protect those who prey on them.

Sick, but Staying Out

The health risks are as serious as the physical dangers. The young women say they understand the risks of what they do for a living. They are exposed to sexually transmitted diseases because their encounters involve unprotected sex. They are also exposed to chronic tuberculosis, colds, and other illnesses because they remain outside through the night and the early hours of the morning.

Staying home is rarely an option. “Sometimes we get sick because whether rain or shine, we have to come hustle. We sometimes buy antibiotics when we feel funny in our bodies; but we don’t really go to the hospital or clinic because we don’t have plenty money,” said another young woman who preferred not to be named.

Her account describes a quiet gap in the health system. When something feels wrong, she and her friends buy antibiotics themselves instead of seeking a diagnosis. A clinic visit costs money they would rather spend on food or on a day’s survival. Illness becomes one more problem to be managed alone, and an infection that might have been treated early is left to continue.

A Troubling Sign

The condition of these young women reflects more than individual misfortune. It points to a wider pattern of rising poverty, limited opportunities and growing substance abuse across Liberia. It also raises serious concerns about the vulnerability of girls and about the need for effective social protection, rehabilitation and economic empowerment programs.

The young women themselves have an answer to what they need. They called on the government to provide social and economic opportunities that would help them return to society. They made specific reference to empowerment through vocational and technical skills training.

It is a practical request, not a vague appeal. Skills training offers the one thing that the roadside cannot: a trade that can earn a living without the daily risks of violence, disease, and exploitation. For women who say they have no one to take care of them, the chance to learn a skill may be the difference between survival and a future.

What the Research Says

The accounts from Brewerville fit a larger body of evidence. Several local and international reports, including those from the United Nations, link transactional sex in Liberia to poverty, drug addiction, and the sexual exploitation of young girls.

A United Nations report titled Transactional Sex and Sexual Exploitation in Liberia, published in April 2025, documented concerns about commercial and transactional sex in the country, particularly in Monrovia and in border areas. It found that economically disadvantaged women and girls face increased risks of sexual exploitation, especially in mining and rubber plantation concession areas.

It added that commercial and transactional sex reportedly occurs around major transportation centers and entertainment districts. Sex workers, it said, face health risks, exploitation, discrimination and exclusion from some social and healthcare services.

A report by the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), titled “A Teenage Girl Who Turned to Transactional Sex to Survive,” gave a firsthand account from West Point, Monrovia. It profiled a girl called Mercy, who was 17 at the time of publication. She said that she and her family were forced out of her father’s home when she was 13. While her mother worked to support the family, Mercy began exchanging sex for money to buy food.

The same report described the broader problems facing adolescents in West Point, including poverty, limited educational opportunities, and inadequate access to basic social services. It also discussed how financial hardship can push young people toward activities that provide immediate income but expose them to additional risks.

A 2025 report by the United States Department of State on human trafficking and sexual exploitation in Liberia offered an international perspective. It detailed how women and girls from impoverished rural communities remain vulnerable to trafficking, and how traffickers sometimes promise young women better opportunities in urban areas before sexually exploiting and abusing them.

Read together, these reports and the voices at the roadside tell the same story. Whether in a Monrovia slum, a mining area or a roadside community in Brewerville, poverty and a lack of options leave girls and young women open to exploitation.

Plans on Paper

The government has not ignored the issue entirely. In March this year, it launched the Third National Action Plan Against Human Trafficking, which covers the period from 2025 to 2029. Among other aims, the plan is intended to prevent the recruitment or involvement of women in commercial sexual exploitation.

In December last year, the government launched its National Anti-Drug Action Plan for 2025 to 2030. Within that plan, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection acknowledges the relationship between drug dependency, commercial sex and the vulnerability of women and children. The plan points out that some women are driven into commercial sex work to support their drug habits. It also highlights the effects of substance abuse on children, including neglect, exposure to violence and loss of educational opportunities.

The Ministry of Health has launched Liberia’s National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights and Nutrition Strategy for 2026 to 2031. The strategy seeks to improve adolescents’ access to sexual and reproductive healthcare, nutrition services and relevant information, while addressing the social and behavioural barriers that affect young people.

In October this year, the government launched a Five-Year Strategic Plan for Women and Children, estimated at approximately US$58.667 million. The plan is meant to strengthen institutional performance, improve service delivery, promote gender equality and enhance protection for children and vulnerable populations. Child and social protection, the prevention of sexual and gender-based violence, and services for vulnerable groups are among its priorities. It also aims to address the situation of girls vulnerable to sexual exploitation, particularly where families struggle to provide food, education, and housing.

More Than Launches

Yet the stakeholders who follow these issues are not satisfied. Despite the growing involvement of young girls in transactional sex, they argue, the government’s efforts have been scanty. In their view, the launch of one plan after another is not enough to reduce the problem.

They want the government to go beyond announcements and address the conditions that push girls onto the street. These include growing economic hardship, drug abuse and dependency among young people, limited educational opportunities, and the sexual exploitation that continues to drive women and girls to exchange sex for money, favors, or other necessities.

The distance between a policy document and a roadside in Brewerville is considerable. A plan can be launched in a single day, but its effects depend on funding, staff and sustained follow-through. The young women who stand near the unfinished building each night are the measure of whether those plans work. If skills training, addiction treatment and affordable healthcare reach them, the plans will have meant something. If they do not, the documents will have changed little.

Before Dawn

When Rita finally leaves the site between 3 and 4 a.m., the night’s work is done, but nothing has been resolved. She has earned a few thousand Liberian dollars, enough perhaps for the next day’s food. She has also faced the risks that come with the road: the possibility of violence, the exposure to illness, and the knowledge that tomorrow the cycle will begin again.

Her story and Miatta’s are different in detail. One is an orphan trying to support herself, and the other is a young woman caught in addiction. Yet they share a common wish, which is to be given something better than the road. Skills, support and a chance to rejoin society are not luxuries to them. They are the difference between surviving the night and building a life.

The question that Brewerville poses to the country is a plain one. Plans, strategies and action programmes have been launched in the thousands of words that fill government documents. The young women of the unfinished building are waiting to find out whether any of those words will reach them.

World.title: Pooling Strength for Development, Advancing Common Progress —Marking the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative
World.content:
In September 2021, President Xi Jinping put forward the Global Development Initiative (GDI) at the 76th Session of the United Nations General Assembly, injecting strong impetus into the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and global development endeavors. On 25 September 2026, the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative was held at UN Headquarters in New York. Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a congratulatory letter to the Dialogue. Participants expressed readiness to continue to firmly support the GDI, strengthen solidarity and collaboration, and work together to build a more inclusive, sustainable and resilient future.

As President Xi has noted, development is development is the eternal theme of human society and is key to promoting people’s well-being. Over the past five years, the GDI has been translated from a Chinese vision and proposal into collective global action. More than 130 countries and international organizations actively support the GDI, and they have participated in cooperation under the Initiative. Over 2,000 GDI cooperation projects, tailored to the needs of beneficiary countries, have taken root and delivered outcomes in more than 120 countries. More than 30 GDI cooperation mechanisms and platforms — such as the Global Development Promotion Center Network and the Global Knowledge Network for Development — have been established one after another. More than 10,000 human resources training programs have been organized to share development approaches and practical skills, helping developing countries to build up their capacity for self-reliant development. The GDI helps build a stronger international consensus on putting development first, facilitates mutually beneficial development cooperation, helps fulfill the development aspirations of countries in the Global South, and generated robust momentum for global development.

Liberia is an important member of the Global South family. As a sincere friend and reliable partner of the Liberian people, China has firmly supported Liberia’s national development. When Liberia was hit by the Ebola outbreak in 2014, China offered assistance without delay. Following the COVID-19 outbreak, China provided multiple batches of anti-pandemic aid to Liberia. Chinese medical teams have long worked in Liberia to save lives and safeguard people’s health. In infrastructure, Chinese-aid projects including the two overpasses on the Tubman Boulevard, the National Clinical Diagnosis and Treatment Laboratory, the Fingerprint Laboratory, and the refurbishment and expansion of the Liberia Broadcasting System have been completed, energizing Liberia’s economic and social development. In agriculture, education, human resources and other areas, China has continued to provide food assistance and train professionals, supporting Liberia in pursuing self-sustaining and autonomous development.



The profound changes unseen in a century accelerate across the world, and progress in implementing the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development has fallen seriously behind schedule. The graver the challenges, the more countries need to stand together and jointly advance development. At the above-mentioned High-Level Dialogue, Vice President Han Zheng put forward four proposals: strengthen solidarity and coordination to fully implement the SDGs and fully leverage the GDI’s role as an accelerator; stay action-oriented and implement more “small and beautiful” livelihood projects that deliver real benefits to local people; expand cooperation in priority areas and broaden the scope of GDI cooperation focusing on artificial intelligence (AI), the digital economy, new energy, and disaster prevention and mitigation to foster new drivers for sustainable development; strengthen partnerships and conduct extensive cooperation through relevant bilateral, trilateral and multilateral mechanisms to leverage complementary strengths and create synergy. These propositions will further advance the GDI and create new opportunities for China and Liberia to jointly implement it.

During the meeting between Liberian Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in this May, Minister Nyanti stated that Liberia highly commends and firmly supports the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity and the series of Global Initiatives, and is ready to strengthen multilateral coordination with China within the UN framework, jointly work for a world of lasting peace and shared prosperity. As both China and Liberia are founding members of the United Nations and members of the UN Security Council, China stands ready to work with Liberia to take the fifth anniversary of the GDI as a new starting point. We will enhance cooperation within the UN framework, uphold true multilateralism, pool development momentum, translate more cooperation outcomes into tangible benefits for the Liberian people, and ensure that the fruits of development are shared more equitably by people across all countries.
