World.title: Liberia: House Summons Education Minister, MCSS Superintendent, Teachers Over Prolonged School Closure
World.content:
L-R: Rep. Dixon W. Seboe and Education Minister, Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah

Monrovia — The House of Representatives is expected to question the Minister of Education, Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah, the Superintendent of the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS), Dr. Augurie Stevens, and the leadership of the MCSS Teachers Association over the prolonged shutdown of public schools in Monrovia and its environs.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The appearance, scheduled for Tuesday, October 20, follows growing concerns over the continued disruption of academic activities more than a month after schools reopened for the new academic year.



The House’s decision came during its sitting last Thursday after Montserrado County District #16 Representative Dixon W. Seboe raised concerns about the standoff between MCSS teachers and the government, warning that the continued closure of schools threatens the education and welfare of thousands of students.

Lawmakers unanimously agreed to summon the education authorities and the teachers’ association leadership to explain the dispute, the status of negotiations, and the measures being taken to restore normal academic activities.

Rep. Seboe described the prolonged shutdown as “worrisome,” urging the House to intervene before the disruption causes further harm to students and their families.

Speaking to reporters after the session, the lawmaker stressed that the continued absence of teachers from classrooms demands urgent attention and accountability from all parties involved.

He said the appearance would give lawmakers an opportunity to establish the facts surrounding the dispute, hear the respective positions of the government and teachers, and identify a path toward reopening the affected schools.

Teachers Demand Superintendent’s Resignation

The latest development follows a directive by MCSS Teachers Association President Augustine N. Nyormui, who called on students to stay away from their campuses and instructed teachers, security personnel, education workers, and cleaners to remain off school premises until their outstanding demands are addressed.

Speaking at a press conference in Monrovia, Nyormui maintained that teachers would not return to the classrooms until MCSS Superintendent Dr. Augurie Stevens resigns.

The decision followed a heated debate during plenary after Montserrado County District #16 Representative Dickson W. Seboe raised issues affecting thousands of students of MCSS and requested the intervention of the House. L-R: MCSS Superintendent Dr. Augurie Stevens and MCSSTA President Augustine N. Nyormui

The demand has intensified the standoff, leaving students in several schools without regular instruction despite the reopening of the academic year.

The prolonged disruption has reportedly frustrated students, with some considering protests over their inability to receive lessons.

The dispute has raised broader concerns about the ability of education authorities and teachers’ representatives to resolve their differences while safeguarding students’ right to education.

Lawmakers Seek Answers

In his communication to the House, Rep. Seboe noted that nearly a month had elapsed since the opening of the academic year without a clear indication that the dispute had been resolved or that teachers were prepared to resume classes.

He warned that continued interruptions could have lasting consequences for students, parents, teachers, and Liberia’s already challenged education system.

The lawmaker urged the House to exercise its constitutional oversight responsibility by bringing the relevant stakeholders before the plenary to explain their positions and outline concrete steps toward resolving the impasse.

During Tuesday’s engagement, Superintendent Stevens is expected to explain the administrative situation within the MCSS and respond to concerns raised by teachers.

Education Minister Jallah is expected to present the government’s position, provide an update on negotiations, and outline efforts to restore normal academic activities.

Meanwhile, the MCSS Teachers Association leadership is expected to detail the teachers’ outstanding demands and clarify the conditions it considers necessary for their return to the classrooms.

Rep. Seboe said the engagement would allow lawmakers to hear directly from all sides, establish the facts, and encourage a peaceful and timely resolution in the interest of affected students.

“The appearance will provide us, the people’s deputies, with further insight into the ongoing disagreement and the prospects for reopening schools across the MCSS. As I said, this shutdown is worrisome,” he said.

The outcome of Tuesday’s engagement could prove critical in determining whether the parties can reach an agreement to reopen schools and prevent further disruption to the academic year.

World.title: Can Constructive Journalism Help Liberia Turn National Challenges Into Development Solutions?
World.content:
BEIJING, China — Liberia’s development challenges are well documented, from poor road connectivity and limited economic opportunities to inadequate public services and persistent difficulties attracting investment. But what if journalism could do more than expose these problems? What if it could also identify practical solutions, encourage institutional responses and showcase the country’s untapped potential?

By Willie N. Tokpah

That question is at the center of a two-week international communication seminar bringing together 23 Liberian journalists in China to examine how constructive journalism, public diplomacy and development storytelling could contribute to national progress.



Sponsored by China’s Ministry of Commerce at the request of the Government of the People’s Republic of China, the seminar brings together practitioners from print, broadcast and digital media to explore China’s experiences in international communication, media development and development-oriented reporting.

Among the participants is Willie N. Tokpah of FrontPage Africa, who is joining fellow journalists to examine approaches that could strengthen Liberia’s media capacity and encourage more solutions-oriented public-interest reporting.

For Liberia, the experience raises a critical question: Can journalism become a stronger bridge between citizens’ concerns, government accountability and practical ideas for development?

Beyond Exposing Problems

Constructive journalism moves beyond identifying problems to examine responses, assess results and highlight practical approaches that could be adapted to local circumstances.

It does not require journalists to abandon investigative reporting or soften criticism of public officials. Instead, it complements scrutiny with evidence-based reporting that examines what works, what fails and what lessons can be learned.

In Liberia, such an approach could transform coverage of persistent development challenges.

Reporting on impassable farm-to-market roads, for example, could document farmers’ economic losses while investigating road-maintenance models, financing arrangements and communities that have improved rural access.

Coverage of youth unemployment could examine vocational training, agricultural enterprises and small-business financing, including barriers preventing graduates from entering the workforce.

Similarly, reporting on sanitation, education, healthcare and local governance could scrutinize public spending while examining community initiatives and practical solutions.

The objective is not to manufacture positive news or shield the government from criticism. It is to provide citizens with a fuller understanding of public problems while generating credible information that can inform action.

Chinese Scholars Highlight Journalism’s Development Role

During the seminar’s first week, Chinese communication scholars and media officials encouraged participants to consider how journalism can contribute to national development.

Professor Zang Yanqiu, director of the Africa Research Center at the Communication University of China, described constructive reporting as an approach through which journalists identify problems, alert relevant authorities and examine efforts to find workable solutions.

“The journalism profession should be used for the good of the community,” Professor Zang stated.

She urged participants to produce reports that reflect national consciousness and contribute to development.

Chang Jin, a second-level counselor in the Department of International Cooperation at China’s National Radio and Television Administration, also discussed communication’s role in China’s development experience.

“It is the media responsibility to report in a way that advances the government’s development agenda,” Chang noted.

For Liberian journalists, however, applying these lessons requires adapting them to Liberia’s constitutional protections, independent media traditions and accountability needs.

Journalism must retain its responsibility to question authority, investigate wrongdoing and provide citizens with reliable information. Engagement with public institutions cannot replace independent verification, nor should national image-building take precedence over the public’s right to know.

The challenge is to combine rigorous scrutiny with reporting that helps people understand potential solutions and determine whether promised interventions deliver results.

From Beijing to Anji: Learning Through Experience

Beyond classroom instruction, the journalists travelled to Anji County in Huzhou City, Zhejiang Province, to examine the relationship between communication, tourism, environmental protection and local development.

One major stop was Yucun Village, associated with the development philosophy expressed in the phrase, “Lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets,” linked to Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The village has become a prominent example of efforts to connect environmental protection with economic development, particularly through tourism and environmentally conscious agricultural practices.

For the delegation, the visit offered an opportunity to examine how natural resources and local identity can become economic assets when supported by planning, infrastructure and sustained promotion.

The implications for Liberia are significant. The country’s forests, beaches, rivers, waterfalls and cultural heritage could support tourism, generate employment and attract investment. But these resources require reliable infrastructure, environmental safeguards, accessible services and meaningful community participation.

Through well-researched reporting, Liberian journalists could promote lesser-known destinations, investigate barriers to tourism and document initiatives connecting conservation with sustainable livelihoods.

The objective would be to tell Liberia’s development stories without simply reproducing another country’s model.

What Liberia Could Learn From Rural Transformation

The delegation also visited the Anji County Smart Governance Center, where participants examined the use of technology and administrative systems to coordinate social and economic services.

The experience raised questions about how Liberian county administrations could improve responses to citizens’ complaints, publish clearer information about development projects and enable communities to monitor the implementation of roads, schools, clinics and other public facilities.

Instead of reporting only when projects are launched, newsrooms could follow them through implementation and completion, documenting expenditures, delays, community feedback and measurable outcomes.

Such reporting would help citizens compare official promises with results while giving public officials a clearer picture of local concerns.

The seminar also exposed participants to China’s rural transformation experience, including efforts to address natural-resource depletion and develop alternative livelihoods.

For Liberia, where many rural communities depend on farming, fishing and forests, the connection between environmental protection and economic opportunity is particularly relevant.

However, any adaptation must account for Liberia’s land rights, customary institutions, community consent, environmental conditions and available resources. The lesson is to examine experiences elsewhere and determine which ideas can work within Liberia’s circumstances.

Building Liberia’s International Image Through Better Storytelling

The seminar also examines international communication, public diplomacy, digital media, disinformation and the changing global media landscape.

These subjects have implications for Liberia’s efforts to attract tourism, expand trade, promote investment and strengthen international partnerships.

A country’s image is shaped not only by official statements and diplomatic engagements but also by stories about its people, institutions, economy and natural environment.

Responsible image-building does not mean concealing corruption, economic hardship or governance failures. It means broadening the narrative through credible reporting on entrepreneurship, agricultural innovation, cultural heritage, environmental conservation and community initiatives.

A report about a rural entrepreneur creating jobs, for instance, could examine both the achievement and the obstacles to expanding the business. A tourism feature could showcase a destination while investigating road access, visitor safety and whether surrounding communities benefit economically.

Such coverage could promote Liberia’s potential while retaining the scrutiny necessary to make development claims credible.

Giving Citizens a Voice in Development

Constructive communication also raises questions about how citizens can participate more directly in shaping development priorities.

Local radio stations, community newspapers, online platforms and public forums could provide opportunities for communities to identify problems, propose responses and assess institutional performance.

A community facing recurring flooding, for example, could work with journalists to document affected areas, consult residents and technical experts, examine drainage proposals and follow the response of local authorities.

Similarly, farmers struggling to transport produce could identify priority road repairs and assess whether proposed solutions improve market access.

For this approach to work, citizen participation must be meaningful. Authorities should explain which proposals can be implemented, which require additional resources and why others may not be feasible.

Journalists must then follow up to determine whether commitments produce measurable improvements.

Turning Training Into Results

The two-week seminar combines classroom instruction with field visits, exposing the 23 journalists to China’s experiences in communication, public diplomacy and development.

The real test, however, will come after they return to Liberia.

The lessons could inform newsroom initiatives such as solutions-focused reporting series, investigations into public projects, community development features and multimedia stories showcasing Liberia’s economic and cultural potential.

Newsrooms could adopt standards requiring reporters to identify problems, examine proposed responses, consult affected communities, verify evidence and assess whether interventions are producing results.

These safeguards would help prevent constructive journalism from becoming a public-relations exercise or a platform for repeating official claims.

Ultimately, the value of the approach will not be measured by how positively stories portray Liberia or its leaders, but by whether they improve public understanding, strengthen accountability and help citizens evaluate possible solutions.

China’s experience offers an opportunity to examine how communication can support development and international engagement. But Liberia’s path must be shaped by its own democratic institutions, public needs and social realities.

The country needs journalism that exposes corruption, questions public spending and investigates abuse. It also needs reporting that examines workable alternatives, highlights local innovation and helps citizens understand how development challenges might be addressed.

These responsibilities are not mutually exclusive.

For Liberia, the opportunity presented by the seminar is not simply to learn how another country communicates its achievements. It is to consider how journalists can connect public concerns with evidence, practical ideas and sustained accountability.

If the training leads to more rigorous reporting on development solutions, stronger citizen participation and credible storytelling about Liberia’s potential, its benefits could extend beyond the journalists themselves.

Ultimately, constructive journalism must do more than make government look good. It must help the public understand problems, evaluate responses and demand results.

The 23 journalists are expected to receive international certificates upon completion of the training.

World.title: Beyond The Diploma: YEIB-MANCO CEO Urges Graduates to Embrace Entrepreneurship, Integrity and Service
World.content:
Monrovia — Youth Entrepreneurship and Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO) Chief Executive Officer Joseph Fatorma Sando has challenged Liberian graduates to turn their education into entrepreneurial opportunities, practical solutions and meaningful service to their communities.

By Patience Jones

Sando said academic qualifications alone were insufficient to guarantee success, urging young people to apply their knowledge to address societal challenges, create opportunities and contribute to Liberia’s development.



He made the call on Saturday, October 17, when he delivered the keynote address at the graduation and closing ceremony of St. James Foundation Elementary, Junior and Senior High School in Peace Community, Upper Caldwell, Montserrado County. More than 50 students graduated from the institution.

Speaking on the theme “Beyond the Diploma,” Sando outlined five principles he said should guide the graduates as they transition from secondary education to higher learning, entrepreneurship and professional life: continuous learning, integrity, problem-solving, resilience and community service.

Education Must Translate Into Impact

Sando told the graduates that completing high school should mark the beginning of a lifelong commitment to learning, rather than the end of their educational journey.

He encouraged them to cultivate the habit of reading, acquiring new skills and pursuing excellence in whatever careers they choose.

“The world is fast-changing, and only those who remain curious and committed to excellence will remain relevant,” he said, urging the graduates to make excellence a defining feature of their work.

Whether pursuing careers in medicine, teaching, business, agriculture or other fields, he said, young people should strive to perform their responsibilities to the highest standard.

The YEIB-MANCO chief executive also emphasized integrity, warning that academic certificates without good character could undermine a person’s prospects for lasting success.

He urged the graduates to remain honest and trustworthy, even when doing so becomes difficult or unpopular, arguing that integrity builds the trust necessary for personal and professional advancement.

‘Be a Solution, Not a Problem’

Sando challenged the Class of 2026 to become problem-solvers who identify challenges in their communities and develop practical responses.

He said Liberia needs young people who can use their education and creativity to address local problems instead of merely complaining about them.

According to him, communities across the country face challenges that require innovation, initiative and the active participation of educated young people.

He also cautioned the graduates against allowing setbacks and disappointments to derail their ambitions.

Acknowledging that life after high school would present difficulties, Sando encouraged them to develop resilience, remain determined and continue pursuing their goals despite rejection or failure.

“You will be disappointed, you will fail at times, you will be rejected, but never surrender,” he said, stressing that the ability to recover from setbacks is essential to achieving long-term goals.

Calls for Community Service and Entrepreneurship

Sando further urged the graduates to embrace entrepreneurship, discipline and patriotism, emphasizing that education should benefit not only individuals but also the wider society.

He encouraged them to give back to Peace Community, Upper Caldwell, and Liberia through volunteering, mentoring younger people and participating in community development initiatives.

He said the value of education should also be measured by how graduates use their knowledge and skills to improve the lives of others.

Sando added that Liberia’s development depends partly on a generation of young people who are skilled, ethical, innovative and willing to serve their country.

School Honors Sando for Support to Students

In recognition of his contributions to the institution and its students, the administration and faculty of St. James Foundation Elementary, Junior and Senior High School presented Sando with an academic gown during a special ceremony.

The presentation, which was met with applause from parents, students and community leaders, was conducted by the school’s principal and senior faculty members.

The administration described Sando as a supportive partner and friend of the institution, citing his financial, moral, spiritual and academic assistance to students, particularly children from less privileged backgrounds in Peace Community.

School officials said his continued involvement and encouragement had contributed to efforts to support the education and development of young Liberians.

Responding to the honor, Sando expressed gratitude to the administration and faculty, describing the recognition as humbling and motivating.

He reaffirmed his commitment to supporting education and youth empowerment in Liberia.

The ceremony brought together parents, teachers, community leaders, and other well-wishers to celebrate the graduates’ achievements and encourage them as they prepare for the next stage of their lives.

The program concluded with the presentation of certificates and awards to students recognized for academic performance and good conduct. The class valedictorian delivered a vote of thanks on behalf of the graduating class.

World.title: Liberia: Full Gospel Nigeria Fellowship Equips Liberian Counterparts
World.content:
MONROVIA – Dr. Jude Ememe at the head of a 7-man high-level delegation under the auspices of the Full Gospel Business Men’s Fellowship International Nigeria, arrived in Liberia on Thursday, October 15 and has been involved in series of activities including capacity – building aimed at enhancing the leadership ability of the Full Gospel Business Men’s Fellowship International Liberia.

By Augustus D.R Bortue

Other members of the delegation include Dr. Godwin Edozie, Barrister Isaac Okpanachi, National President of Nigeria (FGBMFI), Bro. Stephen Okruefe and Mr. & Mrs. Joseph Mamodu.



The fellowship established in 1952 by an American Christian businessman, Demos Shakarian, in California is a global movement of Christians from different denominations and diverse expertise, working together to propagate the Gospel of Jesus Christ in fulfillment of the Great Commission.

Although the fellowship started initially with frustration and disappointments characterized by poor attendance in initial meetings and lack of money, it has been organized in about 163 countries worldwide.

In addition, millions of lives have been impacted globally through groups of ordinary Christians laymen inspired by a God-given vision that was originally imparted to Demos Shakarian.

During one of the training sessions held at Evelyn Restaurant in Sinkor, Monrovia, Dr. Edozie said Full Gospel is a spiritual work that has a vision and mission.

In order to become successful in life, Dr. Edozie encouraged his fellow believers to always factor God first in their plan and allow the Holy Spirit to provide guidance and direction in their Christian journey.

Dr. Edozie added that the fellowship is not a church, but rather a network of professionals having strong passion and commitment in winning souls using their God-given gifts and sharing of testimonies which inspire individuals to join the body of Christ,

On Saturday, October 17, a joint breakfast meeting took place at the Bella Casa Hotel on 2nd Street in Sinkor, Monrovia and brought together participants representing four chapters that have been established in Liberia.

In his welcome remarks, the National President of the FGBMFI-Liberia, Arthur Fumbah, extended profound gratitude and described the visit by the

Nigerian FGBMFI as a clear manifestation of their desire to help Liberia become stronger and more effective in managing chapters to the glory of God.

Fumbah reflected on the warm reception accorded to them during their visit to Nigeria in 2019. Regarding progress, he said the guest, Liberia has established four chapters, and expressed optimism that additional chapters would be established in the coming year.

The main speaker at the breakfast meeting was the National President of the FGBMFI of Nigeria, who is a Solicitor, Advocate and Notary Public.

Isaac Okpanachi challenged executives of the Liberian FGBMFI to engage those in authority to always reference God first as they provide stewardship for the country since, in fact, Liberia is a Nation Founded on Christian principles.

He further prayed for the nation and asked God to use the Full Gospel Fellowship in heading and reconciling Liberia.

Moderating the breakfast meeting was Liberia’s FGBMFI Eminent Chapter President, Dr. Nathania T. Blama, Sr., assisted by Bro. Wilson Gaglo-Delali, National Prayer Coordinator, while sister Mama Wesaye led the praise & Worship Team.

World.title: Liberia to Digitalize 16 Key Government Services with World Bank Support
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — The Government of Liberia, with support from the World Bank, has begun taking steps to digitalize 16 priority government services in a move aimed at making public services more accessible, efficient, and responsive to the needs of citizens.

The initiative is expected to introduce a more integrated digital government system, allowing citizens to access multiple public services through a single online platform while enabling government institutions to share information more efficiently.

At the center of the initiative is the proposed e-Liberia Platform, envisioned as a one-stop shop for government services. The project also includes the development of a Government Service Bus (GSB) to facilitate real-time information sharing among public institutions, upgrades to the National Data Center, and the digitalization of County Service Centers across the country.



The initiative could mark an important step in reducing the delays and administrative challenges often associated with accessing public services, although its impact will ultimately depend on effective implementation, reliable digital infrastructure, and citizens’ ability to access and use the new systems.

To prepare for implementation, the Office of the Chief Information Officer of Liberia hosted a working session over the weekend, bringing together representatives from participating ministries and agencies.

The meeting focused on validating the status of the 16 priority services, assessing institutional and technical readiness, reviewing existing digital systems and business processes, and identifying appropriate procurement arrangements to support the initiative.

Participants also examined the technical requirements for integrating government institutions into the proposed digital ecosystem, including the Government Service Bus, e-Liberia Portal, application programming interfaces (APIs), and shared digital infrastructure.

Discussions further addressed outstanding requirements, institutional responsibilities, implementation timelines, and the next steps needed to move the project from planning toward execution.

Speaking at the session, Liberia’s Chief Information Officer, Sheikh Sheriff, praised the Government of Liberia and the World Bank for supporting the initiative, describing it as a significant milestone in the country’s digital transformation efforts.

World.title: Mundubile Bail Hearing Moved To Wednesday After State Seeks More Time
World.content:
The constitutional bail application by opposition leader Mr Brian Mundubile and 17 others accused of treason failed to proceed in the Lusaka High Court after the State said it was not ready. The court moved the hearing to Wednesday, while the accused remain in custody.

The adjournment came after acting Chief State Advocate Chibesa Mulonda asked for more time to file an affidavit opposing the application. A three-judge panel granted the request. The panel comprises Ndola High Court Judge Derrick Mulenga, who leads it, Justice Davies Chibwili and Justice Ireen Wishimanga.

The 18 accused, who include Mr Makebi Zulu, face treason and terrorism-related charges. They had been transported from Mukobeko Maximum Correctional Facility in Kabwe and were at the court premises by 07:00 hours.

Defence lawyer State Counsel Sakwiba Sikota said the accused had been woken at around 04:00 hours and driven to Lusaka on empty stomachs. He said no provision had been made for their breakfast.

“We have hurriedly organised some food for them so that at least they can have something to eat because they were brought with no provision for breakfast,” Mr Sikota said. “The State didn’t seem to be bothered or make an attempt to provide for that.”

Mr Sikota said the defence had served the State with the bail summons the previous Thursday. In his view, that left the prosecution with ample time to prepare its response.

“We had served the State last Thursday; they have had the documents for a number of days now. However, today the State said they were not ready and asked for an adjournment to enable them to put in documents in opposition,” he said.

Under the timetable set by the court, the State was ordered to serve the defence with its documents by lunchtime on the day of the adjournment. The defence must then file any answer and an affidavit in reply the following day, ahead of the hearing on Wednesday at 08:30 hours.

“They have been ordered to serve us with whatever they have in their possession,” Mr Sikota said, adding that the matter would be heard on Wednesday.

The accused were not present in chambers when the adjournment was granted. Mr Sikota explained that proceedings had not moved beyond procedural arrangements, and the legal team later briefed the applicants in the court holding cells.

Mr Mundubile, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) presidential candidate in the general election, is joined in the application by figures from business, the church and the legal profession. Among the other accused are business executive Mr Harry Findlay, former Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba, Mr Patrick Mwansa and lawyer Mr George Chisanga.

The group is linked to alleged militia activities during the general elections. These are allegations they will have the opportunity to answer before the court.

At the heart of their application is the length of their detention. The applicants argue that keeping them in custody while investigations remain incomplete violates their constitutional rights.

They accept that the State is entitled to investigate criminal allegations. They contend, however, that incomplete investigations cannot justify prolonged detention without judicial proceedings.

The applicants say the law guarantees them the right to be brought before a court without undue delay. If they are not tried within a reasonable time, they argue, they must be released either unconditionally or on reasonable conditions.

Court documents show that the applicants also raise alleged irregularities relating to remand warrants, their conditions of detention and their access to medical care. They maintain that despite being arrested last month and remaining in custody, they have not yet been presented before a competent court.

The application cites the alleged apprehension of Mr Ezra Tolopo, Mr Dickson Tembo and Mr Victor Muzyamba at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on 1 August. The applicants claim the three were then held at unknown locations for more than nine days.

The applicants are seeking release pending trial, either unconditionally or on conditions the court considers appropriate. They also want a declaration that their continued detention, without trial within a reasonable time, violates their constitutional rights.

Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha and two others are cited as respondents.

The applicants maintain that no judicial determination has authorised their continued incarceration. They say they are ready to answer the charges against them before a competent court.

The panel led by Judge Mulenga will hear arguments from both the State and the defence on Wednesday at 08:30 hours. The 18 accused remain in detention until then.

World.title: Publish The List: Katuta Demands Names And Evidence On Civil Servants Facing Dismissal
World.content:
Former Chiengi Member of Parliament Ms Given Katuta demanded that Government publish the names of civil servants lined up for dismissal over allegedly supporting the opposition. She also called for the evidence against each of them to be made public, saying dismissals without proof amount to injustice.

Ms Katuta, who stood as an independent presidential candidate in the August general election, was responding to remarks attributed to a senior UPND official that more civil servants seen as working against President Hakainde Hichilema would be removed.

She said threatening public workers with dismissal “in the national interest” without any evidence of wrongdoing was a serious injustice inflicted by Government on its own people. She set out three demands on behalf of citizens.

“We therefore demand as citizens: Publish the list. Who are these civil servants? From which ministries and departments?” Ms Katuta said.

“Show the evidence. How did they work against the government? Where is the proof? Follow due process. Civil servants serve the Republic of Zambia, not a political party.”

Ms Katuta questioned whether it was fair for the ruling UPND to condemn workers in this way without giving them access to due process. She said the reports had left her deeply troubled. “Is this fair? Is this unity?” she asked. “My heart is heavy.”

She traced the pattern back to the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency (ZAMMSA), where she said all employees had been dismissed. In her view, the civil service was now facing the same treatment.

“First, it was the firing of all ZAMMSA employees. Now it is civil servants to be ‘retired in the national interest’. Where is the fairness in this?” Ms Katuta said.

“If someone has a case to answer, let the law take its course. But to condemn a whole group and label them as ‘working against government’ without evidence is not justice.”

Ms Katuta said Government would struggle to promote unity if it continued to target anyone it perceived to be sympathetic to the opposition. She warned that the country was already in a tense atmosphere and that any attempt to inflame it further would be catastrophic.

She pointed to the timing of the remarks, which came soon after the nation observed the Day of Prayer, Fasting and Reconciliation on 18 October.

“My question is simple: How does this promote unity? Our country is already tense,” she said. “We talked about forgiveness, like President Mwanawasa forgiving President Sata. Now, a day later, we are talking about more firings?”

“This will not unite us. It will divide us more. It will create fear in the civil service instead of professionalism.”

Ms Katuta said those responsible for running a disciplined civil service should follow established procedure rather than resort to what she described as emotional blackmail. She called for an immediate halt to what she termed blanket dismissals.

“What is the best way forward? For now, stop this blanket firing. Use disciplinary procedures. Give people a chance to be heard. That is what the law says,” she said.

Looking further ahead, she argued for a public service insulated from party politics. “For the future, let us depoliticise the civil service. Let us remember that governments come and go, but Zambia remains,” Ms Katuta said.

“A teacher, a nurse, a clerk is not UPND or NRPUP or PF; they are Zambians serving Zambians.”

She closed her appeal with a call for genuine reconciliation, saying the nation could only move forward if leaders chose healing over punishment.

“Let us choose reconciliation over retribution. Unity over victimisation. Zambia is bigger than all of us,” she said.

ZAMMSA, the agency Ms Katuta cited, is currently advertising 23 categories of vacancies, from quality assurance and laboratory services to finance, internal audit and risk management. Applications close on 25 October.

Her three demands remain on the table: publish the list, show the evidence and follow due process for every civil servant named.

World.title: Audit Finds K626 Million In Mining Penalties Left Uncollected
World.content:
The Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development failed to collect K626.64 million in penalties from mining licence holders, the latest Auditor-General’s report has found. The report exposes weaknesses in revenue collection and financial management across Government.

The report covers the accounts of the Republic for the financial year ended 31 December 2025. It identifies gaps in revenue collection, financial management, programme implementation and asset management across ministries, provinces and spending agencies.

Acting Auditor-General Patricia Malaila said the shortcomings had resulted in revenue losses and inefficient use of public resources. She said they had also reduced the effectiveness of public service delivery.

Alongside the uncollected mining penalties, the report found that K30.48 million in annual area charges owed by licence holders remained outstanding. Mining was not the only point where money due to the Treasury went uncollected or unaccounted for.

US$433,820 collected on behalf of the Department of Immigration had not been remitted to the Treasury. The Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) was unable to account for customs duties of K41.97 million and temporary imports valued at K9.03 million because supporting documents were missing.

Land revenue showed a similar gap. The Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources could not assess ground rent on 74,840 properties because its land records were incomplete, raising concerns about both revenue collection and the management of public assets.

The Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation had not secured title deeds for 663 Government properties.

On the spending side, the largest figure sits with the Ministry of Health. The ministry has accumulated outstanding obligations of K3.56 billion, made up of employee-related liabilities and unpaid suppliers’ bills, some dating back to 2014.

Ms Malaila warned that these growing obligations were placing pressure on public finances and threatening uninterrupted healthcare delivery. She said they could also expose Government to further costs through penalties, interest and litigation.

The report also cited Mbala General Hospital, which continued to incur costs transporting oxygen from other towns.

Programmes meant to support citizens directly were not spared. Irregularities exceeding K72 million were identified under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), involving inactive and unapproved beneficiaries as well as individuals who benefitted from more than one Government support programme.

Payroll management at the Ministry of Education raised further questions. The audit found that 125 officers who received salaries totalling K1.23 million could not be accounted for. They were neither reflected on staff returns nor recognised by management at the stations where they were reported to work.

The same ministry was also cited for failing to complete the printing and distribution of learning materials under the new curriculum.

One of the starkest findings concerns confiscated mukula logs held at facilities under the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment. Of the 5,595 logs recorded, auditors could physically verify only 27, leaving 5,568 unaccounted for.

Despite the weaknesses, the report records some progress. Unresolved audit findings fell from 33 in 2024 to 27 at the conclusion of the 2025 audit.

Ms Malaila attributed the improvement to continued engagement with controlling officers and to recommendations issued to address weaknesses identified in earlier audits.

She called for timely corrective measures, recovery of public funds where applicable and stronger accountability. Public resources, she said, must be managed efficiently and in accordance with the law.

To address the issues raised, Ms Malaila urged all controlling officers to implement the recommendations in the report without delay. She asked them to strengthen internal controls, improve revenue collection systems, tighten procurement and payroll management, and safeguard public assets.

The findings were released in a statement issued by the Office of the Auditor-General’s head of public relations, Ms Ellen Chikale.

Controlling officers across the affected ministries are now expected to act on the recommendations. That work includes recovering funds where possible and closing the gaps the audit identified in revenue, payroll and asset records.

World.title: RUGBY: Walkovers continues in the top league
World.content:
The Zambia Rugby Union has awarded Red Arrows a 21-0 walkover victory over Kitwe Playing Fields (KPF) after KPF failed to show up for their rescheduled National League fixture.

According to the official league sheet as of 17th October 2026, the result is recorded as KPF 0-21 Arrows, with ZRU rules stating that a walkover attracts 4 points for a win plus 1 bonus point for four tries, while the defaulting team receives a -1-penalty point.

The decision has major implications for both ends of the table.

For Arrows, the walkover pushes them to 49 points from 12 games with 10 wins, keeping them firmly in contention for the title. They remain third but now have two games in hand on leaders Mufulira and Buffaloes.

Mufulira Leopards continue to lead the National League with 59 points from 14 games with 12 wins. The Leopards are one win away from clinching the 2026 title after beating Arrows 19-15 in September to open a 10-point lead earlier in the season. 70fe

Green Buffaloes are second with 50 points from 14 games.

For KPF, the penalty deepens a miserable season. The Kitwe side remains bottom of the eight-team National League with -1 point from 14 games (0 wins, 1 draw, 13 losses), having been deducted a total of 3 penalty points for no-shows. KPF remain the only team without a win this season. 70fe

Walkovers are not new in Zambian rugby. In previous seasons, KPF themselves benefited from a 21-0 walkover when Kansanshi failed to travel to Kitwe.

The ZRU is expected to maintain the result as final unless KPF successfully appeals.

In the Presidents League (Division Two), Lusaka leads with 36 points from 10 games, followed by Konkola with 35 and Nchanga with 33.

In the Women’s League, Buffaloes are unbeaten leaders with 48 points from 10 games, followed by Arrows with 32 points.

The National League resumes this weekend with Mufulira needing just a bonus-point win over KPF to be crowned champions.

World.title: Netball gives voice to deaf team
World.content:
When Kopala Deaf Netball Team took to the court at Mpelembe Secondary School in Kitwe, they did more than compete, they made a powerful statement about inclusivity in Zambian sport.

That statement was recognised when the Copperbelt Netball Association awarded Kopala Deaf the Most Improved Team Award during its Independence Tournament at the weekend, a tournament that brought together 21 teams from across the Copperbelt and Northwestern Province to celebrate Zambia’s independence through netball.

The tournament, graced by Provincial Sports Coordinator Nosiku and senior officials from Mufulira Municipal Council including the Town Clerk and Director of Housing, was held under the theme: Support the Girl Child Through Sport.

And support came from all corners.

In the Under-17 category, which alone attracted 12 teams, Luanshya Municipal Council were crowned champions after beating hosts Mufulira Municipal Council, with Victorious from Kitwe taking third.

Teams from Masaiti, Lufwanyama, Chililabombwe, Kalulushi, Ndola, Chingola, Wusakile Community, Mpelembe Secondary School and Kopala Deaf all featured, showing the depth of young talent emerging.

The Elite category saw Community Queens, sponsored by Kitwe City Council, prove too strong for the field. Kalewa from Ndola finished second while Kansanshi Foundation, who travelled from Solwezi, finished third in a category that also included Destiny and Copperbelt University.

In the Men’s category, which continues to grow in popularity, Kalewa completed a double celebration by taking first place, followed by Copperbelt University and Mufulira Stars. Wusakile Stars also competed.

But beyond the trophies, the stories of the individuals stood out.

Lufwanyama Town Council’s Brinya Makiku was named Upcoming Player of the Tournament, a recognition of emerging talent that the Association hopes will inspire other young girls to stay in sport.

“These awards celebrate not only winning but improvement, emerging talent and growth,” the Association said. “The progress of Kopala Deaf highlights the importance of providing opportunities for teams of all backgrounds.”

The Association said the tournament was more than just competition.

“It served as an important reminder of the role sport plays in building discipline, confidence, unity and positive social values. It provided an opportunity for players, officials and supporters to interact and celebrate the spirit of independence,” it said.

In a strong call to action, the Association urged communities, local authorities, corporate organisations and parents to invest in sport, particularly for the girl child.

“Providing girls with opportunities to participate in sport helps build self-esteem, develop leadership skills and keeps them engaged in constructive activities. It protects young people from harmful behaviours and negative influences,” the Association said.

As Zambia celebrates 62 years of independence, the message from Mpelembe was clear: the future of Zambian netball is not only bright, but also inclusive.

World.title: “Our Lives Are In Danger”: Zambians In South Africa Plead For Help To Come Home
World.content:
More than 250 Zambians living in South Africa are in hiding after a wave of violent attacks on foreigners spread across the country. Families say they have lost their jobs and homes, and they are appealing to Government to bring them back to Zambia before lives are lost.

The Zambians raised the alarm through a flood of phone calls and WhatsApp voice messages. They asked that their plight be brought to the attention of authorities in Lusaka, describing a situation that has worsened steadily since June.

Mr Michael Musonda, who lives in Durban, said about 50 Zambian families were stranded in KwaZulu-Natal alone. Many have been forced into hiding because the attacks are aimed at foreigners generally, not at any single nationality.

“They are not attacking Nigerians only. Even us Zambians,” Mr Musonda said. “We no longer send our kids to school since June this year. We are not working and well-wishers are the ones keeping us.”

He said the situation took a further turn when landlords were drawn into the conflict. “The situation has degenerated after home owners were also threatened and given an ultimatum to evict us,” he said.

In Pietermaritzburg, also in KwaZulu-Natal, Ms Veronica Bwalya described a life lived almost entirely indoors. She said it had become too dangerous to venture out, and that Zambians who did go into town had learnt to stay silent so they would not draw attention to themselves.

“If you go into town, you need to keep quiet without saying anything,” Ms Bwalya said. “Here in Pietermaritzburg, you cannot even pick up a phone call in a taxi. The moment you do that, you regret answering a phone call.”

Her account points to how foreigners are being identified. Speaking a language other than the local ones, even on a phone call, can expose a person to attack.

For Mr Joseph Katoba, also in Durban, the only way out is home. He said the situation had deteriorated to the point where Zambians could be killed unless Government stepped in to repatriate them.

He said nobody could be certain that no Zambian had already died. “We cannot independently say no Zambian has been killed because not all deaths are recorded here,” Mr Katoba said.

“These people are burning our homes. They are grabbing our properties and the authority here is doing nothing.”

Mr Katoba also raised concerns about the response from Zambia’s diplomatic mission. He said some of the stranded Zambians had gone there for help and come away with nothing.

“Some of us have visited the embassy, but nothing has happened. It is like we are not welcome at the embassy anymore,” he said.

The tension is not confined to KwaZulu-Natal. Mr Gift Mubita Nawa described conditions for foreigners in Johannesburg, Gauteng and Mpumalanga as tense. He said Zambians there had lost both their livelihoods and the goodwill of those who first took them in.

“We are not conducting any business here. We are not working for anyone. We were fired in June and even people who were offering refuge to us are now tired,” Mr Nawa said.

“We thought the situation would improve, but it is getting worse every day. All we are asking for is for the government to help us get back home and start a new life.”

Mr Nawa warned that any further delay could be disastrous. He described a violent attack close to his own home to underline the danger.

“Please help us reach out to the government that our lives are in danger. Any further delay in helping us move out of South Africa will leave us dead,” he said. “As I’m talking to you, my neighbour had his hand amputated just last night by this group of South Africans. They don’t want us here. They are saying they want to rebuild their country.”

Women with children are among the most exposed. Ms Charity Malata, a mother of two, said she had been evicted and could no longer leave the house safely to buy food, even if she had money to do so.

“I can’t go out to buy food. I don’t have money. I was evicted, and these people are coming for me and others here. Please, help us come back home,” Ms Malata said.

Taken together, the accounts describe Zambians who have been out of work since June and who now depend on well-wishers whose support is running thin. Their children have been out of school for months, and some say their homes have been burnt and their belongings taken.

The anti-immigrant protests have since spun out of control, and South African law enforcement agencies are overstretched in trying to contain them.

Those who spoke all made the same request. They are asking Government to arrange their return to Zambia, where they hope to rebuild their lives. They say they have nowhere else to turn after their visits to the diplomatic mission brought no help.

World.title: Solwezi residents calls for sidewalk on Mitec-Mine Boom road
World.content:
Road users in Mushitala area of Solwezi district are appealing to the government and Kansanshi Mining PLC to put up a sidewalk on the Mitec-Mine Boom gate dual carriage way road upgrade.

Dorcus Mokya, expressed concern that the road which is under construction will not have a sidewalk for pedestrians.

She explained that the road is very busy with a lot of schools stressing the need for the government to put up a sidewalk as construction is still ongoing.

“We appreciate that the road is being constructed into a dual carriageway but our concern is the safety of road users especially school going children,” Ms Mokya said.

Meanwhile, another road user, William Kamalata, has thanked the government for upgrading the road adding that it will help reduce congestion.

Mr Kamalata stated that once the road is completed, it will reduce the challenges motorists faced in repairing vehicles due to the poor condition the road was in.

He has called on Kansanshi to put up sidewalks for easy and free movement of pedestrians.

Mr Kamalata has further called for the erection of shelters at the designated bus stops.

“This development is commendable, and we have to work together to safeguard the signage that will be put on the road,” he emphasised.

World.title: ACC arrests former Mkushi DEBS over K2.49 million
World.content:
The Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) has arrested and charged Chama District Education Board Secretary, Titus Mbewe, over alleged irregularities involving K2.49 million in contracts for the supply of maize and dried beans under a School Feeding Programme.

Mbewe, 56, faces two counts of abuse of authority of office and one count of willful failure to follow applicable procedure under the Anti-Corruption Act, Chapter 91 of the Laws of Zambia,

It is alleged that between January and December 2025, while serving as District Education Board Secretary for Mkushi District, Mbewe facilitated payments of K1,424,115 to Frelun Commodities Limited for the supply of white maize and K1,073,000 to Ichikwanka Multi-Purpose Cooperative for dried beans before the contracts were approved by the Mkushi Council Secretary.

The total value of the two contracts was K2, 497,115.

It is further alleged that Mbewe authorised full payment to the suppliers before the goods were delivered.

In the third count, allegations are that Mbewe, acting with other persons unknown, facilitated the circumvention of procurement procedures by purporting that the Evaluation Committee and Procurement Committee had evaluated the tenders when they had not.

The alleged offences relate to procurement activities in Mkushi District during the period when Mbewe served as its District Education Board Secretary.

This is according to a statement issued to ZANIS by Anti-Corruption Commission Head – Corporate Communications Joseph Mwenya.

Mr Mwenya stated that Mbewe had been released on bond and would appear in court soon.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 20, 2026
World.content:
Rwandan Govt Critic Found Beheaded in Uganda

Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old former Rwandan army sergeant major and outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded on the outskirts of Kampala, Uganda. Kabera had fled Rwanda and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution. He later gained a following through his YouTube channel, which featured criticism of Kagame's government. Ugandan police said his head had not been recovered. His widow expressed fears for her family's safety. The opposition Rwanda National Congress has called for a thorough investigation, as his killing renews concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. Other critics of Kagame have been killed abroad, including former intelligence chief Patrick Karegeya, who was found dead in Johannesburg in 2014.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

UN Condemns Deadly Drone Strikes Across Sudan

Drone strikes across Sudan have killed and injured civilians, including children, as fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces continues to intensify. The attacks injured at least 19 people at a market in Abyei and targeted locations in Khartoum, including an area near the airport. The strikes reportedly killed at least 19 people, including 10 children, across several states. The United Nations condemned the attacks and raised concerns over the targeting of humanitarian workers, with 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers reportedly killed since the conflict began in April 2023. An estimated 20 million people face acute hunger, with famine risks rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Despite the insecurity, aid agencies continue delivering assistance, including restoring water supplies to thousands of people in Central Darfur. Sudan's humanitarian response plan remains just over 43% funded.

Zimbabwe's Ruling Party to Discipline MPs Who Missed Constitutional Amendment Vote

Zimbabwe's ruling Zanu-PF party plans to discipline Members of Parliament who failed to attend crucial parliamentary sittings during consideration of Constitutional Amendment No. 3 Bill. Party legal secretary Ziyambi Ziyambi announced the sanctions at the party's annual conference in Chinhoyi, naming several senior officials and deputy ministers among those who did not vote, although their reasons remain unclear. The disciplinary move comes as Zanu-PF advances resolutions to postpone its next elective congress from 2027 to 2029, potentially keeping President Emmerson Mnangagwa at the helm until 2030. Provincial leaders defended resolutions supporting his continued leadership and called for constitutional alignment and greater national self-sufficiency in areas such as medicine, technology and industrial production.

Thabo Mbeki Denies Blocking Apartheid-Era Prosecutions at Inquiry Commission

Former South African president Thabo Mbeki has denied allegations that he held secret meetings with former apartheid-era military and police generals to prevent prosecutions for human rights abuses. Testifying before the Khampepe Commission of Inquiry into delayed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) prosecutions, Mbeki said the generals approached him in 1996 seeking a meeting with the ANC over amnesty applications. He argued that former president FW de Klerk and his cabinet should also apply. Mbeki said the ANC subsequently pursued collective amnesty for some of its leaders to encourage the apartheid leadership to do the same, but the courts later overturned the decision. He maintained that his administration never directed the National Prosecuting Authority to halt or suppress investigations, arguing that prosecutions were the NPA's responsibility. He also defended his 2003 parliamentary speech and later arrangements involving pardon requests, saying these aimed to encourage truth-telling rather than grant blanket immunity to those responsible for apartheid-era crimes.

Close 

Nigeria and Rwanda Seek to Strengthen Defence Cooperation

Nigeria's Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has arrived in Rwanda for a five-day official visit aimed at strengthening defence and security cooperation between the two countries. Shaibu held talks in Kigali with Rwanda Defence Force Chief of Defence Staff General Mubarakh Muganga and Army Chief of Staff Major General Vincent Nyakarundi. The discussions focused on implementing existing agreements covering military training, exchanges of instructional and logistics personnel, and other shared security concerns. Shaibu and his delegation also visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial to pay tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and toured the Campaign Against Genocide Museum to learn about the genocide and Rwanda's post-conflict recovery. The visit is scheduled to conclude on October 23.

World.title: South Africa: Tshwane Informal Settlements More Than Double - South African News Briefs - October 20, 2026
World.content:
press review

Tshwane Informal Settlements More Than Double Ahead of Local Elections

The number of informal settlements in the City of Tshwane has more than doubled, reports EWN. The number rose from 220 in 2020 to 502 in 2026, and the municipality spends more than R1.5 billion annually to service them. In the Plastic View informal settlement in Pretoria East, more than 10,000 people live in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions, with sewage flowing through the community from broken pipes. Resident Humbulani Thobo, who has lived there since 2009, accused the city of making empty promises about relocating residents. The municipality provides water tankers and ablution facilities, but concerns over living conditions persist as local government elections approach.

Former Deputy Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya Awaits Bail Ruling

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Former Deputy National Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya is set to learn whether the court will grant him bail when he appears at the Randburg Magistrate's Court, reports SABC News. The defence has requested R20,000 bail. The state opposed his release, describing him as a potential threat to victims. Sibiya faces multiple charges, including human trafficking, the alleged sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl and the rape of an 18-year-old woman. He has been in custody since his arrest last month. The state said that investigations are at an advanced stage. Sibiya denied the allegations and claims he has been set up by the complainant.

Tshwane Residents Warned Against Drinking Contaminated Bronkhorstspruit Water

Residents in Bronkhorstspruit and surrounding areas have been warned not to use tap water for drinking, cooking, bathing or other household purposes, reports EWN. The city has reopened the Bronkhorstspruit Water Treatment Plant after restoring its chlorine supply, but authorities said that the water is still not safe for human consumption. More than 400 gastrointestinal illness cases, including stomach cramps and diarrhoea, were reported between October 7 and 18 after the water supply went without chlorination from September 24 to October 14. Tests detected E. coli and other bacteria in the water, while the National Institute for Communicable Diseases identified norovirus, Campylobacter and Shigella in patient samples. The city has deployed 36 water tankers carrying water from Cullinan, which has tested safe, while independent testing continues. Until authorities confirm the water is safe, residents may only use tap water for flushing toilets.

World.title: Africa: Macky Sall Officially Withdraws His Candidacy for UN Secretary-General Position
World.content:
Former Senegalese President Macky Sall announced on Saturday, October 17, 2026, his withdrawal of his candidacy for the post of Secretary-General of the United Nations.

In a statement released from Marrakech, the former head of state said he wants to promote an international consensus. This announcement follows the vote held on October 16, 2026, at the United Nations headquarters in New York. Sall said that he made this decision with a profound sense of institutional responsibility, and that various consultations and indicative votes held within the Security Council revealed, from the outset, a preference for a candidate from the Latin America and Caribbean region - possibly a woman.

In his written statement, the former head of state said his initiative was motivated by his desire to put nearly forty years of experience in public life at the service of multilateral governance. He expressed his gratitude to the heads of state who supported him in this endeavor, particularly acknowledging the sponsorship of Évariste Ndayishimiye and the support provided by President Bassirou Diomaye Faye. He also thanked the member states of the Security Council who gave him their votes during the consultations.

Macky Sall thanked his campaign team, religious and traditional authorities, as well as all Senegalese citizens, political actors and representatives of civil society, in Africa and elsewhere in the world, who mobilized around his candidacy.



The continent, Sall said, must continue to make its voice heard and advocate for more equitable representation within international bodies, and needs to strengthen its role in global governance.

The former president concluded his statement by expressing his best wishes for success to the person who will succeed António Guterres as head of the United Nations.

World.title: South Africa: From First Jab to the Next - The Data System Tracking South Africa's LEN Roll-Out
World.content:
South Africa's LEN roll-out isn't just about getting six-monthly HIV prevention jabs into people's arms. We also need to know whether people return for their next dose, whether clinics have enough stock and who is being left behind. A digital system linking LEN clinics will help us find out.

South Africa's LEN roll-out isn't just about getting six-monthly HIV prevention jabs into people's arms. We also need to know whether people return for their next dose, whether clinics have enough stock and who is being left behind. A digital system linking LEN clinics will help us find out.

Giving someone their first LEN jab is easy to count. Knowing whether they return six months later is what tells us whether the programme is really working.

A digital system called SyNCH connects LEN clinics in all provinces outside the Western Cape, which uses a different system, allowing health workers to see information about a person's previous LEN doses when they visit another participating clinic.

The information feeds into a dashboard that helps health officials see who is using LEN, where uptake is low and where clinics may need more support.

South Africa still doesn't have a comprehensive national electronic patient record. The LEN system shows what becomes possible when health information can follow a patient between clinics.

Giving someone an HIV prevention injection is one thing. Knowing whether they come back six months later for their next one is another.

That difference matters.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa started rolling out lenacapavir, or LEN, a twice-yearly injection that prevents HIV, in June . But the success of the programme cannot be measured simply by counting how many people receive their first injections.

The health department also needs to know whether people return for their second and third doses. By 15 October just under 79 000 people had received their first LEN dose, and the first group of people who will receive their second dose, will have to do so in early December .

The department needs to see which clinics have high or low uptake, which groups of people are being reached — and which are being missed. And it needs to know whether clinics have enough stock to give people their next injections when they are due.

Without good data, health officials are effectively trying to manage a national programme without being able to see clearly what is happening on the ground.

That is why one of the less visible parts of South Africa's LEN roll-out could turn out to be one of its most important: the digital system behind it.

SA's HIV prevention medicine dashboard (screen grab)

Following a LEN user from one clinic to another

LEN is currently available at 360 public clinics in South Africa. Most of these clinics are connected through an electronic system called SyNCH, short for the Synchronised National Communication in Health system .

SyNCH was developed by the public health intelligence organisation, Health Systems Trust (HST) and ASG Technologies in partnership with the national health department. It was originally built to help manage medicines for stable patients with chronic conditions who collect their treatment from pick-up points outside clinics. It has since been expanded to include HIV prevention medicines — both the daily HIV prevention pill and LEN.

For LEN users, this means something remarkably practical.

When someone receives LEN, their visit is recorded electronically. If they later go to another LEN clinic connected to SyNCH, a healthcare worker can see information about their previous LEN visit, including when they received their last dose.

So a person does not necessarily have to return to the same clinic every six months to continue using LEN.

That matters in a country where people move between towns and provinces for work, study or family reasons.

The exception is the Western Cape, which uses a different electronic patient-record system. LEN users there can move between participating clinics within the province, but their records are not connected to SyNCH clinics elsewhere in the country.

South Africa has spent years trying to build a comprehensive national electronic patient record. We are not there yet. SyNCH is not such a record either. But what is happening with LEN shows what becomes possible when clinics can share important information about an individual patient's care.

A first dose doesn't tell you whether a programme works

The system does more than help individual LEN users.

The information entered at clinics feeds into a LEN dashboard that allows health officials to see what is happening with the roll-out without waiting months for reports to work their way up through the health system.

Officials can see how many people are choosing LEN or the daily HIV prevention pill and break the figures down by age, gender and area — from province all the way down to individual clinics.

That can answer important questions.

Are young people taking up LEN? Are some districts doing much better than others? Are particular groups not being reached? Is a clinic attracting many LEN users while another nearby is seeing very few?

Those differences matter because a national total can hide local problems.

A headline figure might show that thousands of people have received LEN. But it won't necessarily tell officials that uptake is low in one district, that a particular age group is being missed or that a clinic needs extra support.

More detailed data can.

And as the roll-out continues, another number will become increasingly important: how many people come back for their next injection?

LEN protects someone for six months at a time . If large numbers of people receive their first dose but don't return for later injections, the programme will not have the impact we hope for.

Because SyNCH keeps a person-level record of LEN use, the health department can track whether people return for subsequent doses rather than simply counting injections given.

That turns data from a record of what has already happened into a tool for improving what happens next.

Data can also help prevent stock problems

There is another crucial part of the picture: medicine stock.

A successful campaign can create its own problem if demand grows faster than the supply of medicine to clinics.

Digital information can help health officials see how LEN is being used and where stock is running low. That gives managers an opportunity to respond — for example, by moving stock or replenishing a clinic — before shortages interrupt people's prevention.

This is especially important for a medicine that must be given on a schedule.

Someone who has made the effort to return for their next injection should not discover that the clinic has run out.

The dashboard isn't the achievement on its own

It is tempting to think of a dashboard as the innovation. But a dashboard is only as useful as the information underneath it.

Close 

The bigger achievement is connecting what happens to an individual LEN user at a clinic with information that nurses, doctors and programme managers can use.

HST has worked with the national health department and other partners for years to build and support some of the digital systems on which this work depends. LEN shows how that infrastructure can be adapted for a new public health programme rather than building a separate system from scratch each time.

There is a broader lesson here.

South Africa has many ambitious health policies and programmes. But launching an intervention is only the beginning. We need to know whether people are actually getting it, whether they continue using it, whether clinics have enough stock and whether the people who could benefit most are being reached.

That requires good data.

The same principle applies far beyond LEN. A health system needs to be able to follow people through care, whether they are using HIV prevention, collecting HIV or TB treatment, or receiving long-term care for conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure.

Technology on its own won't fix South Africa's health system. Nor will another dashboard.

But when health workers can see the information they need to care for someone, and managers can see problems early enough to do something about them, data becomes more than numbers on a screen.

It becomes part of healthcare itself.

Ntombi Sigwebela is the chief executive officer of Health Systems Trust.

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Uganda: Police Break Silence On Murder of Rwandan Dissident Beheaded in Mpigi
World.content:
Police have launched investigations into the murder of a Rwandan dissident whose headless body was discovered in Mpigi District, with the victim's missing head yet to be recovered.

Sgt Maj Robert Kabera, 50, a former Rwanda Defence Forces (RDF) soldier who was critical of President Paul Kagame's leadership, was found dead on Saturday morning, October 17, in Luwala Village, Kammengo Sub-county.

Police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke told journalists on Monday that officers had registered a murder case after the discovery of the body.

"We acknowledge that we registered murder of male adult averagely 50 years whose head was cut off and up to now it hasn't yet been recovered. We recovered the body minus the head. He was identified as Robert Kabera by his relatives," Rusoke said.



He said police received the report on Saturday, although investigators believe the killing could have occurred either during the night of October 16 or in the early hours of October 17.

According to Rusoke, local residents discovered the remains and alerted police. Kabera's relatives had also become concerned after he failed to communicate as he usually did.

"The remains were discovered by locals who informed police. Incidentally relatives were concerned about their person who usually wouldn't take long to communicate," he said.

Police officers who visited the scene found the headless body, which was subsequently taken to Mulago City Mortuary as part of the investigation.

Rusoke said investigators were examining the circumstances surrounding the killing and other details that could help establish what happened.

"We are investigating that murder and any other details relevant to the murder or any circumstances surrounding his life," he said.

Kabera reportedly fled Rwanda for Uganda around 2020 after raising concerns that his life was in danger.

His killing comes against the backdrop of his reported criticism of the Rwandan leadership. However, police have not publicly established a motive for the murder or indicated whether his political views were connected to his death.

Investigations are ongoing, with the recovery of his missing head among the outstanding details in the case.

World.title: South Africa: Mbeki Denies Secret Deals With Apartheid-Era Generals
World.content:
At the Khampepe Commission, Thabo Mbeki rejects claims of political interference, explaining the ANC's amnesty bid and distinguishing presidential pardons from prosecution decisions.

Former president Thabo Mbeki has told the Khampepe Commission of Inquiry into delayed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) prosecutions that the only occasion he met former apartheid military and police generals was when they had approached the ANC, stating they would not apply for amnesty if then president FW de Klerk and his cabinet did not do so as well.

On the first day of his much-anticipated appearance, the former president denied any secret meetings and testified that former generals approached him in 1996, while the TRC was in progress, to request a meeting with the ANC committee tasked with amnesty applications.

President, not prosecutor
