World.title: South Africa: Hundreds of Children Fall Ill After Tshwane Fails to Chlorinate Water
World.content:
Public was not warned that water was unsafe for drinking

More than 400 people, mostly children under four, fell ill in Bronkhorstspruit and nearby areas this month.

For three weeks, Tshwane didn't chlorinate water drawn from a river polluted with sewage, and didn't warn residents.

Residents may use tap water only to flush toilets until it is safe again.

Contaminated drinking water in Tshwane has led to hundreds of cases of acute gastrointestinal illnesses. Government investigations have found that the City of Tshwane failed to chlorinate water for three weeks, resulting in high levels of E. coli and other cloriforms.

Between 7 and 18 October 2026, 408 cases, predominantly in children under the age of four, were recorded in Tshwane's Region 7, which includes Bronkhorstspruit, Zithobeni, Dark City, Rethabiseng, and Sokhulumi. No deaths have been reported.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The crisis peaked on 13 October, when 72 new cases were reported in a single day, overwhelming local clinics and Bronkhorstspruit Hospital in north-eastern Gauteng.

Investigations conducted by the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD) and the Department of Water and Sanitation (DWS) linked the cases to contaminated municipal tap water from the Bronkhorstpruit Water Treatment Works. Further specimens are being collected to decide whether to declare an outbreak.

Laboratory analyses of stool specimens found pathogens including Norovirus, Campylobacter, and Shigella, according to an official joint statement by national, provincial, and local health authorities issued on Monday.

Water quality testing by the Department of Water and Sanitation, conducted on 14 October, confirmed severe bacterial contamination, detecting "extremely high levels of E. coli and total coliforms in the water".

Earlier this month, GroundUp reported on residents' continued concerns about discoloured water and potential illness.

Zithobeni resident Nicky Sibanda said she and her one-year-old had no choice but to drink the discoloured water from their tap, which led to diarrhoea and stomach pains.

"I'm worried and want to know when this problem will come to an end," Sibanda said on Monday. "The colour of our tap water has not changed. The municipality still does not send trucks to deliver drinking water and we are suffering. We are still buying water from other people who sell it."

Another resident of Zithobeni, Selina Maphosa, said she is worried about the safety of her two children, aged five and eight.

"I'm always worried that my children might drink tap water and fall ill when playing with other children at other homes," said Maphosa.

"Another problem is that the municipality does not give us full information about this problem. We heard last month that they were investigating this problem but they did not tell us anything more about it. We have many questions that need answers."

Upstream sewage pollution

The root cause of the outbreak stems from raw sewage contaminating the municipal water source.

The Bronkhorspruit treatment works abstracts raw water directly from the Bronkhorstspruit River. The river "is badly contaminated with sewage pollution from upstream dysfunctional wastewater treatment works (WWTW) under Victor Khanye Municipality as well as from dysfunctional [City of Tshwane] sewage pump stations," the joint statement read.

Due to supplier disruptions, Tshwane failed to chlorinate water at Bronkhorstspruit WTW for nearly three weeks, between 24 September and 14 October. The metro then "failed to warn residents in the affected areas of Bronkhorstspruit that the water being supplied had not been chlorinated and therefore should not be drunk or used for cooking, washing or bathing, even after boiling".

At a media briefing on Monday afternoon, Tshwane mayor Nasiphi Moya said the supplier had quadrupled its prices, negotiations failed, and then officials had not informed the city's leadership of the chlorine shortage at the plant. Disciplinary action will be taken against the officials.

Authorities shut down the plant on 14 October, restored chlorine supplies the next day and reopened the plant on 16 October. 36 water tankers were deployed.

Rand Water will be appointed to oversee urgent repairs and conduct ongoing water safety tests. The Water Research Commission is doing independent testing and investigating the causes.

Until full safety compliance is re-established, tap water in the area remains restricted to toilet flushing.

A broader crisis

Close 

Water management expert Dr Anthony Turton recently told GroundUp that South Africa's water network relies on an "indirect reuse model," where treated sewage effluent flows back into rivers and dams before being abstracted by municipal drinking plants.

However, when upstream sewage infrastructure collapses, treatment facilities are pushed far beyond their engineering limits.

"None were designed to convert raw sewage into potable water, which is what they are now being asked to do," he said.

"In my professional opinion, the sewage crisis is what will destroy water security in South Africa. It is an existential threat to the national economy," said Turton.

Tshwane's 2025 Green Drop (an audit of wastewater systems) score fell to 33.8%, with six wastewater systems critically underperforming, persistent sewage spills, dysfunctional pump stations, inadequate monitoring and engineering capacity, and ongoing infrastructure failures contributing to pollution.

On Monday, GroundUp reported on how the Rietvlei WTW, once supplying about 5% of Tshwane's water, has not been working for the past year due to pollution.

World.title: Rwanda: Rwanda, Nigeria Army Chiefs Discuss Training, Skills Exchanges
World.content:
Nigeria's Chief of Army Staff, Lt Gen Waidi Shaibu, arrived in Rwanda on Sunday, October 18, for a five-day official visit aimed at strengthening defence cooperation between the two countries.

On Monday, Shaibu visited Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) Headquarters in Kigali, where he paid a courtesy call on Chief of Defence Staff Gen Mubarakh Muganga and held bilateral talks with RDF Army Chief of Staff Maj Gen Vincent Nyakarundi.

Shaibu said the two sides had committed to implementing existing memoranda of understanding covering military training, the exchange of directing staff and logistics personnel.

"As the outcome of today's discussion, we have made key promises to implement the various memoranda of understanding that have been there between both countries in the area of training, exchange of directing staff as well as logisticians," he said.

The discussions also covered defence and security developments of mutual interest to the two countries.

Shaibu arrived in Rwanda on October 18 along with his delegation and are scheduled to conclude their visit on October 23.

Earlier on Monday, they visited Kigali Genocide Memorial, where they paid tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

They also toured the Campaign Against Genocide Museum to learn about the Genocide, its impact and Rwanda's journey of rebuilding.

World.title: Senate Republicans might survive the blue thunderstorm. Uh, I think.
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

With everyone and his brother predicting that a blue tsunami will wash over the Senate as well as the House, I want to write something contrarian.

This way, if the Republicans do hang on to the Senate, I’ll get credit for defying the conventional wisdom. And if they don’t, I won’t get kicked out of the punditocracy – folks will just say well, he put a lot of caveats in there.

THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND

The truth is, I don’t know who is going to capture the upper chamber, and neither do you.

And neither do all the pontificators and speculators online or on the air.

I do know the GOP is pouring tens of millions into contests they might otherwise lose, giving their people – even scandal-scarred Ken Paxton – a huge advantage on the airwaves in the final two weeks. But money doesn’t always move voters once they’ve made up their minds in this era of early voting.

Is Maine’s Susan Collins liked enough to hang one more time against aggressive Troy Jackson (and thankfully not weirdo Graham Platner), when Donald Trump shouts every day ‘Pretend I’m on the ballot’?" We got it, Mr. President.

Josh Turek is an Iowa legislator and also a wheelchair basketball player who suffers from spina bifida. His GOP opponent, Rep. Ashley Hinton, says she doesn’t want "endless wars" but welcomes a Trump visit.

Embed:

She’s talked about such issues as open borders and transgender surgery. Turek has focused on the Iran war and soaring health premiums because Congress failed to amend the Affordable Care Act.

World.title: UNC settles Trump admin probes into alleged campus antisemitism, race-based admissions
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill that will close 18 active federal investigations and a separate Justice Department compliance review involving alleged antisemitism and race discrimination at the university.

The voluntary settlement agreement does not require a monetary payment, and the university does not admit to any wrongdoing or liability. The deal, which will remain effective until the end of 2028, allows UNC to maintain its eligibility for federal funding.

Under the agreement, UNC will appoint an internal "Merit & Civil Rights Administrator" and establish a "Title VI Coordinator" position in its compliance office to address complaints about antisemitism and race-based discrimination.

The university said Elizabeth Hall, associate vice chancellor for university compliance, was appointed to serve in both roles in addition to her existing duties. She will be the point of contact for the Justice Department and oversee UNC's reporting obligations.

DOJ SUES UCLA OVER ALLEGED ‘JUDENREIN’ CONDITIONS DURING ANTI-ISRAEL ENCAMPMENT

"This announcement reinforces our commitment to the fair and equal treatment of everyone at Carolina," UNC Chancellor Lee H. Roberts said in a statement. "For at least a decade, through different presidential administrations, U.S. universities have faced heightened public scrutiny across a range of issues. We’re proud to resolve those issues at Carolina in a way that protects our mission and affirms the civil rights of everyone in our community."

The agreement also requires UNC to provide mandatory antisemitism training to students, faculty and staff.

UNC will also prohibit face masks used to conceal an individual's identity, subject to certain exceptions, as part of the deal, which said student groups "shall be subject to discipline for antisemitic discriminatory conduct."

President Donald Trump and administration officials have accused pro-Palestinian protesters of antisemitism. But protesters, including some Jewish groups, contend that opposing Israel's military offensive in Gaza is not antisemitic and that support for Palestinian rights does not indicate support for extremism.

The settlement agreement also said UNC will adopt what the Justice Department called a "color-blind admissions system," barring the university from using race or altering its admissions process to change the racial composition of its student body. However, it does not prevent UNC from considering how applicants overcame adversity at a personal level, and the university may consider aspects of family background, such as poverty, if those considerations are applied consistently.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS

UNC must also maintain race-blind policies governing student benefits, scholarships, financial aid and programming, according to the agreement.

The administration has argued that policies favoring certain racial groups over others violate federal anti-discrimination law.

The deal said UNC will send any antisemitism and race discrimination complaints it has received to the DOJ and the Department of Education on a quarterly basis.

As part of the agreement, the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights will close 18 active investigations into UNC, while the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division will close a separate 18-month compliance review opened in April 2025.

"Title VI requires that all students — regardless of their ancestry or race — receive equal treatment under the law at federally funded colleges and universities," Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon said in a statement.

"Higher ed policies and practices that tolerate antisemitism or favor certain racial groups over others, frustrate our color-blind justice system. The Civil Rights Division commends UNC for its cooperation in meeting its obligations under federal law without the need for litigation; we hope other institutions will take note and do the same," she added.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In 2023, the Supreme Court rejected affirmative action at colleges as it struck down ​race-based admissions programs at UNC and Harvard.

The administration has targeted universities across the country with probes and threats to pull federal funding in response to pro-Palestinian protests on campus, diversity initiatives and transgender policies.

The federal government has also settled with some other schools, including Columbia University, which last year agreed to pay more than $200 million to resolve federal probes, and Brown University, which agreed to provide $50 million over 10 years to Rhode Island workforce-development organizations as part of its settlement.

Harvard, which has been a primary target of the administration's threats, has not yet made a deal.

Reuters contributed to this report.

World.title: Rays punch their ticket to the World Series, taking down Guardians in Game 6 to set up series with Brewers
World.content:
The 2026 World Series is set.

The Tampa Bay Rays will take on the Milwaukee Brewers, as they defeated the Cleveland Guardians, 7-3, in Game 6 of the ALCS to win the American League pennant.

The Brewers, who shockingly swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, have been watching this ALCS patiently to see who their opponent will be.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Tampa Bay won Game 5 on the road, which is always a pivotal tilt when the series is tied at two games apiece, and they didn’t squander their first trip back home at Tropicana Field.

With a sold-out "Trop," the Rays used their momentum to get the job done.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Richie Palacios got the Rays on the board first in the bottom of the second inning after a clutch, two-out double to make it 2-0 early.

Then, with the game at 3-1 in favor of Tampa Bay, it was their superstar, Junior Caminero, hitting what felt like the series-sealing home run that sent the Trop into rapture.

Caminero turned on an inside pitch and was willing the ball to stay fair, as it smacked off the foul pole and the celebration ensued. Caminero stopped before hitting first base, screaming in elation with the crowd and his nearby teammates in the dugout as he understood making it a 5-1 game in the bottom of the seventh inning was a back-breaker for the Guardians.

Caminero took his time rounding the bases before touching home plate, and the Rays fans in the stadium matched his energy the entire time.

Cleveland, though, wouldn’t go down without a fight. They found some juice in the ensuing frame, scoring twice to make it a 5-3 game. But as they’ve done all season, the Rays responded when they needed it.

Yandy Diaz hit his own home run, and there was no doubt about the 416-footer he sent over the left field wall to give his squad a four-run lead.

As the top of the ninth began, Bryan Baker, the Rays’ lockdown closer, took the mound to finish the job in Game 6. He got Steven Kwan and Jose Ramirez to both ground out to first base before Chase DeLauter popped out foul to punch Tampa Bay’s ticket into the Fall Classic.

This marks the first time the Rays have been to the World Series since the 2020 COVID-19-shortened season, while the Brewers are in for the first time in 44 years.

World.title: Terry McLaurin carted off, Mike Evans hurt as 49ers hold off Commanders 23-17 on brutal MNF
World.content:

Top Commanders wideout Terry McLaurin had to be carted off the field in the first half with an apparent left knee injury after going down without contact.

Teammates and Niners players alike took a knee for McLaurin as he exited, leaving Washington facing a 13-3 deficit that grew to 20-3 by halftime behind a Brock Purdy touchdown pass to George Kittle and two Christian McCaffrey scoring runs.

A McDonald's in Paris was left ransacked and heavily damaged after cost-of-living protests exploded into riots and widespread looting that also targeted restaurants, cafés and grocery stores across the French capital — with the city now issuing curfews in two places, The Associated Press reported.

The McDonald's on Boulevard de Magenta near Gare de l'Est suffered smashed windows and extensive damage inside, according to Le Monde.

Computer screens were damaged — while an ice cream machine continued spilling vanilla onto a ketchup-covered floor, the outlet reported.

MASSIVE FIRE DESTROYS 400-YEAR-OLD FOOD MARKET, LEAVING HISTORIC LANDMARK IN RUINS

Intruders even attempted to cook french fries before a man and his dog drove about 20 people from the restaurant, a security guard told the publication.

Fox News Digital reached out to McDonald's for comment about the vandalism.

The American-based fast-food chain was hardly the only food business to be caught up in the destruction.

A neighborhood café was burned out, a wine shop was destroyed and supermarkets were among the businesses targeted as unrest swept Paris.

Among the hardest hit was La Barrique, a neighborhood café near Place de la République that was burned out, according to Le Monde.

World.title: Elissa Slotkin calls backlash to threat of prosecution comments 'manufactured outrage'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., called the backlash against her comments that the threat of prosecution could deter young people from working for the Trump administration "manufactured outrage" during television interviews Monday.

During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event, Slotkin drew criticism after a clip went viral showing her saying she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump and push a "deterrence message" for young people.

"I want young people coming out of school to say, ‘Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.’ I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that,’" she said. "I want that deterrence message," Slotkin said.

While speaking with CNN's Jake Tapper on Monday, Slotkin responded to a comment from Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, who wrote that it was "absolutely disgraceful" to "threaten young Americans for participating in politics and serving their country" with legal retribution.

MIKE DAVIS: SEN SLOTKIN REVEALS HER INSIDIOUS SCHEME TO TARGET YOUNG CONSERVATIVES

"Yeah, well, look, that’s manufactured outrage," Slotkin responded. "That’s his specialty. I think the thing that I’ve heard from my own Republican colleagues and peers, including interns and folks who work around the Hill who come to our events, they’ll tell you, 'I was worried. My parents were worried, you know. It’s really messy. I’m not sure what to get involved in.' Politics, in general, has become messy."

"But, you know, when you’re being forced by this administration, for instance, to sign a contract that is given over to a company that Trump Jr. is on the board of, and you know that that’s a problem," she added.

Slotkin then referenced her viral video from 2025, in which she and five other Democratic lawmakers urged military members to "refuse illegal orders." She claimed that in both circumstances she was only encouraging people to reject illegal activity.

"My point is, do not get yourself involved in illegal activity," she said. "It’s the same thing I was talking about a year ago. Whether you’re the uniformed military or a civilian in government, if you’re being asked to do something by the president or his team, that’s illegal, you have a responsibility to reject that. That is my point, and that was the point I was trying to make."

SLOTKIN SAYS DEMOCRATIC PARTY NEEDS 'NEW LEADERSHIP': 'OLD MODELS ARE NO LONGER WORKING'

Fox News Digital reached out to Lee's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

The White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's previous comments on Slotkin.

"That's a hell of a statement. Slotkin said that there should be prosecutions in order to scare people from going into politics. That's a Democrat and that's what they do. That's all they're good at — and you know what? That's why they're getting their a--es kicked," Trump said.

Slotkin reiterated that she had no intention of targeting people for prosecution solely because of their political affiliation and only cared about people "breaking the law."

"If you are violating the law, then you should be held accountable, and that includes people who are supporting that activity. That’s the point I was trying to make. You’re not breaking the law? No problem. We can have disagreements all day long, and certainly Democrats and Republicans do. I don’t care if it’s just freedom of speech. I care if you’re breaking the law," Slotkin told CNN.

PENNSYLVANIA SOCIALIST DEMOCRAT SAYS HE OPPOSES IMPRISONMENT EXCEPT FOR 'LAWLESS MAGA THUGS'

During a separate interview on MS NOW, Slotkin suggested some of the backlash she received from Republican critics could be attributed to her gender.

"I think when you choose to call out their corruption, they clearly don't like that," Slotkin said on MS NOW's "Deadline: White House." "They're clearly trying to change the conversation given what the midterms are and the state of the economy, the state of things around the country. I do think there's something about being a woman and criticizing them and calling them out on that corruption that really gets under their skin, obviously, or they wouldn't respond."

World.title: Richard Riehle, character actor best known for ‘Office Space,’ dies at 78
World.content:
Richard Riehle, a prolific character actor whose bushy mustache and knack for portraying beleaguered middlemen made him a favorite of Hollywood casting directors for decades, has died, his representatives said Monday.

He was 78. Riehle’s representatives said he died over the weekend but did not provide details about the cause.

Riehle was best known for his supporting role in Mike Judge’s corporate satire “Office Space” as Tom Smykowski, an anxious product manager who rages against the prospect of getting laid off. (“I have people skills! I am good at dealing with people! Can’t you understand that?”)

He left an impression even with scant screen time, whether playing a racist quartermaster in “Glory,” a guard who allows Harrison Ford to flee in “The Fugitive,” a mob banker who gets cursed out by Joe Pesci in Martin Scorsese’s “Casino” or a kindly auto mechanic who helps out Kristen Wiig in “Bridesmaids.”

Riehle’s hundreds of credits include scores of TV roles, such as Principal Ed Rooney on the short-lived sitcom “Ferris Bueller,” a gruff grandfather on “Grounded for Life” and a police officer on “The West Wing.” He most recently appeared as a prison warden on HBO’s dark comedy “Barry.”

“Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity,” his talent agency and management company said in a statement.

“Grounded for Life” star Donal Logue paid tribute to Riehle on Facebook, describing his co-star as “an amazing human being” and a “consummate professional.”

Richard Riehle at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles in 2019. Rodin Eckenroth / WireImage

“He was an actor’s actor — humble, kind, and incredible at his craft,” Logue wrote. “I had to apologize to him after his final network audition for ‘Grounded’ because he made me laugh so hard, I broke character and fell to the floor.”

Riehle made his screen acting debut as an unnamed bartender in the 1977 road-trip movie “Joyride,” the first of more than 400 credits across film and television.

Richard Mathias Riehle was born on May 12, 1948, in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin. He attended the University of Notre Dame, where he joined the campus theatrical group and grew fond of stage acting.

“I always wanted the role that would bring something out of me, force me to find something extra,” Riehle told Notre Dame Magazine for the winter 2011-12 issue. “The lead isn’t always the best part in a play or a movie.”

World.title: Tampa Bay Rays advance to World Series, will face Milwaukee Brewers
World.content:
Tampa Bay will face the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series after the Rays on Monday won the American League Championship Series over Cleveland.

It will mark the third World Series berth for the Rays, who are searching for the franchise’s first MLB title after appearances in 2008 and 2020.

Cleveland took a 2-1 ALCS lead before Tampa roared back with successive wins in Game 4 and Game 5 to set up Monday’s clinching 7-3 win in Game 6.

Tampa jumped to an early lead after a double by Richie Palacios drove in two runs in the second inning. One inning later, a sacrifice fly by Jonny DeLuca brought in another run for a 3-0 lead. When Cleveland trimmed the lead to 3-1 in the sixth inning, Tampa answered with a two-run homer by Junior Caminero in the seventh.

Tampa Bay Rays' Richie Palacios reacts after a single during the sixth inning at Tropicana Field on Monday. Julio Aguilar / Getty

Cleveland applied pressure again by scoring two runs in the eighth to cut the lead to 5-3, but Tampa was ready for another answer in its next at-bat. A two-run homer by Yandy Diaz extended the lead to 7-3.

When the Brewers and Rays meet in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday, a first-time champion will be guaranteed. The Brewers are making their first World Series appearance since 1982. It will be a showdown of the teams that finished with the best records in the National and American leagues. Milwaukee finished with an MLB-high 103 wins, while Tampa had 98. The teams played three times in the regular season with Milwaukee winning twice, but all three games occurred during the first week of the season.

Tampa Bay Rays' Junior Caminero celebrates a two-run home run against the Cleveland Guardians on Monday. Phelan M. Ebenhack / AP

The Rays have advanced to baseball’s biggest stage despite building a roster using the third-lowest payroll. Milwaukee wasn’t a big spender, itself, ranking 19th in payroll. Yet the clubs from small markets with relatively low payrolls found ways to play the best baseball in each of their respective leagues this season en route to the World Series.

Tampa entered Monday’s Game 6 allowing just 1.0 walks and hits per inning pitched while sweeping the New York Yankees in the divisional round, then facing Cleveland. The Rays’ postseason star has been pitcher Drew Rasmussen, who has allowed three earned runs combined in his three appearances.

Few would have expected this season from Tampa after the franchise finished its 2023 and 2024 seasons in fourth place in the AL East while finishing lower than .500 each year. Making matters even more difficult was that the team didn’t even have its home stadium available for much of that stretch, after Hurricane Milton tore the roof off of Tropicana Field in downtown St. Petersburg in October 2024. It took until August for the Rays to host games in the stadium again, following a $60 million roof renovation.

World.title: Vance declines to endorse Netanyahu after Trump offers full support for re-election
World.content:
Vice President JD Vance declined to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, a day after President Donald Trump publicly backed Netanyahu as he seeks re-election this month.

“I’m not getting involved in the Israeli elections,” Vance said in an interview on Mark Halperin’s show “2WAY Tonight.”

“I’m not anti-endorsing him; I’m not pro-endorsing him,” Vance added.

Trump weighed in on the election Sunday, strongly backing Netanyahu’s re-election bid.

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so. Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that the post represents his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.”

Vance said Monday that Trump has “the most effective endorsement in American or international political history.”

He further defended his refusal to get involved in the race by saying he endorses “American candidates,” adding “that’s what I’m focused on” as the midterm elections approach.

Vance traveled to Hungary this year to stump for then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who was voted out of power in April after 16 years.

Vance also reiterated Monday that he has not decided whether he will run for president in 2028. But should he do so, Vance said, he thinks Trump will endorse him.

“I really have not made up my mind about what to do in 2028. I just haven’t focused on it,” Vance said. “I think if I run, the president will endorse me right away, right at the beginning.”

World.title: Trump uses antisemitic slur in defending Sen. Roger Marshall at rally in Kansas
World.content:
President Donald Trump used an antisemitic slur Monday in defending Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., after an article said he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid debts when he was a practicing physician.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Kansas, Trump said the reporting made Marshall, who is not Jewish, out to be “some kind of a shylock-type guy,” using a term widely recognized as offensive toward Jewish people.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.

Trump used the same slur last year in a speech to describe exploitative bankers as he was promoting his sweeping domestic policy bill. Some Jewish groups denounced his use of the term.

“Shylock” is a Jewish character in William Shakespeare’s play “The Merchant of Venice” sometimes called a usurer. The Anti-Defamation League, in a guide for educators teaching the play, says, “Shylock, and by extension, all Jews, are presented as money-hungry, conniving, and cruel.”

Trump at the time denied having knowledge of the antisemitic connotations of the term, saying he had “never heard it that way” and adding, “To me, shylock is somebody that’s a moneylender at high rates.”

Former President Joe Biden faced backlash in 2014 for using the word, which he later apologized for.

Trump speaks at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty

Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, faced backlash after The New York Times reported last month that he sued more than 700 patients for unpaid bills, which resulted in scores of arrest warrants for missed court dates. His lawyer said Marshall had no involvement in the warrants or the arrests, and Marshall called the story a “hit job.”

“You got screwed with that stuff,” Trump said Monday about the reporting, addressing Marshall onstage. He did not mention the Times by name.

Marshall, who has represented Kansas in the Senate since 2021, faces Adam Hamilton in a closer-than-expected race. Hamilton is a megachurch pastor and former Republican who said he decided to run as a Democrat this year after having considered a bid as an independent. Hamilton has picked up a number of endorsements from influential Republicans and Democrats in the state.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report characterizes the race as a “toss-up.” NBC News lists it as competitive but leaning toward the GOP.

World.title: Voters reject separation of Alberta from Canada in referendum
World.content:
Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, results showed early Tuesday, delivering a victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity amid President Trump's trade war and annexation threats.

The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.

With more than 1 million votes counted, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation.

"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.

Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots. Albertans were deciding whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could have lead to a second vote on separation.

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.

Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said Albertans have long been mistreated by Ottawa.

"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us and not return anything."

Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.

"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.

Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than health care.

Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that will not disappear.

Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

World.title: Hegseth meets Netanyahu ahead of elections, possible Iran war restart
World.content:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.

The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.

Hegseth confirmed in an X post that he was in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility on Monday, sharing a photo of himself addressing American service members who he said were "on a historic mission." He did not specify his location or mention Israel.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.

Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.

Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.

Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections.

Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.

Netanyahu told Israeli media last week he is not planning to launch renewed strikes against Iran before the Oct. 27 elections, saying, "it is not convenient for us."

Mr. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, calling him "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."

The U.S. president has maintained a close relationship with Netanyahu, though he has put pressure on Israel at times. Over the spring and summer, the Trump administration urged Israel to ease up on striking Lebanon, home to Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.

The administration has also encouraged Israel to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank and cut a longer-term deal with Hamas in the Gaza Strip.

Last month, Trump envoy Jared Kushner suggested the upcoming Israeli elections may have delayed progress in Gaza, saying at a conference in Kyiv: "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."

World.title: Zelenskyy says it's Putin who wants an endless war, not him
World.content:
Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Monday that his country had been subjected to another night of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners."

Zelenskyy has accused the U.S. of limiting intelligence, and possibly other assistance to Ukraine amid renewed tension with President Trump, who accused the Ukrainian leader over the weekend of not wanting to end the war. Mr. Trump has significantly softened the U.S. government's policy toward Russia, easing sanctions to allow Russian energy sales in a bid to ease U.S. gas prices.

Zelenskyy says the moves risk emboldening Moscow and enabling it to continue and intensify its four-and-a-half-year, full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The target of the most recent strikes was energy and other infrastructure, Zelenskyy said, adding that a medical clinic, school, metro station and "ordinary residential buildings" were also hit.

A woman stands amid rubble outside a house damaged by a Russian strike in Dnipro, Ukraine, Oct. 19, 2026. Mykola Miakshykov/Ukrinform/NurPhoto/Getty

Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite technology, to intercept Russian drones. The network is crucial to Ukrainian forces as it enables them to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones and other weapons.

The Trump administration has denied making any changes to the intelligence it shares with Ukraine, or deliberately slowing down Starshield data.

A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday, "There has been no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."

Asked Saturday if the U.S. government was responsible for the change in Starlink service in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about, but it wasn't deliberate … we have nothing to do with that."

"The United States — nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it's been restored. It's back to where it was before," he said, without elaborating on what he meant by "it sort of happened."

Denys Sienik, Ukraine's chargé d'affaires and current top diplomat in the U.S., told CBS News in a statement later Saturday that Ukraine had still not received a response from the Pentagon or Musk's SpaceX to inquiries about Starlink or Starshield service, "including confirmation that unlimited speeds have been restored and that Starshield is operating as it did previously."

"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," Zelenskyy said Monday in a post on X, adding that there had also been "delays in certain types of vital supplies at the level of the U.S. Department of War."

He did not expound on his assertion that the Pentagon was delaying shipments of supplies.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is seen during an interview at his office in Kyiv, Ukraine, Oct. 18, 2026. Olga Ivashchenko/Bloomberg/Getty

The Ukrainian leader issued the statement amid an increasingly terse exchange of accusations with Mr. Trump who, over the weekend, accused Zelenskyy of not wanting the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion to end.

In a Truth Social post, Mr. Trump said Zelenskyy "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump argued.

The U.S. president has over the last month walked back sanctions on Russia — that had support from a majority of Republicans and Democrats — that were intended to increase financial pressure on Moscow over its assault on Ukraine.

"Ukraine never wanted this war," Zelenskyy said in another statement shared Monday on social media. "We took positively literally EVERY attempt of partners to end this war with dignity."

Just over a week ago Mr. Trump declared in a social media post that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," which would mean a halt to attacks on the other country's energy infrastructure. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to any such deal, and within hours Ukrainian authorities reported new Russian attacks on refineries.

A worker sweeps up rubbish outside the Chalet Ice Arena, which was damaged in a Russian ballistic missile attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, Oct. 19, 2026, amid Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Sergei SUPINSKY/AFP/Getty

Zelenskyy said "again and again Russia's answers" to efforts at diplomacy were new attacks.

"Putin does not want the end of this war, or even any de-escalation steps," he said, adding: "It is very important to call things by their names. Call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine protect lives. When the supply of missiles to Ukrainian air defense is blocked, and Russia receives a weakening or postponement of sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality from partners. In reality, the war continues, and continues only because of Russian strikes — the Russian desire to prolong this war."

The Kremlin, meanwhile, has attempted to frame Russia as a willing partner in peace efforts.

Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday that Moscow values U.S. mediation efforts, but that reaching agreements without the participation of representatives from Kyiv is impossible. There have been direct talks, mediated by the U.S., between Ukraine and Russia, but so far the meetings have yielded little more than prisoner swaps, not ceasefires.

The Wall Street Journal first reported Sunday evening that Putin had proposed a meeting between U.S., Chinese and Russian officials to discuss solutions to the Ukraine war, but without a seat for Ukraine at the negotiating table. The newspaper said he proposed the idea for a summit during a call with Mr. Trump on Oct. 9.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Monday in a post on X that "a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."

World.title: California billionaire tax could backfire, Stanford study says
World.content:
California voters next month will decide on whether to tax billionaire wealth, a proposal designed to generate billions of dollars to shore up the state's healthcare system. But Stanford economists are now cautioning that the tax could backfire, leaving the state with less in tax revenue than before.

Seven billionaires have already publicly moved out of California, removing about $540 billion, or 30%, of the state's total billionaire wealth from potential taxation, according to Stanford University economists Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh in a new working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research. The billionaires who have left the state include venture capitalist Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

Because additional billionaires have likely quietly moved since the tax proposal was announced, the measure may ultimately generate only about $30 billion, far less than the $100 billion estimated by its proponents, the economists said. If enacted, the tax would apply a one-time 5% state tax on billionaire wealth.

To be sure, $30 billion is still a sizable amount of new tax revenue. But future income tax losses from those billionaire departures could more than offset that windfall, the economists calculated.

California could lose roughly $1 billion to $3.5 billion a year in income tax revenue due to its shrinking billionaire population, the paper's authors estimated. If those losses persist permanently, their value in today's dollars would exceed the wealth tax proceeds by about $39 billion, the economists said.

"These findings suggest that the Billionaire Tax Act will not fulfill the primary functions for which it was designed," Jaros and Rauh wrote. "Although the Act was designed to raise revenue, behavioral response prior to voting has eroded most of the projected tax base."

The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), a healthcare worker union that introduced the ballot measure, refuted the research.

The proposition's "sole purpose is to ensure that billionaires finally pay their fair share to prevent a collapse of California's healthcare system," Debru Carthan, vice president, SEIU-UHW, said in a statement to CBS News. "And Californians like me are seeing right through these misinformation campaigns."

The tax would replace cuts to healthcare spending introduced in the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill tax and spending law, allowing millions of Californians "to keep their healthcare while preventing their premiums from skyrocketing," Carthan said.

Other economists have come to different conclusions about the tax. Economists including Daron Acemoglu of MIT and Joseph Stiglitz of Columbia University, both Nobel Prize winners, have signed their support for the measure, pointing out that California has attracted more venture funding since the wealth tax was announced.

"What will allow California to thrive in the future is not letting a handful of billionaires live tax free: it is adequate public spending on health, education and public infrastructure, key engines of economic growth to which it is only fair to ask the ultra-wealthy to contribute," they wrote in a September letter of support for the tax.

Ahead of the vote on the ballot measure, called Proposition 40, voters in California are apparently divided on the tax. About 46% of likely voters say they favor Proposition 40, while 43% are opposed, according to a new poll from Citrin-Politico.

Dave Regan, the leader of the union that introduced the measure, told CBS News' Jo Ling Kent that he's "pretty confident" the tax will pass.

"There's never been a proposal like this anywhere in the world, so it's a novel idea," Regan said. "We are facing an emergency."

World.title: France vows to crack down after protests spiral out of control
World.content:
Paris — French officials implemented local curfews Monday as the nation reeled from a weekend of violence. Widespread anti-government protests in many large cities descended into riots, with damage to historic properties and thousands of arrests.

A curfew issued by Paris police on Monday will be in effect for the Place de la République and the Les Halles neighborhood. The curfew will be in effect from 11 p.m. local time Monday until 6 a.m. Tuesday. Gatherings in Paris after 8 p.m. were also banned, CBS News' partner network BBC News reported.

In Nice, a curfew was in effect from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., the city's mayor announced. A curfew covering that same time frame was also in effect for Lyon, according to the BBC.

In hard-hit Marseille, France's second-largest city, all large gatherings were banned Monday in the wake of the violence, which started weeks ago as protests by young people furious over the state of their schools, but quickly snowballed into national demonstrations over the rising cost of living and declining public services.

The 19th-century town hall in the city of Limoges was burned to the ground on Saturday by masked rioters who hijacked marches across France, looting stores, torching cars and buildings and clashing with police as the protests turned violent.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested, France's Justice Ministry said.

The U.S. State Department issued an advisory Monday urging Americans to "avoid the areas of the demonstrations."

A man walks past a row of burned vehicles on Rue Yves Toudic, destroyed amid nationwide protests against the cost of living, in central Paris, Oct. 19, 2026. Kiran RIDLEY/AFP/Getty

In an address Sunday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron, vowed that "those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable."

Speaking Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed at least some of the violence on "an ultra-left movement intent on orchestrating profound disorder in the country leading up to the presidential election" in April.

He said police "had lost control" during the unrest, and as the Yellow Vests protest movement, which organized the weekend rallies that turned violent, called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday, he called for regional authorities to impose "partial" and "localized" curfews to protect businesses.

"I'm absolutely determined to restore public order," Lecornu said, adding that the government was ready to impose a national state of emergency, "if needed."

Speaking of the alleged agitators, Lecornu said there was "⁠an entire network that could be mobilized to challenge the presidential election schedule and the very holding of the presidential election," adding that the government was committed to protecting the country's democratic process.

⁠"There is no way we will allow violent minorities to impose an agenda of violence and, quite obviously, prevent us from holding this election," he said, acknowledging that the protests by high school students over classroom conditions were legitimate, but adding that "the freedom to demonstrate is being undermined."

While French officials have not suggested any link between the unrest and immigration, President Trump claimed one in a brief social media post on Monday, saying: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"

Damage to landmarks

Capital city Paris has seen the worst of the unrest, and residents woke up Monday to streets littered with debris and burned vehicles. But severe damage was inflicted across the country, with centuries of heritage being damaged or destroyed by flames.

Fire guts the historic City Hall building in Limoges, central France, during protests Oct. 17, 2026. PASCAL LACHENAUD/AFP/Getty

Video captured the moment the clock tower of Limoges' historic town hall, in southwest France — a landmark that had stood for nearly 150 years, surviving both World Wars — was engulfed in flames and came toppling down.

The tourist office in the eastern city of Lyon stood for years in one of France's most famous, beautiful city squares. But vandals, many of them masked, rampaged around the building and set it on fire, too.

The city hall in Marseille, on the Mediterranean coast, which dates back to the 1600s, was also stormed and vandalized with graffiti.

Protesters block entrances to the Louvre Museum in Paris to express their support for a nationwide student protest movement, Oct. 19, 2026. Luc Auffret/Anadolu/Getty

On Monday, hundreds of protesters gathered outside Paris' iconic Louvre Museum in support of the school students who initiated the demonstrations more than a month ago.

What protesters say they want

The protests began as demonstrations by high school students about a month ago, with thousands taking to the streets peacefully to vent frustration over crumbling schools, overpacked classes and teacher shortages.

But it grew into a nationwide outpouring of anger over the soaring cost of living — salaries that aren't keeping up with inflation, and crumbling public services.

More than 500,000 people took to the streets on Saturday, when the unrest peaked. But as the government alludes to, there have also been opportunists — people and groups looting, vandalizing and attacking police as they try to control the crowds.

"There are so many reasons," Kamil Alahyan, 18, told French news agency AFP. "The politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been raking in more and more wealth over the last 10 years … everyone has a different reason."

Anae, a 24-year-old student in Grenoble, told AFP she had completed her studies but now has "no income. I've got no money. I don't necessarily have a secure future. Our planet is burning. And we've got a government that's making a joke out of us!"
