World.title: Rays will face Brewers in World Series to produce a first-time champion
World.content:
Rays will face Brewers in World Series to produce a first-time champion

toggle caption i David J. Phillip/AP

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Yandy Díaz's bat backed up his boast, and the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series again.

Díaz and Junior Caminero each hit a two-run homer, Freddy Peralta pitched 5 1/3 gritty innings and the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night to win their third pennant in 29 seasons as a major league franchise.

The Rays will face the NL champion Milwaukee Brewers in the first matchup in which both teams are seeking their first World Series title since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals.

Sponsor Message

Game 1 is Friday night in Milwaukee.

"We got one more bite!" Rays manager Kevin Cash told his team as the clubhouse celebration started.

Díaz, who guaranteed a Game 6 victory through an interpreter on Sunday, made sure the Rays wouldn't let this one slip away. He gave them a four-run lead with a 416-foot shot off Hunter Gaddis in the eighth.

"Yandy had a claim to back and he did his part," Rays President of Baseball Operations Erik Neander said. "That was unbelievable."

Díaz's drive to left field all but wrapped up Tampa Bay's first World Series appearance since losing to the Los Angeles Dodgers in six games at the end of the pandemic-shortened 2020 season.

"I'm really glad he backed it up, that's for sure," Cash said. "We know when Yandy goes, our offense seems to really take off."

The loss by Cleveland extended its World Series championship drought to 78 years.

"I couldn't be more proud of our group," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. "It just hurts. It stings. Really felt like we had a team to go and just weren't able to get there."

On the 18-year anniversary of their first AL pennant in 2008, the Rays jumped ahead 2-0 in the second on Richie Palacios' two-run double and clinched it with closer Bryan Baker on the mound.

Sponsor Message

The Guardians wouldn't give up and had the go-ahead run at first base in the eighth when Kevin Kelly struck out Brayan Rocchio to leave the bases loaded after two runs had scored earlier in the inning.

Peralta, the ALCS MVP, allowed one run and five hits to earn his second win of the series in his third appearance. He threw six scoreless innings to win Game 2 and got two critical outs in relief in Game 4.

"I'm very happy to be here, to be part of this great group and this great organization," said Peralta, acquired from the New York Mets before the trade deadline in early August. "This is not only mine. We all earned this. This is for the boys."

A sellout crowd of 40,230 fans waved yellow-and-blue rally towels, rang cowbells and chanted "Let's go Rays!" throughout the night at Tropicana Field, which needed major renovations after Hurricane Milton shredded the roof two years ago and caused extensive damage throughout the stadium.

toggle caption i David J. Phillip/AP

The Rays played their 2025 home games across the bay in Tampa at the New York Yankees' spring training complex, got new ownership before this season and secured a new stadium deal for a ballpark to be ready in 2029 near the NFL's Buccaneers. They returned to the Trop to win 55 games in the regular season. Only the Brewers had that many home wins this year.

"This is for you!" Caminero yelled to the crowd from a microphone on the field after the game. "Let's go! I can't hear you!"

After sweeping the New York Yankees in the Division Series, the Rays fell behind the Guardians 1-0 and 2-1 in this series before taking three straight games.

Caminero gave Tampa Bay a cushion with his first career postseason homer in the seventh. The two-time All-Star sent a drive off the left-field foul pole to make it 5-1, becoming the first player to go deep on a splitter by All-Star closer Cade Smith.

Sponsor Message

The slugger turned around before reaching first base, looked toward his dugout and pounded his chest with both arms, cupped his ear rounding second to hear more cheers, stopped before reaching the plate, pointed into the stands at former Rays outfielder Randy Arozarena and imitated his crossed-arms pose before touching home.

"I saw him and I told him — before I got to home plate, I said: `Look at me,' and I hit a homer. I said, `He called it,'" Caminero said.

"My guy. Come (with) me every game," Caminero added. "Travel with us for Milwaukee."

Caminero hit 42 homers in the regular season but needed 33 at-bats to get his first in October.

The Guardians answered against Tyler Wells and Ian Seymour by loading the bases with two outs in the eighth on two singles and a walk. Seymour walked Patrick Bailey to force in one run and hit Angel Martínez with a pitch to force in another. Kelly entered and fanned Rocchio on three changeups.

"Credit to our guys. It's a gut punch there in the seventh. And our guys came right back," Vogt said. "Our guys never quit. They never stopped fighting. That's who they are."

Caminero led off the Tampa Bay second with single off opener Shawn Armstrong, who took the loss in his second start in three games. Left-hander Tim Herrin replaced Armstrong. Chandler Simpson reached on a fielder's choice and stole second before Victor Mesa Jr. walked. Simpson advanced to third on Jonny DeLuca's flyout to center. After Mesa stole second, Palacios looped a double to right-center for a 2-0 lead.

Armstrong, also the opener in Game 4, faced the first four batters, becoming the first pitcher in postseason history to start a game after pitching both of the previous two days.

DeLuca's sacrifice fly off Joey Cantillo made it 3-0 in the third but the Rays missed an opportunity to break it open after they loaded the bases with no outs.

Sponsor Message

Nathaniel Lowe's RBI single in the sixth drove in Cleveland's first run.

World.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
World.content:
Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity

toggle caption i Ty O'Neil/AP

EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for national unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats.

With more than 1 million votes counted, 77% supported remaining in Canada, while 23% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.

The referendum wasn't a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.

"Albertans made a clear choice," Carney said. "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada."

Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its center.

toggle caption i John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP

Alberta's separatists, however, saw a silver lining.

Sponsor Message

"We don't have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better," said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada.

"Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," Smith posted on social media.

Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta's future.

"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.

Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday.

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.

Sponsor Message

Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won't disappear.

Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity.

"Vote like Canada's future depends on it, because it does," he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.

Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.

Separatist advocate Jeff Rath said that he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as UCP leader and said that the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.

Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada's federal government.

"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything."

toggle caption i Ty O'Neil/AP

Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.

"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.

Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than healthcare.

With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, "It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves."

Jake Graham, 35, of Calgary, attended a Carney rally wearing maple leaf pants and a Canada hockey jacket. He hopes that the vote ends the debate.

"I hope this squashes this for a long time to come and that it's clear and decisive, that these grumblings disappear for a while and we can be a united Canada," he said.

World.title: DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate
World.content:
DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes as election tensions escalate

toggle caption i Frederic J. Brown/AFP via Getty Images

The Justice Department announced on Monday it was charging 28 noncitizens with election crimes in California, signaling a further escalation over the state's voting system that looks like it will continue through Election Day and beyond.

The DOJ also filed an emergency request in federal court to stop California from processing ballots returned by people on the voter rolls whom the federal government says are "likely noncitizens." The state has asked for specific information on how the federal government came to its conclusions, but has not received it.

"This Department of Justice will not look the other way while noncitizens vote in federal elections," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said at a press conference on Monday announcing the election crime charges. "Unfortunately the same can't be said for California and L.A. County."

Sponsor Message

Noncitizen voting has never been found to be a widespread problem in American elections, but the Trump administration is devoting significant resources to uncovering the ineligible voting that does occur. The DOJ has been announcing handfuls of new charges almost every day as early voting gets underway in many states.

The Justice Department's latest request in federal court is a continuation of a saga that began this summer with President Trump's primetime speech on election integrity. It took a major turn last week with the delivery of a flash drive to Los Angeles County that contained 20,000 names and a 48-hour deadline to investigate them. Local and state officials declined to do so, and the federal government sued.

McCotter escalated the dispute further on Friday by warning California officials in a letter that they could be criminally prosecuted for knowingly processing ballots "cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens." President Trump wrote on Truth Social that evening: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

Taken together, the threats have local officials and election experts worried that the adversarial posture of the Justice Department towards California portends more actions to come aimed at delegitimizing results in this fall's midterms.

Sponsor Message

"There's a few things to be worried about," said Rick Hasen, an election law expert who runs UCLA's Safeguarding Democracy Project. "One is the risk of disenfranchising eligible voters. The other is the risk that it further undermines voter confidence in the electoral process by making it seem like [noncitizen voting] is a major problem when it is not. And the third risk is that this is going to be used as some sort of pretext to try to seize ballots or interfere after the election is over."

Dana Lewis, the Republican county recorder for Pinal County, Ariz., said local officials nationwide are watching and communicating about what's happening in California, the same way they did when the FBI raided an elections office in Fulton County, Ga. in January.

If those officials are administering a race this fall that is close or contested, they feel they could be next, she said.

"When this impacts another jurisdiction, you automatically have to feel that," Lewis said. "If it's happening in Georgia, if it's happening in Colorado or California, we're all watching."

New criminal charges against noncitizens in California

All 28 people charged in California on Monday are green-card holders, and all appeared on the list of 20,000 names the DOJ gave California officials last week, according to DOJ officials.

A number of them do not appear to have actually voted, and some registered to vote more than 20 years ago. Many are accused of making false statements in their naturalization applications, which ask whether applicants previously registered to vote or claimed U.S. citizenship.

Previous research has shown that when noncitizen voting and registration occurs, it is also often the result of bureaucratic error and not intentional fraud. New Jersey revealed this summer that a software glitch at the DMV registered more than 6,000 people to vote even though they had indicated they were noncitizens.

Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for California's Central District, downplayed that possibility on Monday, however.

"It's not something that just happens to you," Essayli said. "They either attested to it when they got a driver's license, or they went out of their way to file a voter registration form, and they swore under oath that they were a citizen."

Sponsor Message

In the past seven weeks, the Justice Department has charged 113 noncitizens across 20 states with voting and registration crimes, officials said at Monday's press conference.

UCLA's Hasen said the charges seem to be meant to make noncitizen voting "look like a bigger issue than it is."

"Given that there's over 20 million registered voters in California, this is quite a small number of allegations," Hasen said. "And we don't know how many of these allegations will even pan out. And so even if all of these were in fact people who were illegally voting, it's a drop in the bucket compared to the number of voters in California."

Recent polling suggests a sizable portion of the American public thinks immigration enforcement will be present at voting locations this fall, despite federal law banning armed federal agents from the polls. Non-white voters are more likely than white voters to say they fear voting could put them at risk of being questioned by immigration authorities despite being citizens.

In an interview earlier this fall with NPR, Los Angeles County's top voting official, Dean Logan, alluded to those worries.

"Given everything leading up to this election, what we're trying to remind voters is the best way to secure the election is through your participation," Logan told NPR. "Don't be distracted by the litigation. Don't be distracted by the mis- and disinformation. If you have questions, let us know, let us answer them. But don't let this keep you from voting," he said.

"Because if you're not voting, none of the rest matters, right?"

An unprecedented demand by DOJ

The Justice Department's request that a federal judge block California and Los Angeles County from processing ballots from the list of 20,000 "likely noncitizens" it gave state officials last week is unprecedented and an especially unusual request given that voting is already underway.

Sponsor Message

California officials have argued that complying with the Department's demand to set the ballots aside would be unlawful and noted the DOJ has not confirmed that the voters on the list are noncitizens.

"The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber wrote to the DOJ's McCotter on Oct. 13.

"Withholding ballots from some duly registered voters and segregating and refusing to tabulate voted ballots submitted by others, is an unprecedented suspension — and even denial — of voting rights," she wrote.

Los Angeles County's assistant county counsel, Peter Bollinger, wrote to McCotter on Oct. 15: "we are not authorized to, or are prohibited from, taking the actions requested in your letter under both federal and state law. The actions described would disenfranchise those in question without due process." The same letter noted the list of names from the DOJ included voters from outside Los Angeles County, whom the office does not maintain any records on.

Both letters cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law that bars states from systematically removing ineligible voters from state voter rolls during the 90 days before an election. The law is supposed to prevent mistakes that could erroneously purge eligible voters right before an election without giving voters time to correct errors.

There are also questions about the methodology the Trump administration used to come up with its tally of 20,000 likely noncitizens and its accuracy. A July letter to California from the Department of Homeland Security alleged the state had a potential of 190,000 noncitizens on its rolls.

In Monday's press briefing, McCotter said the 20,000 figure represented the people the Justice Department had the most confidence were noncitizens after DHS cross-referenced various government databases and other records with identifying information.

McCotter and other DOJ officials blamed California for not handing over its entire voter roll — including partial Social Security Numbers and driver's license numbers — which they said could help shed more light on the citizenship status of these voters. So far 26 federal judges have dismissed DOJ demands for that data across the country.

Sponsor Message

In the Justice Department's Monday filing for a restraining order preventing California from counting ballots from the 20,000 individuals, the DOJ wrote: "Once illegally cast ballots are counted and commingled with lawful votes, the resulting harm may be impossible to remedy. The urgency is heightened because of the fundamental right to vote and to have one's lawful vote counted without dilution."

A half dozen voting and civil rights organizations filed to intervene in the case last week to argue the DOJ's demands are unlawful.

Election experts have said the DOJ's lawsuit against California seems more about sending a political message or teeing up future challenges than winning this case in court, given that the constitution gives states the authority to administer elections.

"I expect this lawsuit to go nowhere," UCLA's Hasen wrote last week.

World.title: Judge chastises Trump administration plan to push ahead overhaul of DC golf course
World.content:
Judge chastises Trump administration plan to push ahead overhaul of DC golf course

toggle caption i Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images

In a tense hearing on Monday, federal Judge Ana C. Reyes sharply rebuked administration lawyers over President Trump's apparent intent to defy the court and proceed with a major renovation of the historic East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C. Only days before, the judge had temporarily blocked the government from moving forward with the project.

During the hearing, which ended without a decision, Reyes chastised the government attorneys, who had previously told the court that renovating the links was still in its conceptual stage. So when Trump posted his detailed plans for a new golf course on Sunday, Reyes wanted to know who was responsible for misleading the court.

Sponsor Message

"Do I believe the president of the United States or do I believe you?" she asked.

During the hearing, Reyes frequently exhibited frustration and annoyance. "I have, on the one hand, the president of the United States saying to the American public three times now, I think, in the last two days, there is a final plan to redesign the golf course," she said. "Then I have you all telling me and, you know, witnesses saying what they're saying, that there's no final plan. Which is it?"

Trump has said that he wants to turn the three existing courses at the East Potomac Golf Links into a single, "championship-style golf course." But in February, a D.C. preservation group and two individuals challenged the U.S. Department of Interior and the National Park Service over the planned renovations, arguing that the renovated course would inflate tee-time costs for a facility that was originally intended to be "open to all people."

toggle caption i Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP

In May, the judge ordered the administration to give notice of any substantial construction work on the course, including the removal of more than 10 trees. Despite the order, late on Friday, Oct. 9 — just before a holiday weekend — government officials notified the court that it planned to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases.

Sponsor Message

Bulldozers began taking down hundreds of trees the next day. During a three-hour emergency hearing last week, Reyes called the government lawyers out for not giving enough prior notice for the tree removal. She did not believe the argument that the tree felling was part of routine maintenance, saying she was "beyond disappointed" by the action and ordered a 24-hour halt.

Judge: "Every single benefit of the doubt"

"I do not know how I could have made it any plainer that I did not want what was to happen, to happen," she said, adding: "I have given the government every single benefit of the doubt that it would not do precisely what it has done."

On Friday, the White House filed a motion requesting that Reyes remove herself from the case, accusing her of bias. The judge declined to step aside.

Ahead of the hearing on Monday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Reyes was a "crazed lunatic" and said that renovation work did not need court approval. "Work is scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY!" he said. The president's post appears to contradict a response filed by Department of Justice lawyers the previous day indicating that "the plan is not final because the Park Service has not completed its review."

Trump has described the golf course as "old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect." The prospect of a complete renovation has alarmed residents who are concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.

A protected landmark

The century-old golf links were also one of the first public courses to be desegregated. "This is not just some putt-putt course," Reyes told the attorneys, who appeared in court on Monday. The park holds "a deep amount of meaning for the people of the district, and is protected as a historic landmark."

Sponsor Message

The White House has said that it is simply carrying out a 2019 preservation plan , but plaintiffs seeking to block the changes have said that Trump's stated desire to redevelop the course goes well beyond that. Among other things, the 2019 plan recommends removing invasive vegetation that doesn't contribute to the historic landscape, but not healthy, native species.

World.title: Schools struggle to measure how much AI experiments are helping
World.content:
Schools struggle to measure how much AI experiments are helping

Schools are experimenting with AI, and a lot of them are encountering the same problem: It's hard to measure whether the technology is good or bad for students.

Transcript

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

Schools across the country are experimenting with AI in classrooms. In some districts, AI chatbots give students feedback on their work. But how should schools measure whether these experiments are helping students or harming them? Lee Gaines reports from one school in Dayton, Ohio.

LEE GAINES, BYLINE: A high school senior is giving an angsty AI chatbot advice.

N: I feel like a therapist, like I'm actually helping him.

GAINES: The student, N, was part of an experiment last school year at the Alternative School at Jackson Center in Dayton. NPR is only using N's first initial because of the stigma associated with attending a school that serves students with behavioral challenges.

N: I kind of built this connection with him trying to get to the point of his issue and why he's, like, feeling this way.

GAINES: The him he's referring to is an AI chatbot named Jordan. Jordan asks students for advice, like what to do when you feel you can't meet adults' expectations. The idea is to get students to open up about their feelings.

N: I've been through similar things like Jordan, so it's - like, it's easier for me to try to help him get through it.

GAINES: The chatbot grades students' responses, and N gets high marks. There's just one problem - there's no way to quantify how much the chatbot is helping students. The best the district can do is ask students and staff.

MIKE KENTZ: Every test, every experiment that I try to measure in some sort of concrete way, I can only get as far as perception.

GAINES: Mike Kentz is a consultant who helped Dayton administrators design and evaluate the chatbot. He's been running into the same problem a lot of school AI experiments have encountered - it's hard to measure whether the technology is good or bad for students. Robin Lake leads the Center on Reinventing Public Education.

ROBIN LAKE: It's been frustrating to see that innovation is tackled without a lot of attention to evidence building.

GAINES: Lake's organization has been tracking AI adoption in schools. She says educators often struggle to measure the value of technology in classrooms, including when it comes to AI.

LAKE: The technology is moving so quickly. Tools are being produced at such a rapid pace. And everybody is feeling overwhelmed in schools and saying, you know, I don't know what works.

GAINES: That's one reason Mike Kentz is cautious about scaling up the Jordan chatbot in Dayton.

KENTZ: I don't think it should be immediately input into their district or any others as some sort of, you know, full-scale solution.

KATELYN SCHOENHOFER: We wrestle with what does success really mean when it comes to AI use.

GAINES: Katelyn Schoenhofer is the AI specialist for Wichita Public Schools in Kansas. The school system is slowly introducing students to a range of AI tools from a few different companies. Last year, the district hosted an AI exploration day for middle schoolers.

SCHOENHOFER: They got to make educational games and code those games and share them with their friends.

GAINES: And some high school students are using an AI math tutor. Until educators figure out how to measure the value of these AI initiatives, Schoenhofer says these experiments will remain small in scale, but they will continue.

SCHOENHOFER: We are still going ahead with caution but with optimism with our students because it is something that is going to impact their lives. It is something they need to be educated about.

GAINES: Robin Lake with the Center on Reinventing Public Education agrees that the answer isn't to stop experimenting because if that happens...

LAKE: We will set our kids back from being able to navigate a world that is changing outside of schools faster than we can possibly imagine.

GAINES: Lake says states and the federal government need to establish guardrails around these experiments so schools can try to prepare students for what's to come. For NPR News, I'm Lee Gaines.

(SOUNDBITE OF TYLER, THE CREATOR SONG, "ANSWER")

World.title: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
World.content:
Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'

toggle caption i Mick Tsikas/AAP Image via AP

MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.

Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.

Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.

toggle caption i Lukas Coch/AAPIMAGE via AP

The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.

Sponsor Message

"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.

"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.

Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.

Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.

Sponsor Message

In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.

World.title: 2026 midterms could be the most expensive on record. And, Macron condemns protests
World.content:
2026 midterms could be the most expensive on record. And, Macron condemns protests

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The 2026 midterm elections are set to become the most expensive on record. More than $15 billion has been raised to influence the outcome and control of Congress.

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

🎧 Democratic nominees in House and Senate races are raking in incredible amounts of donations, even though the Democratic Party remains unpopular, NPR's Stephen Fowler says. Republicans are also unpopular, largely due to issues like the war in Iran, gas prices and the economy. A few megadonors, such as Elon Musk, are donating money to super PACs to try to push voters to elect Republicans. In the 13 competitive races highlighted in the Cook Political Report, Republicans are being outraised by a 5-to-1 margin. Both parties are spending heavily, indicating that Democrats might have a chance to win in several locations. Currently, 75% of planned ad buys are in toss-up races or those leaning Republican.

At least one person died and more than a dozen were injured in a major Ukrainian drone strike yesterday on Saint Petersburg, Russia's former imperial capital. The attack targeted strategic sites, including a key port oil terminal. Over the weekend, Russian missile strikes in Ukraine killed at least 11 people. This conflict continues as President Trump says that relieving pressure on Russia is the best way to end the war.



🎧 The recent attack on Saint Petersburg appears to mark the largest one on the city since Russia's 2022 invasion, NPR's Charles Maynes tells Up First. While it's unclear how many drones struck the city, Russia's Defense Ministry reported intercepting 1,000 drones across various regions that night. Trump seems to be working to protect Russian oil facilities after cutting a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel. The move was aimed at lowering gas prices for U.S. voters before the midterm elections. Trump has called previous Ukrainian strikes a "disgrace," even as Russia continues to strike Ukraine, Maynes says. He adds that the president blames President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for attacks that allegedly raise U.S. fuel prices, despite economists attributing the price increase mainly to Trump's war in Iran.

French President Emmanuel Macron denounced violence over the weekend that he says has overshadowed largely peaceful protests across the country. The unrest began as a student protest for better conditions and has expanded to include public-sector workers protesting high energy prices, the rising cost of living and social inequality. The Interior Ministry reported about 2,300 arrests and nearly 1,000 injured police officers.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Eleanor Beardsley, who was in the streets of Paris yesterday, witnessed burned bikes, shattered glass and graffiti on looted stores saying things like "tax the rich." She spoke with 23-year-old Sarah Berlia, who says she believes these actions come from a frustrated generation facing dwindling rights and opportunities. Beardsley says the protest culture in France often attracts "troublemakers," but the scale of current events is massive. The protests have had political implications, as France is six months away from a presidential election. Far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has joined the protesters, while far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, has condemned the violence and the government.

Living better

toggle caption i Siv Dolmen for NPR

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

Saunas are gaining renewed attention in the wellness world for their potential to improve mental health. This trend reflects the growing interest in the broader wellness movement and social connection, especially post-pandemic. While scientists understand how saunas affect the cardiovascular system, they are just beginning to explore their impact on mental health. Here's what they know so far.

🥵 When our skin detects heat, it sends signals to a primitive brain area that prompts our body to cool down. This pathway also influences mood and pleasure, which is associated with depression.

🥵 Heat triggers an anti-inflammatory response similar to the effects of exercise, which is known to help with depression and other mental health issues.

🥵 Heating people up can act like a "thermoregulatory workout," helping their bodies cool down more efficiently over time.

Picture show

toggle caption i Jennifer Teresa Villanueva

Artist Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has captured her family's everyday life through her lens for eight years, revealing moments of love, care and sacrifice within their Chicago home. The personal project took root in 2018, sparked by her grandmother's hospitalization. It started as a way to better understand her grandmother's daily routines, and soon it blossomed into a heartfelt exploration of the immigrant experience. "I am interested in what happens when the camera enters a home where everyone already knows one another," Villanueva told NPR. "There is no distance between photographer and subject. I am photographing the people who raised me, and I am also photographing the home that raised me." See photos from the project and read more about Villanueva's work.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Charles Tasnadi/AP

Noah Adams, a writer and broadcaster who hosted All Things Considered for 18 years, has died. He was 84 years old. Trump announced over the weekend that he plans to close and renovate the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C. The golf course is already at the center of a legal battle. An Air Force service member died Saturday after a rappelling accident during a pregame ceremony at the Alamodome ahead of the University of Texas at San Antonio's football game against Navy. World.title: A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming
World.content:
A Kelvin wave raised sea levels on the West Coast. More are coming

toggle caption i Dillon J. Amaya/North Carolina State University

One of the first major signs of this year's "Super El Niño" has reached the U.S. It's called a Kelvin wave – a deep ocean wave that's currently raising sea levels along the West Coast.

Scientists have long known about Kelvin waves, but this year, the phenomena grabbed the public's attention with video explanations receiving thousands of views across TikTok and X .

"It does surprise me – I mean, here it's been around all this time," says Mark Cane, who created one of the first models to forecast and predict El Niño . "I'm sure Lord Kelvin is happy in his grave."

Sponsor Message

(Lord Kelvin, the British physicist who also developed the Kelvin temperature scale, first described the wave back in the late 1800s.)

Kelvin waves can develop along the equator during El Niño years, when a vast region of water in the Pacific Ocean becomes much warmer than usual.

Some of this warm water, in the form of a Kelvin wave that stretches thousands of miles, moves slowly east beneath the ocean's surface until it reaches South America. Then it splits, traveling north along the West Coast and as far south as Chile.

"It's like an enormous bathtub sloshing around," Cane says, professor emeritus of earth and climate sciences at Columbia University. "But the slosh is very peculiar, because it only goes west to east along the equator in a Kelvin wave."

These are not the massive, highly visible waves that crash into shorelines during major storms and hurricanes .

"It's not a wall of water, it's not a tsunami, it's not a wave you can surf," says Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor of atmospheric sciences at North Carolina State University. "It's a planetary-scale wave."

A Kelvin wave's impact is gradual, raising sea levels as it moves up the coast, and bringing with it an elevated risk of floods and warmer water temperatures.

Sponsor Message

What's the impact?

Kelvin waves can increase the risk of flooding and coastal erosion.

By themselves, Kelvin waves don't cause flooding, Amaya says. Instead, they load the dice, making flooding more likely by raising sea levels.

"It makes the background conditions more favorable towards coastal flooding, but what you need are triggering factors," Amaya said, such as a major storm or very high tides.

Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says Kelvin waves raise the chances of a "triple whammy" along the California coast: "El Nino, the high tide and the storm surge all coming at once."

That's exactly what some Southern California communities experienced in early October. Sea levels were already higher than normal because of the Kelvin wave – about six to eight inches, Amaya says. Then, when Tropical Storm Rachel hit, a storm surge flooded neighborhoods and left oceanfront homes partially submerged .

"That storm surge was almost certainly made more devastating because of the Kelvin wave," Amaya says.

Warmer water temperatures

toggle caption i Dillon J. Amaya/North Carolina State University

Kelvin waves also bring warmer water up the coast, which can be disruptive and put stress on marine life .

"We've seen tropical fishes in places that we don't normally see them," Amaya says. "Like a whale shark was spotted off the coast of San Diego."

The Kelvin wave can push down nutrient-dense cold waters that support productive marine ecosystems. Amaya says researchers have already seen evidence of sea birds dying in response to warmer water temperatures along the coast.

When is the next Kelvin wave?

There are usually five to six Kelvin waves during a strong El Niño year, Amaya says.

Amaya predicts the next Kelvin wave will reach San Diego in late October or early November. Several more waves are expected through the fall and early winter, he says. Kelvin waves usually subside before the peak of El Niño.

Sponsor Message

World.title: Canadian who stole a Las Vegas flamingo after drinking '30 to 40' beers convicted of animal cruelty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas. Unless you drink "30 to 40 beers" and steal a flamingo — because that will make international news.

A Las Vegas court convicted an Ontario man of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at an iconic Las Vegas hotel in what prosecutors called a drunken and malicious act.

Mitchell Fairbarn was accused of "willfully, unlawfully, maliciously and feloniously" injuring the flamingo in the early morning hours on March 3, according to the indictment viewed by CBC News. He pled not guilty and his trial started last week.

After jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts, Fairbarn remained in custody pending a Dec. 1 sentencing hearing. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony conviction, plus six months of jail time for the misdemeanor conviction.

"I thought it was something that we could joke about for the rest of our lives," Fairbarn, described by various Las Vegas media outlets as a contractor from rural Ontario, said in court Friday.

The façade of the Flamingo hotel in Las Vegas is seen at night on Las Vegas Boulevard in this file photo. (Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

Fairbarn told the court that on the day of the incident, he drank "30 to 40" beers over the course of 24 hours while he was in Las Vegas for a construction expo, he said in video footage of the trial posted by multiple media outlets.

Fairbarn entered the flamingo habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino around 5 a.m. on March 3, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal, and took the bird because he thought it would be a "silly joke" with his friends.

"I thought it would be, at the time, funny," Fairbarn said.

The Flamingo's wildlife habitat, which the hotel says spans four acres and is certified by the National Wildlife Federation, is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, among other birds, turtles and fish.

Peachy was shaking, bleeding: witness

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo by the neck in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway. He spent about 15 minutes with the bird, and two-to-three minutes with it in his room, reported 8NewsNow, citing police evidence heard in court.

Two of Fairbarn's friends testified earlier this week that they had been out drinking, then woke up in their hotel room to find the flamingo there before moving it to the hallway, notes Fox 5 Las Vegas.

A hotel facilities engineer searching for Peachy eventually corralled the bird into a corner with a towel, and told the court Peachy was shaking and bleeding.

The flamingo was injured during the incident, suffering seven to eight missing feathers, broken feather shafts and blood loss consistent with trauma, the bird's treating veterinarian testified in court, according to Fox5 Las Vegas.

Peachy, who is 27 years old, needed antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and weeks of pain medication, the news outlet reported.

CBC News has reached out to the Las Vegas Justice Court for access to court filings and has not yet received them. But multiple local media outlets present in court have aired footage from court where Fairbarn doesn't deny his actions — just his intent.

His lawyer Joshua Tomsheck said Monday it was a drunken act and no harm was intended. When Tomsheck asked Fairbairn Friday if he had any malicious intent "in your mind or your heart when you picked up that bird," Fairbarn shook his head and answered, "no."

CBC News has reached out to Tomsheck, but has not yet received a response.

Fairbarn testifies during his trial at the Regional Justice Center on Friday in Las Vegas. He says he didn't intend to hurt the flamingo he took up to his hotel room in March. (Benjamin Hager/Las Vegas Review-Journal/The Associated Press)

Justice delivered: animal rights advocate

Prosecutors said Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor and video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it. But Tomsheck said his client regrets his actions while intoxicated and never meant to harm the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," Tomsheck said in court Monday.

"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

Fairbarn told the court Friday that he has remained under house arrest in Nevada since the incident. Court records viewed by CBC News show he had to surrender his passport as one of his bail conditions.

Jurors began deliberations after both sides presented closing arguments Monday morning.

Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state's animal cruelty laws, told The Associated Press he believes justice was delivered on Peachy's behalf.

"I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you're not going to do it in Nevada," he said outside the courtroom after Monday's verdict.

The Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, which reside at the hotel's wildlife habitat. (Ceasars Entertainment)

Peachy has since recovered, according to Fox 5 Las Vegas. But the flamingo is just one of several recent cases involving animal cruelty at Las Vegas casinos, reports the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

In June, a woman was charged after allegedly jumping into the fountain at The Venetian and grabbing a duckling named Daffy. In May, a teen girl was arrested and accused of stabbing three horses the the South Point Arena & Equestrian Center so they couldn't compete in a barrel race.

World.title: 'Not out of the woods': Family rallies around soldier badly burned in CFB Wainwright fire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Before he was airlifted to hospital and intubated, Cpl. Sean Hiatt — the second-youngest in a family of 12 — managed to call his mom and tell her he'd been injured in a training accident at CFB Wainwright.

The 24-year-old was coherent at the time, according to his sister, and it gave the family hope.

Now they're focused on his immediate care, and taking things 12 hours at a time.

On Saturday afternoon, Hiatt suffered burns to about half of his body when wind gusts of up to 90 km/h pushed a grass fire one kilometre in less than a minute and onto a group of soldiers doing live-fire training.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 were injured. Hospitals across the province took in the wounded, including University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton where Hiatt’s medevac landed.

“He was, and still is, sedated and intubated, he was completely wrapped up, they didn’t know the degree at that point because they had to get him stable,” Hiatt’s sister Kelly Patterson said in an interview with CBC News.

“It is really rough…. It was a shock to see him like that.”

Of the injured, 19 are in critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a news conference on Sunday.

One of those is Hiatt, from Edson, Alta., about 200 kilometres west of Edmonton.

One by one, family members began showing up at Hiatt’s bedside — brothers, a nephew, sisters and parents — to be with the guy they describe as “happy going”and “cheerful.”

'He's a fighter'

Patterson says her brother “perked up” with every visit, breathing a little bit better and “looking a little brighter."

The road ahead is going to be long and Patterson says Hiatt is “not out of the woods.”

Doctors are still concerned about lung damage and have yet to begin skin grafts. He faces weeks in the ICU and months longer in hospital.

The family is leaning on prayer and the knowledge that Hiatt is "a fighter.”

“He got out of there so he’s going to make it,” said Patterson.

'The whole community is feeling this'

Meanwhile, 200 kilometres from Hiatt’s hospital bed, he and the other injured and fallen soldiers are on the minds of folks in Wainwright, a town deeply connected to its base.

“Everyone’s really connected, everyone really cares for each other,” said Grade 12 student Rylan Pow. “It really was heartbreaking honestly.”

Grade 12 students showed up Monday morning with bouquets of flowers to pay their respects to those who were injured and killed in Saturday's fire at CFB Wainwright. (Gilbert Rowan/CBC)

On Monday morning, with their principal’s blessing, Pow and his entire class from Blessed Sacrament School showed up with their teacher to lay flowers at the town’s memorial clock cenotaph.

Teacher Janae Wildboer said she was in a panic when she learned of the fatal fire and wondered what she could do to help.

“Our school just wanted to do something to honour those who have lost their lives,” said Wildboer. “The whole community is feeling this; it's heavy and we're just now supporting where we can.”

'Still kind of in shock'

Down the street, outside of the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29, which was set up Monday as a referendum polling station, David Campbell finished voting and then turned his mind back to the tragedy.

"Everyone's still kind of in shock,” said Campbell, who has lived in the area for more than 40 years.

“The base is very important, a lot of people work here. We’re farmers and we have cattle in the community pasture, we work with the military all the time, they live in town here, a lot of them.

“They’re part of the community, we know so many of them. Their kids are in hockey, my grandkids are playing hockey with a lot of the kids. It's very devastating.”

Smoke in the air

As the winds changed direction Sunday night and into Monday, the smell of smoke drifted in and out of the community. Fire Chief Aime Smyl warned that could continue in the days ahead.

The fire is still burning but considered contained, said Smyl in his social media post Monday afternoon. It’s not expected to breach the fire guard.

Local MP and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre attended the Wainwright cenotaph with flowers Monday morning. (Josh McLean/CBC News)

Smyl also thanked the seven other fire services that stepped up to help with Saturday’s grassfire response.

“I am also humbled by the number of departments that reached out to help,” he wrote.

By Monday morning, some of Smyl’s firefighters had been awake for three days, according to Local MP and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who showed up at the cenotaph with flowers after a meeting with the fire chief.

Poilievre thanked the first responders, “who ran towards and not away from the fire” to help.

“It has been a phenomenal show of the best of Canada here in Wainwright.”

World.title: Curling controversy: Unusual finish generates boos, ruffles feathers at Slam event
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Grand Slam of Curling's competition committee plans to meet this week to discuss an unusual finish at the Co-op Invitational that sent two Canadian teams into the playoffs and led to pointed words from an American rink left outside the cutline.

Boos were heard throughout Victoria's Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre when teams skipped by Matt Dunstone and Brendan Bottcher were not aggressive in the final end of their round-robin finale Friday night.

Both teams deliberately threw stones through the house early in the end before Bottcher scored one for a tie that forced a shootout. That gave both sides enough points to advance and eliminated Danny Casper's rink from playoff contention.

"They're on ESPN in the U.S. and [Sportsnet] in Canada, thousands of people are watching it, I'm sure, and it looks horrible," Team Casper second Ben Richardson said from Victoria over the weekend. "It definitely leaves a bitter taste in my mouth.

"I can't speak [for] all the people that watched it, but it's definitely not a good look for our sport.”

Normally, a one-point game would lead to a tense eighth and final end. But with the stakes clear — reach the shootout and you're guaranteed a playoff spot — both rinks chose a passive style down the stretch.

When it became obvious both teams were comfortable with a tied score, many spectators voiced their displeasure that any late-game excitement had been scuttled.

"Don't be upset with the players, be upset with the format," said Dunstone, who earned two points for the 6-5 shootout victory.

Bottcher picked up one point for the shootout loss, giving him seven points overall and the final berth. Casper, who would have played a tiebreaker if the game was decided in regulation, missed the cut with six points.

"I understand why both of them would want a shootout," Richardson said. "I don't understand why both of them would not try to win in the last end. I completely disagree with that."

At issue for many were the early shots in the eighth end.

WATCH | Schwaller beats Ramsfjell in men's final: World No. 1 Schwaller beats Norway's Ramsfjell in Co-op Invitational men's final | Duration closed caption 2:09 Switzerland's Yannick Schwaller earns the second Grand Slam of Curling title of his career with a 7-3 victory over Norway's Magnus Ramsfjell in the men's final at the Grand Slam of Curling's Co-op Invitational in Victoria

Walker miss raised eyebrows

Team Dunstone lead Ryan Harnden drew the button, and Team Bottcher lead Geoff Walker flashed his first rock. The Walker miss raised the eyebrows of Team Casper third Luc Violette.

"You would always see a team throw a corner guard in that situation if they were trying to maximize their odds of winning the game outright," he said.

Harnden's second shot stopped at the top of the four-foot ring. Walker then made a double-takeout and his shooter rolled out.

Violette said the flash improved Dunstone's chances to steal. He would have expected Harnden to follow with a tight centre guard in that situation.

"Instead, they lobbed one right on top of it to leave an easy double," he said.

For second stones, Team Dunstone's Mark Nichols deliberately threw his first rock through the house, and Team Bottcher's Tanner Horgan did the same thing.

That sparked boos and jeers throughout the venue. Some spectators shouted "Borrrrr-ing!" while others yelled out "Shame! Shame!"

The broadcast team also sensed what was happening.

"Both of these teams, if this game goes to a shootout, will get into the playoffs," said on-air host John Cullen. "This looks like maybe a bit of a handshake agreement that both teams are saying, 'Let's do it."'

"I doubt that there's any agreement," analyst Brent Laing replied. "I think they're both just smart enough to know there's no need [to] take on any risk, and the other guy thinks the same thing."

After exchanging hits, Dunstone's final rock settled on the 12-foot ring and Bottcher drew the button for one point. Both skips said there was no agreement in place to play for the draw.

WATCH | Weekend recap: Grand Slam of Curling's Victoria stop: That Curling Show returns with a weekend recap of GSOC Victoria | Duration 29:28 The beloved That Curling Show returns with Devin Heroux accompanied by Canadian curling legends, Joanne Courtney and Brad Gushue as they recap the first stop in the Grand Slam of Curling in Victoria BC.

'How the scoreboard played out'

"In eight, they threw a rock in the house and Geoff's first rock picked," Bottcher said in a text message. "That said, our team knew we needed a point to qualify given the format."

Dunstone, reached on the phone from Victoria, said: "there was no conversation whatsoever."

"It was just how the scoreboard played out," he said.

Nic Sulsky, CEO of GSOC owner The Curling Group, said while he likes the 3-2-1-0 scoring system that's in its second season of use on the circuit, he wasn't impressed with what transpired.

"It was a little too obvious, it was a little too raw," he said. "And I feel for the Casper boys. But at the end of the day, fans are in the stands watching rocks being thrown through the house.

"I'm not a supporter of [that] in a situation like [Friday] night."

The seven-member competition committee was expected to meet Thursday or Friday, Sulsky said.

Dunstone went on to lose his quarterfinal to eventual champion Yannick Schwaller of Switzerland while Bottcher dropped his playoff opener to Canada's Brad Jacobs.

"This isn't why we didn't win this weekend," said Violette. "But at the same time, if this were another sport, I do think there would be some sort of sanction or something that happens as a result of a scenario like we saw play out."

"I feel like this was, I guess, a step back in us feeling confident in the integrity among teams at our highest level," he added.

The next stop on the circuit is the Nov. 3-8 GSOC Masters in Medicine Hat, Alta.

World.title: Findings from fatal CFB Wainwright fire investigation will be made public, top commander says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's top military commander committed on Monday to publicly releasing the findings of the investigation into the fire at the training range in Wainwright, Alta., which claimed the lives of four soldiers and left dozens of others injured.

There are three separate parallel investigations underway — two military and one civilian, said Gen. Jennie Carignan, the chief of the defence staff, in her first interview since a sudden brush fire swept through an exercise area at the sprawling military base.

Speaking on CBC's Power & Politics, Carignan said the military's investigative service is on the scene and there will be a board of inquiry (BOI), a technical investigation into the circumstances, as well as a civilian coroner's investigation by the province of Alberta.

The military is under no obligation to proactively release its findings. Normally, the board reports to the defence chief and the minister. In fact, it took public pressure for the board of inquiry investigation into the 2004 fatal fire aboard HMCS Chicoutimi to be made public.

Carignan said she was drafting the terms of reference, which set out the scope of the inquiry, for the board, but she couldn't commit on Monday to saying when the review panel will convene.

"We want to make sure that the board of inquiry starts on firm ground," Carignan told host David Cochrane, referring to the instructions she is preparing.

"I want to make sure that we also make the findings public once the board of inquiry is completed."

WATCH | Carignan speaks about training near brush fires: 'Normal' for Armed Forces to conduct training near fires: top military commander | Duration closed caption 0:59 Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan says that Canadian Forces personnel on the ground determine whether or not to continue training. She spoke with Power & Politics following the deadly fire on Saturday at CFB Wainwright.

Separately, Carignan said the Canadian Forces fire marshal is reviewing what happened. The RCMP have been asked to assist Alberta's medical examiner.

There were tributes in the House of Commons on Monday to the soldiers killed in what military officials describe as a swift-moving brush fire that overwhelmed members of C Company 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry who were using the Wainwright training range to prepare for deployment to Latvia.

The military said the brush fire was already burning when a sudden change in the wind drove it toward roughly 84 troops who were practising hand grenade throwing and small group attacks at one portion of the exercise field.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark all died in the fire. Another 39 troops were injured, 19 of them critically.

Carignan said it's normal for troops to continue training even if there's a brush fire nearby because it adds to the realistic conditions they'd face in combat. There are however, she said, limits and safety is paramount.

"The folks on the ground make a determination on how this could affect training, and mitigation measures are put in place," Carignan said. "To address this, we also have firefighting equipment or support on site to respond to potential fires, of course, depending on the magnitude."

Military regulations dictate the range safety officer makes the call on whether an exercise can continue and under what circumstances.

Retired colonel Rory Fowler, a former military lawyer now in private practice, suggested the public should temper its expectations about what it will see in the board of inquiry report, particularly if there is blame to be had.

"BOIs are not supposed to investigate wrongdoing," Fowler said. "In fact, a little over 10 years ago, [the regulation] was amended to remove an article that directed that a BOI was to identify if anyone was at fault."

Fowler said if there is blame, it might be handled through the military justice system — or disciplinary system.

PHOTOS | The aftermath of the fire:

"Unlike a coroner's inquest, the underlying purpose of a BOI is not to serve a public purpose other than the governance of the Canadian Armed Forces," Fowler said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, after paying tribute to the fallen soldiers, said he has confidence in the system.

"The military wants to get to the bottom of what exactly happened," Carney said. "There's a few processes that we'll go through here and we will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary."

In his House of Commons remarks, Carney committed to giving the military "all the resources that they need" to investigate.

WATCH | Carney on the military investigation: Carney says military 'aided by' feds and RCMP to investigate CFB Wainwright fire | Duration closed caption 0:39 Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Canadian military has 'started a comprehensive investigation' into what caused the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright to get answers 'as expeditiously and transparently as possible.'

Military law expert and retired colonel Michel Drapeau said Carignan's commitment to releasing the findings is important, but only "a first step."

Drapeau, who has represented families at a number of boards of inquiry over the past 20 years, said there needs to be more transparency as the process unfolds.

He'd like to see a commitment to proceedings being held in public where the families can attend.

"National security is not at stake here," Drapeau said. "The family has a right to know, and the Canadian public has a right to know."

Drapeau has long advocated for an independent body — such as an inspector general — that would conduct arm's-length investigations.

"There is merit to the argument that the Canadian Forces should have in place a mechanism for true public inquiry," Fowler said.

World.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Québec Maple Syrup Producers president Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn't miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.

Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions. As a result, the producers' association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.

Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.

"Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero," Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits.

That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.

Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

"We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available," Goulet said. "Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established."

Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.

In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year.

"It's always hard to beat an exceptional year," Turenne said.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have.

However, he believes the industry can still grow. "There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves," he said.

Investments from Quebec City "are too low for our liking," says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly elected Parti Québécois government.

"When we’re told that we have an industry that's thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level," he said.

For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States.

"We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent," Turenne said.

“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.

Industry concentrated in Quebec

While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec.

More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group's report, released Thursday.

When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.

In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.

This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.

"Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry," Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers' group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry's importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.

In some municipalities, "if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages," Goulet said.

World.content: Writes Ivison: “Earlier this month, I wrote that universities across the country are finally getting together to address the epidemic of antisemitism that has broken out on campuses across the country. I referred to a review of antisemitic incidents at Toronto Metropolitan University undertaken by retired justice Mary Lou Benotto and delivered to TMU last August. At the time, I said pages from the report were redacted on privacy grounds (several students were charged after the protests under review). But I was wrong. The pages that were redacted were taken out to remove Benotto’s conclusion, stated clearly, that the university’s own codes of conduct were breached — a finding that would have forced TMU to take action that it apparently did not want to take.”

World.title: Alberta poised to reject separating from Canada in historic referendum
World.content:
Article content

Alberta’s referendum vote comes at a time when Western resentment toward Eastern Canada is at its highest level in decades, particularly following the tail end of the Trudeau era. While Alberta has never had a popular and explicitly separatist separation movement in the same vein as Quebec, many people in the province have long harboured deep grievances over how in their view the province has been underrepresented in confederation and mistreated by Ottawa. Their concerns include anything from anger over Ottawa’s restrictive environmental policies to frustration over the province’s lack of seats in the House of Commons and Senate compared to its population.

World.title: High personal income taxes drag down Canada’s tax competitiveness, new study finds
World.content:
Article content

Estonia earned the top spot in the OECD for its tax code for the 13th year in a row. It has a 22 percent tax rate on corporate income that is only applied to distributed profits and a flat 22 percent tax on individual income that does not apply to dividends. Estonia is followed at the top of the rankings by Latvia and New Zealand in the rankings.

World.title: Scott Stinson: Ontario’s electricity-import deal with U.S. undercuts Doug Ford’s energy tough talk
World.content:
Article content

The new deal to import electricity to Ontario would seem to undermine any future sabre-rattling that Ford might do on the energy file, although there are several caveats to be noted here. The Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) is, as the name suggests, not making decisions at Ford’s behest. And its contract with Alpha Generation is a short-term arrangement to provide electricity in case Ontario needs it during the cold winter months and while the Pickering nuclear plant is undergoing a refurbishment. In the days since the Alpha contract was announced, the IESO said that Ontario will still be a net exporter of electricity to the United States and that it exported seven times as much as it imported last year. The new contract is about increasing the flexibility of the provincial power grid during the high-peak demand of the winter months.
