World.title: Mozambique Ends Minibus Fuel Subsidy
World.content:
MOZAMBIQUE · TRANSPORT

Key Facts —Decision The government has ended the temporary fuel compensation paid to licensed minibus operators, known as chapas, in the Maputo metropolitan region. —Cost Over three months the state paid 307 million meticais (about US$4.9 million) to operators, according to figures from the transport authorities. —Monthly aid A 15-seat minibus received 35,000 meticais a month, about US$553. —Fares The operators’ federation, FEMATRO, proposes rises from 1 November, while the metropolitan transport agency offers 3 to 5 meticais. —Rate used Dollar figures use about 63.24 meticais per US$ (RT, 20 October).

Mozambique has ended the fuel compensation it paid to chapas, the privately run minibuses that carry most commuters in Greater Maputo. Operators now want higher fares from 1 November and warn of service disruption if they do not get them.

For US readers, the dispute shows how fuel-price shocks tied to the Middle East reach a country that Washington and US energy firms watch as a coming gas exporter. It also tests the government’s budget room.

Subsidy Withdrawn After Three Months

The aid was announced in May and ran for three months in Maputo, Matola, Boane, Marracuene and nearby towns. A 15-seat minibus got 35,000 meticais a month (about US$553), and larger buses received more, according to Club of Mozambique.

The authorities paid 307,004,619 meticais in total (about US$4.9 million), covering 2,476 vehicles in the first month, 2,565 in the second and 847 in the third. Government spokesman Inocêncio Impissa called it a temporary measure, and a transport official said the state found more sustainable ways to manage public transport.

File photo: chapa minibuses in Maputo. Foto: A Verdade, CC BY 2.0

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mozambique Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Aid Began

Fuel prices jumped on 7 May, when diesel rose 45.5% to 116.25 meticais a litre (about US$1.84) and petrol rose 12.1%. Portuguese state broadcaster RTP linked the rise to the Middle East conflict.

Operators struck in Maputo and Matola on 8 May, leaving thousands of commuters stranded. The state then agreed to pay compensation to avoid an immediate fare rise.

In late July chapas again stopped in part of Maputo and Matola over late payments. Later, fuel queues formed in late September, and a ministerial diploma now eases customs deadlines for fuel imports.

The Fare Fight

FEMATRO, the road transporters’ federation, proposes raising an 18-metical fare to 30 meticais (about US$0.47) and a 15-metical fare to 25 meticais (about US$0.40) from 1 November. The metropolitan transport agency has countered with a rise of 3 to 5 meticais (about US$0.05 to US$0.08).

FEMATRO first asked for 20 meticais more, which the council rejected, according to Club of Mozambique. Its representative Jorge Manhiça warned of service disruption on 2 November if the proposal is rejected, saying operators would otherwise keep accumulating losses.

What It Means for US Readers

Mozambique’s government projects growth of 9.5% in 2029 once large liquefied natural gas projects start, so urban stability matters to US energy and aid interests. A transport stoppage in the capital would be an early test of that outlook.

Costly imported fuel also leaves Mozambique exposed to oil-price swings. US travellers to Maputo should expect possible disruption to minibus services around 1 and 2 November.

What Is Not Known

The final fares have not been set, and reports differ on how far apart the two sides are. Some operators reportedly accept a smaller rise only if aid continues, while others back higher fares.

The government has not published the legal text ending the aid, and the number of operators paid late has not been reported. It is also unclear what support, if any, will replace the subsidy.

The big picture: Mozambique explained — economy, politics, society and daily life in one read.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Mozambique end the chapa fuel subsidy?

The aid was a temporary measure that lasted three months after fuel prices jumped in May. A transport official said the government found more sustainable ways to manage public transport.

How much did the subsidy cost?

The authorities paid 307 million meticais, about US$4.9 million at 63.24 per dollar. A 15-seat minibus received 35,000 meticais a month.

Will Maputo minibus fares rise?

FEMATRO proposes rises from 1 November, while the transport agency has offered 3 to 5 meticais. No final fare has been announced.

What is a chapa?

A chapa is a privately run minibus taxi. It is the main form of public transport in Maputo and nearby towns.

World.content:
Kenya · Mobile Money · 20 October 2026

Key Facts —Who. Safaricom, Kenya’s largest mobile operator and the company behind the M-Pesa mobile money service. —What. Payments of KSh500 (about US$3.85) or less to a Lipa na M-Pesa till are free, and Pochi la Biashara payments up to KSh200 (about US$1.54) are free. —When. The Pata More campaign began on 1 August 2026, and the till change took effect on 7 August with no end date reported. The Pochi offer is reported to run to 31 October. —Who benefits. Prime Business Africa puts the number of small businesses affected at more than 7 million. —Rate. We used 129.82 Kenyan shillings per US dollar, the RT price of 20 October. —Still unknown. Whether Safaricom will extend the Pochi offer past 31 October.

Safaricom has made M-Pesa payments of up to KSh500 (about US$3.85) to business tills free since 7 August 2026, and no end date has been reported for that change. A separate offer for its Pochi la Biashara wallet, free up to KSh200 (about US$1.54), runs to 31 October.

M-Pesa is the mobile phone payment service that millions of Kenyans use for everything from market stalls to taxis. For visitors and US companies that sell into Kenya, the offer shows how cheap digital payments have become a competitive weapon.

What Changed for Traders

Safaricom raised the free limit for Lipa na M-Pesa, its till system for shops, from KSh200 to KSh500 from 7 August, according to Prime Business Africa. Payments above KSh500 still carry a 0.55% charge, which tech-ish reports is capped at KSh200 (about US$1.54) per transaction.

For Pochi la Biashara, a wallet for small sellers, payments of up to KSh200 are free, up from KSh100. For larger payments the charge is capped at KSh50 (about US$0.39), down from KSh108 (about US$0.83) in the top band, TechMoran reports.

Charges for moving money out of a business till were cut by up to half, Prime Business Africa reports. Examples cited by TechMoran include a transfer of KSh45,000 to KSh250,000 costing KSh54 (about US$0.42), down from KSh108.

A street stall in Nairobi, the kind of small trader Safaricom’s campaign targets. File photo. (Photo: Ninara, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Why Safaricom Did It

Safaricom launched Pata More on 1 August and says it wants to make digital payments affordable for small traders. A company statement quoted by Prime Business Africa reads: “When it’s cheaper to pay digitally than with cash, the whole economy wins.”

At a launch in Nakuru, Fawzia Ali, Safaricom’s chief consumer business officer, cited the pressure on households after a fuel price rise, The Standard reported. The campaign also offers a daily data bundle of 250 megabytes for KSh20 (about US$0.15).

Which Cuts End and Which Stay

TechMoran and business.co.ke report that the Pochi offer runs from 1 August to 31 October. Prime Business Africa calls it a 90-day promotion, and the till and payout changes carry no end date in the reports we reviewed.

We found no Safaricom statement on what happens to the Pochi offer after 31 October. Anyone who sells through M-Pesa should check the current rates with the company before 1 November.

What It Means for You

Travellers who buy from stalls, kiosks and taxis in Kenya often pay with M-Pesa, so lower charges help the small sellers they deal with. Companies that use M-Pesa to collect payments from Kenyan customers should watch what happens to the Pochi rates after 31 October.

For investors, the cuts show how Safaricom trades fee income for loyalty among small merchants. The company has not said what the campaign costs it.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Safaricom will extend the Pochi offer or let the old charges return on 1 November. The company has not said how much revenue it gives up.

The reports we reviewed do not include a Safaricom primary statement, so traders should confirm rates with the company. Our report on the Safaricom sale appeal covers the company’s ownership dispute, and our Kenya section has more.

Which M-Pesa payments are free under Pata More?

Payments of KSh500 (about US$3.85) or less to a Lipa na M-Pesa till are free. Pochi la Biashara payments of up to KSh200 (about US$1.54) are also free.

What do larger till payments cost?

Payments above KSh500 still carry a charge of 0.55%, according to TechMoran, which tech-ish says is capped at KSh200 per transaction. Transfers out of a business till were cut by up to half.

When do the M-Pesa fee cuts end?

The Pochi offer is reported to run from 1 August to 31 October 2026. The till change from 7 August has no reported end date.

Who is eligible?

The cuts target small businesses such as market vendors, bodaboda riders and matatu operators. Prime Business Africa puts the number of small businesses affected at more than 7 million.

Will Safaricom extend the Pochi offer?

No extension has been announced. We found no Safaricom statement on what happens after 31 October.

World.title: OPEC Fund Eyes Uganda Railway Loan Approval
World.content:
UGANDA · INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE

Key Facts —Who The OPEC Fund for International Development, a Vienna-based lender, sent a team led by Senior Country Manager Kemi Afun-Ogidan. —What The team is appraising a proposed €150 million loan (about US$168 million) for Uganda’s Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), starting on Monday, 19 October 2026. —When The fund targets board approval by 30 November 2026, about six weeks after the mission began. —Cost The Malaba to Kampala line is estimated at €2.7 billion (about US$3.0 billion), with export-credit agencies expected to cover 60%, development banks 25% and Uganda 15%. —Rate used Dollar figures use EUR/USD of 1.1214, the 19 October close.

The OPEC Fund for International Development began appraising a proposed €150 million (about US$168 million) loan for Uganda’s Standard Gauge Railway on Monday, 19 October. The fund says it is targeting board approval by 30 November.

For US investors and suppliers, the loan is a step toward financial close on East Africa’s biggest rail project. The line runs from Malaba on the Kenyan border to Kampala and is estimated at €2.7 billion (about US$3.0 billion).

Appraisal Mission Under Way

The OPEC Fund team opened its week-long visit with an entry meeting at the railway project’s headquarters in Kampala, according to Daily Monitor and Nile Post. It is due to meet officials from the finance and works ministries and inspect the Malaba to Kampala corridor.

The appraisal covers engineering designs, implementation arrangements, disbursement schedules and environmental and social safeguards. The loan has not been approved.

File photo: Kampala, Uganda. Foto: Todd Huffman, CC BY 2.0

How the Project Is Financed

The proposed loan equals about Shs697 billion in local reports. Uganda’s financing plan has export-credit agencies covering about 60% of costs, development finance institutions about 25% and the government about 15%.

The Islamic Development Bank approved €650 million (about US$729 million) for the project in June 2026. It would fund the 553-metre Jinja Nile Bridge, the 2.12-kilometre Mbuya to Kampala tunnel, six stations and three workshops.

Timeline and Early Works

The main construction period is planned to last 48 months from commencement. Reports differ on the target: Nile Post says construction starts in January 2027, while Daily Monitor calls January 2027 the target for financial close.

Early works under a limited notice to proceed, valued at €75 million (about US$84 million), are reported to be nearing completion. Land compensation and the remaining financing are still outstanding.

Official Position

Kemi Afun-Ogidan, the fund’s senior country manager, said at the entry meeting that approval would make this its largest single financing commitment to Uganda since it began operating there in 1976. She said the fund is targeting board approval by 30 November.

The two reports we reviewed from 19 October carry no public opposition or formal objection. Earlier coverage points to financing completion, land compensation and the timing of the main contract as the main concerns.

What It Means for US Readers

Board approval would give the project a second large development-finance commitment after the Islamic Development Bank. It could also help unlock the much larger export-credit tranche.

The 48-month build offers openings for engineering, rail and logistics suppliers. US firms tracking East African infrastructure should watch whether financial close slips past January 2027.

What Is Not Known

The loan is a proposal until the OPEC Fund board votes, and no board date has been published. Its interest rate, term, fees and conditions have not been disclosed.

It is unclear whether the export-credit tranche is fully committed. The Finance Ministry’s earlier target of November 2026 for concluding financing differs from the January 2027 date, and we could not establish which is current.

The fund targets a board decision by 30 November 2026. The appraisal mission began on 19 October, about six weeks earlier.

It is €150 million, about US$168 million at the 19 October EUR/USD rate of 1.1214. Local reports put it at about Shs697 billion.

The Malaba to Kampala line is estimated at €2.7 billion, about US$3.0 billion. Export-credit agencies, development banks and the government are to cover 60%, 25% and 15%.

Reports differ: January 2027 is called the construction start by one outlet and the financial close target by another. Construction is planned to take 48 months.

World.title: Ethiopia May Gain Voice in IMF Quota Reform
World.content:
ETHIOPIA · IMF

Key Facts —Quota Ethiopia’s IMF quota is SDR 300.7 million (roughly US$400 million), a share set long before its economy grew. —Reform The IMF says it is exploring a quota realignment, possibly with a new formula, but no decision has been taken. —Loan Ethiopia’s four-year IMF programme is worth SDR 2.556 billion (about US$3.4 billion), and about US$2.65 billion has been paid out. —Next review Talks on the next loan review are expected in November 2026, with a Board decision in early 2027. —G-24 The G-24 group of developing countries asks to protect the quota of the smallest and poorest members.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is exploring a reform of its quota system that could give Ethiopia a bigger share and louder voice in the Fund. A group of developing countries, the G-24, says any new formula must also protect the smallest and poorest members.

For US readers, the debate decides how much weight fast-growing African economies get in an institution the United States leads as its biggest shareholder. It also shapes who can borrow from the Fund and on what terms.

Ethiopia’s Share Lags Its Growth

A quota sets a member’s financial contribution, its voting power and its access to IMF loans. Ethiopia’s stands at SDR 300.7 million (roughly US$400 million), a figure that reflects the weight of its economy years ago.

Zeine Zeidane, who has led the IMF’s African Department since April, said Ethiopia has been growing fast for two decades. “If there is a new formula, it’s likely that Ethiopia will be one of those benefiting,” he said.

G-24 Asks for Protection of the Poorest

Iyabo Masha, who heads the G-24 Secretariat, said the group is calling for “protection of the quota of the smallest and the poorest member”. She also noted that three or four G-24 members rank among the world’s ten largest economies, so the bloc itself is split between fast growers and small members.

The IMF’s governing committee endorsed guiding principles for a realignment in April 2026. The last general review, the 16th, ended in December 2023 without a new formula.

File photo: IMF headquarters in Washington. Foto: International Monetary Fund, public domain

Loan Programme Continues

Ethiopia’s four-year Extended Credit Facility is worth SDR 2.556 billion (about US$3.4 billion), or 850% of its quota. The Board approved it on 29 July 2024.

On 1 July 2026 the Board completed the fifth review and released about US$464 million, bringing total payments to about US$2.647 billion. It also brought forward about US$200 million to ease external financing pressure.

The sixth review could start from 15 October 2026, which the IMF calls the earliest window rather than a deadline. An IMF spokesperson said talks are expected in November, with a Board decision in early 2027.

Tension on the Horn of Africa

A separate backdrop is the dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea. On Wednesday, 14 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke by phone with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and urged restraint and dialogue.

The State Department said all countries in the Horn of Africa must respect their neighbours’ sovereignty and territorial integrity. The IMF debate is not linked to that dispute in any source we found.

What It Means for US Readers

The United States holds the largest quota of any IMF member, so any new formula moves its share too. A larger Ethiopian voice would also change how Washington and its partners negotiate over African debt and lending.

Ethiopia’s programme also shows the IMF still lends large sums to a country with heavy debt and external pressure. US firms and lenders following Ethiopia’s restructuring will watch the next review closely.

What Is Not Known

No new quota formula has been agreed, and the size of any Ethiopian increase has not been published. It is unclear which measures of economic weight, such as output, reserves or trade, a final formula would use.

Neither the Ethiopian government nor neighbouring states have commented publicly on the reform, according to the reports we reviewed. The Board date for the sixth review has not been set.

Sources

The Reporter Ethiopia · IMF press release 26/235 · IMF: members’ quotas · IMF: Zeine Zeidane · Ahram Online

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an IMF quota?

A quota is a member country’s share in the Fund. It sets how much the country contributes, how many votes it holds and how much it can borrow.

Why could Ethiopia gain from a new formula?

The IMF’s African Department director says Ethiopia has grown fast for two decades while its quota stayed small. A new formula would likely raise its share.

What does the G-24 want?

The G-24 asks to protect the quota of the smallest and poorest members. Some of its own members are also among the ten largest economies.

When is Ethiopia’s next IMF review?

The IMF expects talks in November 2026, with a Board decision in early 2027. The earliest window for the sixth review opened on 15 October.

World.title: Coast Guard member Lionel Logan dies following shooting in Corozal; police investigation continues
World.content:
Coast Guard member Lionel Logan dies following shooting in Corozal; police investigation continues

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have confirmed that 35-year-old Belize Coast Guard member Lionel Logan has died after being critically injured in a shooting along the Philip Goldson Highway near Carolina Village, Corozal District, on Sunday evening.

Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed during Monday’s police press briefing that Logan succumbed to his injuries earlier that day. His death comes less than 24 hours after gunmen opened fire on a vehicle carrying Logan and several other passengers.

Logan, a resident of Libertad Village, was travelling in a black Chevrolet Equinox with 35-year-old Julian Dyer, a construction worker from Corozal Town, and other passengers after leaving a football game in Carolina Village.

According to initial reports, a black van carrying approximately four men pulled alongside their vehicle, and its occupants opened fire, striking Logan and Dyer.

Logan suffered multiple gunshot wounds, including injuries to his abdomen and the back of his head. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital in Belize City, where he remained in critical condition before succumbing to his injuries on Monday.

Dyer sustained injuries to his right forearm and lower abdomen and was treated at the Corozal Community Hospital. A nine-year-old girl travelling in the vehicle also suffered a minor injury reportedly caused by shattered glass.

The bullet-riddled Chevrolet Equinox was subsequently discovered abandoned in the San Antonio Village area.

Police are continuing their investigation into the deadly attack. A motive has not been publicly established, and the police have not announced any arrests in connection with the shooting.

World.title: Police investigate whether improperly parked car contributed to fatal bus crash that killed Sherri Mejia and 4-year-old Taleenie Garbutt
World.content:
Police investigate whether improperly parked car contributed to fatal bus crash that killed Sherri Mejia and 4-year-old Taleenie Garbutt

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating whether a car parked partially in the path of oncoming traffic contributed to Saturday evening’s fatal collision between a National Bus Company bus and a Toyota Corolla on the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway.

The accident, which occurred between Miles 37 and 38 near San Juan Village, claimed the lives of Sherri Mejia and four-year-old Taleenie Garbutt.

During Monday’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith said investigators believe the car had stopped along the highway to allow a passenger to relieve themselves.

According to preliminary findings, the bus was travelling in the opposite direction when its driver apparently attempted to swerve to avoid the parked car but was unable to prevent the collision.

Smith said an examination of the scene and the vehicle suggested that the car had not been parked completely off the roadway and may have been partially obstructing the lane used by oncoming traffic.

Mejia died at the scene, while Taleenie later succumbed to her injuries while receiving medical treatment. Four other occupants of the car were injured.

According to public reports, Taleenie’s father, Walton Garbutt, sustained a broken foot and a knee injury requiring surgery.

Police have obtained a urine sample from the bus driver and served him with a notice of intended prosecution.

Investigations continue to determine the precise circumstances of the collision and whether traffic violations contributed to the deaths.

World.title: Police launch internal investigation into chokehold used during arrest in Unitedville
World.content:
Police launch internal investigation into chokehold used during arrest in Unitedville

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Police Department has launched an internal investigation into a viral video showing an officer placing a man in a chokehold during an arrest in Unitedville, Cayo District.

During Monday’s press briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith explained that chokeholds are classified as deadly force under the department’s policies and procedures manual, comparable to discharging a firearm or striking someone in the head with a baton.

Smith said such force should only be used as a last resort when there is an imminent threat of death or grievous bodily harm. The internal investigation will determine whether the officer’s actions were justified under those circumstances.

She also suggested that less-lethal alternatives, including pepper spray, could have helped de-escalate the confrontation, but noted that the officers involved did not appear to have that option readily available.

The man involved has been identified as Samuel Parham, whose family has publicly questioned the officers’ actions following the October 16 incident.

Police confirmed that Parham has since been charged with grievous harm after an officer reportedly suffered a broken arm during the confrontation.

Smith said investigators had obtained additional footage showing an officer being thrown to the ground, an incident that was not visible in the shorter recording she initially reviewed.

The Professional Standards Branch is investigating the matter, and police are encouraging witnesses to cooperate as investigators seek to establish whether the use of force was justified.

World.title: Belize City man accused of raping ex-girlfriend in her home with her son present despite restraining order, remanded to prison
World.content:
Belize City man accused of raping ex-girlfriend in her home with her son present despite restraining order, remanded to prison

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 26-year-old Belize City construction worker has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged with allegedly raping and assaulting his former girlfriend despite an existing protection order against him.

Shadron Gillett, of Iguana Street, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, October 19, where he was charged with rape, harm and damage to property in connection with an incident involving a 28-year-old woman on July 2, 2026.

According to the allegations, the woman was resting on her verandah around 3 p.m. when Gillett approached her and insisted on speaking with her. She reportedly reminded him of the protection order and demanded that he leave.

The woman told police that when she attempted to record him with her cellphone, Gillett grabbed the device and smashed it. During a subsequent struggle, he allegedly damaged another cellphone before the confrontation moved into her bedroom.

The complainant alleged that Gillett grabbed her by the neck, ordered her to stop screaming for help and struck her in the head with a surge protector before sexually assaulting her.

During the alleged attack, the woman’s son reportedly knocked on the door. Gillett allegedly ordered him to leave, but the woman urged her son to remain. She further alleged that Gillett punched her in the mouth before fleeing the residence.

Police subsequently charged Gillett with rape, harm and damage to property involving two cellphones valued at a combined $1,300.

No plea was taken on the rape charge, which is an indictable offence to be tried before the High Court.

Gillett was offered bail of $5,000 with one surety of the same amount or two sureties of $2,500 each. His bail conditions prohibit him from interfering with the complainant or her family and require him to remain at least 100 yards away from her.

However, he was unable to meet bail and was remanded to prison until he can do so. His next court appearance is scheduled for December 28, 2026.

World.title: Augustine sisters acquitted of burning down mother-in-law’s $32,000 home in Crooked Tree
World.content:
Augustine sisters acquitted of burning down mother-in-law’s $32,000 home in Crooked Tree

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two Belize City sisters accused of burning down their former mother-in-law’s home in Crooked Tree Village more than four years ago were acquitted of arson on Monday after a nine-member jury returned a unanimous not guilty verdict.

Janiene Augustine, 27, and her younger sister Janiece Augustine, 23, broke down in tears as the verdict was delivered before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in the High Court. The jury, comprising six women and three men, deliberated for approximately two hours before reaching its decision.

The sisters were accused of intentionally setting fire to a woman’s home on July 16, 2022, destroying a wooden structure valued at $30,000 and household contents worth an additional $2,000.

Prosecutors alleged that Janiene, who had been living at the property with her then common-law husband and their children, was motivated by a dispute that resulted in the common-law husband putting her out of the house two days before the fire.

The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including testimony that the sisters had entered the property shortly before the blaze. However, no witness testified to seeing either woman start the fire.

In his summation, Justice Pilgrim highlighted the absence of scientific evidence establishing that the fire had been deliberately set. He reminded jurors that the burden rested entirely on the prosecution to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Both sisters denied setting the house ablaze, maintaining that they had visited the property only to collect Janiene’s belongings.

The women were initially charged in April 2024, nearly two years after the fire, following directives from the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Janiene was represented by attorney David McKoy, while Janiece was represented by attorneys Leeroy Banner and Lesly Mendez.

Monday’s unanimous verdict brings the lengthy criminal proceedings against the sisters to an end, with both women cleared of the arson charge.

World.title: Coast Guard member Lionel Logan critically injured, Julian Dyer shot in attack on SUV in Corozal
World.content:
Coast Guard member Lionel Logan critically injured, Julian Dyer shot in attack on SUV in Corozal

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A member of the Belize Coast Guard was critically injured and another man wounded after gunmen opened fire on a vehicle travelling along the Philip Goldson Highway near Carolina Village, Corozal District, on Sunday evening, October 18, 2026.

The victims have been identified as 35-year-old Lionel Logan, a Belize Coast Guard member from Libertad Village, and 35-year-old Julian Dyer, a construction worker from Corozal Town.

According to initial reports, the men were travelling in a black Chevrolet Equinox with several other passengers after leaving a football game in Carolina Village when a black van carrying approximately four men pulled alongside their vehicle. Occupants of the van reportedly opened fire on the SUV, striking both men.

Logan sustained multiple gunshot wounds to his left forearm, lower abdomen and the back of his head. He was transferred to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital in Belize City, where he was listed in critical condition. His current condition has not been independently confirmed.

Dyer suffered pellet injuries to his right forearm and lower abdomen. He was treated at the Corozal Community Hospital but subsequently discharged himself.

A nine-year-old girl travelling with her mother also sustained a minor cut to the palm of her right hand, reportedly caused by shattered glass. Both managed to escape from the vehicle during the attack.

The Chevrolet Equinox was later found abandoned in the San Antonio Village area with multiple apparent bullet holes and shattered windows.

The motive for the attack remains unknown, and no suspects have been publicly identified. Police investigations continue.

World.title: Deon Jones, Lloyd Faber injured as gunman opens fire on group socializing on King Street
World.content:
Deon Jones, Lloyd Faber injured as gunman opens fire on group socializing on King Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an attempted murder incident in Belize City that left two men injured after a gunman opened fire on a group socializing on King Street on Saturday night, October 17, 2026.

The victims have been identified as 27-year-old Deon Jones and 43-year-old Lloyd Faber, a stevedore, both residents of Belize City.

According to police, around 10:20 p.m., four men were socializing in a yard on King Street when an unidentified male emerged from behind a building and fired several shots in their direction, striking Jones and Faber.

Police received reports of the shooting around 10:30 p.m. and responded to the scene, where they learned that both injured men had already been transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital for treatment.

The extent of their injuries has not been disclosed, and police have not established a motive for the attack.

The shooting comes amid renewed concerns about gun violence in Belize City, following a series of murders reported earlier this month.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Minister of Foreign Affairs and OAS discuss Belize-Guatemala relations
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and OAS discuss Belize-Guatemala relations

By Zoila Palma: Today, Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca met with Ambassador Antonia Urrejola, Special Representative of the Secretary General of the Organization of American States (OAS) for Belize-Guatemala relations, to discuss matters relating to the Belize-Guatemala relationship and ongoing regional engagement.

The meeting was attended by Oscar Arnold, Chief Executive Officer for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, and Directors of International Affairs, Ambassador Ayesha Borland and Ambassador Alfonso Gahona.

World.title: Where is the outrage?
World.content:
Minister of religion Lisean Gordon delivering the sermon during the Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday. Looking on are Mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager (left) and moderator Leisa Dawson. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CARTERWOOD, Trelawny — Minister of religion Lisean Gordon has criticised what she described as the public’s readiness to demand justice when police officers use force, but silence following the killing of two members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last Friday.



Preaching under the theme ‘Let the Children Know’ during a Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday, Gordon said the lack of comparable demonstrations demanding justice for the slain cops reflects a troubling imbalance.

“They may be somebody’s father, somebody’s son. Nobody came out because we have placed in the heart of ungodly people that we are allowing them to take over this country, all in the name of politics,” said Gordon as she addressed the service hosted by the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) in Trelawny and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

Two members of the JCF’s Special Operations Branch, Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose, sustained fatal gunshot wounds during a firefight with men who had barricaded themselves inside a house in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday.

Three civilians, Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle, also died in the incident while a 10-year-old girl was left nursing a gunshot wound.

Delivering the sermon, Gordon condemned the tendency to vilify members of the police force without knowing the circumstances surrounding an encounter, and charged that media coverage and circulating recordings often fuel premature judgements.

Gordon linked the hostility towards law enforcement personnel to a broader erosion of respect for authority, and contended that political allegiance is encouraging Jamaicans to excuse behaviour they might otherwise condemn.

“There is something called the hidden curriculum, which we sometimes forget about. The hidden curriculum: What they see us do is what they will do,” said Gordon, who is also an educator.

She also took issue with verbal attacks against political leaders, including Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Mark Golding, warning that adults risk normalising disrespect among children who observe and absorb their behaviour.

“This disrespect that we put up with…because we are affiliated to a party, and to politics, it must stop. Disrespect is disrespect, and everybody who leads us needs to be respected, whether they are on the Opposition side or they are on the ruling side,” declared Gordon.

She argued that while children are taught to assert their rights, adults are neglecting the importance of responsibility and accountability.

“But we teach them about their rights, but no longer teach them about their responsibility,” Gordon said as she insisted that parents and other adults must uphold discipline, principles, and respect rather than retreat from the challenges of raising the younger generation.

She warned that Jamaica faces a dangerous escalation of disorder if the erosion of these values continues, describing the threat as a storm more severe than Hurricane Melissa.

“I am afraid of what is coming to Jamaica. There is a storm coming that is worse than Melissa… It’s called a storm of lawlessness, it’s called the storm of disorder, and it’s coming towards us. It’s worse than a Category 5,” said Gordon.

The minister of religion urged Jamaicans to reflect on the values they are passing on to their children as she argued that a meaningful inheritance extends beyond material possessions.

Meanwhile, mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager, in his remarks, called on Jamaicans to preserve the legacy of the national heroes through their everyday actions rather than limiting remembrance to speeches and ceremonies.

“Our national heroes stood firm in the face of adversity, injustices, challenges, and paved the way for the freedom and opportunities we enjoy today,” Gager said.

He urged citizens to serve their communities, stand up for what is right, invest in young people, and work together to build a better Jamaica.

Gager also underscored the Church’s role in strengthening families and communities through prayer, mentorship, compassion and outreach, helping young people embrace their heritage and recognise their potential.

World.title: Ochie ‘Lovers Rock’ getS Hollywood pop-in
World.content:
Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, hangs out with promoter of Lovers’ Rock: A Night of British Reggae on Friday in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

A Hollywood power player showed up at Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae last Friday.

Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, surprised the packed house at Ocean’s 11 Bar and Restaurant in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

Fallon popped into the venue with Wayne Jobson, the Jamaican impresario who is an influential figure in the Southern California reggae scene.

Steve James, who started ‘Lovers Rock’ in 2025, was surprised when the American comedian appeared.

“I was very shocked! We had received an indication that he might attend, but there is a big difference between hearing that someone may show up and actually seeing them there,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “When we saw him we were pleasantly surprised and delighted. His attendance was certainly an unexpected highlight of the evening.”

James said Fallon mingled with patrons, most of whom are fans of lovers’ rock, the genre that emerged in the United Kingdom during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Since 2014 Fallon has hosted his late-night talk show, which is consistently one of the top-rated in the United States.

Beres Hammond also attended Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae, which saw a performance from singer/bassist Lloyd Parks.

The South Florida-based James, who hosts the Real Rock Radio show, led the line-up of selectors who played songs that defined the lovers’ rock movement. Others manning the turntables were Martin Mitchell; Twinn Spinn from Fetedayzradio.com; DJ Jacko from King Jammy Sound System; Buppy C from

Vibes FM London; and Lady Gee, formerly of Choice FM London and Vibes.

“The atmosphere was fantastic! Many patrons expressed how much they had missed hearing this kind of music. For them, it was more than just a night of entertainment; it was a nostalgic journey that transported them back to their days in the UK,” said James, who is considered an authority on lovers’ rock.

The genre produced several stars, most of whom were born in the United Kingdom to Jamaican parents. They include Janet Kay, Peter Hunnigale, and Maxi Priest.

Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae was first held during Reggae Month last February at Pon Top Seafood Grill and Bar in Kingston. The second staging took place at the same venue in May.

The fourth is scheduled for Kingston in February.

World.title: Netball Jamaica boss talks up Sunshine Girls’ chances in Horizon Series
World.content:
Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls will face England’s Roses in the four-Test Horizon Series, with the first two games set to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena. The Sunshine Girls will then welcome England to Jamaica on December 5 and 6. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

NETBALL Jamaica (NJ) President Karen Baugh has promised entertainment galore as the Sunshine Girls look to tackle England’s Roses in the Horizon Series next month.

The four-Test series was announced at a press conference held at S Hotel in New Kingston on October 13, 2026. The first two games are to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena.

The Sunshine Girls are set to welcome the Roses to Jamaica on December 5 and 6.

“When Jamaica and England meet on a netball court you can expect intense competition, a bit of drama, excitement, and if Jamaica has anything to do with it, a little extra flair,” Baugh said.

“…This is much more than just two netball matches… it is an international sporting event, a celebration of our Sunshine Girls, and an opportunity to showcase the best of Jamaica netball and Brand Jamaica. This is definitely a rivalry worth watching.”

The Horizon Series — contested in honour of netball icons Molly Rhone of Jamaica and Jean Hornsby of England — began in 2024 with a classic.

Baugh recalled her favourite match, one she ranks alongside the 2026 Commonwealth Games win over Australia.

“That first match here against England, [in] the last second, we were leading by one and Shanice [Beckford] literally ran down the clock to prevent them from scoring again — and we won in the last second to tie the series. We went on to win the last game and won the series 2-1,” she said.

That Jamaica team had trailed 1-0 after the England leg — drawing the first, losing the second — before coming home to win the series.

In 2025 Hurricane Melissa forced the cancellation of the Jamaica leg, and England won the two matches played in England.

“The trophy, our trophy, is currently in England so we have a question to settle in 2026: Will the Rhone Hornsby Trophy be coming home?” Baugh asked.

In a historic first, Jamaica’s men’s team, The Suns, have been invited by England Thorns to play the curtain-raiser in London.

“It is a great opportunity for the male players to showcase their talent, and we wish The Suns every success in what is promised to be an exciting contest,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that for the home leg of the series, fans will get two matches for the price of one. England’s Roses Pathway team will tour Jamaica for a three-match series against the Jamaica Development Squad.

The first match will be on December 3, with the other two serving as curtain-raisers on December 5 and 6.

“You want to come really early. You want the place to be electric,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that the series forms part of preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Australia and comes on the back of a stellar year.

At the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, the Sunshine Girls won silver, stunning world number one Australia 46-45 in the semi-final before going down to New Zealand in the final.

“That was a statement to the world that Jamaica is among the very best in world netball,” Baugh said.

World.title: READY TO COMPETE
World.content:
Jamaican winger Jamone Lyle (centre) is expected to feature prominently for Jamaica at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Qatar in November. Here he is seen dribbling away from Canada’s Eloi Breton (right) and Ulrich Zamble during the Concacaf Under-17 Qualifiers encounter between Jamaica and Canada in Costa Rica on February 11, 2026. (Photo: JFF Media)

WITH the FIFA Under-17 World Cup now less than 30 days away, national under-17 Head Coach Wendell Downswell says the group have had to make the most of a less-than-ideal preparation period as they look to ensure they’re ready to compete at the tournament.

The young Reggae Boyz are set to make their third appearance at the global eventwhen it kicks off in Qatar on November 19. Jamaica have been drawn in Group E with European giants Italy, Ivory Coast and Uzbekistan.

The team booked their spot back in February at the 2026 Concacaf U-17 Qualifiers. However, they haven’t been able to secure international matches since.

Downswell, though, says they have made the best of the options available to them.

“It’s not been the ideal preparation that we have had because we were not able to get an international game; we were exploring at least two international games,” he

told the Jamaica Observer.

“However, we have been having camps — probably about four to five with the core of the players — which is good. And what we do is we prepare them in such a way that we use the Premier League teams and the Tier 2 teams as part of the measuring stick to see where we are in terms of the necessary preparation, and the boys have been responding very positively.”

“The coaching staff have explored all the possibilities to stretch these players somewhat similar to opposition that we’ll be up against in the tournament itself. So, hopefully this level of preparation, this kind of limitation that we have, will be of utmost significance for us going forward.”

Downswell says the technical staff have been closely keeping track of all the players they intend to select for the squad. However, he says several factors, including the ongoing ISSA Schoolboy Football, season haven’t made life easy.

“We release them and then some of them come back, [and] some come back with injuries here and there, knocks here and there,” he said. “[But] we have been having conversations with them. We have another camp coming up on the 6th and we have been having dialogue with the schools, so they won’t be released from the 6th up to our departure on the 14th.”

Downswell, who previously guided Jamaica’s U-17 team to the 2011 World Cup, says the players have been put through extensive preparation on and off the field, ahead of the tournament.

“We’ve put in place tactical preparation and the mental aspect of the players to get them fully focused regarding this task ahead. We have placed a lot of emphasis on the mental aspect of preparation, and the players have been responding in a positive way,” he said.

“Also, the whole preparation going in[to] international [games] — how we play the first 10 minutes, 5 minutes, the various tactical manoeuvres that we have done for the players to assimilate and adapt from a tactical standpoint — these are some of the things that we have been working on.”

Jamaica struggled in their two previous World Cup appearances, exiting at the group stage in 1999 and 2011 without recording a win in six matches.

Donwswell, though, is confident these young Reggae Boyz can break that trend and create history for the country. “I’m very upbeat, very enthusiastic about going, and at the same time our intention is to compete,” he said.

“Our first game’s against Italy [so] what we will do, the fact that we haven’t gotten much international exposure, so to speak, since February, [the plan] is using each game as part of our preparation and hoping that it lends itself in such a way that we are able to come out of the zone and take it from there.”

The squad, which is expected to feature new senior Reggae Boyz Jahmarie Nolan and Jamone Lyle, is set to be finalised by the first week of November.

World.title: When Granny’s Jamaican House Becomes the Mood Board
World.content:
Crochet, embroidery and handmade textile details bring texture and unexpected craftsmanship to the table.

Remember Granny’s house? The mahogany furniture that was built to last several lifetimes. The crocheted doilies strategically placed on every available surface. The lace and eyelet curtains. The tufted sofas and chairs that were definitely not for everyday sitting. The cabinet filled with the “good” glasses and patterned china that nobody was allowed to touch. And, of course, those decorative lampshades.

For years, many of us would have looked at these things and thought: old fashioned. Today? Put them on a mood board and suddenly they’re vintage, layered and chic.

Welcome to the wonderful cycle of design, where what was once considered old can become the next big trend.

Take mahogany, for example. In an old Jamaican home, dark, heavy wooden furniture was everywhere — dining tables, sideboards, coffee tables and those formidable chairs that seemed almost indestructible. After years of lighter woods dominating event design, deeper wood tones are beginning to feel sophisticated again. Pair mahogany with contemporary florals, beautiful linens and modern lighting and it takes on an entirely different personality.

Then there’s eyelet and lace. We remember them as curtains blowing at the window or perhaps a tablecloth brought out when company was coming. Now those same textures can inspire gorgeous linens, napkins and decorative details for weddings. Styled correctly, they feel romantic and intentional rather than old-fashioned.

And let’s talk about lampshades. Those decorative fabric shades that were once a fixture in Jamaican living rooms are finding their way back into stylish interiors and event design. Table lamps are appearing on dinner tables, bars and lounge areas, creating a warm, intimate, residential feeling that overhead event lighting simply cannot replicate.

Then there are the tufted sofas and chairs. Once associated with formal living rooms and furniture that children were warned not to climb on, tufting is having another moment. Used selectively in a contemporary lounge setting, a beautiful velvet tufted sofa or statement chair can add richness, character and just enough old-world glamour.

Even patterned china is having its moment. Remember those beautiful plates displayed behind the glass doors of the cabinet? Mix-and-match floral china, coloured glassware and vintage silver pieces can now transform a tablescape and make it feel collected rather than rented straight from a catalogue.

And yes, even crochet deserves another look. Perhaps we don’t need a doily under every vase, but crochet, embroidery and handmade textile details can bring texture and craftsmanship into an event in a way that feels personal and unexpected.

That’s really what this return to nostalgia is about.

We spent years trying to make everything sleek, minimal and perfectly matched. Now there’s something refreshing about a room that feels as though it has a story. The Jamaican homes many of us grew up visiting were layered. Things were collected over generations. Furniture was kept, repaired and passed down. The “good” pieces had meaning.

The trick is not to recreate Granny’s entire living room at your wedding.

Choose the memory, then reinterpret it.

A mahogany table with contemporary flowers. Eyelet linen with modern tableware. Patterned china against an unexpected tablescape. A beautiful lampshade incorporated into a bar or dinner setting. A tufted velvet sofa paired with contemporary coffee tables.

Suddenly, it isn’t old-fashioned. It’s nostalgic Jamaican style with a modern point of view.

So perhaps the next time you walk into an old Jamaican home and see that lampshade, embroidered cloth, tufted chair or piece of mahogany furniture you once thought was terribly outdated, don’t be so quick to dismiss it.

You might just be looking at your next event mood board.

Shikima Hinds

Managing Director

World.title: Fi Wi Land: Beyond the duppy stories, discover the value of Jamaica’s bats
World.content:
Often misunderstood and surrounded by folklore, bats are among nature’s hardest-working environmental protectors, helping to control insect populations, pollinate plants and disperse seeds. Discover more about these fascinating creatures as the Jamaica Observer in association with the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) premieres ‘Fi Wi Land’ on Monday.

In the debut episode, host Carlysia Ramdeen is joined by NEPA Environmental Officer Damany Calder who shares insights about bats, their importance to Jamaica’s ecosystems and why they deserve greater appreciation.

The new 12-week environmental series by the Jamaica Observer and NEPA explores Jamaica’s unique wildlife, ecosystems and natural resources while highlighting efforts to protect the island’s environment for future generations.

Catch the premiere on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: Proud moment for Barnswells as husband and wife conferred with national award
World.content:
Councillor Scean Barnswell and wife Danielle pose for a photograph after receiving their Badge of Honour for Gallantry at the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards at King’s House on Monday, October 19. 2026. (Photo: Llewellyn Wynter)

It was a historic and proud moment for the Barnswell family from Clarendon, when the husband and wife team of Councillor Scean Barnswell and Danielle Anna-Marie Barnswell stood on the dais at King’s House Monday morning to accept their national award – the Badge of Honour for Gallantry, from Governor General Sir Patrick Allen.

The occasion was the 2026 Ceremony of Investiture and Presentation of National Honours and Awards.

The Barnswells were among 149 Jamaicans who were honoured for outstanding contributions in various fields.

The two were recognised for their “quick and courageous” actions that led to the rescue of a six-year-old girl who was reportedly abducted from the St Thomas More Preparatory School in May Pen Clarendon on December 9 last year.

“In growing up you’re told to mind your business but in Jamaica, the children are all our business so in this case I’m happy we did that and I wouldn’t change anything,” said Mrs Barnswell during rehearsals for Monday’s ceremony.

Scean Barnswell is the councillor for the Hayes division in the Clarendon Municipal Corporation and a former Mayor of May Pen. He is looking to return to that position as the balance of power in the corporation recently swung from the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) to the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP).

This came after the JLP-elected councillor for the May Pen North division, Tanya-Lee Williams, resigned from the JLP, giving the PNP a clear 12-10 majority in the corporation. The PNP has stated that this gives it the right to appoint the mayor and deputy mayor but a court injunction granted last Friday has stalled those plans. The PNP has said it will be going back to court.

According to reports from December 2025, Barnswell and his wife spotted a man walking with a small child along Bustamante Highway and, sensing something was wrong, immediately intervened. Their actions resulted in the safe recovery of the child and the capture of the suspect, who was arrested by the police.

In a statement at the time, the PNP described the incident as an act of humanity, noting that Councillor Barnswell showed decisive, selfless leadership in a moment of crisis. The party said his response reflected the values of community vigilance and public service and urged others to do likewise.

WATCH: Barnswell honoured for rescuing abducted six-year-old

The PNP also expressed gratitude to members of the public who raised the alarm and commended the Jamaica Constabulary Force for its swift response.

“It emphasised the importance of strong community–police partnerships in protecting children and preventing crimes of this nature,” the party said.

-Lynford Simpson
