World.title: Cyberangriffe kommen nicht nur zu Bürozeiten
World.content:
An diesem Vormittag wartet die IT-Abteilung von Babor auf einen Cyberangriff. Genauer gesagt auf das Ergebnis eines Cyberangriffs, den sie selbst in Auftrag gegeben hat: Ein Penetrationstest soll zeigen, wie gut die Systeme des Kosmetikherstellers geschützt sind. Denn die Bedrohungslage verändert sich. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert nicht nur, wie Unternehmen arbeiten, sondern auch, wie sie angegriffen werden. Phishing-Mails lassen sich heute in Sekunden auf ihre Opfer zuschneiden, Schadsoftware kann sich automatisiert an Abwehrmechanismen anpassen, und Angriffsmuster entwickeln sich schneller weiter, als klassische Sicherheitskonzepte nachziehen können. Für Unternehmen werden damit zwei Fragen immer wichtiger: Wie schnell erkennen sie einen Angriff und wie reagieren sie darauf?

Ein Härtetest für die IT-Sicherheit

Gemeinsam mit den Expertinnen und Experten von Vodafone und SITS hat das Team die eigene IT-Infrastruktur einem kontrollierten Cyberangriff ausgesetzt. Die Frage ist, wie gut die Systeme einem echten Angreifer standhalten würden und vor allem, wie früh ein solcher Angriff erkannt wird. „Das Ergebnis haben wir mit Spannung erwartet“, sagt Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor. Für die IT-Abteilung ist der Test mehr als eine technische Übung. Babor betreibt rund 200 Server am Hauptsitz in Aachen, dazu kommen weitere Rechenzentrumsstrukturen an unterschiedlichen Standorten. ERP-Systeme, Datenbanken und Kollaborationstools bilden die Grundlage der täglichen Geschäftsprozesse. Weltweit vernetzte Standorte mit Tochtergesellschaften in Europa und Nordamerika sowie mehr als 1000 Mitarbeitern machen die Infrastruktur zusätzlich komplex. Entsprechend hoch sind die Anforderungen an ihre Absicherung. Die bisher eingesetzte Sicherheitslösung stieß zunehmend an ihre Grenzen. Gesucht war ein Ansatz, der nicht nur automatisiert auf verdächtige Aktivitäten reagiert, sondern die gesamte Infrastruktur rund um die Uhr im Blick behält und bei Bedarf Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten hinzuzieht. Inzwischen ist ein solches Security Operations Center (SOC) bei Babor im Einsatz. Der Penetrationstest sollte deshalb auch zeigen, wie gut die neue Sicherheitsarchitektur im Ernstfall funktioniert.

World.title: French riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates
World.content:
Police officers stand near a fire during an unauthorized demonstration marked by riots and clashes with law enforcement at Place de la Republique in Paris on October 18, 2026. | Gauthier Bedrignans/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS — Looting and rioting across France over the weekend are threatening to reshape the contours of the French presidential race.

Far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen is seizing on the crisis to cast herself as the candidate of law and order, but there are risks for her too. Many voters see her as a highly divisive leader whose 2027 victory would only deepen the societal fault lines exposed by the riots.

Far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, widely tipped to challenge Le Pen in the second round next year, is also treading carefully as rivals accuse him of encouraging the rage on the streets that has morphed into pillaging and arson.

World.title: Spanish left-wing chaos dampens Sánchez’s hopes of election miracle
World.content:
With negotiations stuttering, an exasperated Mónica García, health minister and candidate for the left-wing Broad Front, warned on social media that the left risked getting “trapped in egos, worries, internal disputes and electoral and/or personal calculations that are good for nobody except the right.”

The Broad Front took shape shortly after the election was called in order to bring together several parties to the left of Sánchez. But after several days of frantic discussions, prominent left-wing party Podemos did not join the united ticket — except in the Canary Islands and the Valencia region — hampering the far left’s overall electoral prospects.

“The only way for [Sánchez] to be able to govern again is for there to be a strong presence to the left of the Socialists,” said Kiko Llaneras, polling analyst for media outlet El País, who pointed out that “the Broad Front isn’t actually that broad.”

He added, “The big question is whether this new movement will be strong enough to allow the left to form a majority — and that’s going to be very difficult.”

Defying the odds

The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the junior partner in the current Socialist-led government; the Catalan Comuns; the communist-led United Left (IU); Más Madrid; and an array of regional left-wing parties. The lead candidate of the ticket will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.

Spain’s electoral system rewards united platforms, and the Broad Front is not as inclusive as a similar alliance — created in 2023 and including Podemos — which helped Sánchez defy the odds and form a new administration after the last election.

World.title: Trump says he is open to trilateral summit with Putin and Xi
World.content:
The president told reporters that such a meeting would focus on denuclearization, not the war in Ukraine as Moscow had suggested earlier.

President Donald Trump said Monday he was open to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, but said such a meeting would not focus on the war in Ukraine.

Trump told reporters at the White House that he would participate in a summit with both leaders if the purpose was to discuss denuclearization. The comments came after reports that Putin had proposed that the three leaders meet on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in China to discuss how to end the war in Ukraine.

“I would do it, not so much for Ukraine,” Trump said. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They have not been doing much. And the same thing with China. We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons, denuclearization. And anytime I can have a meeting on denuclearization.”

World.title: EU Parliament launches probe into fake email seeking to sway internal election
World.content:
The email disparaged the work of Portuguese EPP lawmaker Sebastião Bugalho ahead of the EPP’s vice-chair elections. When asked, Bugalho’s office said he “will obviously not comment on forged emails.”

Pedro López de Pablo, the EPP’s press director, said: “The group has been informed that there will be an investigation.”

The Parliament’s probe was announced by EPP group chair Manfred Weber to all the group’s lawmakers at a closed-door meeting on Monday afternoon, according to four people in the room. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive internal matter.

Halicki sent his request for an investigation by Belgian authorities to Parliament President Roberta Metsola on Friday. “As I know, the Parliament immediately reacted, and the investigation has been launched,” he said, referring to the internal probe.

The email comes amid a fierce campaign for the EPP’s vice-chair positions, which are to be voted on on Tuesday. Twelve lawmakers, including Bugalho and Halicki, are battling it out for 10 spots.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misstated Pedro López de Pablo’s role. This article was updated Oct. 19 to correct his title to press director.

World.title: After looting spree, France tells online resellers to crack down on traffic of stolen goods
World.content:
During a government press conference earlier in the day, Minister for Small Businesses Serge Papin said officials were working on “coordination between investigators and online platforms” to identify the individuals behind suspicious listings. A specific protocol is expected to be put in place, according to a government source speaking to POLITICO.

A spokesperson for Vinted France said the sale of stolen goods, or soliciting the purchase of such goods, is strictly prohibited on the platform. "We have a zero-tolerance policy on this matter," said the company representative. "Since this past weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings that may involve stolen goods, and we have stepped up our monitoring of suspicious listings."

Other platforms weren't immediately available for comment.

The discussions with the reselling websites are also likely to touch on longer-term questions around platform responsibility and the monitoring of illicit trade within the EU’s digital marketplace.

The issue of looted goods sold on online marketplaces “is a new dimension and the Commission is happy to look at it in collaboration with French authorities," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told POLITICO.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has instructed local authorities to enact “partial curfews” Monday evening to prevent further looting and rioting. Papin said a “special support fund” will be set up to provide financial assistance to the estimated 3,000 local businesses affected by the weekend’s unrest.

Eliza Gkritsi contributed to this report.

World.title: Ryanair CEO calls EU chief Ursula von der Leyen 'useless' and demands tax on US and Chinese airlines
World.content:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary has called European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen "useless", accusing her of talking about competitiveness while doing nothing to deliver it.

 

In an interview with Euronews, O'Leary said "You have that ship of fools in the European parliament, redesigning more regulations designed to increase the cost of air travel when consumers want lower fares."

O’Leary attacked EU environmental taxes that apply only to flights within the bloc. American, Asian and Chinese carriers are exempt, even though he says they produce more than half of Europe’s aviation emissions.

"Nobody would design a stupid system like this, other than the European Parliament and Ursula von der Leyen. If you're serious about competitiveness, tax the Americans when they land here in Europe.

"Ursula von der Leyen’s afraid to do anything except talk. You know, she’s useless," O’Leary told the Europe Today programme. "Europe has a road map for being more competitive, it’s called the Draghi Report. Two years later, not one of its recommendations has been implemented and Ursula von der Leyen hides in the Berlaymont doing nothing except giving speeches."

He called for a "fair and reasonable" levy on every flight landing in or taking off from Europe.

Former Italian prime minister Mario Draghi published the report in September 2024. It warned the EU faced a "slow agony" without radical reform and called for up to €800 billion a year in extra investment.

Last month a report by the Joint European Disruptive Initiative said the bloc has implemented 26% of the recommendations outlined by Draghi and claimed "progress is real, but it is not in sync with the pace of the world."

'Belgium, France and Germany are not competitive'

O’Leary was in Brussels to announce Ryanair’s winter schedule. The airline is cutting a million seats and 20 routes from Belgium after Bart De Wever's government raised its air travel tax from €2 to €7 per ticket.

"We’re moving aircraft to those countries who are competitive," he said. "Belgium is not competitive. France is not competitive. Germany is hopelessly uncompetitive."

O’Leary warned passengers to expect higher fares. Ryanair has locked in this year’s fuel at about $67 a barrel by agreeing the price in advance, which protects it from rising oil costs. He expects that price to double next year as the protection runs out.

"We guarantee no fuel surcharges," O’Leary said, "but there is no doubt that airfares are going to rise significantly in 2027 because of much higher oil prices."

His warning comes as war in the Middle East pushes oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude, the international benchmark, closed at $109.86 a barrel on Friday, its highest level since May, and has since topped $110 as tanker attacks threaten supplies from the Persian Gulf.

World.title: Spain versus Morocco: this is how the military forces of both countries stand in 2026
World.content:
The Royal Moroccan Air Force's first F-16 Block 72 carried out its maiden flight on 6 October in Greenville, South Carolina, Lockheed Martin has announced. It is now progressing through pre-delivery testing after some delays in the programme. It is the most eye-catching piece of a rearmament drive that is being closely watched in Spain.

 

But, with the numbers in front of us, how much military weight does Morocco actually have today compared with Spain? Spain is still far ahead in terms of budget and easily dominates at sea. Rabat, by contrast, has more soldiers and rocket artillery, a capability the Spanish Army has lacked for the past 15 years.

Defence spending: more than six to one

The clearest gap is in spending. According to the latest report by Sipri (Stockholm International Peace Research Institute), Spain allocated around 34.287 billion euros to Defence in 2025, 50% more than the previous year, pushing its military burden up to 2.1% of GDP. Morocco came to 5.645 billion euros, up from 4.920 billion in 2024. That increase keeps it as Africa's second-biggest military spender, behind Algeria, which spent 22.660 billion.

Behind that lies the size of each economy. Morocco closed 2025 with a GDP of 138.668 billion euros, according to the World Bank, while the Spanish economy was around 1.69 trillion euros. Twelve times larger.

Does Morocco really spend 10% of its GDP on Defence?

It is one of the figures most often circulated, but it does not fit with Sipri's time series. The institute itself puts Morocco's 2025 military spending at 3.54% of GDP. The 10% looks much more like another indicator: Defence's share of public expenditure, which Sipri calculates at 10.28% for 2025.

Something similar happens with the budget figures. Morocco's 2026 finance law authorised future spending commitments for the National Defence Administration of 157.170 billion dirhams, around 14.7 billion euros, a multi-year line that is often presented as if it were spending in a single year. What will actually be disbursed in 2026 in payment appropriations comes to 55.300 billion dirhams (5.157 billion euros).

Spain, meanwhile, hit 2% of GDP in 2025 and aims to consolidate that in 2026, although it remains the only ally to have refused to sign up to the 5% target for 2035.

Manpower: more troops south of the Strait

Here the balance tips the other way. Several sources converge on Morocco having between 195,000 and 200,000 active-duty personnel and some 150,000 reservists. In addition, unlike Spain, Morocco maintains compulsory military service, reintroduced in 2019. In troop numbers, Morocco's military strength comfortably exceeds Spain's.

This is where the oft-quoted 400,000 figure, which has gone viral in various media, should be treated with caution. The number comes from Global Firepower's profile updated on 21 January 2026, which also credits the African country with some 250,000 reservists, and, as of publication, no other independent record backs it up.

The Spanish Armed Forces have a staffing problem. On 1 January 2025 there were 116,739 military personnel in active service, below the legal minimum of 130,000 set by the Military Career Act, and the year ended with 832 fewer troops. The reserve is even weaker: at the start of 2024 there were 3,091 voluntary reservists.

Aviation: Eurofighter versus F-16 Viper

Spain flies more aircraft, but faces a longer-term question mark. FlightGlobal's World Air Forces 2026 directory credits it with 81 EF-18 Hornets and 67 Eurofighters, with another 45 on order. The first Halcón, a twin-seater, rolled out of the Getafe plant on 1 June, and the second batch will start to be delivered in 2030.

The problem is what comes next. Spain shelved the F-35 in August 2025 in order to buy European, and in June 2026 the FCAS, the fighter it was banking on, fell apart between France and Germany. Paris will now develop its own aircraft on its own.

Morocco is taking a different path. Washington approved in 2019 the sale of 25 F-16 Block 72s for some 3.380 billion euros, plus 23 kits to upgrade the F-16s it already operates.

A series of aircraft 'paint' the Spanish flag in the sky over Madrid on 12 October 2025. AP Photo

And the F-35? There are signs of advanced talks, but the deal remains in the realm of the possible and would still need final approval from the US administration and Congress. Specialist media have spoken of 32 aircraft costing around 13.5 billion euros spread over 45 years, including maintenance, but there has been no official confirmation.

In helicopters, Rabat already has 12 of the 24 AH-64E Apaches it ordered and is expecting the rest in phases between 2026 and 2027. Spain will upgrade its 18 Tigers to the MKIII standard. Morocco has also completed delivery of the Israeli Barak MX system, with three batteries and 225 interceptor missiles with a range of up to 70 kilometres, according to Sipri's database.

Ground forces: where Rabat presses hardest

It is on land that Morocco's military strength comes closest to Spain's. Rabat operates the US M1A2 Abrams and, although opacity makes an exact count impossible, some 200 units are estimated to be in service and another 150 on order. Spain fields 220 Leopard 2E tanks and around 50 2A4s, and plans to upgrade them to the 2A8 standard.

The most striking asymmetry is in multiple rocket launchers. Global Firepower credits Morocco with 185 systems and Spain with none; the Army lost that capability when the Teruel system was withdrawn in 2011. Morocco, by contrast, combines Chinese systems with Israel's PULS, already in service, and is awaiting the US HIMARS, of which Washington has approved the sale of 18 launchers.

There is a paradox here. Spain's Silam programme was to be based precisely on PULS, but the contract was cancelled because of the embargo on Israeli military technology imposed by the government; on 30 December 2025 Escribano and Rheinmetall Expal presented the Defence Ministry with a national alternative. In the meantime, the Moroccan Army is already receiving 8x8 WhAP armoured vehicles assembled in the country.

Moroccan army soldiers parade during celebrations marking the 50th anniversary of the Royal Armed Forces of Morocco on 14 May 2006. AP Photo

At sea, the gap is vast

The Navy is Spain's big safety cushion. Its backbone consists of five Álvaro de Bazán-class F-100 frigates, whereas Rabat's flagship is a single FREMM frigate. On top of that Spain has the LHD Juan Carlos I, which serves as an aircraft carrier, and two Galicia-class amphibious assault ships.

Under water there is simply no comparison, as submarine capability is one of Morocco's historic shortfalls. The S-81 Isaac Peral has been in service since November 2023, and the S-82 Narciso Monturiol has been undergoing port and sea trials since the summer, with delivery scheduled for the last quarter of the year; it will be the first to be fitted from the outset with air-independent propulsion. On the surface, the F-111 Bonifaz frigate, first in the new series, will join the fleet in 2028.

The Washington factor in Morocco's military strength

What has changed in 2026 is the political backing behind the purchases. Morocco and the United States signed at the Pentagon a military cooperation roadmap for 2026-2036, and by February the Royal Armed Forces had already tested the Link-16 tactical communications system, until now reserved for NATO members.

The US Senate has gone a step further: a clause in its defence bill instructs the Pentagon to deliver within 180 days a ten-year plan to turn Morocco into its most capable military partner in Africa. The United States already accounts for around 60% of Morocco's arms imports.

Rabat also wants to manufacture at home. The government has authorised ten defence industrial projects worth around 231 million euros in investment, and a letter of intent envisages producing in the country a long-range autonomous strike system, the Irifi, with a declared range of around 2,000 kilometres.

Spain has other cards to play. Its defence industry places it among the few countries capable of designing and building its own conventional attack submarines, and it belongs to NATO, although the geographical scope set out in Article 6 of the Washington Treaty does not explicitly include Ceuta and Melilla.

What the rankings don't measure

In the 2026 Global Firepower index, Spain ranks 18th out of 145 and Morocco's military strength appears in 56th place. It is the most frequently cited ranking, but it does not publish an auditable methodology and acknowledges that it relies on the CIA World Factbook and unidentified sources.

The trend, in any case, is upward. Morocco's military strength was ranked 59th in the 2025 edition and 61st in 2024. Nor does the index keep pace with deliveries: it gives Spain zero tanker aircraft, even though the Air Force is taking delivery of its third A330 MRTT this year.

The real friction between the two countries has not, moreover, involved fighters or armoured vehicles. At the end of July, the arrival of migrants in Ceuta led to a mass crossing by sea and over the breakwater at the border, the most serious crisis between the two countries since 2021.

The next figure to be scrutinised in Madrid will arrive soon. Mohammed VI on Saturday chaired in Rabat the Council of Ministers that approved the general guidelines of the 2027 budget, and the Defence allocation will be known once the draft reaches Parliament.

World.title: France presses resale platforms to remove 'stolen' goods after unrest
World.content:
Six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, the country was rocked over the weekend by some of its worst street violence in years, with thousands of shops damaged, many looted. The unrest came after weeks of student demonstrations demanding better conditions in schools.

 

More than 3,000 businesses suffered damage, according to the authorities. Since Sunday, screenshots have circulated on social media showing online resale listings for items allegedly stolen during the weekend unrest.

"Stolen items from this weekend are being offered for sale on certain platforms," digital minister Anne Le Henanff said on X.

"We expect these platforms to remove the listings in question without delay," she said.

She convened representatives of six platforms for a meeting in the presence of interior and justice ministry officials.

"They will also be required to cooperate closely with state authorities so that those reselling stolen goods can be prosecuted," Le Henanff added.

According to the French commerce ministry, representatives of Vinted, Amazon, eBay, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok as well as French online retail association Fevad were invited for talks.

Contacted by AFP, Vinted said it applied a policy of "zero tolerance" in such cases and was cooperating "actively with law enforcement and the French authorities".

"Since this weekend, our teams have acted immediately to identify and remove listings that may involve stolen goods, and we have strengthened monitoring of suspicious listings," the Vilnius-based second-hand platform said, without specifying the scale of the problem.

eBay said it was "not in a position to confirm an increase in listings that may be linked to thefts committed over the weekend".

The online auction platform said it used "proactive technological tools" to detect the sale of stolen goods.

World.title: France to impose new curfews where 'situation requires it', PM Lecornu says
World.content:
France will impose new curfews in areas where needed on Tuesday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said, adding that the measures introduced in several cities the previous day had "helped keep the night calm".

 

France was rocked by some of its worst rioting in recent years on Saturday, just six months before the country elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron.

Accused of failing to anticipate and contain the street violence, the government has pledged to restore order and had announced partial curfews in Paris and some other cities on Monday.

"Targeted curfews have contributed to calm overnight," Lecornu wrote on X.

"Tonight new curfews will be decided where the situation requires it. These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the mayors," he said.

Police confirmed the night had passed without major incidents across France.

Several cities, including Paris, the southwestern city of Bordeaux and Nice on the French Riviera, introduced partial curfews on Monday in response to urban unrest that followed weeks of student demonstrations over poor learning conditions in high schools.

While some restrictions, such as those in Paris, initially applied only for the night from Monday to Tuesday, others, particularly in Bordeaux and Nice, were set to remain in force for several days.

During the night, a helicopter flew over the French capital's Place de la Republique, one of the epicentres of the unrest, sweeping a powerful searchlight across the square to monitor compliance with the curfew.

In Lyon, despite a ban on demonstrations, around 500 people gathered on Monday evening outside the tourism office that was set on fire, to show support for shopkeepers affected by looting, according to organisers.

The word "LYON" had been spelled out on the ground with candles.

A banner hung on a fence nearby read "Anti-Rioters Lyon" and "Doucet Resign", referring to Green mayor Grégory Doucet, an AFP journalist said.

The smashed window of a looted bank after violence erupted during nationwide protests against rising living costs in Marseille, 19 October, 2026 AP Photo

Under pressure, the government scheduled another series of emergency meetings on Tuesday, including talks involving representatives of major social media platforms.

Finance Minister Roland Lescure pledged support measures for shopkeepers and craftspeople.

Patrick Martin, the head of France's Medef business lobby group, on Tuesday accused the state of having "failed" during the urban unrest that hit at least 3,000 businesses, according to preliminary estimates.

World.title: Protests in France: Russian interference "quite certain" says French politician
World.content:
French poltician Patrick Molinoz, vice-president of the French Mayoral Association claims that recent violence in France was "planned", citing a "certain" Russian intereference.

 

French cities have recently been embroiled in waves of violence and protest, with widespread looting and destruction in major cities. This wave has been "completely different" from prior protests, according to Molinoz. Interference was "definitely on social media", additionally claiming "some of the attacks were planned."

World.title: Police patrol Paris streets under overnight curfew
World.content:
Paris police imposed an overnight curfew on Monday in two areas of the capital, after a weekend of some of France’s worst rioting in years.

 

People may not enter or stay in Place de la Republique or the Les Halles shopping district from 11pm until 6am on Tuesday. Gatherings and demonstrations are barred from 8pm.

On Monday evening, police guarded the two spots and asked passers-by to take other routes.

Some people had their identity papers checked. A helicopter with a searchlight passed over Les Halles several times, and the streets stayed quiet.

The prime minister had earlier asked prefects to impose ‘very limited’ and ‘localized’ curfews to prevent more looting.

World.title: At least 14 killed and seven injured in landslide at illegal gold mine in Colombia
World.content:
A landslide at an illegal gold mine in southwestern Colombia killed 14 people and injured seven, a regional official said on Monday.

 

Armed groups in Narino, an illegal mining hotspot on the border with Ecuador, control the clandestine gold trade as well as trafficking drugs and engaging in extortion.

Videos shared on social media show people and a backhoe evacuating bodies from the mine to a canoe on a nearby river.

Narino's Peace and Security Secretary Alex Gonzalez gave the revised death toll to the Caracol television channel, adding that the search for survivors had ended.

Rescue teams struggled to reach the site due to the difficult terrain and the presence of criminal groups, the governor's office said.

"Communities have no other economic alternatives than these extremely risky activities. Traditional small-scale mining has practically disappeared," a source from the office told the AFP news agency.

Mine accidents in Colombia are frequent, particularly at unregulated sites.

Locals in the municipality where the mine collapsed on Monday have reported selective killings carried out by armed groups over suspicions of collaboration with security forces and rival organizations, or of stealing gold.

World.title: Ryanair CEO calls Commission President Ursula von der Leyen 'useless'
World.content:
Michael O’Leary, CEO of Irish airline Ryanair, has criticised European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s green policies, arguing that they add “complexity and cost”. He also branded the European Parliament a “ship of fools”, claiming its green laws are driving up the cost of air travel.

 

O’Leary is set to announce Ryanair’s winter schedule as the airline cuts one million seats in countries including Belgium, following an increase in air passenger taxes, and Germany, which he has described as “hopelessly uncompetitive”.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: Japan probe sets course for Mars moon
World.content:
The MMX spacecraft is on its way to Mars' moon Phobos to collect surface samples that could help answer long-standing questions about the formation of the Solar System.

A Japanese spacecraft successfully set off on a journey to one of Mars' moons late Monday in a race to become the first mission to return samples to Earth and potentially unlock the mysterious origins of the Solar System.

The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is expected to reach Mars in August 2027. It will attempt to collect samples from Phobos, the larger of the planet's two moons, and deploy the German-French rover IDEFIX to explore the surface.

Pioneering mission heads to Mars moon — and back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX probe lifted off into a pitch-black sky from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41 a.m. local time (1941 GMT Monday), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.

Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet as the spacecraft blasted into space, shaking hands and embracing. Thousands of people tuned in to watch the livestream despite the early hour.

An hour later, JAXA announced that the probe had successfully separated from the H3 rocket and was "beginning its journey towards the Martian system."

"I'd dreamt of this day, so I'm incredibly happy," said JAXA scientist Mari Aida. "Right now I feel really relieved."

The agency also received signals from the spacecraft as expected, confirming it was operating normally.

Making way for science

Scientists hope the probe's discoveries will help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.

"The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars," Nicky Fox, administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a message broadcast on the JAXA live stream.

The mission is a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companies Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

JAXA also hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, unlocking a key piece of knowledge about the formation of the Solar System.

One theory holds that Mars' two moons formed after a giant celestial body collided with the planet. Another hypothesis suggests the moons are asteroids captured by Mars' gravity. Confirming either theory would help scientists determine "how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets," JAXA said, referring to the four rocky planets closest to the sun.

Probe to reach destination in August 2027

The probe is due to arrive near Mars around August 2027, where it will orbit one of the planet's two natural moons, Phobos.

A French-German rover named IDEFIX, after the dog from the Asterix comic series, will be the first vehicle to travel across Phobos to conduct surface observations and help ensure a safe landing for the Japanese probe. It is no bigger than a microwave oven.

Once MMX arrives on Phobos, it will spend about two hours collecting at least 10 grams of material from the moon's surface before launching back into space. It will also study Mars' other natural moon, Deimos, during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian region in 2030.

Phobos, the larger of the two Martian moons, orbits the planet three times a day Image: JAXA/DLR/dpa/picture alliance

Another objective of the mission is to explore the possibility of using Phobos as a "natural space station" by establishing the requirements for a round trip.

Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock measuring about 22 kilometers (14 miles) across.

The mission, which aims to complete the first round trip to the Martian region, is a collaboration involving US and European space agencies along with several private technology companies.

US and Chinese space agencies have also been competing to become the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars to Earth. NASA's Perseverance rover, which has been exploring the planet since 2021, has already collected samples. The return mission, however, was canceled by US President Donald Trump's administration after a congressional vote in January.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

World.title: India news: Rubio set to hold talks with S Jaishankar
World.content:
Skip next section Rubio heads to India for talks on trade, energy and emerging technologies

10/20/2026 October 20, 2026 Rubio heads to India for talks on trade, energy and emerging technologies

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to land in Mumbai as he begins his second official trip to India this year and holds talks with Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.

The meeting between Rubio and Jaishankar is expected to focus on "energy, trade and investment, defense, critical and emerging technologies," according to a report in the Indian newspaper The Indian Express.

During his visit, Rubio is also expected to travel to Jamnagar, in the western state of Gujarat, where he is set to visit billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance oil refinery.

Rubio's trip comes amid tensions in relations between the US and India over visa restrictions and tariff threats.

However, speaking in Samarkand on Monday, Rubio said Washington and New Delhi were "very close" to an agreement. The visit is being seen as part of a US effort to repair ties.

How India has become Russia's trade lifeline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The trip also comes days after the US paused sanctions on Russian oil imports.

Speaking in Samarkand, Rubio also said the US had considered the India-US trade deal when deciding to waive sanctions on Russian oil. India is a major importer of Russian oil.

Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors "including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies."

"You also can't unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue," he said.

World.title: Canada: Alberta rejects separation bid, CBC projects
World.content:
Voters have decisively rejected a proposal to begin the legal process toward Alberta's independence, dealing a major blow to a movement driven largely by economic grievances.

Canada's Alberta province has overwhelmingly rejected a plan to begin the process of seeking independence from Canada.

Canadian public broadcaster CBC projects a decisive victory for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76% support for remaining in Canada after roughly a third of the votes had been counted.

According to unofficial results from the chief provincial electoral office, Elections Alberta, nearly 77% favored staying with Canada with roughly one million votes counted, whereas 23% sought independenced.

The nonbinding referendum asked residents whether they wanted to stay in Canada or start the legal steps needed for a future binding vote on separation. Although it was not a full-on referendum, a positive vote for the separatists would have put in motion further steps to pursue that end.

The vote marks the first such Canadian independence referendum held outside Quebec, where past independence movements have been driven by language and cultural differences.

Alberta's independence movement was fueled by the influx of large numbers of Canadians angry about COVID-19 regulations, mixed with a high level of resentment toward Ottawa and Canada's eastern provinces.

Settling the question of independence once and for all?

On Monday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, posted on social media that, "Albertans have voted for a stronger Canada in a united Canada."

Smith will address Albertans on Tuesday evening to speak about the results of the vote.

Smith, who opposes independence from Canada, was forced to call the vote after being pressured from within her United Conservative Party and said she hoped that holding the vote would put the question of breaking away from Canada to rest for good.

Home to the world's fourth-largest oil reserves, Alberta is largely rural and conservative.

Its independence campaign was largely fueled by economic grievance. The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass but is much more sparsely populated, with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

Independence-minded Albertans feel that too much of their revenues go to the federal government and that leaders in Ottawa have been unfair to the province over energy and environmental policy.

The push for independence has also been actively fanned by US President Donald Trump, who has been exceedling belligerent towards one of America's oldest and most-trusted allies, often ranting about making Canada the 51st US state as well as starting an unnecessary trade war that remains ongoing.

In the run-up to the vote, Alberta independence advocates held meetings at the US State Department in Washington, D.C., as well as receiving coaching from US Republicn political operatives. Trump's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called Alberta a "natural partner," whereas Trump's biggest donor, trillionaire Elon Musk, recently posted on X that Alberta "should separate" from Canada.

Monday's result is a significant setback for separatist groups and their supporters and a much-needed win for Prime ​Minister Mark Carney as ​he ‌attempts to keep the country unified amid the ongoing trade war with ‌the US.

Why Canada's trust in the US may not recover anytime soon To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Australian MP seriously hurt in suspected car attack
World.content:
Helen Haines, an independent federal lawmaker, suffered severe injuries in what Australia's prime minister has called a deliberate attack by a man in a car.

An Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday has lost one of her legs, local media reported, citing sources.

Independent MP Helen Haines underwent surgery overnight after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that one leg had been amputated.

Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?

Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars.

The driver, described as a 43-year-old man, has been arrested, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.

Local barber ran to assist

Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.

Barber Ricky Jefferies has been called a hero for restraining the driver Image: Seven Network/REUTERS

Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.

"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't ​pull it ‌out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.

Jefferies said he then held the man down until ‌police arrived.

"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and ‌he was ​no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.

Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."

"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.

Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese

Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.

"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Prime Minister Albanese has said the incident seemed 'no accident' Image: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA/picture alliance

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."

At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.

Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.

World.title: Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years
World.content:
Veteran journalist Christiane Amanpour on Monday said she was leaving her role at CNN after 43 years at the network.

"After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless nights, as you can imagine, I've decided to separate from CNN," Amanpour, 68, said in a statement.

"This daily show on CNN and PBS will come to an end at the end of this year. But CNN and I have worked out a smooth transition where we continue doing Amanpour once a week through to June," she said in a video message posted on social media.

Amanpour, who became famous for her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones, did not give a reason for her departure.

That said, her move to resign comes weeks after CNN's parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), was formally taken over by Paramount Skydance.

After a yearlong process, Paramount closed its merger with WBD on October 6, uniting two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN — under one roof.

The merger has drawn concerns over the independence of the newsroom at CNN as the merged company's owners, the Ellison family, are close allies of US President Donald Trump.

Trump bans media outlets from White House To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"You know I've always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you as long as I am here and beyond. That's especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides, political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field," she said, without directly referring to the deal.

What to know about Amanpour's career

Amanpour, who was born in London to an Iranian father and British mother, joined CNN in 1983 as an assistant. In the next few years, she went on to cover major wars in the 1990s, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War.

Amanpour has interviewed many world's leaders, reported from conflict sites and interviewed newsmakers from hotspots such as Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, Rwanda and the Balkans.

Amanpour is one of the most recognized international correspondents [PHOTO: 2004] Image: Chris Helgren/REUTERS

She said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."

In a memo, CNN Chief Executive Mark Thompson praised Amanpur for "43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship."

"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally," Thompson said.

World.title: Zelenskyy accuses US of delaying Patriot missile shipment
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the United States of delaying deliveries of air defense missiles already paid for by European allies, as relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorate.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the US administration of delaying the delivery of crucial missiles needed by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

He told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" even though they had already been paid for by Ukraine's European allies.

The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place.

What did Zelenskyy say?

The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles, with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine.

He also said that Ukraine's European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US .

"The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval."

Ukraine urgently needs more air defence missiles like the Patriot system Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

Earlier on Monday, he said Ukraine had again not received any early warnings about incoming Russian missile strikes. The country is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia.

There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data.

The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions.

US says it's not withholding intelligence

The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings, cutting off electricity to more than half a million households.

"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack.

The US, though, dismissed claims it was withholding information, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisting that Washington had not paused its intelligence sharing with Kyiv.

On Monday, Trump doubled down on his previous complaints about alleged ingratitude from the Kyiv administration.

"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that," Trump told reporters in Washington on Monday.

Regarding the easing of sanctions and the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow, Donald Trump strongly criticized Zelenskyy for calling out the deal.

"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

World.title: At least four dead after flooding in eastern Spain
World.content:
At least four people have died in Spain as torrential rain has battered the country's eastern Mediterranean coast. The severe flooding had left more than 450 people stranded on rooftops, in buildings or in cars.

At least four people have died after heavy rain and severe flooding across eastern Spain, forcing hundreds of people to flee. The worst-affected areas are in the Valencia and Alicante regions, on Spain's eastern Mediterranean coast.

In the town of Oliva, two bodies were recovered on Monday. One victim was a 79-year-old woman found at her home, while another was a man who died from a heart attack at a campsite.

In Sagunto, a man drowned while swimming at the beach, while in Catalonia, a woman died after falling into a rain-swollen stream in Catalonia.

Emergency services have rescued more than 450 people who were stranded by the rising water. Some had to be airlifted from rooftops, flooded buildings and vehicles, while others were brought to safety by boat.

Roads were underwater on Monday Image: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

Residents use buckets to drain water from their homes in Daimuz Image: Ana Beltran/REUTERS

Pile of furniture on a muddy street Image: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

Emergency restrictions

Authorities imposed emergency restrictions across several municipalities, asking people to stay indoors. Most restrictions have since been lifted.

The Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, including Mallorca and Ibiza, were also affected, with schools closed, and some flights cancelled or delayed.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said military emergency teams were assisting with the rescue efforts and pledged full government support.

The latest flooding comes almost two years after the Valencia region suffered a devastating flood disaster that killed more than 220 people.

World.title: French authorities impose partial curfews in Paris, Nice
World.content:
Donald Trump has blamed the French unrest on immigration Image: Jonathan Ernst/REUTERS

US President Donald Trump on Monday cited the unrest in France as an example while warning of what he alleged could happen in the United States if opposition Democrats were in power, without providing evidence to support the claim.

At a rally supporting the Republican Senate candidate in Kansas, Trump described France as a formerly great nation that had been "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists."

"When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what ​the radical Dumocrats want to do to America," he said, using the altered version of his opponents' name that he often employs as an insult.

Ahead of the rally, Trump told reporters at the White House that he had warned French President Emmanuel Macron he was "making a big mistake."

"The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn't the deal," he said, adding: "We closed our borders. He didn't."

The US president's return to his signature anti-immigration, anti-Muslim rhetoric, which he used to some effect in his election campaigns, comes as his party seeks to avoid a drubbing in the November midterm elections.

His comments echo previous remarks by Republican colleagues. Vice President JD Vance, for example, argued that the French protests occurred because "Western liberals imported the third world into France."

World.title: Última hora de la actualidad política, en directo | Feijóo confirma negociaciones con Vox para las listas del Senado: “Sería un error facilitar al sanchismo el control”
World.content:
El PP busca una fórmula en la que los ultras no concurran a la Cámara alta el 29-N para lograr una mayoría más holgada frente a la coalición de izquierdas | El Gobierno aprueba un paquete para mejorar prestaciones sociales

Momentos clave Momentos clave Hace 2h Roger Llanes susituirá a Bernabé como delegado del Gobierno en la Comunidad Valenciana

El líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha confirmado que el PP y Vox están negociando para encontrar una fórmula en la que los ultras no concurran a la Cámara alta el 29-N, con la vista en lograr una mayoría más holgada frente a la coalición de PSOE y Frente Amplio. “Sería un error facilitar al sanchismo el control”, ha explicado en una entrevista en Cadena Cope. Este martes, el Consejo de Ministros aprobará un paquete de medidas de carácter social. Entre ellas figura una inversión de 45 millones de euros para crear 2.000 nuevas plazas en residencias universitarias de Madrid, Castilla-La Mancha, Andalucía, Castilla y León, la Comunidad Valenciana y Cataluña, con el objetivo de impulsar alojamientos asequibles para estudiantes. Además, el Ejecutivo dará luz verde a una batería de iniciativas para ampliar la protección social en casos de incapacidad por patologías asociadas a la menopausia, reforzar la prestación para víctimas de violencia de género y mejorar las condiciones de otras pensiones, como las de viudedad. Por otra parte, el Tribunal Constitucional celebra desde este martes un pleno en el que tiene previsto amparar al exconseller catalán Jordi Turull frente a la negativa del Tribunal Supremo a aplicar la ley de amnistía al delito de malversación.

World.title: “Repetí curso, pero también me saqué la oposición en dos años y medio y fui la número uno”
World.content:
La jueza que pide que se enseñe empatía en el colegio | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 6)

Dakota Sampedro fue una de las juezas más jóvenes de España y Ana Rosales, la alumna más destacada en su provincia de la PEvAU de 2024. Ambas charlan sobre cómo la vocación no la determina ni la excelencia académica ni los baches en los estudios, y abogan por la práctica del debate y el fomento de la empatía en el colegio para evitar conflictos futuros

El testimonio de Dakota Sampedro (Gijón, 30 años) demuestra que una mala temporada académica puede quedar enterrada en la excelencia de una carrera: “Repetí curso, pero también me saqué la oposición en dos años y medio y fui la número uno de mi promoción”, explica. El motivo de su transformación tras ese complicado tercer curso de la ESO fue los ánimos de su familia y su propia voluntad. Y, sobre todo, que encontró una motivación, un propósito: el Derecho. En 2022 consiguió entrar en la Escuela Judicial, en una prueba cuya ratio es de aproximadamente 20 aspirantes por plaza. Y desde 2025 ocupa la plaza número 1 de la Sección Civil y de Instrucción del Tribunal de Instancia de Torrox (Málaga).

“Las buenas notas te pueden dar muchas herramientas y ayudar a abrir muchas puertas, pero no te dan la respuesta definitiva a qué vas a ser en la vida”

Su caso sirve de inspiración para Ana Rosales (Alcalá la Real, Jaén, 20 años), una estudiante de ADE y Derecho en la Universidad de Granada. Ambas historias tienen puntos en común: las dos fueron estudiantes muy aplicadas. Rosales llegó a ser la mejor nota de la PEvAU en la provincia de Jaén en 2024. Cuenta que fueron sus profesores los que le insuflaron confianza: “Se me brindaron todas las oportunidades y herramientas posibles”.

“Gracias a mis profesores entendí que también había lugar para la gente que se esfuerza diariamente y que pretende alcanzar la excelencia académica”

Rosales y Sampedro comparten en Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación, una reflexión sobre qué hace el sistema con personas como ellas, que persiguen (sin desistir) el mejor desempeño académico. Rememoran a esos docentes que las espolearon, reconocen que un buen expediente no exime de las dudas vocacionales y recogen todo lo que descubrieron en las incontables horas de estudio. “Aprendí sobre todo a conocerme a mí misma”, desvela Sampedro. Como profesional y mediadora, afirma que algunos de los problemas que llegan al juzgado se podrían minimizar desde las escuelas. “Deberían enseñar a respetar los derechos de los demás y valores como la responsabilidad, que tú sepas que tus actos tienen consecuencias”, precisa.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.
