World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prague’s Día de Muertos Festival Returns to Holešovice on November 5th
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will host the fifth annual Día de Muertos festival on November 5, bringing Mexican food, live music, traditional decorations and family activities.

The event, organized in cooperation with Jarritos and Nuevo Progreso, will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Halls 13 and 11 will host a Mexican market and a carnival for children.

Visitors can arrive throughout the day, with the food stalls opening at lunchtime.



The selection will include Mexican and South American specialties, tortillas, grilled dishes and Jarritos soft drinks. A special beer brewed by Falcon brewery for the occasion will also be available.

The food zone will remain open until 10 p.m., giving visitors time to sample different dishes and explore the festival’s other attractions.

One of the main attractions will be a traditional ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, prepared by the Mexican Embassy. Decorated with photographs, flowers, candles and personal objects, the altar will introduce visitors to the traditions behind the holiday.

Día de Muertos is dedicated to remembering deceased family members and loved ones.

In Mexican tradition, the holiday celebrates their continuing place in family life and the belief that their spirits return to visit the living. Its customs differ from Halloween, combining remembrance with food, music, flowers and colorful decorations.

Hall 11 will become the PEDRO Kids’ Zone from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., with a program designed for children and families.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holešovická tržnice (@holesovickatrznice)

Activities will include dance workshops, Mexican music, crafts, stories about the holiday and a game in which children throw balls at illuminated skulls. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet a Xoloitzcuintle, the Mexican hairless dog traditionally associated with guiding souls to the afterlife.

Costumes are welcome, and the organizers have divided the program into six one-hour sessions beginning at 1 p.m., 2 p.m., 3 p.m., 4 p.m., 5 p.m. and 6 p.m.

Admission costs CZK 100 per person for adults and children aged three and older. Tickets are available through GoOut and at the venue, subject to availability. Each ticket covers one hour of activities, after which visitors can explore the rest of the festival.

The program will also feature mariachi musicians, stilt walkers, colorful masks and costumes, and a festival parade. DJs will provide music throughout the day, while a screening of the animated film Coco will offer another introduction to Mexican traditions surrounding death and remembrance.

World.title: Danish-Japanese Chain Sticks’n’Sushi to Open First Prague Restaurant
World.content:
Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Czech restaurant in central Prague on Wednesday, November 4, introducing its combination of Japanese cuisine and Danish design to the local dining scene.



The restaurant will occupy a site on Jungmannovo náměstí in Prague 1. Ahead of the official opening, guests will be able to sample the menu at half price from November 1 to 3.

Those interested in attending the preview must register online. Registered guests will then receive a link to book a table for one of the available dates.

The menu combines sushi, sashimi and salads with kushiyaki, Japanese-style grilled skewers. The restaurant will also offer set menus intended for sharing, making them suitable for groups.

Among the dishes are Beef Tataki, served with miso aïoli, truffle ponzu and crispy Jerusalem artichoke, and the Temaki Setto, which allows diners to assemble their own hand rolls with ingredients including lobster, Wagyu tartare and avocado.

Another addition is the Ebi Sando, a sandwich featuring crispy shrimp, truffle and miso aïoli. The Sticks Setto features skewers of Japanese Wagyu beef, Iberian pork, shrimp and miso-marinated black cod, served on a hot stone at the table.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sticks’n’Sushi Czech Republic (@sticksnsushi_cz)

The drinks list includes sake, Japanese teas, cocktails and premium spirits. The restaurant will also serve a Japanese rice lager brewed for the chain by Danish brewery Mikkeller.

Zbyněk Pokorný, chief executive of Sushi Group s.r.o., which is bringing the concept to the Czech market, said the opening followed nearly two years of preparation.

“We believe that the combination of Japanese quality, Danish hospitality, and a strong focus on the overall guest experience is a perfect fit for Prague,” Pokorný said. He added that the company was looking forward to welcoming its first guests.

Reservations can be made through the company’s Czech website.

About Sticks’n’Sushi

Founded in Copenhagen in 1994, Sticks’n’Sushi was established by brothers Jens and Kim Rahbek, who have Danish and Japanese roots, and Thor Andersen. The first restaurant opened in a basement space in the Danish capital.

The business has since expanded into an international restaurant group, with locations in Denmark, Germany and the United Kingdom. Its interiors draw on Japanese and Danish influences, with individual restaurants featuring their own design elements within the brand’s overall concept.

World.title: Hungary and Slovakia want EU to ease Russian energy ban rules
World.content:
Hungary and Slovakia are calling for greater flexibility and more EU funding as the bloc prepares to end Russian energy imports in 2027, warning that replacing existing supplies could prove costly for Central Europe.

Hungary and Slovakia are urging Brussels to ease the rules surrounding the phase-out of Russian gas and provide more funding to expand regional energy infrastructure, Euronews reports. They argue that their geographical position and dependence on existing supply routes make it harder and more expensive to diversify their energy sources.

Under the European Union’s plans, Russian energy imports to Central Europe are due to end in 2027, raising concerns in both countries about energy security, industrial competitiveness and the cost of replacing existing supplies.

Hungary and the EU are heading in the same direction on energy policy, but Hungary wants to move at a slower pace. Photo: depositphotos.com

Slovakia warns of energy supply challenges

Slovakia has historically served as an entry point for Russian oil and gas, but it now risks becoming a destination at the end of alternative supply routes, alongside Hungary, as the EU moves away from Russian energy.

Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava attended by European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen, Slovak Deputy Prime Minister Denisa Saková called for discussions with the European Commission on how the next EU funding period could address the region’s needs.

“We would like to discuss with the European Commission how the next EU funding period and the availability of EU funds can meet our needs, particularly regarding the expansion of oil and gas infrastructure in the Visegrád Four region,” Saková said.

Saková also stressed the importance of preparing new supply agreements ahead of the 2027 deadline, arguing that energy security requires clear rules for delivering oil and gas throughout the region.

If you missed it: Only one year left to use Russian gas: will the Hungarian economy truly grind to a halt without it?

V4 pushes for lower electricity bills

The latest appeal follows pressure from all four Visegrád countries at the European Council summit on 15–16 October. They called on EU leaders to reconsider measures intended to ease electricity costs across Central Europe. Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the EU’s Emissions Trading System (ETS), the bloc’s carbon market, and postponing the introduction of its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.

The countries argue that high energy prices are making it harder for their industries to invest in electrification, the transition from fossil fuels to electricity-powered processes and technologies. The US-Israeli war against Iran has contributed to rising energy prices, adding to the pressure on households and businesses across Europe.

According to energy think tank Ember, wholesale electricity futures in Central Europe are now more than 60% above pre-crisis levels, leaving consumers in the region facing a particularly heavy financial burden.

Brussels acknowledges the problem but insists on limits

European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen acknowledged the “serious” situation facing Central European households but maintained that any response should consist of targeted and temporary measures.

He also warned against solutions that could undermine the EU’s broader objective of reducing its dependence on imported fossil fuels.

“We used to be dependent on Russia. We’re moving out of that. Now, that is good. But the current situation shows that we are now dependent on the global market, and events in the Middle East can affect citizens here in Bratislava,” Jørgensen said.

Hungary and Slovakia seek alternatives to Russian supplies

Budapest and Bratislava argue that meeting the EU’s energy diversification requirements will be particularly difficult without additional financial support. Both countries want investment in infrastructure that would allow them to receive oil and gas through alternative routes.

The Visegrád countries already have access to several non-Russian energy sources and supply routes. However, these alternatives can be more expensive, and the extent to which they are integrated into national energy systems varies across the region. Hungary and Slovakia therefore want Brussels to recognise these differences when deciding how to distribute EU funding.

Hungary has also challenged the EU’s plan to phase out Russian energy imports in court, with Slovakia supporting its legal action. Both countries argue that ending Russian supplies could put their industries at a competitive disadvantage compared with businesses elsewhere in the EU.

World.title: Billions, big promises and debt: opposition Fidesz and Mi Hazánk attack Tisza’s 2027 budget
World.content:
The debate on the 2027 budget should be conducted once the draft is known, Fidesz parliamentary group leader János Bóka said at Monday’s sitting of parliament, responding to the prime minister’s speech before the agenda. Our Homeland’s group leader, László Toroczkai, said the prime minister had not said in his speech what the budget would cost, while the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP) group leader called next year’s budget hostile to the middle class.

Fidesz’s Bóka complained that Péter Magyar had spoken for more than two hours about a budget that has not yet been submitted. He added that the prime minister had not mentioned such key parameters as inflation, economic growth and the public debt figures on which next year’s budget was based.

The government, he insisted, was not keeping a single election campaign promise to each occupational group, and there would be no wage rises of the scale Tisza promised.

Read more about the 2027 budget:

Hungary’s 2027 budget: PM Magyar reveals major tax cuts, family allowance and pension rises

Péter Magyar announces huge housing and road spending reforms, food price cap removal

Meanwhile, Toroczkai said the prime minister had spoken about railway development, a rental housing construction programme and much else that would require the 6 trillion forints in European Union funding. He said that Tisza lawmakers and government members had earlier called that sum the cornerstone of the 2027 budget.

Bence Rétvári, the group leader of KDNP, called next year’s budget hostile to the middle class, employers and workers. The budget, he insisted, sought to smash the pillars of the earlier economic system that could have formed the basis of economic growth built on Hungarian businesses and Hungarian employers.

The government, he complained, had stripped the Fiscal Council of its veto right, although the council could genuinely have determined whether “the great pile of promises” would indebt Hungary.

World.title: Kremlin sends message on Ukraine war as possible Putin-Trump-Xi summit emerges – Without Zelensky
World.content:
Russia highly values US mediation efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday. Speaking at a press briefing in Moscow, Peskov said a final settlement would require the participation of someone from Kyiv willing to take responsibility.

“The American side continues its mediation and peacemaking efforts, and we highly value them,” he said.

Peskov also confirmed that the possibility of a trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump had been mentioned during Putin-Trump contacts, given that all three leaders could potentially attend a summit in China.

However, no substantive proposals or agreements had been discussed regarding such a meeting or its possible agenda, he said.

Ukraine: This would not help end the war

Responding to the initiative in a separate statement, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US and Russia could help end the war sooner.

“A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite,” he said.

Commenting on unrest spreading across Europe, Peskov described the situation as “a major crisis,” saying disturbances in France’s largest cities had spread to Italy and were beginning to affect other countries.

“These are disturbances that are effectively already bordering on chaos,” he said, adding that the situation was an internal matter for the countries concerned.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Russian government reshuffle

Peskov also addressed the proposed reshuffle of the Russian government, describing personnel changes as “a normal part of its work.” Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin had proposed changes to the Cabinet, which Putin had approved, he said.

The necessary parliamentary procedures for approving the new nominees would now begin, Peskov added, noting that all deputy prime ministers would continue performing their duties until the relevant presidential decrees were issued.

The reshuffle includes a proposal to appoint Finance Minister Anton Siluanov as deputy prime minister while retaining his finance portfolio. Peskov said the move reflected the need for stronger coordination of fiscal discipline amid the current economic situation.

The Finance Ministry’s role in maintaining macroeconomic stability was particularly important at the present time, he said, highlighting budget discipline and the need to coordinate the work of several government departments.

Asked about a proposal by Russian businesses to finance the development of new air defense systems to protect industrial facilities, Peskov said the initiative had not been discussed in detail at the Kremlin and fell within the government’s remit.

He also referred journalists to explanations previously provided by Mishustin’s press secretary, Boris Belyakov, regarding the government reshuffle.

World.title: New winter forecast reveals what could be in store for Hungary this year
World.content:
Europe is heading towards a potentially snow-poor winter in 2026–2027, with the latest seasonal models pointing to below-average snowfall across much of the continent. Hungary is also expected to see less snow than usual, while a strong El Niño could influence when the heaviest snowfall arrives.

The latest seasonal forecast suggests that winter sports enthusiasts and snow lovers across Europe may be disappointed this year. According to an analysis by Severe Weather Europe, which combines data from six seasonal weather models, much of the continent is expected to receive less snow than average during the winter of 2026–2027.

The October update paints a less snowy picture than the forecasts published in September, with all major European regions showing a downward trend in expected snowfall. The biggest shortfalls are projected in southern and central Europe, although western Europe is also likely to experience significantly less snow than usual.

For Hungary, the outlook is similarly disappointing. The models show no indication of above-average snowfall, with the country potentially receiving less snow than the long-term average throughout the winter.

Where will Europe see the biggest snowfall shortages?

The most pronounced snow deficits are forecast along Norway’s western coastline, in northern parts of the United Kingdom and across the western Balkans. Much of southern Europe is also unlikely to experience particularly snowy conditions.

Above-average snowfall is expected in only a handful of areas, mainly in north-eastern Europe and some northern mountain regions. Parts of Scandinavia could fare better, while certain areas of the Alps may also see more favourable conditions.

The new projections suggest that regions receiving close to their usual snowfall levels could be among the luckier parts of Europe this winter.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

February could bring the best chance of snow

The forecast also examines how snowfall could be distributed throughout the season, suggesting that the timing of winter precipitation will be just as important as the overall amount.

December is not expected to bring above-average snowfall to any of Europe’s major regions. This could mean a slow start to the winter, with more substantial snowfall arriving later in the season.

February stands out as a potentially snowier month in parts of north-eastern and east-central Europe, as well as some northern areas of the continent. Certain parts of Germany and Poland, Ukraine and southern Sweden could receive more snow than usual.

By March, the signal for above-average snowfall is expected to persist mainly in Europe’s northernmost regions. Southern Europe, meanwhile, is not forecast to see above-average snowfall in any of the winter months.

Hungary is not expected to benefit from this late-season pattern, with the models showing no clear prospect of above-average snowfall even in February.

How could a strong El Niño influence the winter?

A strong El Niño is expected to be one of the major factors shaping global weather patterns during the 2026–2027 winter.

El Niño occurs when sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean become warmer than usual. This can influence atmospheric circulation, affecting the distribution of precipitation and cold air across different parts of the world.

Its effects vary by region, but the phenomenon is associated with winter weather patterns that can favour a slower start to the snowfall season in some areas, followed by more significant snow events later on.

However, seasonal forecasts are not precise predictions of individual weather events. Conditions can change as winter approaches, and the latest projections should be treated as an indication of the likely overall pattern rather than a guarantee of how much snow a particular location will receive.

World.title: German gardener steals 22 gold bars from woman in Hungary, gets arrested by police
World.content:
A 62-year-old German man has been arrested in Hungary on suspicion of stealing 22 gold bars worth more than HUF 13.6 million (approximately EUR 37,500) from a woman’s garden after she showed him exactly where they were buried.

Gardener turned gold digger

According to Hungarian police, the woman had previously purchased 64 investment gold bars for more than EUR 100,000. In June 2025, she buried 22 of them in a box in the garden of her home in Somogy County, southern Hungary.

Later that year, she hired an acquaintance to build a garden pond on her property. To prevent the buried gold from being disturbed during the work, she showed the contractor the precise location of the box and explicitly warned him to avoid the area.

Gold sold to a dealer in Kaposvár

The woman recently learned that the man who had been carrying out work at her property had sold a substantial quantity of investment gold to a dealer in Kaposvár, police said. Suspecting that something might have happened to her own gold, she returned to the garden and dug up the box. She discovered that its contents had disappeared, with the resulting loss estimated at more than HUF 13.6 million.

The discovery prompted a police investigation into the suspected theft. Investigators focused on the contractor after learning that he had sold investment gold in the nearby city. The case highlights how the woman’s attempt to protect her valuables by warning the worker about their hiding place may have inadvertently provided the suspect with the information needed to find them.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Suspect arrested at home

Police arrested the suspected perpetrator at his home during a night-time operation on 15 October. Officers searched the property and seized approximately HUF 1.5 million in cash. The 62-year-old German national was taken to the Fonyód Police Station for questioning. He was questioned on suspicion of theft involving property of significant value, according to the Hungarian police.

Authorities have not disclosed whether the seized cash is believed to be connected to the sale of the gold bars or whether any of the missing bars have been recovered. The investigation is ongoing. The man is suspected of committing the offence and has not been convicted.

World.title: What is Wekerle Plusz? Here’s the new housing programme the government offers instead of Orbán’s Home Start
World.content:
Hungary’s government will replace the previous administration’s Otthon Start housing loan scheme with a new programme offering more targeted support for young homebuyers, housing savings and energy-efficient renovations from 2027.

The Wekerle Plusz programme will retain subsidised 3 per cent mortgages for eligible buyers of new homes, while loans for existing properties will carry a fixed 5 per cent interest rate. Prime Minister Péter Magyar outlined the plans during his parliamentary presentation of the 2027 budget. Unlike Otthon Start, which had no age limit, Wekerle Plusz will be available to applicants aged 18 to 41 seeking to buy or build their first home.

Stricter conditions for subsidised home loans

Under the new Wekerle Plusz scheme, the fixed 3 per cent mortgage rate will apply to newly built homes and house construction. Buyers of existing properties will be offered loans at a fixed 5 per cent interest rate. Applicants must also commit to living in the purchased property for at least five years.

Neither the applicant nor their spouse may hold a 50 per cent or greater ownership share in another residential property, a condition intended to limit investment purchases and direct support towards people seeking a home of their own.

Marriage and having children will not be eligibility requirements. The government also plans to reduce the commissions banks receive on subsidised loans. Existing Otthon Start loan agreements will remain valid, according to the announcement.

Magyar criticised the previous scheme, arguing that it had not adequately helped young people without substantial savings or financial support from their families. He claimed that 59 per cent of subsidised loans had gone to the wealthiest 10 per cent of the population, with some properties purchased for investment rather than owner-occupation.

State support for housing savings returns under Wekerle Plusz

Wekerle Plusz will also introduce a state-supported housing savings scheme to help prospective buyers build up the deposit needed to purchase a property. People who save regularly for years will receive a non-repayable state contribution on their deposits, writes Telex.

The contribution will amount to 10 per cent during the first five years, increasing to 20 per cent from the sixth year onwards. The scheme is intended to make it easier for young people to accumulate the initial capital required for a mortgage.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Bigger loans and grants for home renovations

The third pillar will support energy-efficiency improvements. The maximum subsidised loan will rise from HUF 6 million to HUF 15 million, with a fixed interest rate of 3 per cent. Applicants may also qualify for a non-repayable grant covering 30 to 50 per cent of eligible costs, capped at HUF 7.5 million.

To qualify, renovations must deliver energy savings of at least 30 per cent. Properties in the poorest energy condition will be eligible for the highest level of support. The funding can cover improvements such as insulation, replacement windows and modernised heating systems. The scheme is intended to be available nationwide, without marriage or childbearing requirements and regardless of age, according to the announced plans.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar announces huge housing, food price cap scrap and road spending reforms

Other housing measures to continue

The government has also confirmed that the preferential 5 per cent VAT rate on new homes will remain in place in 2027. Existing family support measures, including the babaváró loan, CSOK housing subsidies and rural CSOK, as well as household utility price reductions, will remain unchanged.

Separately, the Wekerle Sándor Housing and Student Accommodation Construction Programme will allocate HUF 30 billion in EU funding in 2027 towards affordable rental homes and student accommodation. A further EUR 550 million is planned over the following three years.

The government’s stated aim is to make housing support more accessible to young people and households with limited savings. The final impact will depend on the detailed eligibility rules and implementation of the new programme.

World.title: What happened? Macron cancels Budapest visit, von der Leyen confirms 23 October appearance and speech
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron will not attend Hungary’s 70th anniversary commemorations of the 1956 Revolution, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is expected to deliver a speech in Budapest.

Macron’s visit was never officially confirmed by France

French President Emmanuel Macron will not attend Hungary’s state commemorations marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution on 23 October, the French Embassy in Budapest has confirmed to Telex.

The embassy said Macron would not take part in the commemorations, adding that his possible visit to Budapest had never been officially confirmed by the French side.

The announcement comes after Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in an interview with Hungarian YouTube channel Partizán last week that several foreign leaders, including Macron, would travel to Hungary for the anniversary.

Although earlier reports suggested the French president had agreed to attend, the embassy’s statement has now claimed otherwise. It also raises the question: how did the potential visit come to be reported before France had officially confirmed it?

It is likely that Macron will not be coming to Budapest due to the unrest in France.

Péter Magyar and Emmanuel Macron in June 2026. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Von der Leyen to address the Budapest ceremony

While Macron will be absent, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is set to attend the 23 October commemorations in Budapest and deliver a speech, according to 24.hu, citing information provided by the European Commission.

Von der Leyen is expected to arrive in the Hungarian capital on Friday. She had originally been scheduled to attend a summit in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, but that event was postponed, making her Budapest appearance possible.

Photo: Anadolu Agency

Zelensky will also miss the anniversary

Magyar previously said that virtually every head of state and government had been invited to the event, with Russian President Vladimir Putin the exception. Speaking to 444.hu, the prime minister said he could not recall whether the number of invited politicians was 100 or 150.

Macron is not the only prominent foreign leader who will be absent. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was also invited, but Magyar has said he will not attend.

The 1956 Revolution began as a popular uprising against Soviet rule and became a defining symbol of the country’s struggle for freedom and independence.

Hungary prepares for large-scale commemorations

The government is organising an expanded, day-long programme for the 70th anniversary, with events planned both in Budapest and elsewhere in the country. In the capital, activities are expected to take place at several prominent locations, including Kossuth Square, Andrássy Avenue, the river embankments and Bem Square.

World.title: Péter Magyar announces huge housing and road spending reforms, food price cap removal
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has announced a series of economic measures, including a new housing support scheme to replace the Otthon Start programme, expanded funding for affordable rental homes and student accommodation, the gradual removal of food price margin caps and a HUF 100 billion road repair programme planned for 2027.

Speaking on Monday, 19 October, Péter Magyar outlined plans to reshape housing support, help young people buy or build homes, improve energy efficiency and increase public investment in roads. Several of the measures are due to begin next year, while the government also pledged to retain existing family support schemes and household utility price reductions.

Wekerle Plusz to replace Otthon Start

The government plans to launch the Wekerle Plusz housing programme, replacing the Otthon Start (Home Start) scheme with a system Magyar described as fairer. He argued that, although Otthon Start had a worthwhile objective, its implementation disproportionately benefited wealthier households and investors.

According to the prime minister, 59 per cent of loans under the programme went to the wealthiest tenth of the population, with some state-supported purchases made for investment purposes rather than owner-occupation.

Under Wekerle Plusz, people aged 18 to 41 would be able to access fixed-rate loans at 3 per cent interest to buy or build a new home. Loans for existing properties would carry a fixed 5 per cent interest rate. The government also intends to reduce banks’ commissions associated with the loans.

The wider Wekerle Sándor housing construction programme would direct HUF 30 billion (EUR 82.6 million) in EU development funding towards affordable rental housing and student accommodation in 2027. A further EUR 550 million is planned over the following three years, alongside bank and private-sector financing.

Prime minister Péter Magyar also confirmed that the preferential 5 per cent VAT rate for the construction and purchase of new homes would remain available next year.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Housing savings and renovation support

The government also plans to introduce a Wekerle Plusz housing savings scheme. People saving part of their salaries over five to ten years would receive a state contribution equivalent to 10 per cent of their deposits during the first five years, rising to 20 per cent from the sixth year onwards.

A separate home renovation support and loan scheme would focus on energy efficiency. The maximum available loan would rise from HUF 6 million (EUR 16,500) to HUF 15 million (EUR 41,300), with a fixed interest rate of 3 per cent.

Applicants could also receive non-repayable state support covering 30 to 50 per cent of eligible costs, capped at HUF 7.5 million (EUR 20,700). The largest grants would go to homes with the poorest energy ratings.

Prime minister Péter Magyar said the rules governing the family home creation allowance, the rural version of that scheme, the baby-expecting loan and household utility price reductions would remain unchanged.

Photo: MTI/Hegedűs Róbert

Food price controls to be phased out

Péter Magyar also announced plans to phase out the government’s food price margin cap, a measure that limits the retail margins charged on certain products.

He argued that the policy had failed to make shopping cheaper, claiming that retailers had offset losses by raising prices on other goods and that domestic suppliers had been pressured to accept discounts. The government wants to encourage quality food production and competition between retailers through genuine promotions.

The announcement comes as the government says food inflation has eased and prices for several products have fallen. The timing and detailed arrangements for ending the margin cap were not specified in the announcements.

More on the Hungarian government: PM Péter Magyar reveals major tax cuts, family allowance and pension rises for 2027 budget plans

HUF 100 billion for roads in 2027

A HUF 100 billion (EUR 255.6 million) road development and pothole repair programme is planned for 2027. Péter Magyar said the government would spend more than HUF 400 billion (more than EUR 1.1 billion) on road repairs and development next year, while continuing inherited projects, including the Mohács bridge, the expansion of the M1 motorway and construction of the M49 motorway.

The government also intends to review road concession fees, reducing the budgetary burden from HUF 566 billion to HUF 320 billion (from EUR 1.56 billion to EUR 881 million). Péter Magyar said this would save HUF 246 billion, adding that taxpayers should receive better roads and better value for money.

The announcements set out an ambitious agenda for housing affordability, consumer prices and infrastructure. The impact will depend on the final programme rules, implementation timelines and how the planned spending is delivered.

World.title: How Serbia’s Ruling Party Turned State Institutions into ‘Vote Machines’
World.content:
Employees at the cadastre service of a small municipality in provincial Serbia were taken aback. Last month, they were asked to put their names on a list pledging their votes to the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS.

“This has never happened before; everyone is in disbelief, even older colleagues who have been working here since the era of [Slobodan] Milosevic,” said an employee who spoke to BIRN on the condition of anonymity.

Despite their disbelief, everyone in the office added their names to the list.

“We all signed reluctantly, because the next step is that they transfer us as punishment to other towns that are hard to get to,” the employee said.

Employees at the Republic Geodetic Authority, RGZ – the state body responsible for land registries and which has a staff of over 2,000 – are among the most recent to become acquainted with SNS’s long-standing practice of demanding that employees of state institutions and public companies (and sometimes private ones), vote for the party and attend its campaign rallies.

This practice finally reached the RGZ employees ahead of the parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25, but it is a mass, systemic abuse that has been going on for years, observers say.

Since 2014, the OSCE’s election-monitoring arm, the ODIHR, has regularly reported on the pressure faced by voters who work in the public sector. European Commission reports have been noting the same issue since 2017.

A 2022 public opinion survey conducted by the Belgrade-based NGO CRTA, based on a representative sample of 1,075 respondents, found that 14 per cent of Serbia’s population had been pressured to vote for a particular party.

BIRN spoke with eight RGZ employees from across Serbia who reported that they are being pressured to vote for the SNS and to attend party rallies.

They said the pressure started after the new acting director Dalibor Babic was appointed in August this year.

“Ever since the new acting director arrived, they’ve been pushing us for the first time to sign the list. Since the response was very poor, they brought in a party ‘commissar’ to harass people and force them to sign,” said an RGZ employee.

The same person told BIRN that people were forced to attend an SNS campaign rally in Belgrade.

“Ahead of the rally at the [Belgrade] Arena there was a hunt to get us to sign up to go. Turnout was catastrophic even then – not even those who had signed [showed up],” the employee said, referring to an SNS rally held on October 3.

An RGZ employee in another municipality told BIRN that they were asked to go to the SNS rally in Novi Sad, which was supposed to be held in mid-September 2026.

“The week when they announced the rally in Novi Sad, we were told that the new RGZ director had asked people to go there in support of him. In other words, we should go to the SNS rally, but it was really supposed to be our support for the new director,” the employee said. “I just told them I’m not interested in any of it and that they shouldn’t ask me.”

This employee said that they have not suffered any consequences yet.

“So far, nothing. I’ve actually been wondering how many times I’ll be able to tell them no,” the employee said.

The RGZ did not respond to BIRN’s questions.

Under pressure

World.title: US Concessions to Dodik Strengthen Moscow’s Hand in Bosnia
World.content:
Back in October 2025, Milorad Dodik, leader of Republika Srpska’s ruling SNSD party and former president of the Serb-led entity, met Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Minsk, Belarus, and spoke of the “high level of strategic cooperation” between Republika Srpska and Moscow.

The next day, the US Treasury Department removed him from its sanctions list, together with 47 others. The Treasury gave no reasons; the State Department later pointed to “constructive actions taken by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska in recent weeks”. Eleven months on, there is enough on the record to judge the result.

American officials have dealt with Dodik before. In January 1998, Dodik became prime minister of Republika Srpska, presented as the moderate alternative to the hardliners who had run the entity through the 1992-5 war in Bosnia, and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright pledged $5 million in budgetary support. When she visited Brcko in March 2000, Serb protesters chanted “Dodik, traitor” at her motorcade.

That history matters for two reasons. First, Dodik is a pragmatist who has spent three decades adjusting to whoever holds power in Washington, Brussels or Moscow, which is why conditions can move him and an unconditional opening will not. The man Washington once backed against the hardliners became the hardliner it sanctioned.

World.title: Kosovo Risks Losing More EU Funds After Deadlock Delayed Reforms
World.content:
But two years on political instability in Kosovo has delayed ratification of the agreements needed to begin implementation. As a result, Pristina has received only 61.8 million euros in pre-financing. This was just 7 per cent of its total allocation.

Earlier this month, Kosovo’s squabbling parties reached a deal that many hope will put the legislature back on track after three elections in two years and a debilitating row over who should be appointed president.

But much work remains to be done, and much time has been lost in political wrangling, election campaigns and post-poll negotiations.

Kosovo’s Head of Negotiations with the EU, Jeton Zulfaj, states that all the required reforms must be implemented by the end of December, or Kosovo will forfeit more than 90 million euros.

“A total of 131.4 million euros in funding from the European Union’s Growth Plan must be allocated to this package of reforms,” Zulfaj told BIRN.

After three failed attempts, parliament narrowly passed the anti-money laundering law on Friday, one of the key laws in the reform package that would enable Kosovo to join the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). Kosovo’s non-membership of SEPA had been costing its citizens some 55 million euros per year.

However, 16 other laws still need to be adopted by December.

“Securing the votes, especially for some of these laws, remains a challenge,” Zulfaj admitted.

Kujtim Dobruna, director of ECIKS, an NGO focused on sustainable economic development, investment promotion and public-private sector growth in Kosovo, said that losing EU funds simply due to failure to meet the criteria was irresponsible.

“For a small economy like Kosovo, more than 100 million euros is a significant amount, especially when we still face basic infrastructure problems that should have been resolved long ago,” he told BIRN. “Kosovo cannot afford this.”

Following a June deadline, Kosovo submitted its first formal disbursement request in July. In its request, Kosovo claimed progress in anti-corruption, women’s and youth employment, judicial accountability and early childhood education enrolment. But it did not explain the exact extent to which these criteria had been fulfilled.

Kosovo has requested 142.6 million euros, including 66.3 million euros for direct disbursement to the Kosovo Treasury and 76.3 million euros through the Western Balkans Investment Framework, WBIF. Of the total requested, 35.3 million euros was in loans and 40.9 million in non-repayable support.

The European Commission confirmed that the request is under assessment, with the amounts expected to be clarified by the end of October.

“Kosovo risks losing additional funds if it fails to meet a reform milestone by the end of the grace period. For 23 of the 64 milestones, originally due in 2025, that period expired at the end of June 2026,” the European Commission told BIRN.

The Commission is assessing whether Kosovo has met each requirement. “Each milestone effectively has its own price tag, and payments are released based on the level of implementation,” it noted.

In practice, the Commission enjoys broad discretion over how the funds are used and could redirect them to other priorities.

According to the Commission, implementation of the Growth Plan in the region has been highly uneven. While some countries have advanced reforms and secured EU funding, others, including Kosovo and Serbia, are making slower progress.

The €140 million already withdrawn from Kosovo and Bosnia and Herzegovina has remained in the region after being transferred to the European Innovation Council Compartment for the Western Balkans.

The next reporting deadline comes in January 2027, when the grace periods for steps originally due in 2025 expire.

According to the Commission, slow progress in implementing reforms puts Kosovo, Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina at risk of losing hundreds of millions of euros in total. All three countries have seen significant delays in adopting their reform agendas and accessing initial funding, risking permanent cuts to their allocations.

Time running short for complex reforms

World.title: Serbians Linked to Protest Movement Allegedly Hit by Spyware Attacks
World.content:
There is high likelihood that the rector of the University of Belgrade, Vladan Djokic, and a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime, Rade Bajic, were targeted by spyware earlier this year, digital rights investigators from the NGO SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab said on Monday.

Both Djokic and Bajic have been supporters of the student-led movement that has been organising anti-government protests for almost two years. Bajic also investigated official corruption in a failed project in Belgrade linked to the Affinity Partners investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab said that they concluded that Djokic was hacked with Pegasus spyware, created by Israeli NSO Group.

“The infection leveraged a zero-click exploit. No action, such as a click or opening a file was necessary for infection. Our investigation into this case is ongoing,” The Citizen Lab said regarding Djokic’s case.

The Citizen Lab is a research unit affiliated with the University of Toronto that investigates “novel threats to democracy, human rights, and global security in the digital ecosystem.”

In August 2026, Bajic received an Apple Threat Notification. “These notifications are high-confidence indicators of targeting with mercenary spyware such as Pegasus,” The Citizen Lab said

SHARE Foundation said that “surveillance of judicial staff and university officials directly threatens the independence of institutions and their ability to work free from pressure”.

“In the justice system, it can undermine the independence of courts and prosecutors and discourage action in the public interest. At universities, it erodes academic autonomy and freedom of expression,” the organisation said. “When the institutions meant to protect the public interest become targets of surveillance, it is not just individuals who pay the price, but society as a whole.”

It added that these trends are especially concerning ahead of the October 25 parliamentary elections, “when protecting freedom of expression, political activity, and privacy is critical”.

Djokic has been a prominent supporter of the student-led movement and has often been targeted for criticism by pro-government tabloids and officials for months. In March this year, officers from the Anti-Corruption Department of the Criminal Police Directorate also raided the Rectorate at Belgrade University as part of a probe into a student’s unexplained death, a move some said was intended to put pressure on Djokic.

As well as probing official corruption allegations related to the Kushner project in Belgrade, Bajic spoke publicly about political interference in the controversial scheme on the site of the old Yugoslav Army headquarters.

In connection with the project, Serbian Minister of Culture Nikola Selakovic was charged with illegally removing the cultural heritage status of the headquarters in order to pave the way for its demolition and redevelopment. His trial is ongoing.

Last month, citing findings from SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab, the Student Blockade protest movement announced that 14 people – members of the student movement, opposition politicians and activists – had been targeted with advanced spyware.

Lawyers representing one of the targeted student activists, Jelena Kontic, filed a criminal complaint on October 6 with the Prosecutor’s Office for High-Tech Crime over the installation of Pegasus spyware on her phone, allegedly by Serbian security forces.

The latest allegations come six days before the parliamentary elections in Serbia, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party facing a strong challenge from the opposition Student List, which grew out of the protest movement.

World.title: Albania’s Capital Rocked by Chaotic Weekend of Street Unrest
World.content:
Anti-government protest in Tirana on October 18, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Xhemali Moku.

The streets were filled with tear gas fumes, flames from Molotov cocktails and blasts from water cannons as thousands of protesters clashed with police yet again in central Tirana over the weekend.

In the sixth consecutive day of unrest at student-led protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government on Sunday, demonstrators focused their anger on government premises and targeted governing party and opposition headquarters.

Protesters chanted “Rama resign!”, “Revolution” and “Rama in prison, Berisha in prison” – a reference to opposition Democratic Party leader Sali Berisha.

A police station in Tirana was set on fire by a group of people in masks, police said. State Police director Skender Hita said that ten police officers sustained injuries as a result.

“Attacking police officers with Molotov cocktails and other dangerous items constitutes serious violence, which is punishable by law and cannot be justified under any circumstances,” Hita said.

Rama said on Monday said that his government was “ready to talk with anyone but we don’t negotiate with those who commit violence”.

“A red line has been crossed with the attack on the police station. Two hundred and ninety-five people have been injured and this is a very large number,” he said in a televised meeting with police chiefs. Claims have been made that police officers have used excessive force but Rama gave them his unequivocal backing.

The protesters have no public spokesperson and have issued no collective statements since the violence first erupted last week. Their central demand is the resignation of Rama’s government.

Tear gas, water cannons, petrol bombs and stones

Before the protest began on Sunday, Rama delivered a lengthy public address in which he rejected calls for his resignation and accused the opposition, extremist groups and foreign powers Russia and Iran of inciting unrest to destabilise Albania, although he did not provide evidence to support these claims.

He also stated that, two days earlier, authorities had neutralised a drone equipped with explosives, which he alleged was intended to strike the prime minister’s office.

He framed the escalation of the protests as a threat to Albania’s European integration process, insisting that it is not his own grip on power that is being challenged, but rather his goal of joining the European Union by 2030.

He vowed that the state will not back down in the face of violence. “Whoever wants to talk, I am here. Whoever wants to send messages using stones and masks will find the state standing against them,” he declared.

Despite his warnings, demonstrators gathered around 12.30 p.m. in front of the Ministry of Education, where the rally began peacefully, with protesters chanting “Your end is edging closer!” and “Rama, resign!” Soon afterwards, some young protesters started pulling up paving stones and throwing them at the ministry building.

During the unrest, a journalist was hit by a stone and taken away in an ambulance for medical treatment.

Police intervened with tear gas and water cannon to try to disperse the crowd as protesters marched towards the city centre and the headquarters of Rama’s governing Socialist Party. Some attacked the main door of the Socialist headquarters with stones and other objects, breaking its windows.

Several masked people emerged from the building, holding wooden sticks similar to shovel handles, and confronted the protesters. The identity of these individuals and their connection to the Socialist Party remains unknown so far.

Tensions also ran high on Sunday evening as clashes erupted in front of the opposition Democratic Party building when police pushed past security barriers in an attempt to arrest some protesters.

Firing tear gas and water cannons, the police managed to temporarily disperse the protesters, but they soon reassembled and marched on the prime minister’s office.

Eno Bozdo, a Democratic Party MP, described the scenes outside the party building as “unjustified violence”. “It is unprecedented for an opposition party to be attacked with tear gas and violent force [by police],” Bozdo said.

On Sunday evening, a group of 141 Albanian university professors issued a joint statement condemning police violence against students during the protests and demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Rama, calling on the public to join the anti-government protests.

“We call on Prime Minister Rama to listen to the demands of the students and pave the way for peace in the country. We demand his resignation and the creation of a caretaker government,” the statement said.

World.title: Ukraine’s EU Accession Push Is Gaining Momentum, Says Ambassador to Moldova
World.content:
Dniester River water crisis exposes new tensions with Moldova

As well as encouraging cooperation, the war has also complicated Ukraine’s relationship with Moldova, especially over the Dniester River, a key source of drinking water for both countries.

Severe drought has dramatically reduced river flows, pressuring Ukraine’s Novodnistrovsk reservoir and raising concerns about supplies to downstream Moldovan communities, including Chisinau.

According to Ukrainian government figures, water inflows into the reservoir fell to just 24 cubic metres per second on September 17 and 20, about 11 per cent of normal levels and the lowest daily averages recorded since the reservoir began operating.

Moldova’s government reported in late September that the reservoir had fallen below 111 metres, compared with a normal level of about 121 metres.

Arguments over plans to reduce water releases have led to accusations that Ukraine is holding back water. Rohovei strongly rejected those allegations.

“There has been a great deal of speculation recently, including claims that Ukraine is deliberately stopping the water,” he told BIRN. “We could end up blaming Ukraine for the lack of water in the Dniester. By that logic, if there were a solar eclipse, Ukraine would also be blamed.”

The ambassador attributed the crisis primarily to prolonged drought and insufficient rainfall in the Carpathian mountains, where the Dniester originates. “I consider this a natural disaster. The lack of rain and the drought have led to this situation,” he said.

Rohovei warned that releasing excessive volumes from Ukraine’s reservoirs could create additional risks for the functioning of hydropower infrastructure and future water supplies.

“If we take the wrong steps, we could cause an even greater catastrophe,” he said. “Suppose, theoretically, we release the water from the reservoirs, we would have water for two or three weeks. But what would we do afterward?”

Reservoir operators must balance the needs of people downstream, environmental requirements, electricity production and safe water levels. Releasing water faster than it is replaced can help downstream for a short time but worsen shortages in the long run. Ukraine itself was suffering from severe water shortages.

“In Ukraine, we have been forced to ration it,” he said, referring to communities supplied according to restricted schedules. “Ukraine has never deliberately cut off water supplies to the population and will never do so.”

But this crisis shows there is an urgent need for better cross-border water management, clear information about water levels and alternative water sources. “Relying on just one river is very dangerous,” Rohovei warned.

World.title: Hydropower Scheme Threatens to Irrevocably Alter Iconic Neretva in Bosnia, Croatia
World.content:
During a lifetime spent on the Neretva, Miroslav Dugandzic has watched its waters change.

“Fishing has been in my family for four generations,” he said, sitting in his living room in Komin, a village in Croatia near where the Neretva empties into the Adriatic after wending its way through southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Now in his eighties, Dugandzic learned his trade from his father and taught it to his son, Ante, who now runs the family business alongside him.

He fears, however, that his grandson will never get the chance: the tools and techniques Dugandzic inherited were made for a river that no longer exists.

“Some species are gone, they are extinct from this area, because the fish habitat changed a lot,” he said.

World.title: Changes to Dentistry Under Croatian Health Insurance Fund
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – There are changes to certain aspects of dentistry within the scope of the Croatian Health Insurance Fund, with white fillings being part of the shakeup.

Instead of the previous amalgam fillings, the installation of white fillings at the expense of the Croatian Health Insurance Fund (HZZO) has been announced, even when they aren’t going to be placed on the front teeth. Poslovni reports that amalgam fillings entered history on the 1st of July, unless a dentist assesses that such a filling is necessary due to the patient’s particular health needs. This measure was introduced in Croatia on the basis of an EU regulation.

dentists are still charging…

In practice, however, the matter is somewhat different: the use of a white filling still comes with a cost if the patient wants a white composite filling of the kind that, according to HZZO rules, they should receive free of charge on their front teeth. The dentist will most often not offer a choice, but will allegedly place a composite filling and then charge the patient for it. Anyone who wants a free white filling must request it, but must also inform themselves beforehand, because each of the materials used has its own characteristics. We received information that the free white filling visually completely differs from the tooth base and looks “like cement”.

These are glass-ionomer and hybrid glass-ionomer cements, which have good characteristics for replacing the former amalgam fillings, but cannot match composite white fillings. Research in European countries where these materials have been used for about 20 years shows that the disadvantages of glass-ionomers are more frequent chipping, limited resistance to abrasion and erosion, and strength below the values for composite. Persons who had such fillings installed had a higher rate of fractures and abrasions of the fillings than with composites, as well as colour deviations.

economic status and purchasing power in dental medicine

“The key problem is the fact that white fillings do not cover all the indications in which amalgam can be used,” emphasises Irma Šavorić, president of the Association of Contracted Doctors of Dental Medicine MODDUS HR. This means that the choice of material should not be only a matter of aesthetics but also of the concrete clinical situation.

“Indications are key, and problems usually arise when something is not in a specific indication,” Šavorić states. Patients, she says, as a rule do not come with a request for a particular type of filling, but make the decision in conversation with the dentist. In this, the patient’s economic status, i.e. purchasing power, can play a role, especially when there is a choice between a filling covered by insurance and one that requires additional payment. The fact that a certain material is more expensive does not automatically mean that it is more suitable for every situation, this doctor of dental medicine explains.

“Materials have different characteristics and limitations, so the choice should primarily depend on the indication,” she concludes. The price of 30 to 80 euros per tooth will be important for a considerable part of citizens when deciding between the two types of white filling.

the right to free composite fillings until you’re 18

The right to a free composite filling for all teeth, regardless of which tooth is involved, is now held in Croatia by children up to 18 years of age, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers. For all other citizens who do not want to pay extra for such fillings, the health insurance fund will, according to the announcement of the Ministry of Health, secure from 10 to 12 million euros annually.

The MODDUS HR Association was founded in order to clearly define issues related to materials, indications, financing and the position of dentists who work in different models of dental healthcare. From the HZZO they are requesting a correction of the financing model, warning that the existing model could lead to longer waiting times for patients and reduced availability of certain services.

World.title: HŽ to Invest €7.4 Million – Here Are the Croatian Cities Covered
World.content:
October the 20th, 2026 – HŽ is set to invest a fortune in the country’s future railway plans, with multiple Croatian cities covered by the plans.

HŽ Passenger Transport has issued a tender estimated to stand at a whopping €7.4 million excluding VAT for the arrangement and modernisation of six workshops for the maintenance of trains across the country. Poslovni reports that more specifically speaking, these will be located in Vinkovci, Solin, Osijek, Pula and Varaždin. The tender was published on Monday in the Electronic Public Procurement Notice, and offers can be submitted until the 26th of November.

According to the tender documentation, the most money is planned for Solin, where two workshops will be arranged for €2.73 million. For Osijek the estimate is €1.59 million, Varaždin €1.48 million, Vinkovci €998,000, and for Pula €606,000. At all those locations construction, electrical and mechanical works are planned, as well as the procurement and installation of equipment for the maintenance of trains.

For example, for one of the Solin workshops the project states that it is in poor condition and that it needs to be adapted for the maintenance of existing and new trains. Therefore inspection channels for examining trains from below and a platform for inspecting equipment on the roof will be made in it, and the roof, floor and lighting will also be renewed.

The works will be carried out gradually, beginning in January 2027 and continuing until January 2028, and at each workshop they should last 119 days. First in line are Vinkovci, which will take place from the 12th of January to the 10th of May 2027, and the final one is Varaždin, where the works should finish on the 3rd of January 2028, should all go as planned.

The deadlines have (at least according to the documentation) been set so that too many workshops don’t end up being closed at the same time and so that trains can be regularly maintained even during the works. Completed parts of the halls can be returned to use after they pass expert supervision. The most advantageous offer will be selected according to price and quality, and one of the criteria is also the length of the warranty period, which must not be shorter than two years. Bidders can compete for one, several or all locations.
