World.title: China sends naval forces to monitor US warship near disputed shoal
World.content:
US-CHINA RIVALRY. US and Chinese flags are seen in this illustration created on April 10, 2025

The Chinese military's Southern Theater Command asserts that the US warship 'illegally intruded' into waters adjacent to a shoal in the Spratly Islands

BEIJING, China – China’s military said on Tuesday, October 20, it had sent forces to watch a US warship that “illegally” entered waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea.

China views almost all of the busy waterway as its own territory, despite overlapping claims by Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam, with recent tension most pronounced between Beijing and Manila.

The Chinese military’s Southern Theater Command said the Charleston “illegally intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal (Escoda) in the Spratly Islands without Chinese government approval in the early hours of Tuesday.

“The US action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability,” it said.

“The US side should immediately cease such activities.”

China’s navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the ship, it added.

The US Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It generally refers to such missions as “freedom of navigation operations,” though its last known one in the South China Sea was more than a year ago.

Last month, a China Coast Guard vessel rammed a Philippine boat on a refueling mission near the same shoal.

China and the Philippines, which has a mutual defense treaty with the US, both contest sovereignty over Sabina Shoal and the entire Spratly Islands archipelago. – Rappler.com

World.title: Indoor bouldering 101: Sending your first climb
World.content:
Being a first-time climber can be intimidating, whether you’re afraid of heights, unsure if you’re fit enough, or even feel pressured by the gym. But don’t worry, it is easier than it looks, even for beginners.

Indoor bouldering is a sport where you climb short walls following a set of the same colored holds. More than a physical sport, it also involves strategic thinking, as you have to consider where you will place your hands and feet as you get to the top. Hence, climbers use the term “projects” to refer to what climb they are trying to do, as each route is a small physical and mental problem that you get to solve.

It might seem difficult, but don’t worry, as you don’t need to know the perfect way up before you start. Trying a move, adjusting, and trying again is part of the climb. To send your first climb, here are some tips that helped me enjoy and keep climbing.

Gearing up and preparing

Before climbing, it is a must to gear up and prepare; this not only applies to your shoes and chalk, but also to preparing your mind and body.

To get started, wear clothes that you can move comfortably in, and give yourself a few minutes to warm up from head to toe before climbing. This will help you avoid muscle strains and prepare your body for physical activity.

Climbing shoes and chalk are also a must. If you don’t have any of these, every climbing gym will have them in stock. Compared to regular shoes, climbing shoes have a firm sole and allow a tighter fit, helping you to step on small holds better, giving your feet the proper traction. Meanwhile, chalk gives you the proper grip and avoids abrasions or wounds on your hands. For your first climb, focus less on having the perfect gear and more on getting comfortable trying a climb.

Climbing shoes

Ready to get climbing shoes? Looking at the curvature of the soles and their comfort level are the two most important factors to consider so you can get the best pair for your experience level. Here are some climber-recommended options to help you get started.

Budget: ClimbX Rave

If you’re looking for an all-day shoe while still giving you a good fit and performance, ClimbX Rave is a strong pick.

At an affordable price, ClimbX Rave is more of a comfort-oriented shoe with a slight downturn on the soles. So, if you are starting out with climbing, this is a good option for you to find the proper footing and confidence on the wall.

Get ClimbX Rave here. (Also available at Bhive Circuit Makati)

Performance: Scarpa Vapor V and La Sportiva Solutions

For more performance-based shoes, Scarpa Vapor V along with La Sportiva Solutions are two options worth considering.

One main difference between the two is their downturn curve. Solutions gives an aggressive downturn shape and a stiff sole, making it ideal for steep routes. Their shape gives precision and power on small footholds, as it is designed for demanding projects.

Meanwhile, Vapor V is a moderately downturned shoe, prioritizing support and comfort while still giving you good grip and precision.

Get Scarpa Vapor V here.

Get La Sportiva Solutions here.

Splurge: Scarpa Dragon LV

If you just want the top of the line, this shoe is a one-stop shop. Despite its aggressive curve, climbers often find it comfortable due to its soft build aimed at sensitivity. This allows you to feel and hold on to smears, small, and complex holds.

If you’re ready to invest in your climbing journey, this could be a splurge worth considering.

Get Scarpa Dragon LV here.

Mental preparation

It is normal to feel nervous about falling, not being strong enough, or simply climbing in front of other people. I felt those same worries, too when I started. But bouldering gave me the chance to face them one climb at a time. And after realizing that it wasn’t as difficult as I made it to be, bouldering became much more enjoyable.

As an example of facing my fear of heights, a pre-briefing for beginners on proper falling technique taught me how to confidently fall from heights that seemed too high. Furthermore, there are also easy-to-grab holds across all walls that are mainly for assisting me as I climb down; hence, even when jumping off feels scary, climbing down gives me the peace of mind that I can reach a safe height. You do not have to conquer your fear before you start climbing, but starting small can help you build that confidence.

Climbing levels and proper technique

You do not need to be super strong before trying bouldering. Climbing gyms use “tags” to show how difficult each bouldering project is, helping climbers choose a level that suits them best, from V0-V1 being the easiest and beginner-friendly, to V8 being the hardest (some gyms go beyond V8). These are usually color-coded in climbing gyms, so make sure to check, as they vary per gym.

When I started climbing, I depended on my strength to pull me up. This was one “not to do” lesson I learned that led to early fatigue. To guide you on the right path, here are a few basic techniques that can help you rely less on strength and more on technique:

Push with your legs instead of relying only on your arms.

Keep your arms straight when you can so you are not holding yourself up with bent arms the whole time.

Turn your hips toward the wall to help shift your weight from one hold to another.

Use the tip of your climbing shoes to place your feet more precisely, allowing you to pivot.

Pay attention to which direction the holds point and grab it in that direction.

Remember: Climbing is not about rushing to a higher grade. It is about finding new ways to move and enjoying the climbs along the way.

All the technicalities aside, what matters most is whether you enjoy climbing. For me, more than a sport, bouldering taught me how to appreciate doing hard things, facing my fears, having courage, and constantly trying even after experiencing setbacks.

Bouldering might not be the sport for everyone, but it is definitely a sport everyone can do. So if you feel a connection with bouldering, try to send your first project! – Rappler.com

This piece was written by Rappler intern Sebastian Vincent U. Ngo. Basti is a multimedia creative storyteller who focuses on the everyday details that make ordinary moments feel special. He seeks stories and uses design, words, and motion to help people see the familiar in a new light.

World.title: Adamson’s strong start surprises Nash Racela, adds to La Salle’s woes
World.content:
LEADER. Mathew Montebon in action during Adamson's first-round duel against La Salle in the UAAP.

‘I apologize to my players because they really surprised me, the whole team,’ says Adamson coach Nash Racela as his Falcons cap the UAAP first round strong with an upset of defending champion La Salle

MANILA, Philippines – Adamson has exceeded expectations, and even head coach Nash Racela is surprised by the heights the Soaring Falcons have reached.

The Falcons secured the third-best record at 4-3 by the end of the first round of the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament, capping it with a 70-68 stunner over defending champion La Salle Green Archers.

As the Falcons soared, La Salle slipped to 3-4, joining Ateneo in a tie for sixth place.

Few expected Adamson to find itself among the league’s top teams after seven games, with Racela admitting that while he believed in his team’s potential, he did not anticipate such a strong start.

“We should be happy with where we are at right now,” Racela said. “To be honest, as a coach, I knew what we could do as a group. I could see our potential.”

“I apologize to my players because they really surprised me, the whole team. I wasn’t expecting to be at this point after the first round,” he added.

Adamson’s only losses in the opening round came against league-leading NU, Ateneo, and the UP Fighting Maroons.

Against UP, the Falcons controlled much of the game before the Maroons caught fire from beyond the arc in the final six minutes to steal the win.

Adamson nearly suffered the same fate against La Salle, but this time, it held its ground down the stretch. Matty Erolon delivered the decisive blow with a clutch three-pointer to help seal the two-point victory.

The result further complicated the title defense of the Green Archers, who are still leaning on last season’s championship core led by Jacob Cortez, but this time, minus Mike Phillips.

In keeping with its identity, Adamson has built its early success on the defensive end. The Falcons have allowed a league-best 65.86 points per game, making them the toughest defensive team to score against through the first seven games.

Graduating guard Mathew Montebon has also emerged as one of the UAAP’s most productive floor generals after averaging 12.14 points, 2.71 rebounds, 3.71 assists, and 2.14 steals per game in the first round, while shooting 36% from three-point range on more than six attempts per game.

Erolon has provided another scoring option, averaging 10.57 points per contest, while foreign student-athlete Precious Jonah has made his presence felt on both ends of the floor with 10.43 points, 7.71 rebounds, 1.00 steal, and 2.57 blocks per game.

Ray Allen Torres, Mat Edding and Earl Medina have also delivered valuable offensive contributions while helping maintain the team’s defensive intensity.

For Racela, the progress goes beyond the numbers as he has seen his players grow more comfortable in his system and develop greater trust in one another.

“At this point, my players should know that I trust them so well. And I see slowly that they’re building trust in me,” Racela said.

Despite Adamson’s strong finish to the first round, Racela is not letting the team get carried away.

With seven games still to come in the second round, he knows the Falcons have yet to accomplish anything significant.

“Seven games are done, but it does not really mean anything,” Racela said. “Experiential learning. We have to go through fire to learn.”

La Salle will open the second round against the winless UE Red Warriors on Wednesday, October 21, while Adamson takes on the FEU Tamaraws next on Saturday, October 24. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

World.title: Senate panel approves proposed 2027 OVP budget in under 20 minutes
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.

Vice President Sara Duterte skipped the budget hearing to represent her father at the inurnment of a Davao City official, OVP chief of staff Zuleika Lopez tells the Senate finance sub-committee A

MANILA, Philippines – The proposed P785.2-million of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for 2027 hurled the deliberations of a Senate Finance sub-panel on Tuesday, October 20, in under 20 minutes.

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito arrived in the upper chamber at around 10:16 am to open the deliberations of Senate finance sub-committee A on the OVP’s proposed budget.

Ejercito proposed the budget’s approval for plenary consideration at around 10:31 am, extending inter-parliamentary courtesy to the OVP.

“This representation acknowledges the tradition of inter-parliamentary courtesy in respect to the OVP while also assuring to the public that the fiscal year 2027 proposed expenditure program is taken up wth due diligence,” the lawmaker said.

OVP chief of staff Zuleika Lopez represented the agency at the hearing.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked Lopez about the absence of Vice President Sara Duterte at the budget hearing. He noted that last year, Duterte took time out of her busy schedule to lead her agency in defending their budget.

Play Video

Lopez answered, “The Vice President is actually representing former president Rodrigo Duterte in the inurnment of our long serving city planner in Davao City. The schedule for the inurnment is today, October 20. So she’s the representative of the former president.”

Gatchalian, who was Senate finance committee chair during the budget deliberations in the previous year, expressed hope that Duterte would defend the OVP budget at the plenary.

The OVP is proposing a P785.2-million budget for next year — 11% lower than its P889 million budget for 2026. Among their projects are socioeconomic programs targeted to extend aid.

The Senate is on a break in the impeachment trial of Duterte to focus on the proposed 2027 budget. – Rappler.com

World.title: Super Typhoon Champi enters PAR, named Rosal
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 19, 2026, 10:40 am.

Signal No. 1 is raised in parts of Luzon at 11 am on Tuesday, October 20, shortly after the entry of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) into the Philippine Area of Responsibility

MANILA, Philippines – Super Typhoon Champi entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 10:40 am on Tuesday, October 20, becoming the country’s 18th tropical cyclone for 2026.

Champi, also the first tropical cyclone for October, was given the local name Rosal.

In a press conference past 11 am on Tuesday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Rosal was located 1,385 kilometers east of Central Luzon as of 10 am, moving west northwest at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

At the time of its entry, the super typhoon had maximum sustained winds of 185 km/h and gustiness of up to 230 km/h. On Monday evening, October 19, its maximum sustained winds had reached 195 km/h.

Rosal’s latest forecast track shows it is unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines. But due to its size and intensity, the super typhoon will still affect parts of the country.

Even before Rosal entered PAR, PAGASA already said on Monday that the trough or extension of the super typhoon may bring scattered rain and thunderstorms to Catanduanes, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar. Flash floods and landslides can occur.

The weather bureau added on Tuesday morning that it may issue a rainfall advisory in the afternoon, listing the areas expected to see heavy rain from Rosal.

For strong winds, PAGASA already raised Signal No. 1 at 11 am on Tuesday, giving the affected areas lead time of 36 hours to prepare. These areas include:

Batanes

eastern part of Babuyan Islands (Babuyan Island, Camiguin Island, Didicas Island)

eastern part of mainland Cagayan (Santa Ana, Gonzaga, Lal-lo, Santa Teresita, Camalaniugan, Aparri, Buguey, Gattaran, Baggao, Peñablanca)

northeastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, San Pablo, Cabagan, Santa Maria, Tumauini, Ilagan City)

northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

The highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal due to Rosal is Signal No. 2 or 3.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Tuesday, October 20

Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Cagayan, Isabela, Polillo Islands, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Catanduanes, Northern Samar, Eastern Samar, most of Caraga, Camiguin, Misamis Oriental, Sarangani, Davao del Sur, Davao Occidental

Wednesday, October 21

Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Polillo Islands, Bicol, Romblon, Eastern Visayas, Iloilo, Guimaras, Negros Occidental, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani, Zamboanga del Norte

Thursday, October 22

most of the country

In the next 24 hours, Rosal will also affect conditions in various seaboards across the country.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Seaboard of Isabela; eastern seaboards of Batanes, Babuyan Islands, and mainland Cagayan; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur; northern and eastern seaboards of Northern Samar and Eastern Samar – waves up to 4 meters high

Northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon; remaining seaboard of Batanes – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboards of Aurora and northern Quezon; eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group; remaining seaboards of Cagayan and Camarines Norte – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboard of Surigao del Sur; eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining seaboard of Catanduanes – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Surigao del Norte, and Davao Occidental; northern and eastern seaboards of Quezon; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining northern and eastern seaboards of Camarines Sur; remaining seaboards of Polillo Islands, Dinagat Islands, and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group – waves up to 2 meters high

PAGASA said Rosal will move generally west northwest until Wednesday, October 21, before heading generally northwest until Friday morning, October 23. Afterwards, it may turn north northwest to north starting Friday afternoon, until it leaves PAR by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24.

The weather bureau also sees possible intensification in the next 24 hours as Rosal moves over the Philippine Sea, but it could weaken into a typhoon on Thursday, October 22, and into a severe tropical storm on Saturday evening or by Sunday morning, October 25.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Aside from the trough of the super typhoon, other sources of rain on Tuesday include the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) and the easterlies.

The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet, while the easterlies are warm winds from the Pacific Ocean.

Scattered rain and thunderstorms continue to hit Palawan due to the ITCZ, while isolated rain showers or thunderstorms may hit Batanes and Babuyan Islands because of the easterlies.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.

The operation was carried out by two Russian-made Mi-35 attack helicopters, two fighter jets from Magwe and Nyaung Oo, and two drones from the Pakokku-based No. 101 Light Infantry Division, the NUG said.

However, local media reported that at least 15 civilians were killed in the incident.

On the same day, the regime bombed Magyikan Village in Sagaing’s Myaung, injuring one.

The regime’s airstrikes continued on Sunday, as Y-12 utility aircraft bombed Arakan Army (AA)-controlled ethnic Rakhine villages in Rathedaung. Wai Hun Aung, a prominent ethnic Rakhine writer and aid worker, said five people were killed.

The regime also bombed a jetty in AA-controlled Paletwa, Chin State, on the same day, resulting in 20 casualties according to media reports, though there has been no official statement yet.

A regime drone attacked Shwebayet Village in Mandalay’s Singu Township on October 18, killing three people and injuring four women and girls, including a 5-year-old, the Singu People’s Defense Force reported on Monday.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed Ohntaw Village in Magwe’s Pakokku Township on Sunday, killing five including children and senior citizens. Local media reported that four were injured, including a 2-year-old.

At the NCA anniversary event, regime leader Min Aung Hlaing invited 2015 signatories that have been fighting the Myanmar military since the 2021 coup—the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front—to join his peace process. The regime demands that the PDFs surrender.

Lt-Gen Yar Pyae insisted the aerial bombing was conducted for peaceful purposes. “Some parts are military actions, while others are steps to achieve peace,” Yar Pyae said.

World.title: Detained Aung San Suu Kyi Receives UK Royal Package: Regime
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner.”

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Aung San Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Aung San Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home Ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee,” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.

Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.

Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

In response to questions from AFP, the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

Britain condemns what it describes as Aung San Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Sittwe Counteroffensive Hits the Rocks on Nga Pyi Island
World.content:
The Myanmar military’s push to land troops on Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Pauktaw Township has suffered fresh setbacks as the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) strikes regime vessels and tightens its siege on the state capital Sittwe.

Frontline sources said AA artillery hit another navy vessel off the island on Sunday, the third to be damaged in recent days. “The boat was struck and caught fire,” a local source close to the AA confirmed. Intense clashes are raging both on and around Nga Pyi Island as regime forces continue efforts to secure a beachhead despite mounting casualties.

Sources said commanders are driving conscripts forward in near‑suicidal assaults, but few have managed to reach land.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed more than a dozen gunboats and landing craft backed by airstrikes and artillery from encircled Sittwe, in an effort to seize the island. The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor and shield the navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Nga Pyi Island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

“Junta soldiers keep coming despite heavy casualties, but few have made it to shore,” said a source close to the AA.

Meanwhile, AA columns have seized several regime outposts elsewhere in Sittwe and are pressing toward Shwe Mingan naval base and the Sittwe Regional Operations Command.

The assault on Nga Pyi was launched as advancing AA troops threatened to encircle the military’s Sittwe stronghold. Fighting has also intensified just down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

A regime counteroffensive launched from neighboring Magwe, Bago, and Ayeyarwady regions is bogged down amid fierce resistance and heavy losses.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Defense Minister Claims Airstrikes Are Aimed at Achieving Peace
World.content:
Despite widespread domestic and international condemnation of the military junta’s airstrikes on civilian targets, newly appointed regime Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae said the bombing operations were intended to achieve peace.

“Mainly, they [questions raised in the media] are based on human rights and humanitarian concerns regarding the bombings. From our perspective, the current military operations are actually steps taken to obtain peace,” Lt-Gen Yar Pyae, who also serves as chairman of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), said during his closing address to a workshop marking the 11th Anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) on October 16.

The military regime routinely bombs civilian targets in resistance-held territories in an effort to undermine anti-regime groups’ administration and to coerce them into joining its purported peace talks. The tactic worked well in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region, where it managed to force the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and its ally, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), to stop fighting, agree to China-brokered ceasefires and hand over some seized towns.

The regime continues to use the tactic in other regions and states including Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the Arakan Army (AA), an ally of MNDAA and TNLA.

On September 28, the regime conducted an airstrike targeting the busy Indian Market in the AA-controlled town of Kyauktaw, killing at least 50 people. The attack drew fierce condemnation from the UN, the UK, ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and various human rights organizations.

Since the 2021 military coup, the Myanmar military has consistently launched airstrikes across revolutionary strongholds, including the Anyar region (also known as the Dry Zone) and ethnic minority regions—targeting not only military sites, but also schools, hospitals, religious buildings and civilian homes.

Even as it makes peace overtures, the regime continues to engage in heavy fighting with the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) in Bhamo, and clashes are ongoing with the AA in Rakhine State. Airstrikes also continue to target civilians in the Anyar region, where People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) maintain a strong presence.

Amid the ongoing air raids on resistance-held areas, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing made what he called an unconditional peace invitation during the 11th NCA anniversary event in Naypyitaw on October 15. The regime nonetheless continues to pressure the PDFs—the main armed resistance groups across the country—to lay down their arms and surrender.

According to statements made during a press conference at the close of the NCA anniversary workshop, invitations to peace talks were extended to the KIA, but not to the AA.

Furthermore, Min Aung Hlaing stated on October 15 that if ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) wish to engage in politics, they must disarm and form political parties; if they wish to conduct business, they must do so legally; and if they wish to serve in defense, they must join the Border Guard Forces (BGF).

In 2009, the military heavily pressured EAOs to transform into Border Guard Forces. With few exceptions, however, the initiative largely failed.

The KIA, which is currently engaged in intense fighting with the military, was one of the major ethnic armed groups that refused to transform into a BGF at that time. During the Spring Revolution that erupted in response to the coup, the KIA earned the Myanmar military’s ire by providing military training, weapons and combat support to anti-junta PDF forces.

Similarly, following Operation 1027, the AA seized control of most towns in Rakhine State, including a regional military command center. Since then, the regime has launched several offensives to retake lost territory in the state.

While urging PDFs to surrender and asking EAOs to join the BGF, Min Aung Hlaing also told ethnic representatives attending the NCA ceremony that he would cooperate with those willing to work together on peace, while actively finding methods to handle those who refuse to cooperate.

World.title: Solar Mandate Crushes Myanmar Builders as Regime Chief’s Son Profits
World.content:
Contractors warn that a new regime mandate requiring installation of solar power systems in all high-rises and commercial buildings will send construction costs soaring in Myanmar. The directive further squeezes construction companies already pinched by a shortage of materials, import restrictions, and severe currency volatility.

The Yangon City Development Committee’s Engineering Department issued the order on October 1 as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

From November 1, all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar panels sufficient to power elevators and emergency lighting. For commercial buildings, solar systems must be integrated with power supplied by the Yangon Electricity Supply Corporation (YESC).

The order applies to existing projects, buildings under construction, and those awaiting Building Completion Certificates required for habitation.

“We have been handed the order at a time when prices of solar panels and related equipment are rising daily,” complained a Mandalay‑based builder. “Steel and cement prices are already soaring, so this adds yet another burden.”

Meanwhile, industry insiders warn of a scarcity of skilled technicians capable of installing large solar systems, creating technical and financial hurdles. “Household systems won’t power elevators, which require commercial‑grade solar systems,” the manager of a solar dealership explained. “Installation takes at least two months and costs around 100 million kyat.”

Solar imports to feed surging demand created by the new mandate are controlled by Aung Pyae Sone, son of regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

Aung Pyae Sone swiftly cornered the lucrative market after his father’s regime waived tax on solar imports in April 2023 under the pretext of boosting the energy grid. His Venus Essential company also holds licenses to supply solar equipment for projects in Naypyitaw and planned 40-megawatt solar power plants in Taungdwingyi, Salin, Pakokku, Pauk, Chauk and Kyunchaung.

The solar mandate comes as regime energy rationing intensifies with more frequent rolling blackouts this year.

“They cut electricity during extreme heat, then order solar systems to be installed,” said a former political prisoner from Mandalay. “But only one company — belonging to the coup leader son — is allowed to import and sell the equipment nationwide. This is not aimed at solving the power crisis, but exploiting authority for personal profit.”

On October 5, the Electricity and Energy Ministry introduced rolling four-hour blackouts under the pretext of surging demand during the El Niño heatwave. Since then, households in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw have faced daily outages.

The power crisis has driven prices of solar panels and related equipment to record highs. In early August, a 500‑watt panel cost around 650,000 kyat. By mid‑October, the price had surged past one million kyat, putting solar systems beyond the reach of ordinary families.

World.title: An ‘All-for-Arakan’ Approach Is Needed to Address the Rohingya Refugee Crisis
World.content:
As resistance against long-term Rohingya presence in host countries grows, the refugees’ fate is back in the headlines. Malaysia is a recent example. Its government has yielded to growing hate speech against Myanmar refugees, and Rohingya in particular. In September, Malaysia and Myanmar negotiated a controversial repatriation agreement for 5,000 refugees that is not supported by the UN or its refugee agency. Resentment in India and Indonesia has also grown.

Following large-scale Rohingya returns from Bangladesh to Myanmar in the 1970s and 1990s, repatriation efforts started again in 2017, after the enforced flight of 750,000 Rohingya from Myanmar to Bangladesh. Initially, they were based on a Chinese offer to mediate between the two countries. Even though these and later efforts failed, Bangladesh’s pursuit of repatriation continues, and Malaysia has now joined in.

There are many reasons why the repatriation initiatives of the past 10 years have not been successful. A largely unmentioned one is that many initiators wrongly assume that traditional diplomatic relations between states can lead to meaningful dialogue and conflict resolution. This state-centric approach overlooks the key question at the heart of Myanmar’s decades-old volatility: how power and political authority are shared between Myanmar’s center and its highly diverse regions and ethnic nationalities. Moreover, since the country’s 2021 military coup, the regime in Naypyitaw has lost control over much of the country. In Arakan (Rakhine State), the birthplace of most Rohingya refugees—and where some 500,000 of them still live—the current regime has control over only three of the state’s 17 townships.

Today’s Myanmar is in transition. It is a country with multiple centers of authority. In some, local territorial control has been in place for decades; in others, it has been established since the military coup of 2021. These ethnic and regional authorities are not against a federal state as such. They are against the current federal union that is based on a constitution that concentrates significant power at the center, and particularly with the armed forces.

Right now, the key question is whether a new form of federalism can emerge, one that leaves a highly centralized system behind and, instead, focuses on existing and newly emerging centers of political authority. A long road lies ahead but in many parts of the country progress is clearly visible.

Arakan is a prime example. As the territorial dominance of the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA) grows, particularly since 2023, it has been transforming into a central administrative authority with local administrative, security and judicial mechanisms. The Institute for Strategy and Policy in Chiang Mai recently reviewed the progress that has been made and concluded that “despite persistent challenges, a solid institutional framework is emerging”. But it also cautions that following rapid territorial expansion, a performance gap has emerged between public expectations and the administration’s delivery capacity.

A key reason for the delivery gap is that right now Arakan is a war zone with almost daily ground clashes between the AA and Myanmar’s armed forces, as well as attacks by Bangladesh-based Rohingya militias. Moreover, Arakan is now a prime target for attacks by Myanmar’s air force, which deliberately targets civilian structures with bombs of up to 500 pounds. The devastation on the ground is massive, with hundreds of civilians killed and maimed, while schools, markets, clinics and prayer houses have been destroyed. Physical infrastructure is also heavily affected, including by recent massive floods, leading to large-scale disruption of livelihoods and food security.

According to a recent report by the UN Development Programme, 68.4 percent of Arakan’s population (all ethnicities) experience multi-dimensional poverty, while a further 20 percent is at risk of falling into that category. Arakan’s current population is thought to stand at just over 2.4 million, while a Doctors Without Borders report in 2024 estimated that only 636,000 Rohingya remained in Arakan. Today that number will have fallen significantly, as approximately 150,000 more Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since then.

To be clear, Rohingya repatriation from Bangladesh and other countries will take time. Refugees cannot return if armed conflict continues and before the underlying reasons for their flight have been addressed. To achieve this, a central role for both ULA/AA and the people of Arakan, including the Rohingya, is critical. But at the same time, various factions on the Rohingya side stand in the way of a united approach, particularly those supporting armed militias. Moreover, some of them have been used as a divide-and-rule tool by Myanmar’s military-backed regime.

Arakan’s problems are manifold and a broader vision of identity is critically important, one that acknowledges inclusion and equality as basic building blocks for a stable, secure and prosperous Arakan.

This understanding led the Rakhine Advisory Commission of 2016-17, chaired by former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, to focus on solutions to address the legitimate grievances and suffering of all Arakan’s diverse people. Its report and recommendations to Myanmar’s leaders remain highly relevant, based as they are on the central objective of developing conditions in Arakan that will lead to a peaceful, fair, harmonious and prosperous future for all communities. In 2018, the commission published a lessons-learned report focusing on how it operated in Myanmar’s highly politicized and complex context.

Obviously, much has changed since the report was released but it remains relevant, even after the National League for Democracy’s violent removal in 2021. It analyzes Arakan’s situation around three major crises: a security crisis, an economic and development crisis, and a human rights crisis. These crises persist and could form the basis for an all-of-Arakan approach.

Since 2017, the Annan report has been re-acknowledged annually by an overwhelming majority of the UN General Assembly and the UN Human Rights Council. Yet, no efforts have been made to establish how it might serve Arakan’s people under their current circumstances, and particularly since 2024, when most of Arakan came under the control of the ULA/AA.

Any process leading to a comprehensive plan for Arakan will be complex, not least because of the wide range of actors, functioning at diverse levels. In “The Dilemma of Hard Choices”, published in August, the Center for Arakan studies identifies the heterogeneity of agents as a key issue and adds that it is compounded by the problem of ownership, where most states, armed groups, civil society and international bodies each deflect overall responsibility while pursuing their own narrow strategic interests.

Precisely these diverging interests would make the Annan report a helpful starting point for dialogue. For good reasons, the commission’s recommendations are not highly prescriptive. Its general understanding was that, while basic principles of governance and human rights should guide the implementation process, details could be developed as part of dialogue processes. The report contains 88 recommendations on a comprehensive set of issues, ranging from economic and social development to freedom of movement, citizenship, health, access to justice, intercommunal cohesion, humanitarian access and internally displaced persons.

Obviously, dialogue cannot be based on the Annan report alone, but it could be a starting point. Additional questions must be raised to take account of developments since 2017. The first is the clarification of victimhood. Who are the victims of decades of oppression, persecution and violent conflict? A second is the “fog of war” that distorts a clear view of what is happening on the ground.

Obviously, it is not necessary to argue that the Rohingya are victims; that is accepted around the world. But what about the other communities in Arakan—the Rakhine, the Maramagyi, the Mro, the Chin, the Hindus and others?

They too are victims, yet their plight has been getting far less attention. They too have had their villages bombed and burned, their clinics, schools and livelihoods destroyed, while thousands are displaced in areas where relief goods cannot reach them. But their plight is not as widely documented. Acknowledgment that all Arakan’s people are victims could be a first step in reconciliation. And clearly, there are different degrees of victimhood and these too must be acknowledged.

The second point concerns the current “fog of war” and the urgent need to establish independent investigations. As in other places around the world, violent conflict, displacement and hunger obscure a clear view of developments on the ground. In such situations, deliberate disinformation thrives. We should not pretend that we have a clear view of what is happening in Arakan and in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. Lack of independent access and blocked internet facilities compound the problems.

Independent investigations will be needed to establish what has happened in Arakan and Bangladesh since 2017. While a significant body of research about the Rohingya exists, research on Arakan’s other communities remains scant. Moreover, research should also focus on disturbing allegations about what has been happening in Bangladesh. How did Rohingya militias manage to get a firm grip on the population in the refugee camps? Where did funding for their arms and operations come from? And how can large numbers of refugees and militia fighters continue to cross the Bangladesh-Myanmar border seemingly unnoticed?

Since 2018, the Independent Investigating Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) has been collecting and preserving evidence to facilitate criminal prosecutions of those most responsible for atrocity crimes. But it only shares its findings with investigative, prosecutorial and judicial authorities in national and international courts. As a result, a vast body of information remains inaccessible to the public. Moreover, IIMM’s mandate does not cover other truth-seeking needs, such as documenting and public acknowledgment of crimes through truth and reconciliation bodies and publicly accessible archives. These limitations underline the importance of establishing additional mechanisms to ensure that accountability is pursued as an integral part of transitional justice and reconciliation. This should be part of a comprehensive approach: an all-for-Arakan approach.

Using the Annan report as a credible starting point for dialogue could be a first step towards creating a better understanding of the needs of all Arakan’s people. Moreover, its repeated recognition by the UN General Assembly might help to rally much needed support for such an exercise at a time when resources are scarce.

Laetitia van den Assum is a former Dutch diplomat. She was also a member of the Rakhine Advisory Commission (2016-2017), chaired by Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General.

World.title: US Holds Second Round of Talks With Myanmar Regime as Concerns Grow Over Policy Shift
World.content:
U.S. officials held a meeting with Myanmar miliary regime officials in Tokyo last week, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the meeting.

It was the second round of talks between the two countries within a month. A U.S. delegation led by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance visited the regime’s capital Naypyitaw in mid-September.

Vance also led the delegation in Tokyo, which included over a dozen U.S. officials, while the identities of regime representatives and the issues discussed remained undisclosed, according to Reuters.

At the September talks, the U.S. delegation met with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing and secured the release of American businessman Adam Castillo, who had been detained upon returning to Yangon in June 2026 over a lawsuit filed against him.

The U.S. outreach led by Vance has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters reported, citing current and former officials as well as others familiar with the U.S. policy shift.

The Irrawaddy has learned that during the Naypyitaw meeting, the U.S. side urged the regime to reduce attacks on civilians, crack down on money-laundering gangs, engage with ethnic armed groups, release political prisoners and allow unfettered distribution of humanitarian assistance.

Observers noted that the Trump administration has shifted its policy from isolating the Myanmar military-installed government to engaging with it.

The National Unity Government (NUG), a leading anti-regime revolutionary organization, said it was not overly concerned by the increasing engagement between the U.S. and the military junta.

Speaking to The Irrawaddy, NUG Foreign Affairs Minister Zin Mar Aung said the U.S. is engaging with both sides—the military regime and the revolutionary groups—purely based on promoting its own interests, without granting legitimacy to anyone.

“Its [U.S.] policy is already clear. They are taking a transactional, practical approach to tackle issue like TOC [transnational organized crime]. They will discuss matters that are crucial to U.S. interests,” she said.

“So, this is nothing unusual. Nor is it a shift in policy. Since the Trump administration took office, this is how the U.S. has been dealing with [all] countries, not just Myanmar.”

Banya Khung Aung, Secretary 2 of the Interim Executive Council of Karenni (Kayah) State, which largely controls the eastern Myanmar state, told The Irrawaddy he is concerned that increased U.S. engagement with the regime will harm the country’s federal democracy and human rights movements, whether financially, technically or operationally. As evidence, he pointed to the Trump administration’s recent cuts to USAID funding for Myanmar.

“If you look carefully at Donald Trump’s policies, everyone knows that he engages with all [sides] and highly considers his national interests. So, I am not surprised with [the administration’s ongoing] engagement with the regime,” he said.

He noted that foreign governments are no longer prioritizing democracy and human rights, and are instead focusing on their national and common interests.

“Because of that, whether it is a government or a dictatorship, if there are benefits for America, it is almost certain they will engage.”

Bertil Lintner, a Swedish journalist, author and strategic consultant who has been writing about Asia for more than four decades, echoed Banya’s comments.

“I am not surprised. Democracy has never been a top priority for the Trump administration. And more countries are starting to acquiesce to a fait accompli. The military-dominated government is there to stay for the foreseeable future.”

Following the 2021 coup, the U.S. under Joe Biden imposed sweeping sanctions against top regime generals—including Min Aung Hlaing and his family—as well as military-owned conglomerates.

But Trump has shifted U.S. policy from isolating the regime to engaging with it, including delisting junta cronies accused of aiding and abetting regime war crimes and crime against humanity committed against their own people.

Meanwhile, the country, whose economy has collapsed under the regime, has become a hotspot of transnational organized crime. Chinese-run scam syndicates under the protection of several armed organizations, including regime-controlled or aligned militia groups, defraud huge sums from victims globally, including Americans, who have lost billions of dollars annually in recent years.

Regarding U.S. engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma, said, “It looks like President Trump has been scammed by sham President Min Aung Hlaing. Trump is rewarding a criminal for committing more crimes.”

She warned that U.S. engagement with the regime not only poses risks to the country’s pro-democracy movement, but also endangers civilians in Myanmar and across the region. She noted that Min Aung Hlaing has escalated the country’s conflicts, causing mass displacement, while also driving a boom in transnational crime that targets victims regionally and globally.

“Embracing Min Aung Hlaing is embracing a nest of vipers. He has been intensifying threats to regional human security and economic stability,” Stothard said.

The U.S. State Department said it engages will all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting U.S. interests and has raised the need to cease violence and release political prisoners, according to the Reuters report.

World.title: Chinese Jet-Fuel Refinery to Bypass Sanctions, Myanmar’s Blood Timber Flows to China, and More
World.content:
China‑backed refinery lets regime bypass jet fuel sanctions

Myanmar’s military regime has restarted the Thanlyin No.1 Oil Refinery near Yangon, allowing it to bypass jet fuel sanctions and sustain its deadly air raids on the civilian population. According to Nikkei Asia, Phase 1 is designed to produce 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually, roughly equal to Myanmar’s import volume last year.

The refinery, operated by Myanma Petrochemical Enterprise (MPE), was taken offline in 2017 but rebuilt after the 2021 coup. The engineering, procurement and construction contract was awarded to Peiyang Chemical Engineering Service Corporation (PCCS), a Singapore-registered subsidiary of Peiyang Chemical Equipment in Tianjin.

Anhui Tiankang Group supplied nearly 400 measuring devices for the various chemical processes, coordinated by Tianjin Sainuo Oil & Gas Technology. Some modules were fabricated in China and shipped via Singapore to Thilawa Port.

The regime says the project will reduce foreign currency outflow and stabilize supply. It has heavily relied on air power since 2022, killing thousands of civilians, and this dependency has only increased as the territory it controls continues to shrink. In the most recent atrocity, 50 civilians died and nearly 60 were injured when the regime bombed a busy market in Rakhine’s Kyauktaw.

China becomes biggest buyer of Myanmar’s blood timber

China has become the dominant buyer of Myanmar’s timber since the 2021 coup, according to UN Comtrade data cited by Australia’s Wood Central.

Last year, China’s purchases climbed to US$147.3 million, nearly double the pre-coup total of $78 million, while Western imports collapsed from roughly the same amount to just $1.2 million worth, according to Forest Trends, a Washington‑based non‑profit that monitors global forest trade and conservation finance.

The group’s analysis shows China’s share of Myanmar’s reported wood exports rose from 25.5 percent in 2019 to a peak of $228.7 million in 2024, nearly 80 percent of the total, before settling at 74.1% in 2025. Nearly three‑quarters of China’s imports since the coup were bound for companies registered in Yunnan Province.

Myanmar’s total reported wood exports rose from $304.3 million in 2019 to $370.6 million in 2022 but then fell to $198.9 million last year after the regime lost control over most of the border with Yunnan in Shan and Kachin states. But China continues to import timber through border crossings now controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Western buyers’ share now accounts for just 0.6 of Myanmar’s blood timber, but Forest Trends warns that the decline does not necessarily mean sanctions are working. Instead, the group believes much is “re-exported” to the West after “transiting through China,” though the flow is harder to trace.

Kokang scam warlord sentenced to death

A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three leaders of Myanmar’s notorious Wei clan to death as Beijing continues its public reckoning with the Kokang scam syndicates. The Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court convicted Wei Huairen and two others of running violent fraud compounds that trafficked Chinese nationals, forced them into online scams, and murdered at least two victims.

According to Chinese state media, the Wei family’s network generated 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion) through online scams, drug trafficking, illegal casinos, and prostitution. Courts also handed life sentences to three associates and prison terms to 55 others, describing the gang as the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar.”

The Wei clan was one of four family crime syndicates in Kokang, which is now controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA). Wei Huairen was the chief of the regime-aligned Kokang Border Guard Force (BGF), in which capacity he created a much-emulated model of quasi-official armed protection of online fraud parks. The ruling follows earlier executions of Ming and Bai clan members.

Beijing renews outreach to Myanmar’s party leaders

The director‑general of the Chines Communist Party’s International Liaison Department, Peng Xiubin, met leaders of nine Myanmar political parties in Yangon on Tuesday, though none associated with the bona-fide opposition.

Present at the meeting were the usual suspects from the ruling Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) as well as a few co-opted ethnic political parties like the Arakan Front Party (AFP) and Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party (SNDP). Discussions focused on “bilateral ties” and Myanmar’s “peace and reconciliation,” according to participants.

SNDP chair Sai Aik Pao told the Popular News propaganda outlet that he urged Peng to help the central regime regain control over the Muse–Mandalay trade corridor, pushing out the MNDAA and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

“China has influence” over those armed groups, he was quoted as saying.

While the USDP remains at the center of party-to-party ties, China also often flies other party leaders to Kunming and Beijing for “study tours” and “cooperation forums.” Shortly after the regime announced its planned elections last year, the department hosted a delegation of several Myanmar political parties in Beijing.

Shan groups warn against MNDAA’s ‘Sinicization’

Eight Shan civil society and youth groups published an open letter to the MNDAA on Oct. 9, warning that its boorish cultural and administrative practices in northern Shan State threaten ethnic coexistence and China–Myanmar border stability.

The letter warns that the MNDAA’s military control is only temporary and urges it to respect local ethnic traditions, languages, and rights. The groups accuse the Chinese-speaking group of erasing Shan, Ta’ang and Burmese scripts from public signboards and replacing them with Chinese characters. They argue that imposing Chinese-style governance and financial systems without consultation undermines trust and risks fueling resistance.

Such actions could even jeopardize the future of the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), the letter warns, referring to the pet project of the MNDAA’s paymasters in Beijing.

Ta’ang civil society groups have similarly condemned the MNDAA’s actions. In April, six Ta’ang organizations said replacing Ta’ang signs with Chinese amounted to erasing an ethnic identity—a violation of international human rights law.

The MNDAA is busy consolidating its control of all major trade corridors linking to Yunnan Province.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Kazakhstan Tops World Fencing Rankings for First Time in History
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s men’s fencing team has topped the International Fencing Federation (FIE) world rankings for the first time in the country’s history, following a gold-medal victory at the World Cup stage in Casablanca, Morocco, the Kazakhstan Fencing Federation announced.

The team opened the 2026-2027 season with the victory, building on a series of major international titles over the past 12 months. Kazakhstan had entered the Casablanca competition ranked third in the world, behind Switzerland and France, but moved to the top after winning the tournament.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated the team on its achievement, wishing the athletes further success representing Kazakhstan at the world’s most prestigious competitions.

A historic winning streak

Kazakhstan’s rise to the top of the rankings follows a series of victories at major international competitions. In November 2025, the team won gold at the Islamic Solidarity Games in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. In June 2026, it became Asian champion in New Delhi, India, before claiming the world championship title in Hong Kong in July. In September, the team also won at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

For many years, the leading positions in the men’s team were dominated by established fencing powers, including France, Italy, Hungary and Switzerland. In Asia, Japan and South Korea had previously reached the top of the world rankings. Kazakhstan has now joined that group, marking a first for the country.

Kazakhstan Fencing Federation President Mirbulat Abuov highlighted the significance of the Casablanca victory, particularly because the team competed with a refreshed lineup.

“I would first like to congratulate the athletes, coaches and the entire team on this historic result. What makes this achievement especially valuable is that we competed in Casablanca with a renewed lineup,” Abuov said.

The team consisted of Kirill Prokhodov, Vadim Sharlaimov, Alexander Fedotov and Kirill Pavlov.

“With this lineup, we defeated France, a 23-time world champion in men’s team epee. This is an absolute record in the discipline. Kazakhstan’s victory confirms that our country has not only strong leaders but also young athletes capable of defeating the world’s best teams,” he said.

Road to gold in Casablanca

Kazakhstan began its campaign with convincing victories over Türkiye, 45-20, and Hong Kong, 45-28. In the quarterfinals, the team overcame Egypt 45-39 in a closely contested bout. The semifinal brought a clash with France, one of the most successful teams in the discipline. Kazakhstan took an early lead and maintained its advantage to secure a 45-39 victory.

In the final, Kazakhstan faced Russia, which was competing at a World Cup event under its national flag for the first time after an extended break, according to the federation’s announcement. The Kazakh fencers maintained a narrow advantage throughout the match and won 45-40 to secure the gold medal and the top position in the FIE world rankings.

The result marks a milestone for Kazakhstani fencing, demonstrating the team’s ability to sustain its success at major international competitions while developing younger athletes capable of competing at the highest level.

World.title: KMG International Posts Higher Profits as EBITDA Climbs to $469 Million
World.content:
ASTANA – KMG International, a subsidiary of Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company KazMunayGas, reported a 73% year-on-year increase in consolidated earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) to $469 million in the first nine months of 2026, the company announced.

Net profit reached $269 million, up 219% compared with the same period last year. The company’s results were supported by refining operations at Romania’s Petromidia refinery, as well as higher sales volumes across KMG International’s retail businesses.

Refining and fuel production

Petromidia processed 4.087 million tons of feedstock during the reporting period. Average daily processing reached 14,670 tons, equivalent to approximately 97% of the refinery’s designed capacity.

Total petroleum product output amounted to 3.977 million tons, including 1.793 million tons of diesel, 1.103 million tons of gasoline and 369,000 tons of Jet A-1 aviation fuel. The figures highlight the refinery’s continued role in KMG International’s operations, with processing volumes remaining close to its designed capacity.

Retail sales increase

KMG International’s retail companies sold a combined 2.272 million tons of petroleum products, a 5% increase year on year. The growth was driven primarily by higher wholesale sales in Romania, alongside increased sales volumes in Moldova.

Sales of non-fuel goods and services in Romania also rose, increasing 3% compared with the first nine months of 2025. EBITDA in the retail segment reached $87 million.

KMG International said it continues to implement measures to improve operational efficiency, maintain the reliability of its production assets and strengthen its financial stability.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expects Mild Winter, With Above-Normal Temperatures and Snowfall
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is forecast to experience a relatively mild winter, with temperatures above the climatic norm in most regions and increased precipitation expected across parts of the country, mainly in February.

The winter is expected to bring moderate precipitation overall, although some areas in the north, northwest, northeast and central parts of the country may receive above-normal amounts. Blizzards, strong winds, fog and icy conditions are also possible in various regions, reported Kazhydromet, the national hydrometeorological service, on Oct. 16.

Forecasters warn of significant temperature fluctuations throughout the season, which could contribute to the formation of an ice crust within the snow cover.

In December, average air temperatures are expected to be 2°C above the climatic norm nationwide. Precipitation is expected to remain near normal across most of Kazakhstan, with above-normal levels in parts of the north, northeast and east. The Kyzylorda Region is forecast to receive less precipitation than usual.

In January, temperatures are expected to be 1-2°C above the climatic norm across most of the country, while near-normal conditions are forecast in the northwest. Precipitation is likely to remain near normal, with higher levels in parts of western Kazakhstan and below-normal levels in areas of the south and southeast.

February is forecast to be warmer than usual across most of Kazakhstan, with temperatures 1-3°C above normal. Precipitation may exceed the climatic norm across much of the country, although several western and southern areas are expected to see near-normal levels, while parts of the southwest may receive less than usual.

Overall, the outlook points to a relatively mild winter, though sharp temperature fluctuations, strong winds, blizzards, fog and icy conditions may still pose challenges in some areas.

World.title: Protect Teens With Stronger Safeguards and Parental Choice, Not Social Media Bans, Says Meta
World.content:
ASTANA — Protecting teenagers online requires more than privacy settings and messaging restrictions, as ensuring that recommended content is age-appropriate remains a challenge, said Philip Chua, Director of Public Policy, Products (APAC) at Meta, in an exclusive interview with The Astana Times.

Chua said Meta is extending its approach to online safety from protective account settings to the content teenagers encounter, including posts from accounts they follow and recommendations generated by algorithms.

“Fundamentally, algorithms are a way of sorting a lot of content that we have to potentially show a person, and figuring out what to show first. Algorithms are neutral. They are neither inherently good or inherently bad,” he said.

Meta has introduced content settings inspired by movie-rating criteria for ages 13 and older, designed to limit teenagers’ exposure to sensitive material across recommended content and accounts they follow.

The approach is part of a wider discussion over how technology companies and governments can protect younger users without unnecessarily restricting digital access. For Kazakhstan, Meta is recommending stronger protections within existing platforms, alongside age verification systems that would reduce the need for users to share personal information with individual applications.

“What we are recommending to governments, including in Kazakhstan, is this idea of an app store or OS-level [operating system-level] approach to age assurance,” he said.

The proposal would allow applications to receive age-related information through app stores or operating systems rather than requiring families to provide the same personal details separately to multiple platforms.

Can social media safeguards prevent harm?

While Meta has expanded protections for teenage users, their effectiveness also depends on how successfully the company can prevent inappropriate material from appearing in recommendations and other content. Some videos, for example, may comply with platform rules while containing suggestive music, language or themes unsuitable for younger audiences.

When asked how Meta addresses such material, Chua explained that the company combines artificial intelligence and human review to enforce its community standards, while applying additional content restrictions to teenage accounts.

He said these measures are designed to reduce exposure to inappropriate content, although technology cannot guarantee that every potentially harmful experience will be prevented.

“So what we would expect is never 100%. I think technology will keep getting better. But our commitment here is to really avoid any content that A, doesn’t belong on our service, but B, also removes a lot of what you would perhaps say is borderline, potentially sensitive, not something that you want somebody 13 and above to see,” he said.

Age verification raises privacy questions

Ensuring that these protections reach the intended users presents another challenge: determining their ages accurately while limiting the collection of personal information.

Chua described age assurance as an industry-wide issue involving technological limitations and privacy concerns, particularly when young people use numerous applications. Meta uses information provided by users alongside technology that analyzes behavioral patterns to estimate whether an account belongs to someone younger or older than 18.

The accounts people follow, for example, can offer clues about their age.

“The example that I like to use is if you are following Backstreet Boys on Instagram, you are probably slightly older as compared to if you are following Blackpink,”he said.

Such patterns can help platforms estimate ages without relying exclusively on more intrusive identity-verification methods. However, Chua said the number of applications used by young people raises questions about how widely their personal information should be shared.

“And I think, more importantly, the issue that we are seeing is that insofar as a young person can use up to 40 apps every day, should every app be collecting age and personal information? And what does that mean in terms of how that data can be compromised?” he said.

Under Meta’s proposed approach, age assurance would take place at the app-store or operating-system level, allowing applications to provide age-appropriate experiences without separately collecting the same information. According to Chua, parents could provide their children’s age information when first setting up a device, with app stores and operating systems helping ensure that applications apply suitable protections.

“If there is a way that we can, on a one-stop basis, on a once-off basis, just collect that information at the OS level or the app store level, that’s going to protect privacy and streamline the amount of data that needs to be shared with any app,” he said.

Balancing online protection and digital access

The question of how to protect young users while respecting privacy forms part of a broader policy debate over whether governments should strengthen safeguards within existing platforms or restrict access to social media altogether.

“We have seen that a ban on social media actually does not result in a decrease of time that a young person spends online. We have seen that a ban on social media results in young people finding ways to circumvent the system or finding ways to migrate to other apps that may not be regulated, potentially could be less safe, and generally would not have spent the same kind of investment that big social media companies have spent all these years to protecting young people,” he said.

Australia became a prominent test case when restrictions on social media accounts for users younger than 16 took effect on Dec. 10, 2025. Early findings from the country’s eSafety Commissioner indicate a decline in account ownership among children ages 10-15, although many continued accessing restricted platforms. The long-term effects remain under evaluation.

Chua said restrictions could also leave young people feeling excluded from online communities or encourage them to seek alternative platforms with fewer safety measures.

For Kazakhstan, he recommended building on safeguards already introduced by major technology companies, combining restrictive default settings for teenagers with parental choice rather than adopting blanket prohibitions.

“We need to respect the role of parental choice. Those two ingredients, I think, are very important ingredients in how you can have a balanced regulatory framework so that we are not in a situation where we are denying young people access to digital skills and cutting them off from their digital lives,” he said.

Government restrictions and access to online platforms

Government restrictions on social media access, particularly during politically sensitive periods, present a separate challenge involving regulatory authority, platform compliance and the public’s ability to communicate online.

When asked how Meta approaches such restrictions, Chua said maintaining working relationships with governments is central to the company’s public policy activities.

“Our first principle here is really to collaborate and have a very good working relationship with governments around the world because we believe we share a common interest on preserving access to the internet, preserving the digital conversation and that’s going to be a very important part of our work,” he said.

Chua noted that discussions with governments often concern content that may be inappropriate or illegal under national legislation. Meta seeks to enforce its own policies while complying with applicable laws, including in Kazakhstan, where content regulation remains part of its engagement with policymakers.

He linked these regulatory questions to Kazakhstan’s ambitions in AI and the digital economy, noting that decisions about online access also have implications for the opportunities available to younger generations.

“We also know that Kazakhstan has a very young population and I think the country has a lot of ambitions for the future and so I think this is why we are talking about AI and innovation and investment into the country at the same time we are talking also about how we can ensure a balanced regulatory solution,” he said.

“We want to make sure that we don’t outright restrict access to important digital skills that are critical for the future,” he added.

World.title: Kazakhstan Resolves Long-Running Dunga Oil Dispute, Paving Way for New Development Plan
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has reached an agreement to resolve a yearslong dispute over costs at the Dunga oil field in the Mangystau Region, clearing the way for a development plan targeting 67.4 million barrels of oil production through 2039, the Energy Ministry said in a written response to The Astana Times.

The agreement was signed on Oct. 5 by Kazakhstan’s Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov and KazMunayGas Deputy Chairman Ruslan Balykbayev, in the presence of representatives of PSA LLP, the country’s authorized body overseeing production-sharing agreements, and Dunga Operating GmbH, the field’s operator.

The ministry said the settlement would allow the parties to proceed with a new development plan for 2026-2039, which envisages substantial capital and operating investments in the field.

The document is expected to be submitted for signing to the consortium’s foreign partners, Oman Oil Company Limited and Thailand’s PTTEP Corporation.

The Dunga field was discovered in 1966 in the Tupkaragan district of the Mangystau Region in western Kazakhstan, entered trial production in 2000 and has been under full-scale development since 2007. The field operates under a production-sharing agreement originally signed between Kazakhstan and Oman Oil Company Limited in May 1994. In 2019, Kazakhstan and the consortium agreed to extend the Dunga production-sharing agreement by 15 years, from 2024 to 2039.

In November 2023, Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company KazMunayGas acquired a 60% interest in the project from TotalEnergies for $358.5 million, according to the company’s financial statements.

The acquisition gave KazMunayGas control of Dunga Operating GmbH, which serves as the field’s operator. Oman Oil Company Limited and PTTEP Corporation each hold a 20% stake.

According to KazMunayGas, Dunga produced 677,300 tons of oil in 2025, compared with 630,000 tons in 2024 and 546,900 tons in 2023. Gas production exceeded 51 million cubic meters in 2025.

The dispute centered on whether certain historical expenses incurred by the project’s contractors were eligible for reimbursement under the production-sharing agreement. Such expenses from oil production are usually recovered before the remaining profit oil is divided between the state and investors.

Nurlan Zhumagulov, an energy analyst and founder of the Energy Monitor Telegram channel, said the project’s previous operator, France’s TotalEnergies, and other consortium partners, had recoverable costs amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars. He linked the resolution of the dispute with the field’s future production potential, saying it could help the operator to increase annual oil output to 850,000 tons.

According to Zhumagulov’s estimates, tax payments to Kazakhstan from the project totaled approximately 40 billion tenge (US$88.2 million) in 2025, including 32 billion tenge (US$70.6 million) representing the state’s share of profit oil.

The latest settlement also entails financial compensation to Kazakhstan. The Energy Ministry, however, did not specify the amount in its response to The Astana Times or provide a breakdown of the disputed historical expenses.

“The Dunga oil field has significant potential and is of strategic importance to the country’s energy sector,” said Kazakhstan’s Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov.

“The project’s development has long been hampered by unresolved disputes over non-recoverable costs. The agreements reached allow us to protect the state’s economic interests without lengthy legal proceedings and pave the way for a new investment cycle,” said Akkenzhenov.

The settlement is expected to facilitate implementation of the field’s development plan through 2039, with projected oil production of 67.4 million barrels over the period.
