Follow live updates on the Helen Haines attack Australian intelligence agencies will brief anxious federal politicians about a worsening security environment on Wednesday as independent MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive outside her regional Victorian office. The member for Indi, 65, lost one of her legs and surgeons were trying to save the other at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital on Tuesday. Police held suspect Brendan Nugent, 43, in custody as they investigated potential motives for what they are treating as a targeted attack. The town of Wangaratta came together on Tuesday, just hours after the horrific attack on Helen Haines. Jason South Haines’ parliamentary colleagues described the former nurse and midwife as “the best of us” as they grappled with the rare act of violence against a sitting MP, while the town of Wangaratta, in north-east Victoria, held a vigil and laid flowers outside her office.



The attack on Haines has alarmed state and federal MPs who have been subject to increasingly threatening behaviour in recent years. As One Nation leader Pauline Hanson blamed state premiers and the prime minister for enabling division and hatred, other MPs said it was time for reflection, not finger pointing. The Home Affairs Department, ASIO and Australian Federal Police will address parliamentarians in several sessions on Wednesday, while Victoria is contemplating increased security at next month’s state election. “Everyone in public office carries a level of risk now, everyone,” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said on Tuesday. Federal police have received 1067 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against high officeholders in 2025-26, up from 951 the financial year before. Former independent Indi MP Cathy McGowan, left, and a Haines supporter at a service in Wangaratta. Jason South But Haines seemed to MPs and her constituents an unlikely target, and politicians across the political divide on Tuesday described the non-partisan MP as a kind, decent, respectful and community-driven local member.



“When you go through the different scale of who we would have thought was the most at risk, no one would have thought Helen Haines,” Burke said. “Everybody looks at that and thinks, if it was Helen, it could have been me. Everyone is aware of that. But all our thoughts right now are with Helen.” Witnesses said Haines was retrieving items from the boot of her car on Monday afternoon when a white Toyota LandCruiser conducted a U-turn to ram her against a vehicle, before reversing and hitting her a second time. In what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has labelled a heroic act, barbershop owner Ricky Jefferies intervened by running to the driver’s side of the vehicle and wrestling him to the ground before waiting for authorities to arrive. Ricky Jefferies, the man who detained the alleged attacker, outside his barbershop. Jason South Victoria Police is leading the investigation, supported by the state’s counterterrorism team, the Australian Federal Police and ASIO. Police raided Nugent’s sprawling property near Wangaratta on Monday night, and it remained cordoned off by detectives on Tuesday.



Neighbours described Nugent as an unemployed man with few friends, and said they had become increasingly concerned about his erratic behaviour. He was involved in a road rage incident near Wangaratta last month, where he allegedly threatened a woman with a hammer, but no charges have been laid. The Tarrawingee man has a history of environmental activism but sources who knew him said he had changed dramatically since protesting logging in the local forest. Nugent’s social media history reveals he previously praised Haines and backed her independent campaign in the area. More recently, his posts focused on international issues, including criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza. The property where Brendan Nugent lived. Jason South His father, Rod Nugent, on Tuesday afternoon revealed Haines was a friend for more than 20 years. “What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” he said in a statement. “All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends. We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.”



ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said Monday’s incident had happened in an environment where increased levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation had made violence seem permissible. “I have repeatedly put on the record my concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse. Words matter,” Burgess said in a statement. “I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meets with law enforcement heads in Victoria. Paul Rovere Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said 41 people had been charged with offences relating to threats against high office holders, including politicians, since special national security investigation teams were launched last October.



Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said extra security measures could be imposed at voting booths at next month’s state election, while NSW Premier Chris Minns said he feared such incidents would deter other people from running for political office. Related Article Haines attack Suspect in Helen Haines attack once praised the MP online and had raised concern among neighbours Independent senator David Pocock described it as a “wake-up call”. “As a male parliamentarian, you get some threats. You get the angry phone calls, the awful emails, the anonymous comments,” he said. “But I think we’ve got to look at what’s happening to female politicians, and just the ridiculous amount of threats and abuse that they have to cop, and as Australians, we need to stand up and say this is not OK.” Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Coalition MPs had often discussed the increased threat of political violence as he stressed the importance of keeping an Australian culture of vigorous debate that never crossed the line into violence.



“We need to do everything we can as elected representatives to prevent this ever happening again,” he said. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Haines was a “lovely lady” who worked tirelessly for her community, while Greens leader David Shoebridge said the notion that Haines could be targeted for her work was “horrifying, senseless and shameful”. Hanson described Haines as a “beautiful lady” before blaming Albanese and state premiers for the deteriorating state of political debate. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, whose own security has been recently upgraded, criticised that response. “We all have a role to play and it can’t just be finger pointing. I think it’s a bad move to point the finger on a day like this,” he said. Hanson also revealed she had ordered her cartoon creator to change a One Nation video that mocked Senator Jacqui Lambie’s struggles with vaginal prolapse. After Lambie condemned the cartoon on Monday, Hanson said she should “have a laugh” and “get over it”.



But on Tuesday, she changed tone. “The video went up without my actually seeing it, and I was not aware of the content of the video,” Hanson said. “It wasn’t as tastefully done as it could have been, and I do apologise for that. I’ve already spoken to them about it and changing that.” With Nick Newling and Emily Kaine More from our Helen Haines coverage

World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Star skipper departs as Collingwood’s disastrous season plunges into crisis Hannah Kennelly Updated October 20, 2026 — 6:41pm ,first published October 20, 2026 — 10:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Collingwood’s AFLW team is in crisis after captain Ruby Schleicher announced her departure amid ongoing concerns from senior players about the direction of the women’s program. On Tuesday morning, Schleicher – an inaugural player and dual All-Australian – announced she would not re-sign with Collingwood and would instead return home to Western Australia. Collingwood skipper Ruby Schleicher. Getty Images In an emotional farewell video, the 28-year-old – who had her arm in a sling following a season-ending injury in round nine – fought back tears and said it was time for her to return home and spend time with her family. Her departure comes at a pivotal time for the club, as it faces calls to change its struggling women’s program, with several senior players voicing concerns about a lack of improvement and direction.



To make matters worse, the Pies are anchored near the bottom of the ladder with just one win from 10 matches and facing a potential exodus of players who are out of contract at the end of 2026, including Tarni White, Sarah Rowe, Mattea Breed, Lauren Butler and Bri Davey. Related Article Analysis

AFLW They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success? Vice-captain Jordyn Allen signed a three-year deal in 2024, but tried to seek a trade to the Brisbane Lions last year. Collingwood initially offered Schleicher a one-year-contract extension, but later bumped that up to two, as their skipper weighed up leaving the club and the impact that would have on the extensive media opportunities she has in Melbourne, including her work as a commentator and presenter for Fox Footy. But the skipper’s untimely departure has given Magpies fans a sense of déjà vu after losing star player Chloe Molloy in 2023 amid the club’s consistent struggles to perform on field.



“This has been a really tough decision to come to, but one that, sitting with it probably feels the best for me and my career and my life at the moment and that’s to head home back west,” she said in announcing her departure on Tuesday. “It’s clearly not a decision that’s probably even still sitting completely right, I’m not sure if it will, it may take a long time to.” West Coast are the front-runners for the inaugural player’s signature, offering a four-year contract. Schleicher informed her teammates on Tuesday morning that she was leaving.



“I can’t put into words the gratitude I feel for this place and the role it has played in helping me grow up,” Schleicher said in a statement. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Why I have an issue with the Nick Blakey trade to North Melbourne Peter Ryan Sports reporter “Being an 18-year-old coming across, those first couple of years away from home, as someone who is really close to their family, was something I struggled with. “This has been a really tough decision for me to make but one that is ultimately the best for where I am in my life and career. “The family that Collingwood has become for me – the staff, admin, footy department and the girls I’ve played with – has meant so much.



“I’ll always consider myself a Collingwood person, and thank you to the Magpie army, who have embraced me, whether it’s walking down the street or at our games.” Former No.1 draft pick Ash Centra posted a lengthy tribute to Schleicher on social media, praising her as a leader, mentor and friend. “Thank you for leading by example, for the way you carry yourself and for the way you care for people,” Centra posted. “You’ve taught me so much, not just about footy but about life, about believing in myself, about being a better person, and about what it really means to show up for the people around you.”



Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly also released a statement thanking Schleicher for her contribution and praising her leadership skills. “Ruby has represented the black and white with great resilience and character and has played a key role in supporting the next generation of Collingwood players on and off the field,” Kelly said. Collingwood Football Club chief executive Craig Kelly. AAP “While we are disappointed to see Ruby depart our club, we respect her decision to return home. We thank Ruby for everything she has given to Collingwood and wish her all the very best for the next chapter.” Brit Bonnici will become the only inaugural player left on Collingwood’s AFLW list.





Schleicher’s announcement came just one week after Kelly met with the Pies’ AFLW team and staff to address concerns about the club’s women’s the program. In a recent interview, Kelly told the Herald Sun he and the club were “fully committed” to turning around the side and rejected claims he did not care about women’s football. St Kilda recently announced an independent investigation ino their program following their poor season and resignation of long-time coach Nick Dal Santo, however Kelly ruled out commissioning an external review at Collingwood. Collingwood declined to comment further when contacted by this masthead. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘As tall as you can go’: The NYC-style density plan for Melbourne’s future
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly ‘As tall as you can go’: The NYC-style density plan for Melbourne’s future Angelica Snowden and Alex Crowe October 20, 2026 — 6:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio has implored Melburnians to embrace high-rise, high-density living as the city’s population races towards 9 million. But as de Blasio decried urban sprawl – constructing homes further away from city centres on urban fringes – as a “massive failure” of the Western world, former Victorian premier Steve Bracks told The Age’s Melbourne Assembly on Tuesday that it could be too late. Former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio argued for an end to urban sprawl at Tuesday’s Melbourne Assembly event. Justin McManus “I think the genie is already out of the bottle. We are already a sprawling city,” Bracks said. “What we need is a hard full stop on the city. We should be protecting the green wedges … [and] encouraging our planning scheme development at activity centres around our transport hubs.”



Held at Federation Square, the second day of the inaugural forum brought together industry leaders, decision-makers and the community. As well as the pillar of shaping the city, it focused on education and innovation, with experts discussing how to attract and keep the brightest minds and commercialise research breakthroughs. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Melbourne Assembly day two as it happened: PM, ex-New York mayor share visions for more liveable Melbourne Melbourne’s planning policies were at the centre of the debate, ahead of next month’s state election in which Labor’s “activity centres” are on the ballot, with the Coalition vowing to abolish the zones where developers are allowed to bypass local planning rules to build high-rises up to 20 storeys. The government implemented the plan in response to surging house prices and population growth, with activity centres spread across the city near transport hubs in a bid to shift population growth away from the urban fringes into established suburbs. Bracks pointed out that Melbourne was five times the size of New York, and suggested that instead of imitating de Blasio’s hometown, increased density should be targeted in the activity centres.



The former New York City mayor, however, urged authorities to “reverse” sprawl and build “as tall as you can go” closer to the CBD, backed by careful planning to include amenities and services. “The reality of people’s quality of life, living far from the centre is going to get harder and harder,” he said. “People want culture and connection more than ever. You must embrace height and density. You must turn away from sprawl.” Loading It may be politically easier to sprawl, but it is more costly to society, Grattan Institute chief executive Aruna Sathanapally told the forum’s panel on shaping the city. Where developers invest in the construction of homes on urban fringes, the cost of supplying residents with access to jobs, and infrastructure for water, electricity and roads is straddled to state governments, she said. “I don’t accept that it’s cheaper if you actually take those costs into account to sprawl. It can be much more efficient to use infrastructure densely in your existing cities,” said Sathanapally, who pointed out that the handbrake on density was the rising cost of construction and poor construction productivity.



Architect Sarah Lynn Rees also advocated for greater density – but in a way that connects people to their homes and neighbourhoods, and factors in the needs of families. “We’re putting people in white boxes and expecting them to live a life of thriving within their community, but they’re so disconnected from it, and they don’t have the space that they need,” Rees said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the Melbourne Assembly. Justin McManus Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used his address to reveal Victoria would receive $350 million in federal funding to connect “last mile infrastructure”, particularly basic utilities, to new housing in the state’s growing suburbs and regions. In the face of criticisms of urban sprawl, Albanese nodded to the outer suburbs including Frankston, Point Cook, Dandenong, Melton, Sunbury and Cranbourne as the “powerhouse” of Melbourne.



Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece said density was a key plank of the City of Melbourne’s 25-year city plan, including its target of building 120,000 new homes in the next 25 years. He pointed to Fishermans Bend, Macaulay, Arden and West Melbourne as having “huge tracts of land”. “Melbourne is blessed in that it has plenty of underutilised land that can be developed very close to the city,” he said. Loading “These areas can accommodate our population growth in sustainable, high-density suburbs with plenty of green space.” But he said it was crucial major infrastructure was delivered by the state government based on long-term strategic planning and independent advice, not the “short-term political considerations and electoral maps” that influenced projects such as the Suburban Rail Loop and the West Gate Tunnel.



“I would urge the next government, whoever it is at the end of November, to reverse the decision to abolish Infrastructure Victoria and preserve its independence,” he said. “Any proposed major project should be subject to independent analysis … the government of the day can then select from this menu. If it’s not on the menu, then you can’t go committing billions of dollars, leaving it to future generations to pay off.” Loading The education and innovation debate was kicked off by Professor Marek Tesar, the faculty of education dean at the University of Melbourne, the presenting partner for Melbourne Assembly. The internationally recognised scholar in early childhood education asked the audience to consider who the future Melbourne was being designed for, pointing out that a four-year-old living here today would by 2080 have experienced more than half a century of the decisions being discussed.



“We need to ask the four-year-olds,” he said, urging leaders to consider the views of children who refused to “accept that the world must remain effectively as it is”. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly “I’d love to see Melbourne develop a network of youth innovation hubs connected to schools, libraries, universities and neighbourhoods across the city,” Tesar added. “Places where all young people could work with mentors on real problems: biodiversity, disability access, loneliness, robotics, transport, housing, climate change ... not just classroom exercises.” Doherty Institute director Professor Sharon Lewin took up the theme with her insights into how Melbourne can become the destination of choice for the world’s best researchers and innovators. Lewin, who runs the world-renowned biomedical research hub in the Parkville precinct, spoke about what could be learnt from Australia’s past and the way her parents were welcomed from war-torn Europe as survivors of the Holocaust.



“The great cities of the future will compete for many things: for investment, for technology, for companies. But above all, they will compete for people,” she said. “Talent will go somewhere. We need to welcome that talent … Just as Australia did all those years ago for my parents.” Lewin also argued for a more comprehensive effort to achieve bigger economic gains from Melbourne’s research capability. “We are really good at discovery. We’re not always that good at what happens next,” she said. Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

World.title: November 1 is looming. But Sam Walker is keeping contract talks on hold
World.content:
SportNRLRugby League World Cup November 1 is looming. But Sam Walker is keeping contract talks on hold Nick Wright October 20, 2026 — 7:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Kangaroos debutant Sam Walker says he has put all thoughts of his club future on hold until after he makes his Test debut for Australia. The premiership-winning Roosters halfback is set to line up in the green and gold for the first time on Sunday as part of a new-look halves pairing with Tom Dearden, with Cameron Munster named on the bench and Mitchell Moses’ World Cup campaign over due to a leg injury. Sam Walker in Brisbane at Kangaroos training on Tuesday. Getty Images Walker will become one of the hottest properties on the open market if he hasn’t inked an extension with the Tricolours come the November 1 free agency deadline. The 24-year-old has said he hopes to sign a new Roosters deal before then, with his camp reportedly seeking close to $1.7 million a season over four years from 2028. The Roosters are reportedly prepared to offer Walker around $1.5 million a season.



Now with an NRL premiership and three Maroons caps on his resume, Walker is poised to become one of the highest-paid players in the game. But he’s determined not to let his contract situation distract him from his looming Kangaroos debut. “There’s no looking at that at the moment,” walker said on Tuesday. “My goal is completely on Sunday, and once that all happens I’ll be able to sit down and have a good look about it. Sam Walker celebrates with Roosters fans after winning the grand final. Getty Images “But at the moment, my goal is to represent Australia and get that jersey done first.” Walker and Dearden came up through the Broncos’ academy together, but have not played alongside each other at the scrum base. Walker replaced an injured Dearden (syndesmosis) for this year’s State of Origin series, in which he starred in game one and claimed man of the match honours in game two.



Munster is expected to come straight back into the No.6 jumper after being given a rest against Fiji at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday, but Walker was not viewing the battle in Brisbane as a shootout between him and Dearden for the right to join the Melbourne Storm champion in the halves. “We’ve almost grown up with each other, our families have known each other for a very long time, and Tommy and I have been mates for a long time,” Walker said. Loading “There’s no talk about that [a shootout]. Whatever is best for the Australian side – we’re really clear on that. Our focus at the moment is Sunday, and putting our best foot forward for our country.” In another world, Walker could have been wearing England colours at the World Cup, having been born in Leeds, but he joked that his family “would’ve killed me if I represented anyone other than Australia”.



Related Article Rugby League World Cup Is the Kangaroos battle with Walsh heating up? Not in Tedesco’s eyes Walker has had to overcome plenty of obstacles to don the green and gold, most recently a syndesmosis injury suffered in round 26 that could easily have ended his season. Incredibly, he was cleared to return for the Roosters’ preliminary final against the Dolphins barely a month later, putting himself firmly in the frame to succeed the injured Nathan Cleary and Moses. “I had to work really hard there for about a month and sacrificed a lot. I had to work really hard at my rehab and make sure I could put myself back in the best position for the Roosters,” Walker said. “I’m really proud of the team at the Roosters for getting into a position where I could allow myself to come back because we had a coupe of weeks there where it was knockout footy.



“I was really confident [I would come back], once they gave me the timeline of when I could possibly get back on the field I had a really clear goal and set my targets on that.” Walker will feature in a new-look spine against Fiji, with he and Dearden joined by fullback James Tedesco (replacing Reece Walsh) and hooker Blayke Brailey, who makes his own Test debut with Harry Grant rested. Blayke Brailey will make his debut for Australia on Sunday, having toured in last year’s Ashes but not played. Getty Images Brailey established himself as one of the more creative dummy-halves in the NRL this season, earning his maiden NSW call-up in the process and managing 15 try assists and 14 linebreak assists in Cronulla’s run to the semi-finals. The 28-year-old was adamant that his style would not clash with Walker’s, with both players eager to attack when they sensed an opportunity.



Related Article NRL 2026 62 tries in 53 games: The attacking phenom leading World Cup’s NRL hopefuls “I know he plays ad-lib, he likes to be off the cuff, he likes to be all-out attack – so hopefully that complements my game well,” Brailey said. “I think the way he moves and the way he plays [suits me]. I was a half myself, and I kind of know where he’s going to be and how he’s going to play, so hopefully we do link up and really connect. “In this team, what you see you back yourself. I know Kevvie will give us full rein where whatever you see, you take … it’s a luxury we have in our team where we have so much strike.”

World.content:

The NSW Liberal MP whose 690-word speech sparked the corruption watchdog’s investigation into his own party says he would pay the price of whistleblowing again as he announced he will exit politics at the 2027 election. In announcing his resignation, Ray Williams acknowledged the personal toll of exposing allegations of impropriety within his own party. His sole motivation in making the “unpleasant decision” was to ensure the Liberal Party upheld the “highest standards possible”. Liberal backbencher Ray Williams announced he will exit politics at the next election. Wolter Peeters “I want to make it clear that at no time have my actions been motivated by any malice or personal agenda. In fact, I knew that I would be shunned as most whistleblowers are, right or wrong. I happened to be right and more so than I initially understood,” the Kellyville MP wrote. “There is no place for corruption in any organisation including my own. However, the sad reality is that in Australia, as a whistleblower, career opportunities quickly disappear and people choose not to associate themselves with you.”



Related Article Operation Rosny The late-night speech that blew apart the NSW Liberals The veteran MP wrote that regardless of that, he would “do it all again if ever I was faced with the choice of doing the right thing on behalf of my party and my community”. The statement, which circulated among Liberal MPs on Tuesday afternoon and obtained by the Herald, is expected to be formally released on Wednesday morning. In a parliamentary speech in 2022, Williams detailed his concerns about “undemocratic political processes” within the Liberal Party, questioning how popularly elected mayor Michelle Byrne and six sitting Liberal councillors were replaced by the Liberals’ state executive “without the usual preselection processes normally afforded to such positions”. The backbencher alleged Christian Ellis and other senior members of the party “were paid significant funds” to install new councillors on The Hills Shire Council who would support property developer Jean Nassif future development applications.



Then-Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet referred Williams’ claims to the Independent Commission Against Corruption the next morning. The allegations sparked the corruption watchdog’s high-profile Operation Rosny probe which finished public hearings in late September. Presiding commissioner Fabian Gleeson, SC, has 180 days after final submissions to hand down his findings from the blockbuster corruption inquiry. William’s exit leaves Byrne as the early frontrunner to succeed him in his northwestern Sydney electorate, said a Liberal source on the condition of anonymity so they could speak freely. With Australia’s migration settings facing severe political pressure, the former state multiculturalism minister said he dedicated himself to “ensuring everyone who called NSW home and did the right thing, was treated equally and respectfully”.



“Sydney can be proud that we have integrated more people from cultural backgrounds more successfully than any other city in Australia,” he wrote. Williams joins Liberal James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor as the party MPs who will exit politics in March next year. World.title: The new tech shopping for you while you sleep
World.content:
LifestyleFashionMelbourne Fashion Week The new tech shopping for you while you sleep Courtney Thompson October 20, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of the most memorable scenes from the 1995 cult classic film Clueless (a movie full of memorable scenes) occurs early on, inside Cher Horowitz’s bedroom. After waking up, Horowitz, played by Alicia Silverstone, walks over to her closet and consults a computer for what she should wear to school that day. The computer shows her different combinations of her clothes, and informs her when something clashes via an aggressive “MISS-MATCH” warning. When she finds an outfit she wants to wear, it gives her an image of what it would look like on her. In 1995, the scene felt like a far-flung possibility. In 2026, it’s not that far off how AI is shaping the way we interact with fashion and shopping today. Models wearing local designers Perple (left) and Gotham (right), who “reject AI perfectionism”. Justin McManus Like all industries, AI is disrupting fashion. In 2023, Oroton was one of the first local labels to experiment with augmented reality (AR) similar to Cher’s computer in Clueless, unveiling AR windows at the Queen Victoria Building in Sydney and Queen Street Mall in Brisbane where customers could virtually try on their bags in the windows.



Since then, AI has become deeply embedded in every stage of how people shop online, improving fit recommendations, virtual try-on, trend forecasting and stock management. Related Article Fashion Week The style lesson to borrow from Nicole Kidman’s Paris Fashion Week look According to a new report by Stripe and Thoughtworks, 81 per cent of shoppers in Australia and New Zealand have already used AI to help them shop online. “Most use it for advice rather than buying and the businesses we talk to are asking, not whether this is coming, but how quickly they need to build the trust, capability and infrastructure to keep up,” says Kathryn Heffernan, Thoughtworks managing director for retail and travel, APAC. One of the most recent developments has been agentic commerce, with spending on the technology projected to grow from $5 billion to $47 billion by 2030.



Traditionally, when you shop online you do all the work: search, scroll, filter, compare and then buy. Agentic commerce outsources the bulk of that labour to an AI assistant. You tell the assistant what you’re looking for – “a cotton midi dress for a summer wedding that is under $300 and will arrive by the end of the week” – then it goes out, finds sites with options in your size, and compares them for you. If you allow it, the assistant can also make the purchase. In 1995, Cher Horowitz used a computer program to help pick out fashionable outfits. Today, 81 per cent of shoppers do too. CBS via Getty Images Heffernan says it’s a welcome advancement for time-poor people who want to cut back on the admin of online shopping.



“Comparing options is tedious: opening tabs, checking fabrics, decoding size charts. An AI assistant can read product descriptions, reviews and size guides in seconds and pull them into one side-by-side summary,” she explains. “Done well, it can also help people buy less but better. When it’s easy to compare fabrics, care instructions and reviews, you can make a more considered choice rather than an impulse one. That depends on the tool being built to serve the shopper rather than to push more sales, which is why trust matters so much.” In this process, however, the joy of discovery is lost. Ask any fashion editor, and they’ll tell you about the meditative state they enter when they start trawling online websites for the specific cut of black pants they’ve spent months searching for. Likewise, designers are still figuring out how they can meaningfully integrate AI into their business without affecting their creative output.



Editor's pick Trends Is it a belt? Is it a corset? No, it’s a cummerbund “AI has helped me code my website and add plugins that track sales and improve the site layout,” says Gautam Kapoor, founder and designer of Melbourne-based label Gotham. While the technology is helpful, Kapoor isn’t worried about it impeding their creativity. “AI usually creates from what has already come before. Designing involves going back and forth with an idea many times, and that push and pull is what creates something original and unique,” Kapoor says. “In fashion, this happens in the toiling process, when prototyping a garment, and I don’t believe AI could replicate that.” On Wednesday evening, Gotham will be one of nine designers showing designs as part of the Cult Status runway at Melbourne Fashion Week.



Chris Ran Lin, Club Venus, Hunter Gatherer x BSL, Liandra, Perple, R.Sport, Toilè Studios, Wah-Wah Australia and Wilson Jedd Adams are all inspired by subcultures that sprout from the underground, their work challenging the hyper-perfection of AI in favour of experimentation and individuality. “AI has made me value the importance of the creative journey at a deeper level and appreciate the unique perspective designers across all mediums bring to their art form,” says Huiliana Chandra-Curry, designer of slow fashion label, Perple. “Without a doubt, the importance of well-made, intentional garments will continue to command respect and attention. In an era where AI models will homogenise aesthetics, there is an opportunity for originators to find their people.” See more from Melbourne Fashion Week: A look from sustainable fashion brand Amy Cottrell on the runway at Melbourne Fashion Week 2026. World.content:
NationalWACourts What tobacco crime kings pay enforcers to blow up rival Perth stores Rebecca Peppiatt October 20, 2026 — 6:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The paltry amount crime bosses will pay someone to do their dirty work has been revealed in court as a man who helped ram raid and set fire to a Midland tobacco shop was sentenced. Darryl John Campton, 23, was a drug addict and a career criminal somehow recruited by an organised crime gang in November 2025 to target a store that refused to sell their illegal vapes and smokes. Loading Now he’s heading to jail for his involvement and he didn’t even get paid. Campton was sentenced on Tuesday in the Perth District Court to 4½ years over a spate of offending in September and November 2025, that included the raid on the Great Eastern Highway shop that caused almost $20,000 worth of damage.



The incident was caught on CCTV with Campton seen in the footage with two other men using a stolen car and a street sign to “battery ram” the metal shutters on the front of the shop. They’re later seen peeling apart the metal so they can get inside, pour some fuel from a jerry can and set the shop on fire before fleeing the scene. Campton was paid $5,000 for being the getaway driver. One of his co-offenders carried out the task in return for having his drug debt wiped. Judge Belinda Lonsdale said Campton was “susceptible to pressure from peers” as a result of “a dysfunctional childhood” that included abuse, leading to drug use and anti-social behaviour.



During the hearing, the 23-year-old was also sentenced over a terrifying nighttime burglary in which he woke the occupant of an Iluka property by standing in his bedroom doorway with a hatchet in his hand and a bandana covering his face. He told him to be quiet before stealing keys to a BMW which he later dumped in nearby bushland. He was arrested and confessed to the crime, but two months later was at it again, this time breaking into the home of a Craigie acquaintance. It was his car that was used an hour or so later in the Midland ram raid. The court was told Campton’s history of offending and drug use stretched back into his childhood, including a suggestion he was suffering from fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. “The impetus for this offending is to feed his long-standing and insatiable drug habit,” the court was told. Judge Lonsdale sentenced him to a total of 4½ years in prison – two years for his involvement in the attack on the Midland store which is the same sentence as one of his co-offenders.

World.title: Security briefing for anxious MPs as Helen Haines loses leg, remains in critical condition
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Security briefing for anxious MPs as Helen Haines loses leg, remains in critical condition Natassia Chrysanthos Updated October 20, 2026 — 6:50pm ,first published 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Follow live updates on the Helen Haines attack Australian intelligence agencies will brief anxious federal politicians about a worsening security environment on Wednesday as independent MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition after being struck by a four-wheel drive outside her regional Victorian office. The member for Indi, 65, lost one of her legs and surgeons were trying to save the other at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital on Tuesday. Police held suspect Brendan Nugent, 43, in custody as they investigated potential motives for what they are treating as a targeted attack. The town of Wangaratta came together on Tuesday, just hours after the horrific attack on Helen Haines. Jason South Haines’ parliamentary colleagues described the former nurse and midwife as “the best of us” as they grappled with the rare act of violence against a sitting MP, while the town of Wangaratta, in north-east Victoria, held a vigil and laid flowers outside her office.



The attack on Haines has alarmed state and federal MPs who have been subject to increasingly threatening behaviour in recent years. As One Nation leader Pauline Hanson blamed state premiers and the prime minister for enabling division and hatred, other MPs said it was time for reflection, not finger pointing. The Home Affairs Department, ASIO and Australian Federal Police will address parliamentarians in several sessions on Wednesday, while Victoria is contemplating increased security at next month’s state election. “Everyone in public office carries a level of risk now, everyone,” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said on Tuesday. Federal police have received 1067 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against high officeholders in 2025-26, up from 951 the financial year before. Former independent Indi MP Cathy McGowan, left, and a Haines supporter at a service in Wangaratta. Jason South But Haines seemed to MPs and her constituents an unlikely target, and politicians across the political divide on Tuesday described the non-partisan MP as a kind, decent, respectful and community-driven local member.



“When you go through the different scale of who we would have thought was the most at risk, no one would have thought Helen Haines,” Burke said. “Everybody looks at that and thinks, if it was Helen, it could have been me. Everyone is aware of that. But all our thoughts right now are with Helen.” Witnesses said Haines was retrieving items from the boot of her car on Monday afternoon when a white Toyota LandCruiser conducted a U-turn to ram her against a vehicle, before reversing and hitting her a second time. In what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has labelled a heroic act, barbershop owner Ricky Jefferies intervened by running to the driver’s side of the vehicle and wrestling him to the ground before waiting for authorities to arrive. Ricky Jefferies, the man who detained the alleged attacker, outside his barbershop. Jason South Victoria Police is leading the investigation, supported by the state’s counterterrorism team, the Australian Federal Police and ASIO. Police raided Nugent’s sprawling property near Wangaratta on Monday night, and it remained cordoned off by detectives on Tuesday.



Neighbours described Nugent as an unemployed man with few friends, and said they had become increasingly concerned about his erratic behaviour. He was involved in a road rage incident near Wangaratta last month, where he allegedly threatened a woman with a hammer, but no charges have been laid. The Tarrawingee man has a history of environmental activism but sources who knew him said he had changed dramatically since protesting logging in the local forest. Nugent’s social media history reveals he previously praised Haines and backed her independent campaign in the area. More recently, his posts focused on international issues, including criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza. The property where Brendan Nugent lived. Jason South His father, Rod Nugent, on Tuesday afternoon revealed Haines was a friend for more than 20 years. “What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” he said in a statement. “All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends. We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.”



ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said Monday’s incident had happened in an environment where increased levels of grievance, intolerance and polarisation had made violence seem permissible. “I have repeatedly put on the record my concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse. Words matter,” Burgess said in a statement. “I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meets with law enforcement heads in Victoria. Paul Rovere Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said 41 people had been charged with offences relating to threats against high office holders, including politicians, since special national security investigation teams were launched last October.



Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said extra security measures could be imposed at voting booths at next month’s state election, while NSW Premier Chris Minns said he feared such incidents would deter other people from running for political office. Related Article Haines attack Suspect in Helen Haines attack once praised the MP online and had raised concern among neighbours Independent senator David Pocock described it as a “wake-up call”. “As a male parliamentarian, you get some threats. You get the angry phone calls, the awful emails, the anonymous comments,” he said. “But I think we’ve got to look at what’s happening to female politicians, and just the ridiculous amount of threats and abuse that they have to cop, and as Australians, we need to stand up and say this is not OK.” Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Coalition MPs had often discussed the increased threat of political violence as he stressed the importance of keeping an Australian culture of vigorous debate that never crossed the line into violence.



“We need to do everything we can as elected representatives to prevent this ever happening again,” he said. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Haines was a “lovely lady” who worked tirelessly for her community, while Greens leader David Shoebridge said the notion that Haines could be targeted for her work was “horrifying, senseless and shameful”. Hanson described Haines as a “beautiful lady” before blaming Albanese and state premiers for the deteriorating state of political debate. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, whose own security has been recently upgraded, criticised that response. “We all have a role to play and it can’t just be finger pointing. I think it’s a bad move to point the finger on a day like this,” he said. Hanson also revealed she had ordered her cartoon creator to change a One Nation video that mocked Senator Jacqui Lambie’s struggles with vaginal prolapse. After Lambie condemned the cartoon on Monday, Hanson said she should “have a laugh” and “get over it”.



But on Tuesday, she changed tone. “The video went up without my actually seeing it, and I was not aware of the content of the video,” Hanson said. “It wasn’t as tastefully done as it could have been, and I do apologise for that. I’ve already spoken to them about it and changing that.” With Nick Newling and Emily Kaine More from our Helen Haines coverage

World.title: Star skipper departs as Collingwood’s disastrous season plunges into crisis
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 Star skipper departs as Collingwood’s disastrous season plunges into crisis Hannah Kennelly Updated October 20, 2026 — 6:41pm ,first published October 20, 2026 — 10:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Collingwood’s AFLW team is in crisis after captain Ruby Schleicher announced her departure amid ongoing concerns from senior players about the direction of the women’s program. On Tuesday morning, Schleicher – an inaugural player and dual All-Australian – announced she would not re-sign with Collingwood and would instead return home to Western Australia. Collingwood skipper Ruby Schleicher. Getty Images In an emotional farewell video, the 28-year-old – who had her arm in a sling following a season-ending injury in round nine – fought back tears and said it was time for her to return home and spend time with her family. Her departure comes at a pivotal time for the club, as it faces calls to change its struggling women’s program, with several senior players voicing concerns about a lack of improvement and direction.



To make matters worse, the Pies are anchored near the bottom of the ladder with just one win from 10 matches and facing a potential exodus of players who are out of contract at the end of 2026, including Tarni White, Sarah Rowe, Mattea Breed, Lauren Butler and Bri Davey. Related Article Analysis

AFLW They’re an AFL powerhouse. So why can’t Collingwood’s women’s team find success? Vice-captain Jordyn Allen signed a three-year deal in 2024, but tried to seek a trade to the Brisbane Lions last year. Collingwood initially offered Schleicher a one-year-contract extension, but later bumped that up to two, as their skipper weighed up leaving the club and the impact that would have on the extensive media opportunities she has in Melbourne, including her work as a commentator and presenter for Fox Footy. But the skipper’s untimely departure has given Magpies fans a sense of déjà vu after losing star player Chloe Molloy in 2023 amid the club’s consistent struggles to perform on field.



“This has been a really tough decision to come to, but one that, sitting with it probably feels the best for me and my career and my life at the moment and that’s to head home back west,” she said in announcing her departure on Tuesday. “It’s clearly not a decision that’s probably even still sitting completely right, I’m not sure if it will, it may take a long time to.” West Coast are the front-runners for the inaugural player’s signature, offering a four-year contract. Schleicher informed her teammates on Tuesday morning that she was leaving.



“I can’t put into words the gratitude I feel for this place and the role it has played in helping me grow up,” Schleicher said in a statement. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Why I have an issue with the Nick Blakey trade to North Melbourne Peter Ryan Sports reporter “Being an 18-year-old coming across, those first couple of years away from home, as someone who is really close to their family, was something I struggled with. “This has been a really tough decision for me to make but one that is ultimately the best for where I am in my life and career. “The family that Collingwood has become for me – the staff, admin, footy department and the girls I’ve played with – has meant so much.



“I’ll always consider myself a Collingwood person, and thank you to the Magpie army, who have embraced me, whether it’s walking down the street or at our games.” Former No.1 draft pick Ash Centra posted a lengthy tribute to Schleicher on social media, praising her as a leader, mentor and friend. “Thank you for leading by example, for the way you carry yourself and for the way you care for people,” Centra posted. “You’ve taught me so much, not just about footy but about life, about believing in myself, about being a better person, and about what it really means to show up for the people around you.”



Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly also released a statement thanking Schleicher for her contribution and praising her leadership skills. “Ruby has represented the black and white with great resilience and character and has played a key role in supporting the next generation of Collingwood players on and off the field,” Kelly said. Collingwood Football Club chief executive Craig Kelly. AAP “While we are disappointed to see Ruby depart our club, we respect her decision to return home. We thank Ruby for everything she has given to Collingwood and wish her all the very best for the next chapter.” Brit Bonnici will become the only inaugural player left on Collingwood’s AFLW list.





Schleicher’s announcement came just one week after Kelly met with the Pies’ AFLW team and staff to address concerns about the club’s women’s the program. In a recent interview, Kelly told the Herald Sun he and the club were “fully committed” to turning around the side and rejected claims he did not care about women’s football. St Kilda recently announced an independent investigation ino their program following their poor season and resignation of long-time coach Nick Dal Santo, however Kelly ruled out commissioning an external review at Collingwood. Collingwood declined to comment further when contacted by this masthead. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘As tall as you can go’: The NYC-style density plan for Melbourne’s future
World.content:
NationalVictoriaMelbourne Assembly ‘As tall as you can go’: The NYC-style density plan for Melbourne’s future Angelica Snowden and Alex Crowe October 20, 2026 — 6:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio has implored Melburnians to embrace high-rise, high-density living as the city’s population races towards 9 million. But as de Blasio decried urban sprawl – constructing homes further away from city centres on urban fringes – as a “massive failure” of the Western world, former Victorian premier Steve Bracks told The Age’s Melbourne Assembly on Tuesday that it could be too late. Former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio argued for an end to urban sprawl at Tuesday’s Melbourne Assembly event. Justin McManus “I think the genie is already out of the bottle. We are already a sprawling city,” Bracks said. “What we need is a hard full stop on the city. We should be protecting the green wedges … [and] encouraging our planning scheme development at activity centres around our transport hubs.”



Held at Federation Square, the second day of the inaugural forum brought together industry leaders, decision-makers and the community. As well as the pillar of shaping the city, it focused on education and innovation, with experts discussing how to attract and keep the brightest minds and commercialise research breakthroughs. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Melbourne Assembly day two as it happened: PM, ex-New York mayor share visions for more liveable Melbourne Melbourne’s planning policies were at the centre of the debate, ahead of next month’s state election in which Labor’s “activity centres” are on the ballot, with the Coalition vowing to abolish the zones where developers are allowed to bypass local planning rules to build high-rises up to 20 storeys. The government implemented the plan in response to surging house prices and population growth, with activity centres spread across the city near transport hubs in a bid to shift population growth away from the urban fringes into established suburbs. Bracks pointed out that Melbourne was five times the size of New York, and suggested that instead of imitating de Blasio’s hometown, increased density should be targeted in the activity centres.



The former New York City mayor, however, urged authorities to “reverse” sprawl and build “as tall as you can go” closer to the CBD, backed by careful planning to include amenities and services. “The reality of people’s quality of life, living far from the centre is going to get harder and harder,” he said. “People want culture and connection more than ever. You must embrace height and density. You must turn away from sprawl.” Loading It may be politically easier to sprawl, but it is more costly to society, Grattan Institute chief executive Aruna Sathanapally told the forum’s panel on shaping the city. Where developers invest in the construction of homes on urban fringes, the cost of supplying residents with access to jobs, and infrastructure for water, electricity and roads is straddled to state governments, she said. “I don’t accept that it’s cheaper if you actually take those costs into account to sprawl. It can be much more efficient to use infrastructure densely in your existing cities,” said Sathanapally, who pointed out that the handbrake on density was the rising cost of construction and poor construction productivity.



Architect Sarah Lynn Rees also advocated for greater density – but in a way that connects people to their homes and neighbourhoods, and factors in the needs of families. “We’re putting people in white boxes and expecting them to live a life of thriving within their community, but they’re so disconnected from it, and they don’t have the space that they need,” Rees said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the Melbourne Assembly. Justin McManus Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used his address to reveal Victoria would receive $350 million in federal funding to connect “last mile infrastructure”, particularly basic utilities, to new housing in the state’s growing suburbs and regions. In the face of criticisms of urban sprawl, Albanese nodded to the outer suburbs including Frankston, Point Cook, Dandenong, Melton, Sunbury and Cranbourne as the “powerhouse” of Melbourne.



Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece said density was a key plank of the City of Melbourne’s 25-year city plan, including its target of building 120,000 new homes in the next 25 years. He pointed to Fishermans Bend, Macaulay, Arden and West Melbourne as having “huge tracts of land”. “Melbourne is blessed in that it has plenty of underutilised land that can be developed very close to the city,” he said. Loading “These areas can accommodate our population growth in sustainable, high-density suburbs with plenty of green space.” But he said it was crucial major infrastructure was delivered by the state government based on long-term strategic planning and independent advice, not the “short-term political considerations and electoral maps” that influenced projects such as the Suburban Rail Loop and the West Gate Tunnel.



“I would urge the next government, whoever it is at the end of November, to reverse the decision to abolish Infrastructure Victoria and preserve its independence,” he said. “Any proposed major project should be subject to independent analysis … the government of the day can then select from this menu. If it’s not on the menu, then you can’t go committing billions of dollars, leaving it to future generations to pay off.” Loading The education and innovation debate was kicked off by Professor Marek Tesar, the faculty of education dean at the University of Melbourne, the presenting partner for Melbourne Assembly. The internationally recognised scholar in early childhood education asked the audience to consider who the future Melbourne was being designed for, pointing out that a four-year-old living here today would by 2080 have experienced more than half a century of the decisions being discussed.



“We need to ask the four-year-olds,” he said, urging leaders to consider the views of children who refused to “accept that the world must remain effectively as it is”. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly “I’d love to see Melbourne develop a network of youth innovation hubs connected to schools, libraries, universities and neighbourhoods across the city,” Tesar added. “Places where all young people could work with mentors on real problems: biodiversity, disability access, loneliness, robotics, transport, housing, climate change ... not just classroom exercises.” Doherty Institute director Professor Sharon Lewin took up the theme with her insights into how Melbourne can become the destination of choice for the world’s best researchers and innovators. Lewin, who runs the world-renowned biomedical research hub in the Parkville precinct, spoke about what could be learnt from Australia’s past and the way her parents were welcomed from war-torn Europe as survivors of the Holocaust.



“The great cities of the future will compete for many things: for investment, for technology, for companies. But above all, they will compete for people,” she said. “Talent will go somewhere. We need to welcome that talent … Just as Australia did all those years ago for my parents.” Lewin also argued for a more comprehensive effort to achieve bigger economic gains from Melbourne’s research capability. “We are really good at discovery. We’re not always that good at what happens next,” she said. Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website.

World.title: Search underway for man in kayak who went into the sea at Waihi Beach
World.content:
A search is underway for a man who went kayaking at Waihi Beach.

Police said the man went into the sea on Tuesday morning and had not been seen since.

A police spokesperson said a search and rescue operation was underway at the beach after the man was reported missing about 5.40pm.

The kayak was described to be blue with black and white mottled (camo) colour, and was a single seated sit-on-top vessel.

World.title: Ministry of Education pushes back on claims Gloriavale school shut down was rushed
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has pushed back on claims the process to shut down Gloriavale's school was rushed.

The ministry defended its decision to cancel the school's registration in the High Court at Wellington during the second and final day of a judicial review challenging the move.

The Secretary for Education Ellen Macgregor-Reid has twice tried to close the West Coast Christian community's school over student safety concerns.

On Tuesday, counsel for the ministry, Victoria Casey KC disputed Gloriavale's position that the Secretary had only one day to consider relevant information before making her decision.

Counsel for the ministry, Victoria Casey KC. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"She had one working day and a weekend, and with respect the level of annotation throughout the entire report... doesn't support the submission that she didn't pay proper attention to it."

Casey said the entire process took five months which was neither truncated nor unfair - an argument that Gloriavale's lawyer, Richard Raymond KC, did not accept.

Raymond and Casey also tussled over whether Macgregor-Reid's second decision to cancel the 80-student school's registration was a continuation of a process initiated in 2025 or a fresh examination.

Macgregor-Reid first moved to shut down the school in December last year, but it remains open due to the legal challenge by the school's board.

She again confirmed the cancellation in September following a failed Education Review Office (ERO) report that found the school was not a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

Raymond argued the second review of the school had been a "fresh look" and the Secretary missed cruicial steps in the process, such as issuing a notice to comply.

Gloriavale's lawyer, Richard Raymond KC. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

But Casey said such a notice issued in July 2025 remained relevant and argued the school was "absolutely on notice" about the Secretary's safety concerns pointing to December's cancellation bid and a letter to the board in April.

Casey also challenged the request by Gloriavale for the Court to correct the record in relation to information provided to RNZ under the Official Information Act.

The "disputed information" reported by RNZ in June, concerned a letter from ERO to Oranga Tamariki expressing wellbeing concerns, including that Gloriavale's school "knowingly employed staff with prior convictions unsuitable for work with children" and "in at least one instance, the school failed to act when behaviours placing students at risk were identified".

Gloriavale argued the information was false, however, Casey said the Ombudsman rather than the Court was the appropriate place to raise such issues.

Although the "disputed information" wasn't considered by the Secretary in her latest decision, Casey argued that the "substance of the concern was very real," citing a teacher's guilty plea to an historic assault and a recent complaint of an historic sexual assault committed by a staff member.

She said ERO had concluded there was a pattern of institutional failure to act on known risks to children.

Raymond asserted that the board had acted appropriately in response to the recently surfaced allegation.

Justice Karen Grau thanked the parties for the quality of their interesting but dense submissions, warning the public gallery packed with Gloriavale supporters that her decision would take time.

World.title: Police officer who stole police-issued firearm starred in police recruitment series
World.content:
A police officer who stole a police-issued firearm starred in a police recruitment series, and was awarded the Commissioner's Award for leadership in his recruit wing, it can now be revealed.

RNZ earlier revealed a police officer had been charged with stealing a police-issued firearm and being in unlawful possession of a police-issued firearm.

On Tuesday, the officer Steven John Karehana pleaded guilty to the charges. Following his guilty plea an interim suppression order was lifted. Karehana will be sentenced in December.

The summary of facts said Karehana graduated from Police College in October 2024, and was stationed in Whanganui.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

At the time of the offending he was assigned to a team that was based out of an agency site on Victoria Ave, Whanganui.

In March, 2026, police carried out an audit of police-owned firearms in the Central District policing area.

The audit confirmed a glock was missing, presumed stolen on or about 11 February, 2026. The glock is worth $1204.

The summary said the glock was one of several police firearms that were stored among four locked gun safes on the ground floor of the Whanganui Police Station.

Prior to the gun going missing, Karehana asked an associate if they would be able to get rid of a gun if he delivered one to them. The associate said they would.

About 7.15am on 11 February, Karehana entered the Whanaganui Police Station to begin his shift which started at 8am. He then took two glocks and two M4 rifles from the gun safe and put them into lockboxes in a police car.

He and his colleague for the day then went to the Victoria Ave site. Karehana returned to the police station alone about 1.40pm and accessed the gun safe which housed the glock.

"The defendant removed the glock and placed it into his backpack before leaving the building and driving home," the summary said.

"A short time after arriving at his home address in Martin, the defendant delivered the glock to the associate.

"This associate subsequently supplied the glock to another associate and obtained $10,000 cash for it."

Karehana did not know that his associate was going to on sell the weapon, the summary said. That evening Karehana was given $5000.

The glock was recovered by police in June.

When spoken to by police, Karehana denied the allegations.

The 42-year-old starred in the police recruitment video series, Ride Along.

His parts in the series appear to have since been removed from YouTube, and his name has been removed from a press release about the series.

In one episode seen by RNZ, Karehana spoke of his journey to joining the Police.

"I guess for me it was a long journey. Took me around about 20 years from my first application to being accepted into police college, and I've been out for about four months now.

"So I first applied in 2003, and I was denied because of what had happened in my youth, and I applied probably every five years after that until I got a job as a painter, and I stayed in that job for 16 years.

"It wasn't until I went and worked for my iwi, and through that journey, it reignited the love and passion for my community and my people."

A screen grab from Ride Along. NZ Police/Youtube

He said being an older recruit he brought "different life skills, life experiences to the police".

"My why for joining is to be a role model for our people.

"By showing them rather than just talking about it, it can go a long way into helping build those relationships once again."

Karehana's name has also been removed by Police from a press release put out in October 2024 celebrating Wing 378.

The original version, seen by RNZ, said he was awarded the Commissioner's Leadership Award.

"This is the beginning of our journey in the New Zealand Police, but for all of us graduating, there are many people who have sacrificed and worked hard to allow us to be here, and we are very grateful. We could not have done it without you.

"The call to service is one few answer, but it is a selfless sacrifice to put community above self and by graduating today we have all joined a proud and selfless organisation."

In a statement to RNZ, Central District Commander Dion Bennett acknowledged Karehana's guilty plea.

"While I am pleased that Mr Karehana has been prepared to accept responsibility for his actions, I know that I and all his former colleagues are bitterly disappointed that he let down the mana of our uniform but we will all work hard to repair the damage he's caused."

Bennett said as a consequence of Karehana's actions police had removed him from promotional materials in which he featured.

"He has demonstrated that he no longer holds the same values that previously led him to be selected for inclusion in Police promotions," he said.

World.title: Two girls injured after falling from Ferris wheel at Greymouth agricultural show
World.content:
Correction: An earlier version of this article stated three men were injured after falling from a ferris wheel at Rolling Meadows Festival. Two were injured.

Two teenage girls are recovering from injuries suffered in a fall from a Ferris wheel at an agricultural trade show in Greymouth over the weekend.

The girls fell several metres from the ride at AgFest West Coast and hit another girl on the ground on Saturday afternoon.

AgFest West Coast managing director Andy Thompson said it was unclear how far or why the girls fell, and WorkSafe had been notified.

"I didn't witness the incident myself, but it is fair to say more than two or three metres from what I can tell, and possibly more than that," he said.

Thompson said he had spoken to the mother of the girl who was hit on the ground, who said she was okay, but concerned for the teens.

"The other two girls, I have not had a direct report yet from the authorities on their wellbeing but I understand their injuries were minor - still that is just very, very lucky that they weren't injured any further," he said.

Thompson said everyone else was asked to get off the Ferris wheel. Operator Sturgeon Amusements shut down the ride and contacted the safety regulator.

He said police took photos and secured the scene.

The event ran from Friday to Saturday and was only 30 minutes from closing when the girls fell, Thompson said.

"We'd had an incredibly successful day with over 10,000 people attending so it was a real shame that in the final few minutes an incident occurred. All the protocols and procedures we had in place, with the on-ground medical staff, police and communications with St John meant it was handled quickly and professionally."

Sturgeon Amusements has been contacted for comment.

A WorkSafe spokesperson confirmed the regulator had been notified and inspectors were making enquiries to understand the circumstances of the fall.

"An inspector has issued a prohibition notice while our enquiries are ongoing. This notice prevents use of the Ferris wheel while a competent person is engaged to assess the Ferris wheel and provide a report to the owner, Sturgeon Amusements Ltd, and WorkSafe," the spokesperson said.

Two men were injured after falling from a Ferris wheel operated by Event Hire at Rolling Meadows Festival in Christchurch on New Year's Day.

World.title: Scott Watson's appeal being heard in Supreme Court
World.content:
Scott Watson's defence lawyers argue police pressured and "primed" a key witness to identify Watson as the man he saw boarding a yacht with Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in the early hours of New Years' Day.

The argument came as Watson's appeal of his double-murder conviction is being heard in the Supreme Court.

Watson was sentenced to life imprisonment for murdering Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in the Marlborough Sounds and has now been behind bars for 27 years.

The Blenheim friends, aged 21 and 17, were last seen stepping off a water taxi onto a stranger's yacht in Endeavour Inlet the early hours of 1 January, 1998, after a New Year's Eve party at Furneaux Lodge.

Their bodies have never been found.

Watson was found guilty of the murders in 1999 after an 11-week jury trial involving about 500 witnesses.

He appealed his convictions after the trial but the application was dismissed. He made another two applications that were unsuccessful before a 2017 bid for a royal pardon was granted, with the case heard by the Court of Appeal in 2024.

Watson's Supreme Court appeal focuses on one key point - the photo identification process used in the original trial.

Ben Smart and Olivia Hope. NZ Police

Water taxi driver Guy Wallace identified Watson by photo montage on 20 April 1998 as the mystery man with Smart and Hope boarding a yacht - the last place they were ever seen.

Defence lawyer Nick Chisnell KC said that photo montage evidence was "inadmissible" and "tainted", but had been a "crucial part" of the Crown's case.

Chisnell said by the time Wallace was shown the montage, it was about three and a half months after Watson was identified as the suspect, and Hope and Smart disappeared.

"We say that it was profoundly contaminated by outside influences earlier in the investigation," Chisnell said.

He said police had had already shown Wallace a photo of Watson in early January 1998, but Wallace had told police he didn't recognise the man.

Chisnell argued police pressured Wallace in the days after this, saying Watson had been identified by others as the "lone" man, the "sleazy" man, the "mystery man", which suggested he was the key suspect.

"Media saturation" also identified Watson as a suspect and his boat Blade as featuring heavily in the investigation, Chisnell said.

"Then we say the final nail in the unfairness coffin, is the fact that the police created an unfair and improper montage that predisposed Mr Wallace and others to select Mr Watson."

Chisnell referred to expert evidence raised the Court of Appeal which criticised the photo identification process as a "show up" - by police showing a single photo of Watson, and their naming of him to Wallace, they "directly communicated" to an eye-witness who the central suspect was.

"...In my submission, police primed Mr Wallace to identify Mr Watson, and that tainted the identification procedure in that point onwards."

Chisnell KC said a detective applied "moral pressure" to Wallace in a video interview, suggesting he wasn't telling the truth about who he saw, and that he needed to for Smart and Hope's families.

Chisnell also criticised the photograph of Watson police used in Montage B, with his eyes only half open.

He said police could have used other photographs with Watson's eyes fully open, taken from a front on perspective, similar to photos of other people they provided.

He said that Wallace said at time of the trial that he was drawn to this characteristic of the eyes in the photo montage, in the context of a trial about a party and intoxication.

Watson's second lawyer Kerry Cook KC said if this appeal is successful, there shouldn't be a retrial, due to the effect of the passage of time and the media involvement, including news coverage, and books.

"That's very difficult to unwind."

Wallace - a key eyewitness - had died, Cook KC said.

"This case is singular in the way in which the media and the nation has been captured by it, and that has implications."

World.title: Taranaki conservation projects convinced AI can be force for good
World.content:
Two Taranaki conservation initiatives are convinced artificial intelligence can be a force for good in the environmental space.

The 800 Trust is planting native trees and managing pests over about 1600 hectares of retired farmland and former forests in the East Taranaki back country.

It has developed Hark, which uses acoustic sensors and AI to record and monitor forests, analysing bird calls, detecting pests and tracking changes in the environment over time.

Project lead Miranda Wells said AI had huge potential to make wildlife monitoring faster and more affordable.

"Hark is basically a listening device, but it's on the edge, and when I say on the edge, it does all its processing on the device itself, and it's able to listen to many and run many, many AI models in real time and give real time alerts of what has been heard, and that could be a bird, that could be a pest or that could be a chainsaw."

Wells said the device sent a notification to a cellphone and decisions could then be made about what next steps to take.

"So, if your focus is that you're trying to find the last possum in an area, and you get a notification in real time that it's just detected a possum.

"Then you listen to it and you're able to get out of your pyjamas and put your Swanndri on and go out there and find that possum, or if you're after a particular rare bird and you want to know when it's coming into your area so that you can do extra pest control. It also does that for you."

Wells said Hark empowered landowners, individuals, iwi and hapu to understand what was going on in a particular space, in the taiao, the environment.

The 800 Trust and another Taranaki organisation - Wildlife.ai - were recently among 16 Asia Pacific organisations selected to join Google Deepmind's AI for the Planet Accelerator.

Wells, who travelled to Singapore for an initial week-long boot camp with another member of the 800 Trust team, said they worked alongside DeepMind experts and were now working to push the project along before returning to Asia in December.

"Working with Google DeepMind provides an exciting opportunity to push that technology further and explore applications that could benefit conservation projects both here in Taranaki and around the world."

Miranda Wells says AI has huge potential to make wildlife monitoring faster and more affordable. Robin Martin

Wells said despite some personal reservations about the pace AI was progressing at, she was enthusiastic about its application in the conservation arena.

"It's impossible for humans to be out there across the whole of the country monitoring pest control and so we do need to find smart ways of doing things to achieve our goal of being pest free by 2050, and so AI definitely has a purpose and here is a prime example of where AI can be used for good."

Wildlife.ai is developing Wildlife Watcher, an AI-powered camera which can identify and count smaller mammals, reptiles, and amphibians which are typically harder to monitor using traditional methods.

Biologist Victor Anton from Wildlife.ai said the selection of both organisations for DeepMind was a reflection of the broader innovation and commitment of the Taranaki conservation sector.

"To have two Taranaki organisations included in a cohort of only 16 from around the world shows just how advanced our region is when it comes to conservation.

"When it comes to restoring our natural environment, the world truly is watching Taranaki."

Wildlife.ai was also developing a marine monitoring platform - Spyfish Aotearoa - to analyse underwater footage far faster than traditional methods.

World.title: 'A real concern for the future'-  thousands call for review of Selwyn's water pricing
World.content:
Water charges in Canterbury could reach a point where people simply cannot afford to pay, a Selwyn councillor says, as thousands call for the district's pricing system to be reviewed.

An 18 percent water bill hike took effect in July when council-owned organisation Selwyn Water issued its first invoices, a year after the entity was first established.

A petition calling for changes to the pricing structure has attracted 2500 signatures in a matter of days.

Rolleston ratepayer Byron Clarke said the price increase had been a real shock.

"It's a massive rise for anyone to actually deal with at a time when we've got lots of other financial challenges due to the fuel crisis and the knock-on effect on food and so on," he said.

"I can see myself ending up paying over $6000 a year for my rates and the water. That's a massive increase and a real concern for the future."
