Calls for pricing review as Selwyn water prices spike Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Selwyn councillor Tracey MacLeod said she understood the frustration and households could only absorb so much.

"I'm a ratepayer here, I live here. My friends and family that live here are also seeing the same stuff," she said.

"I am very aware that rates increases and water increases may well reach a point where we're all looking around going nobody's going to pay this."

MacLeod said the council had already pushed back on the size of the increase, which Selwyn Water initially proposed at 24 percent.

Clarke said ratepayers deserved a clearer explanation of why costs had risen so much, questioning whether they were paying for future development in the fast-growing district.

"It looks like current residents are paying the price for the future and things are not ideal," he said.

"If we can understand why these things have happened, why that massive increase has happened, it might make it a bit more bearable."

Selwyn mayor Lydia Gliddon said costs were being driven by higher drinking and wastewater standards set by central government, repairing ageing infrastructure and the demands of a growing district.

Gliddon said the council had asked Selwyn Water for a one-year water services strategy so costs, charging arrangements and efficiencies could be examined before longer-term decisions were made.

Selwyn Water deputy chief executive Heather Geddes acknowledged the 18 percent increase had been difficult for some households.

She said some confusion had also resulted from water charges previously included in council rates now appearing on a separate Selwyn Water bill.

"We know [the 18 percent increase] is for a lot of our customers is still a little bit too much to bear and we need to work on that," she said.

Geddes said about 75 percent of the charges passed on to customers related to infrastructure renewals and compliance requirements, while about 23 percent relates to servicing debt.

Selwyn Water was gathering data during its first year to inform future pricing options and planned to consult ratepayers on what constituted fair charges.

"We're really interested in understanding what the community think are fair charges across the district and how we might be able to create different options to make that happen for them," Geddes said.

Selwyn Water and the district council were also working to fix historic water billing issues.

An investigation revealed that council systems failed to capture about 2700 properties between July 2024 and December last year, resulting in up to 2.9 million in unbilled water charges.

World.title: Tedesco parachutes in as Kangaroos captain in first Test since 2023
World.content:
James Tedesco will be elevated straight to the captaincy when he runs out for his first game for the Kangaroos in three years.

Tedesco has been named at fullback for Australia's men's Rugby League World Cup clash with Fiji in Brisbane on Sunday.

It marks the 33-year-old's first cap in green and gold since the 2023 Pacific Championship final, when he led the Kangaroos to a shock 30-0 loss to New Zealand.

Since his last Test appearance, Tedesco has won back his NSW jersey, claimed last year's Dally M Medal and was the Clive Churchill medallist as Roosters captain earlier this month.

On Sunday night at Lang Park, Tedesco will return to the team after coach Kevin Walters made the decision to rotate through his squad to try to find his best line-up.

Rugby League World Cup quick hits From Kalyn Ponga's magnificent Test debut to a mighty Tongan victory years in the making here are the quick hits from week one of the Rugby League World Cup.

Walters named four debutants in the 23-strong squad, with halfback Sam Walker, centre Bradman Best, hooker Blayke Brailey and back rower David Fifita all set to start.

Walker's debut will double as a play-off with halves partner Tom Dearden as both bye to replace the injured Mitchell Moses in the seven jersey for the rest of the campaign.

The bench and extended squad are filled out by starters from the Kangaroos' 24-22 win over the Kiwis in their tournament opener, including regular captain Isaah Yeo and fullback Reece Walsh, who staked his claim in a barnstorming return from injury with a long-range solo try and a try-saver on opposite number Kalyn Ponga.

If Tedesco aims up, it could leave Walters with a major selection call to make at the pointy end of the tournament.

"Those big moments; he hadn't played in six, seven weeks but he turned up in big moments and nailed them," Tedesco, the oldest member of the squad at 33, said of Walsh.

"He was great all week, asking for advice, but it's not a competition. I've got an opportunity and all I can do is make the most of it and do my role.

"Walshy does things on the field so it's about knowing my game and being an experienced leader.

"Walshy, he was soaking up anything I had to say last week and I enjoy that role."

World.title: Aussie Opal's block fires Dream to WNBA finals win
World.content:
Australian rookie Izzy Borlase has helped the Atlanta Dream to their historic first WNBA finals victory, shining in a series-levelling 79–65 triumph over Golden State.

Dream superstar Angel Reese was a dominant figure in game two at San Francisco's Chase Center on Monday (Tuesday AEDT), posting a monster double-double with 30 points and 16 rebounds.

The Dream's win was their first in a title-deciding best-of-seven series, after being swept in their three previous appearances and losing game one against the Valkyries this year.

Coach Karl Smesko's team will enjoy home-court advantage in the next two games as they chase their first WNBA championship.

Borlase could play a key role after being entrusted with almost 17 minutes on court in game two, finishing with two points, one assist, one steal and one block.

The 22-year-old missed all four field-goal attempts in the first half, but sank a pair of free throws and made a huge play to help Atlanta to a 39–37 lead at the main break.

Borlase's block on Veronica Burton late in the second period led to an Allisha Gray (18 points) triple and forced the Valkyries to call a time-out.

It drew huge praise from Reese, who made a beeline for her teammate and celebrated with a chest bump and double-fist to the chest.

Atlanta seized control in a dominant third quarter and took a 60–46 lead after Jordin Canada (13 points) banked a long-range three on the buzzer.

Overrun after leading late in game one, the Dream held firm this time to record their breakthrough finals victory.

Reese became the third player in WNBA history to have at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a finals game.

Another Australian Opals star, Miela Sowah, sat on the bench for the Valkyries and will remain there throughout the finals due to her restricted status as a development player.

World.title: Diamonds boosted by imminent return of vice-captain
World.content:
Diamonds vice-captain Kate Moloney is on track to return from injury and give Australia a much-needed boost for the Constellation Cup.

Moloney was forced to watch the netball world's number-one side suffer a shock 56–50 loss to the Silver Ferns from the sidelines after a finger laceration in the lead-up to the Auckland series opener.

The Diamonds were already without defender Jo Weston (managed), and the experienced duo were sorely missed against the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss It was defender Courtney Bruce's 100th milestone game to start the Constellation Cup but the brand new centurion and her captain Liz Watson were both sent to the bench in Australia's 56-50 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

New Zealand stormed to a 15-goal lead in the first of four matches, forcing Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench captain and midcourter Liz Watson alongside goalkeeper Courtney Bruce in her 100th game.

Jamie-Lee Price took over centre duties against New Zealand's Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan, while Jessie Grenvold was tasked with containing Silver Ferns goalscoring superstar Grace Nweke on debut.

Australia cut the deficit to just six goals in the fourth quarter, but the damage had been done.

Georgie Horjus was the only Diamond who remained on the court for four quarters, finishing with a game-high 19 gains and 38 feeds as wing attack.

With the Diamonds set to name their squad this evening, Marinkovich said Melbourne Vixens captain Moloney's return was imminent.

"We'll definitely see her back in the series," Marinkovich said.

"It was a bit of a nasty laceration to her finger, so we had to wait till it pretty much stuck back together.

"It's just one of those innocuous things that happen at training, but she's been able to do all the running and the movement, and yeah, look forward to having her back."

But the midcourt will not be the only area of focus for tomorrow night's game in Christchurch.

Looking to end their five-year drought on Kiwi soil, the Diamonds will need to find a way past the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger.

With goalkeeper Jackson standing at 192cm and goal defence Burger at 184cm, Australia's attacking roster of Kiera Austin, Cara Koenen, Sophie Dwyer and Sophie Garbin struggled to fire.

Marinkovich is urging her Diamonds to start with "immediacy" on the court.

"We were slightly off our pace [in game one], and our numbers would show that we weren't as aggressive as what we needed to be on the ball," she said.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of Game II between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns on Wednesday, October 21.

AAP

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Ohope Wins's fatal Caulfield Cup fall
World.content:
A Racing Victoria investigation into the fall at the Caulfield Cup that resulted in the euthanasia of Ohope Wins has finished, clearing all jockeys involved of any wrongdoing.

Ohope Wins, ridden by Jye McNeil, and Half Yours, ridden by Mark Zahra, both went down in the final straight at the 150th running of the famous 2,400-metre race.

Zahra and Half Yours fell first after getting tangled in the pack chasing eventual winner Kingswood, with Ohope Wins going over the top of the fallen gelding.

Loading...

Last year's Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours suffered superficial cuts and scrapes, but Ohope Wins was assessed on track as having a "serious racing injury" and was put down by on-course veterinarians.

Both jockeys were thrown from their mounts and taken to hospital, delaying the conclusion of the inquiry into the incident, which once again prompted calls for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths.

After hearing evidence from McNeil, Zahra and three other jockeys in the race, Racing Victoria stewards said they "could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider".

The hearing at Racing Victoria headquarters found contact between Kings Valley and Green Spaces with about 300m to go resulted in the latter becoming unbalanced.

Half Yours ran the rest of the course without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green Spaces, ridden by Rachel King, then turned inward and made more contact with apprentice rider Jabez Johnstone's Kings Valley, who also turned inward, resulting in Half Yours being squeezed for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann.

"A short distance later, Half Yours subsequently fell," the stewards' report read.

"Ohope Wins that was trailing was subsequently brought down when unable to avoid the fallen Half Yours."

The incident has been referred to Racing Victoria's Veterinary Services Department, as is standard practice.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours was recovering well from injuries and would be rested, while Zahra was meeting with doctors today about a timeline for his return to riding.

McNeil was cleared of any injury and is expected to ride at the Geelong Cup tomorrow.

World.title: Collingwood AFLW captain to leave at end of season
World.content:
Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher will leave the struggling AFLW club to return to her native Western Australia.

Schleicher informed the Magpies of her decision on Tuesday after suffering a season-ending shoulder injury in their round 9 loss to St Kilda.

The 28-year-old inaugural Collingwood player is expected to land at West Coast, with the Eagles reportedly offering a four-year contract.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

A two-time All-Australian, Schleicher's departure is a massive blow to perennial competition strugglers Collingwood, who have only won one game after 10 rounds this season.

"This has been a really tough decision for me to make but one that is ultimately the best for where I am in my life and career," Schleicher said in a club statement.

"Collingwood has been my home for my entire adult life … I'll always consider myself a Collingwood person.

"I'm excited for my next chapter, but also for the club's next chapter."

Collingwood chief executive Craig Kelly expressed the club's disappointment in Schleicher's decision.

Schleicher reportedly turned down a one-year deal to remain at the Magpies after strong interest from the Eagles.

Joining the Magpies ahead of the inaugural AFLW season in 2017, the defender-turned-midfielder has played 82 games for the club and took over as captain from Bri Davey in 2025.

Schleicher was moved to the forward line this season under coach Sam Wright and kicked 10 goals before fracturing her shoulder against the Saints.

"While we are disappointed to see Ruby depart our Club, we respect her decision to return home," Kelly said in a statement.

"We thank Ruby for everything she has given to Collingwood and wish her all the very best for the next chapter."

Like Schleicher, Davey is among several senior leaders set to come off contract at the end of this campaign, while vice-captain Jordy Allen's contract runs until the end of the 2027 season.

AAP

World.title: NFL QB in hospital at 4am before London game due to blood clots
World.content:
Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts has blood clots in both lungs, according to his team and his agent, with media reports saying the former Super Bowl MVP is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season.

Hurts was clinically stable but his treatment would involve blood thinners, which would rule him out of contact activities, the Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said in a statement.

The 28-year-old was initially diagnosed with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis after an ultrasound in London before Philadelphia's 19-17 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which Hurts played in.

The current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli. A bilateral pulmonary embolism is where a blood clot travels from a deep vein in the body, often the leg, and blocks an artery in both lungs.

"Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery," the statement said.

"We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners."

It said no long-term effects were expected.

According to an ESPN report, Hurts was in the hospital in London until 4am on the day of the game and did not sleep the night before the contest as a health precaution.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday, local time, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni said the team cared about its players and he trusted the medical staff.

"I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them," Sirianni said.

"We get medical information from our guys, and we always put the players' health first and foremost in every situation. And, you know, that's where we were there."

The Eagles said in a statement on Thursday that their medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the ultrasound results and concluded that "activity and mobility were important" and that Hurts could safely play in the game against the Jaguars, adding that he "played without limitation".

Hurts guided the Eagles to the Super Bowl title in February 2025, throwing for two touchdowns and running in another against the Kansas City Chiefs to earn the game's Most Valuable Player trophy.

Reuters

World.title: Quick hits: Renshaw floored by miracle grab as Bavuma's six stops traffic
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has been shocked by his own miracle grab, while Temba Bavuma's soaring six has stopped the Gqeberha traffic on a day when a soggy outfield threatened to ruin it all.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. A soggy outfield almost ruins it all

Things did not look good as the scheduled start of play approached on day two. Dark skies and pouring rain meant a delay was inevitable.

But within two hours, the rain had ceased, and another hour after that, the sun was beating down in Gqeberha.

The St George's ground staff had a lot on their plate on day two. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

The St George's outfield, however, just wasn't playing ball. Three surface inspections came and went, with the umpires and ground staff determining the soggy turf too treacherous for play on each occasion.

The two areas of particular concern, both deep in the outfield, were simply refusing to drain.

It was Test cricket at its exasperating, excruciating worst, and the threat of an entirely lost day loomed on the horizon.

But five hours after the scheduled start of play, and more than three since the last downfall, the officials finally determined the field fit for purpose.

By the time the Australian bowlers were going through their warm-ups, it was a glorious day in the Eastern Cape.

2. Hazlewood the latest to succumb to sickness

But when the Australians finally got on the field for a 30-over evening session, they were without one of their most dangerous weapons.

Josh Hazlewood was battling sickness and nowhere to be seen at St George's Park, leaving just the — admittedly serviceable — trio of Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc and Scott Boland for the South African batters to contend with.

A day earlier umpire Chris Gaffaney was forced to withdraw from the Test with a bout of food poisoning, the saga no doubt leaving those in attendance wondering if there might be a dish to avoid at the St George's canteen.

Hazlewood is expected to return on day three.

3. Carey poised for 200

Scott Boland picked up from where he left off as play finally got underway. (Getty Images: Richard Huggard/Gallo Images)

It was typically outstanding stuff from Boland as day two belatedly began.

The Victorian had Temba Bavuma swinging and missing dramatically with the first ball of the afternoon. He only had to wait until his second set of the day to claim his third wicket of the match, luring Marques Ackerman into a drive and nicking off the debutant for six.

Meanwhile, behind the stumps, Alex Carey was nearing a major milestone.

And when Mitchell Starc had Matthew Breetzke edging through to the Australian wicketkeeper only moments later, Carey was one take away from becoming the fifth Australian gloveman to take 200 catches in Test cricket after Adam Gilchrist, Ian Healy, Rod Marsh and Brad Haddin.

Carey will hope to join that group on day three.

4. Bavuma interrupts traffic with massive six

It was an absolutely massive six, and it came from absolutely nowhere.

Bavuma had been so composed and diligent in steadying ship after the losses of Ackerman and Breetzke, and looked set to defend his way to stumps.

But the South Africa captain absolutely exploded in hooking Cummins over the backward square leg boundary.

Temba Bavuma's six interrupted the Gqeberha traffic. (Fox Cricket)

The ball sailed over the rope, out of the stadium and then rolled onto the road, where a security guard was forced to weave through the Gqeberha traffic to collect it.

5. Renshaw stunned by own miracle grab

With only a matter of minutes remaining in the day's play, Australia was pushing for the one final wicket that would put them well on top in the game.

Shadows were lengthening, light was fading quickly, and Marnus Labuschagne had just put down a relatively simple catch at leg slip.

Visibility clearly wasn't great but, somehow, Matt Renshaw produced something remarkable.

Renshaw took a remarkable catch late on day two. (Fox Cricket)

It was definitely Carey's catch, but the Australian wicketkeeper was rooted to the spot as Ryan Rickleton edged towards the men behind the wicket.

The ball looked destined to fly between the keeper and slip, but there he was, Renshaw, diving at full stretch and managing to get his right hand between ball and turf.

Matt Renshaw was blown away by his stunning catch. (Fox Cricket)

The Queenslander looked absolutely stunned to have taken the catch that had South Africa rocking at 5-97 at stumps.

World.title: FIFA given deadline to answer questions over failed World Cup sell-off
World.content:
Soccer's governing body in Europe UEFA has given FIFA until November 2 to release documents relating to Gianni Infantino's aborted attempts at a secretive investment plan for the World Cup and other governance issues.

The latest move in a power struggle between the two governing bodies came in the week after UEFA's European delegates were disappointed by what they perceived as a lack of clarity by FIFA president Infantino over the issues at a FIFA council meeting last week.

Infantino provided no documents about the $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) FIFA World Cup sell-off plan he launched and quickly dropped in July amid a fierce backlash led by Europe.

Among the 42 questions that UEFA is demanding an answer to are: Infantino's personal remuneration package, financial payments made to singer Marc Anthony, the handling of US striker Folarin Balogun's disciplinary case, business and political relationships involving Donald Trump and his family, and the operational independence of FIFA's judicial, electoral, and ethics committees.

UEFA asked US federal courts to authorise subpoenas compelling the production of documents and sworn testimony about the abandoned investment plan called FIFA Forward Enterprise.

FIFA lawyers have claimed UEFA is harassing Infantino.

UEFA expresses deep dissatisfaction

The formal letter, signed by UEFA general secretary Theodore Theodoridis on behalf of European FIFA council members, stated Infantino's apology for his actions and subsequent explanation failed to address their core concerns.

"These explanations have not begun satisfactorily to address a number of fundamental questions raised by Council members. Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been [provided]," the letter said.

"The withdrawal of FFE, the recognition of mistakes, and the announcement of 'potential governance reforms' do not answer how the relevant decisions were taken or why the FIFA Council was not involved at the appropriate stage."

UEFA has demanded a response by November 2 — 16 days before the nomination deadline for the presidential election next March 18.

With the next FIFA council meeting scheduled for December 16 in Doha — after nominations close — UEFA insisted that answers cannot wait.

"These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the FIFA Council — nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them," the letter emphasised.

The earlier deadline would give federations time to assess FIFA's answers — or its failure to answer — while they can still nominate or endorse a challenger.

AP

Tech.title: Baseus’ new security camera has a spotlight that tracks and follows moving targets
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Baseus announced a new addition to its lineup of AI-assisted security cameras that’s more proactive about discouraging unwanted visitors instead of just recording and alerting you to their presence. The Baseus Security PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera introduces a motorized spotlight that shines directly on a moving target, even as they’re running across your property, so they know they’ve been detected. The targeted light also improves the quality of video captured in the dark to increase the chances of a subject being identified, and it can assist your family with after-hours activities like taking the dog out.

The Baseus U2 Pro is now available through Amazon in the US for $269.99, while European availability starts on October 15th at €269.99. Alongside the spotlight feature, the U2 Pro pairs a 3K fixed camera designed to constantly monitor a specific area of your property with a second 3K camera that can zoom, tilt, and pan 360 degrees to monitor everywhere else. Full-color night vision capabilities make it easier to identify people, animals, or even the color of a suspicious vehicle.

An included solar panel can be mounted atop the camera or installed a short distance away to ensure it gets adequate sun exposure. Image: Baseus

Using “AI-powered analysis,” the U2 Pro will provide alerts when motion is detected with summaries and descriptions of what was seen that differentiate between people, pets, vehicles, and activities like delivered packages. It’s also smart enough to ignore movements that aren’t relevant, such as tree branches blowing in the wind, or activities that regularly occur so as not to overwhelm you with notifications. Footage is captured only when motion is detected and is stored locally on a 512GB encrypted memory card. It can be accessed remotely through Baseus’ mobile app, while live views from the cameras can also be monitored on Amazon Alexa or Google Home smart devices.

Baseus claims the U2 Pro can be installed in about two minutes using mounts that connect to walls or ceilings. The camera connects wirelessly to your home network and features a rechargeable battery good for up to 150 days of use, although that will potentially be reduced depending on how much activity there is on your property. An included 3W solar panel can be mounted atop the cameras or a short distance away to ensure it can see the sun. Just 40 minutes of sun exposure generates enough power for a full day’s use.

Tech.title: Elon Musk’s proposed SpaceX stock giveaway would go into ‘Trump Accounts’
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

President Donald Trump announced this afternoon that Elon Musk’s SpaceX shares for children will be given through Trump Accounts. Musk said earlier today that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” sometime next year. Musk had thanked Trump Account booster Brad Gerstner for “helping enable this,” and Trump appeared to confirm the plan in a post on Truth Social.

Given the value of SpaceX’s stock on Friday, 72 million shares would be worth approximately $10.5 billion, according to CNBC. “This will be the first of many,” Musk said.

Michael and Susan Dell, Ray and Barbara Dalio, Gerstner, and SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell have all also promised contributions to Trump Accounts. In October, the White House said that after automatically enrolling some 60 million children, over 70 million accounts had been created.

Tech.title: The fossil fuel comeback is here
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.

Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels.

America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn.

“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point”

“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.

While the US still generates 60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the cheapest power source in most of the world.

The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago.

Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively.

New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

Tech.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.

Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.

When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more

To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.

“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.

I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.

CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.

The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds

So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.

Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.

Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.

Tech.title: I tried a $99 plug that promises to track your car and send help when needed — without selling your data
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

My 15-year-old daughter just got her learner’s permit, so when I was pitched a new gadget tailored to teen drivers, I was intrigued. The Miles Plug is a small device that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port and monitors location, driving habits, and vehicle health, along with emergency accident response and roadside assistance.

The idea is that knowing all these things should help me feel more comfortable when my daughter starts driving alone. I tested the (now discontinued) Ring Car Cam when my son was learning to drive, but he hated it and refused to turn it on; I wondered if the Miles could provide the same peace of mind without feeling as intrusive.

Miles Plug is a small device without a screen or battery that plugs into your car’s OBD-II port, This is the rear. It slotted into the port on my Toyota easily.

Billed as “a wearable for your car,” Miles is a tiny cellular and GPS-enabled device that connects to an app to deliver real-time location, alerts, and driving insights (speeding, hard braking, trip recaps). The app also features an AI chatbot called the Miles Mechanic that decodes warning lights, tells you how urgent a fix is, and estimates repair costs.

Miles was developed by cofounders Matt McGovren and Kit Klein, who have a solid smart home pedigree. They worked at Wink in the early days and bring combined experience from Amazon (Ring and Blink), Ubiquiti’s smart home line, and other companies. “We built Miles to support teens and parents together, and keep them on the same team,” said McGovren in a press release. “Parents and teens see the same trips and the same alerts with nothing hidden, building trust instead of suspicion.”

You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product. — Matt McGovren

Miles is available today at mileslabs.com and costs $99, plus $180 for a year of membership ($279 total, or $15 a month). A three-year plan is $396 with the Plug included ($11 a month). All plans are paid upfront with no auto-renewal. Anyone in the family can download and use the app, with each driver getting their own profile and alerts. Miles says it’s compatible with most gas and hybrid cars from 2008 onward and some EVs (there’s a compatibility checker).

While the prices seem steep, McGovren’s pitch is that it covers several services you might already be paying for: “You could piece together a roadside service, a family tracking service … and then you’re looking at $30, $40 a month,” he said in an interview with The Verge. And, unlike your car’s own branded app, Miles isn’t selling your data. Automakers have been caught collecting and selling driving data, with GM being banned from selling data to brokers for five years.

McGovren says Miles will never sell vehicle, trip, or location data, and the app has no ads: “You’re the customer, you’re not the product. Your data is not the product.” He says, “All the vehicle and trip data is encrypted,” adding that “the most sensitive data is end-to-end encrypted.” Additionally, the location data is tied to the car, not the phone, so it stops tracking when you walk away. The app lets you download your data, stop location collection, and delete your account and all its data.

The Miles is very small and works with most gas and hybrid cars made in 2008 or later.

I set up Miles in my 2014 Toyota Highlander I nicknamed Tanya and have been using it for a couple of days. Setup was simple, and the app is clean, uncluttered, and easy to follow. It took me through a few setup screens, including asking to share my phone’s location to relay data from the Plug over Bluetooth when cell service is spotty. I plugged it into my OBD-II port, and it read my VIN and correctly identified my car.

It logs every trip with route, distance, time, and driver initials (I haven’t had my daughter download the app yet; I’m interested to see whose phones it connects to when we’re both in the car). Arrived- and left-home alerts came through promptly, and the events tab flagged hard acceleration and a cluster of three hard-braking alerts when I was running a little late to collect my daughter from work.

Previous Next





1 / 4 This is a demo screen of a car in the Miles app.

I like the home card, which shows a vehicle health summary: engine OK, fuel 63%, battery 13.5V, and the odometer reading. I played with the Miles Mechanic chatbot and asked how my car is and what upcoming maintenance is due; it answered in plain English, telling me the cabin air filter is due at about 140,000 miles, and the oil change and tire rotation at 142,500.

Previous Next

1 / 2 The Control Center lets you see and manage your data.

I haven’t been testing it long enough to comment on battery drain, an issue with earlier products in this space. “It goes to sleep when your car is not driving or not on,” says McGovren. “We use a little bit of data to wake up and sync, but [that] doesn’t have a material impact on the battery.” He advises removing it if you won’t be driving the car for a while.

Beyond car battery life, an obvious concern for prospective users is how long Miles the company will last. Startup Automatic had a similar idea back in 2016, launching the Automatic Pro for $130 that plugged into your OBD-II port, tracked mileage and location, and monitored for crashes over a 3G radio. The service shut down in 2020. Miles is basically Automatic but with a business model; Automatic didn’t initially charge a monthly fee, Miles does.

McGovren says he and his team have seen a lot of “scar tissue from the smart home,” with companies that “thought they could make money later.” Both founders were at Wink during its outage, bankruptcy, and eventual sale to will.i.am’s company. Charging for membership upfront is meant to avoid that type of outcome. He says the company is “well capitalized” and offers a 60-day money-back guarantee to users.

The car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app. — Matt McGovren

Automatic also had several smart-home tie-ins, but at launch Miles doesn’t connect to your smart home. McGovren says they have an MCP server in beta that could deliver “all of this information … to your AI of choice, your home assistant of choice,” he says. “And now the car becomes part of this bigger ecosystem. We aren’t just trying to tie you into our app.” He envisions a future where you own your car’s data and can connect it to any service you want, and be able to ask Alexa, Siri, or Google, “When’s my next oil change?” or “How much gas is in my car?”

Miles is pitched as a solution for monitoring your teen driver, including notifications of possible crashes and risky driving, without also having to monitor their phone. But it also feels like a good solution for anyone with an older car or who doesn’t want to rely on data-tracking apps from insurance companies or car manufacturers but wants easy access to their car’s data. I plan to test it more thoroughly, hopefully try out the MCP integration, and follow up with a full review.

Photography and screenshots by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Tech.title: Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
Tech.content:
writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5. B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t currently offering a discount on the XM6.

The XM6 are a solid upgrade over their predecessor and easily amongst the best noise-canceling wireless earbuds on the market. In his review, John Higgins noted that they do a better job of tuning out other people’s conversations than any other earbuds he’s tested. Sony has also improved the bone-conduction sensor and added AI-powered microphones that help keep your voice clear during calls, even in noisy environments.

The XM6 earbuds also deliver clean, balanced sound with impressive bass, raising the bar of what we expect with Sony’s WF-1000XM series. If you prefer to customize your listening experience, Sony’s Sound Connect app offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to adjust how much surrounding noise you hear without removing the earbuds. You can also personalize the touch controls.

The XM6 earbuds support Sony’s LDAC codec, which delivers higher-quality audio from compatible Android devices, too. New in the latest set is a listening mode that makes music sound more like background audio playing in a cafe, allowing you to listen to your favorite music without getting too distracted from whatever you’re doing.

Tech.title: Amazon is funding a new nuclear plant in Indiana
Tech.content:
Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The proposed plant, which would replace the now defunct coal-fueled Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, aims to provide up to 960 megawatts of carbon-free energy for both the regional power grid and Amazon’s data centers.

No timeline for construction or operation has been announced for the facility, which Amazon says “could” create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The facility in Indiana is targeting to build 12 Xe-100 SMR’s, an advanced (but unproven) reactor that’s still undergoing development and licensing. These reactors can be cooled using either air, water, or a hybrid solution of both, which Amazon says should allow them to be deployed in water-constrained regions without impacting water demand in local communities.

Indiana also happens to be home to a famously expensive and uncompleted energy project called the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant. It was abandoned half-finished in 1983 after $2.5 billion had already been sunk into it, and has been under continued demolition since 2008. Terms for Amazon’s agreement in Fairbanks haven’t been disclosed, so we can’t compare the cost between the facilities.

This marks the second nuclear energy project that Amazon and X-energy are collaborating on, with the collective goal of working with regional utilities to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of new nuclear capacity in the US by 2039. In October last year, Amazon shared an early preview of its first planned nuclear plant, the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington. That project is similarly set to build 12 advanced reactors and create local jobs, but construction isn’t expected to start until the end of this decade.

Amazon is one of several tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, and Google, that are exploring their own nuclear energy projects to power AI data centers. Investing in energy grid infrastructure was also one of the commitments that Amazon outlined in a lengthy blog post earlier this month that aimed to sway some of the growing negativity around data center projects, though it’ll be many years before anyone — including Amazon — can reap the benefits of these new facilities.

Tech.title: Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet
Tech.content:
Estonia-based Blackwall, which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents.

The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025.

Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue. But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic.

Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship.

There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats.

In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot.

In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments.

Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider.

Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers.

Tech.title: Walmart’s Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India
Tech.content:
Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. It is entering a fiercely competitive market that has defeated even previous attempts by Amazon and Google to break in.

The Bengaluru-based company is testing its food-delivery service internally and has expanded the trial from a few hundred employees to upwards of 8,000, according to two people familiar with the matter. It has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders through its logistics arm, Ekart, separate from the riders who handle its quick-commerce deliveries, as it prepares for a public launch.

The employee-only service appears as a separate tab on Flipkart’s main shopping app, alongside its Minutes quick-commerce offering and travel bookings, TechCrunch has learned. It draws on restaurants listed through ONDC, a government-backed network that connects online buyers and sellers across different platforms, as well as restaurants that Flipkart signed up directly.

Riders wearing jerseys bearing the “Eat-in by Minutes” branding have also begun fulfilling orders on the streets of Bengaluru, the southern Indian city where Flipkart is headquartered.

As Flipkart expands its food-delivery operations, it is entering a market that the brokerage firm Bernstein estimates is growing 18% to 20% a year. Online delivery, though, still accounts for just over 15% of India’s broader food-services industry. Zomato, owned by Eternal, and Swiggy together serve an estimated 85 million to 95 million paying customers a year, per Bernstein. That figure shows how dominant the two are, and how much room newcomers have to grow online food ordering in the world’s most populous country, which has more than a billion internet subscriptions.

Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market. Ride-hailing company Rapido, which has already given Uber and its Indian rival Ola a tough fight, has been expanding Ownly, its food-delivery service that charges restaurants zero commission. Meanwhile, Swiggy has launched Toing, a separate app aimed at customers looking for cheaper meals. Both moves reflect growing pressure on the industry’s existing pricing model and the commissions that restaurants pay.

“Monopoly is bad, but duopoly is more pathetic,” said Sagar Daryani, president of the New Delhi-headquartered National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over 500,000 restaurants nationwide. “What one does, the other follows suit.”

Daryani argued that restaurants have long needed alternatives to the two dominant platforms.

Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market. In 2020, Amazon launched a food-ordering service in Bengaluru, but it shut the service down two years later. Google’s Areo app, which offered food ordering alongside other services, also failed to gain traction. Uber also left the market in 2020, selling its Uber Eats business in India to Zomato.

Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it. Zomato and Swiggy built their businesses around delivering meals before expanding into quick commerce. Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery.

“Flipkart’s quick commerce benefit will get passed on to food delivery, so it will be leaner, more efficient,” Daryani told TechCrunch.

Restaurants are also hoping that new entrants will bring down the cost of selling meals online. Daryani, also co-founder and CEO of the dumpling chain Wow! Momo Foods, said Flipkart has proposed a base commission of about 10%, compared with the 20% to 25% that restaurants typically pay Zomato and Swiggy.

Commissions are only part of the expense, though. Once advertising, discounts, and other promotional costs are factored in, restaurants can end up spending 40% to 50% of an order’s value on the established platforms, Daryani told TechCrunch. He expects Flipkart to keep that total cost closer to 15% to 16%, which could mean restaurants keep more money from each order.

Nonetheless, getting restaurants on board is one thing and winning over customers is another. Bernstein estimates that new entrants could save customers just ₹20 to ₹30 (around 20–30 cents) per order by operating more efficiently, which may not be enough to draw customers away from Zomato and Swiggy. The two incumbents could also offer deeper discounts to keep them.

Flipkart is not planning to stay in Bengaluru for long. The company has told restaurants that it expects to launch its food-delivery service publicly by the end of October and to expand to five or six cities by the end of this year, Daryani told TechCrunch.

The food-delivery push also comes as Flipkart’s long-awaited stock-market listing remains uncertain. Chief Executive Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above) recently declined to give a timetable for an IPO, even as the company continues to expand into businesses that could bring customers back to its app more frequently.

Flipkart’s expansion comes as competition in India’s e-commerce market intensifies. Quick-commerce platforms that started by delivering groceries in minutes now sell even the latest iPhones and other discretionary purchases, putting them in more direct competition with Flipkart and Amazon.

Flipkart did not respond to a request for comments.

Tech.title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
Tech.content:
Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society.

Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity, and to take back control instead.

His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the AI Now Institute, a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable.

Last month, Mamdani ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her.

“It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said.

Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting “house-phished,” or tricked by misleading listings.

Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives.

“Nothing has to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.”

He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children. Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack.

“There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,’ he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.”

Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027.

Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI.

“At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said.

President Donald Trump’s Superintelligence Task Force, announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction.

“As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said.

Tech.title: Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly in talks for yet another $45B compute deal
Tech.content:
In Brief

A little over a month ago, Anthropic and AI infrastructure provider Nscale announced a $45 billion compute deal. Now the duo may be about to do it again.

Bloomberg reports that the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still underway and that the details could change.

If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck over the past year. TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.

The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has spooked a certain segment of investors, who worry that companies are spending too much money for too little profit. Still, Anthropic has pressed on with such partnerships, driven by the belief that it will all pay off in the end.

Both Anthropic and Nscale are also currently pursuing IPOs. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is also seeking to go public, although Bloomberg reported on Monday that the company is experiencing investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.

Tech.title: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
Tech.content:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.

However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.

With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?

“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.

Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.

Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.

“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said.

“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”

The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents.

Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.

Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily outperform a frontier model, Solaiman shared.

“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.

In other words, the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

Tech.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
Tech.content:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies. The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents, which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

Tech.title: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
Tech.content:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.

TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.

Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.

TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.

However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.

“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”

AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.

“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.

But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.

Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:

Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.

While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.

Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

Tech.title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
Tech.content:
OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services.

As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks.

“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said.

While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven.

Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer wrote.

Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000.

Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway.

The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X.

Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters.

“[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X.

OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack.

OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.”

Security researchers have raised similar complaints, saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run.

The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

“OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X.

The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview.

OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing.

The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks. Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.
